VIENNA, AUSTRIA—U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright today delivered the U.S. National Statement at the General Conference of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) in Vienna, Austria.

I am honored to represent the United States of America at the 70th IAEA General Conference. This year, as we celebrate the 250th anniversary of the founding of the United States, we reflect on a history defined by a tireless spirit of innovation and bold exploration. It was this American drive that, over seven decades ago, moved President Dwight D. Eisenhower to deliver his historic 'Atoms for Peace' address, sowing the seeds for the creation of this very Agency.

Together, our high-level cooperation has achieved monumental milestones—pioneering global safeguards, securing vulnerable fissile materials across the globe, countering and preparing for radiological and nuclear threats, creating energy abundance, and advancing nuclear science to improve living standards. As the world’s foremost nuclear innovator, the United States remains steadfastly dedicated to the IAEA’s mission.

I would like to take a moment to congratulate Timor Leste on becoming the newest member of the IAEA. America looks forward to working with you.

Thanks to President Trump’s leadership, the United States is ushering in an American nuclear renaissance. President Trump directed the Administration to revitalize America’s nuclear sector, modernizing regulations, improving processes and streamlining advanced reactor testing to rebuild the nuclear industrial base.

This agenda allows the United States to establish an expedited pathway for testing and approving advanced reactors, set standards for converting surplus uranium and plutonium into reactor fuel, and support the energy infrastructure needed for America’s reindustrialization and artificial intelligence.

This highlights that distinct business cycles are influenced by different economic shocks, resulting in varying impacts on the economy. Consequently, indicators that have indicated slack during previous cycles may not hold the same relevance in future contexts. For example, during periods of labor market slack, measures that consider the duration of unemployment can often offer greater insights into the permanence of unemployment and subsequent slack conditions. Conversely, in times of tight labor markets, metrics that evaluate job transitions, including flows into, out of, and among jobs, tend to provide a more accurate depiction of job availability for workers and potential upward wage pressures. Furthermore, the combination of vacancy rates and unemployment, which is included in the definition of efficient u*, can serve as an alternative indicator of maximum employment levels.

It is important to recognize that each estimation methodology examined has inherent limitations. For instance, there are often restrictions on the number of indicators that each model can effectively analyze, which suggests that certain models may be more adept at capturing specific determinants of maximum employment compared to others. This implies that I am unable to identify a single best statistic or model for maximum employment. Instead, I can affirm that a diverse array of models and indicators generally enhances the decision-making capacity for policymakers. In light of the uncertainty surrounding the real-time estimation of maximum employment and the myriad options available, it seems unwise to adopt a singular measure as the basis for monetary policy. The reason is that different business cycles are generated by different shocks that affect the economy in different ways, so that useful indicators of slack in past cycles may not be as insightful in the future. For instance, when there is slack in the labor market, measures taking into account unemployment duration can be more informative about the persistence of unemployment and future slack. By contrast, when labor markets are tight, measures of flows into, out of, and across jobs will give a better measure of the job opportunities for workers and potential upward pressures on wages. Similarly, the vacancy and unemployment ratio combination used in the definition of efficient u* can provide an alternative measure of maximum employment.

Of course, any one of the estimation techniques that I have reviewed has limitations. For instance, there are constraints on the number of indicators that each model can process. This implies that some models will be better at capturing some drivers of maximum employment than others. That is why I cannot point to the best statistic or best model of maximum employment. I can only acknowledge that a rich set of models and indicators only benefits the policymaker. Given the uncertainty in estimating maximum employment in real time and the many options available, I consider it undesirable to adopt one particular measure to guide monetary policy. This is something to bear in mind as I approach the current review of the FOMC's Statement on Longer-Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy, which we call our framework.

It is important to evaluate the timing of monetary policy's impact on the macroeconomy. Contemporary economic literature employs a variety of statistical models to estimate the effects of what are referred to as monetary policy "shocks." These shocks represent movements in the policy rate that do not correlate with systematic responses to incoming economic and financial data and are not anticipated by the public. This focus on the estimated effects of these shocks serves to isolate the consequences that arise solely from actions and communications related to monetary policy. Notably, one significant lesson from this research is that Milton Friedman’s concept of "long and variable lags" remains relevant. A selection of key studies on this topic estimates that it typically takes approximately one to two years for the maximum effects of policy to manifest in economic activity and inflation. These extended lags in the influence of monetary policy on the economy highlight the necessity for policymakers to anticipate economic conditions as accurately as possible. They should strive to proactively understand the effects of various economic shocks, enabling them to respond swiftly when required.

Furthermore, the direction of travel is a critical element to consider when making decisions regarding monetary policy. It is worth noting that credible evidence suggests that contractionary monetary shocks tend to decrease economic activity more significantly than expansionary shocks increase it. To comprehend these asymmetric effects, one can consider the illustrative metaphor employed by Marriner Eccles, who served as the head of the Federal Reserve during the 1930s. Ultimately, understanding these dynamics can help policymakers navigate the complexities of monetary policy more effectively.

Timing Matters The first element to evaluate is the timing with which monetary policy affects the macroeconomy. The contemporary economics literature uses a variety of statistical models to estimate the effects of what are called monetary policy "shocks." Those are movements in the policy rate that are not explained by estimates of how monetary policy systematically responds to incoming economic and financial data and are not anticipated by the public. Focusing on the estimated effects of these shocks helps isolate the consequences solely coming from monetary policy actions and communications. One lesson that emerges from this research is that, broadly speaking, it turns out that Milton Friedman's "long and variable lags" concept still holds. A selection of key studies on the topic estimates that it takes about one to two years for the maximum effects of policy to be observed in economic activity and inflation. These long lags in monetary policy affecting the economy point to why it is important for policymakers to anticipate economic conditions as best as possible and try to be proactive about understanding the effects of different shocks to the economy, so they can act quickly when needed.

Direction of Travel The second element to consider when making decisions related to monetary policy is whether its transmission has been equally impactful during different points in time. For example, credible evidence indicates that contractionary monetary shocks may generally decrease economic activity more strongly than expansionary shocks increase it. To understand these asymmetric effects, consider the following illustrative metaphor used by Marriner Eccles, who led the Fed back in the 1930s.

It is worth noting that the GENIUS Act payment stablecoins do not provide yield and lack federal deposit insurance, which diminishes the likelihood of widespread withdrawal of funds from the domestic banking system. Furthermore, the primary advantage of stablecoins lies in their ability to satisfy the unfulfilled foreign demand for dollar assets, particularly among savers in regions where access to dollars is constrained. In contrast, individuals in the United States and advanced foreign economies, such as those in the euro zone, currently have unhindered access to Treasury securities, dollars, and various financial instruments that offer both yield and deposit insurance. Consequently, I anticipate that the majority of demand for stablecoins will originate from areas lacking access to dollar-denominated savings instruments, thereby enhancing the overall demand for dollar assets.

Moreover, the equilibrium between supply and demand for loanable funds is what determines the neutral interest rate, commonly referred to as r*. In my recent address, I articulated my belief that a multitude of factors are exerting downward pressure on r* and should be taken into consideration when developing monetary policy. Some scholars have endeavored to quantify the extent to which the growth of stablecoins may contribute to a reduction in interest rates. A study conducted in 2024 by Marina Azzimonti and Vincenzo Quadrini projected that, should stablecoins achieve widespread adoption and be fully backed by U.S. securities, they could exert a downward impact of as much as 40 basis points on interest rates.

In assessing the implications of projected growth in stablecoin issuance on the demand for Treasury securities and other highly liquid dollar assets, it proves beneficial to draw a parallel to what many researchers identify as a significant contributing factor during a period of declining interest rates that commenced around the beginning of the 21st century. This phenomenon, which former Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke termed the global saving glut, serves as a valuable point of reference. In his analysis of the global saving glut, Bernanke indicated that the annual U.S. current account deficit expanded by four percentage points of U.S. gross domestic product from 1996 to 2004. Thus, the examination of stablecoin growth and its potential ramifications for interest rates and asset demand is critical for understanding the current economic landscape.

Firms have indicated that innovations focused on financial health may resonate well with customers and can potentially lead to increased revenue, reduced costs, and enhanced profitability of these services. This aspect is notably important, as the private sector is likely to offer these services only if they can be operated profitably. Additionally, some preliminary evidence suggests that the business case for financial health may be stronger than many individuals realize. A case study presented at last year's conference included data that indicated financially healthy customers may be less expensive to serve; they tended to use customer service centers less frequently and experienced lower rates of delinquency on loans. This type of operational efficiency, in conjunction with increased deposits and higher usage of other services, implies that assisting customers in achieving financial health can be beneficial not only for consumers but may also enhance profitability. This alignment of interests appears to be essential for sustainable market adoption.

Furthermore, it has been previously noted that technological innovations, particularly artificial intelligence, have played a significant role in the recent acceleration of measuring financial health. It appears that businesses employing AI may have a promising opportunity to support financial health initiatives. A better understanding of customer behavior can lead to the provision of targeted financial advice as well as the identification of vulnerable customers before they encounter serious difficulties. Additionally, AI can assist businesses in delivering services that are tailored to consumer needs, potentially at reduced costs.

In light of these developments, it is important to recognize that several challenges still exist that may need to be addressed before financial health metrics can achieve their full potential on a large scale. For instance, identifying the most promising variables and measuring them reliably in a scalable, timely, and cost-effective manner will be essential for advancing this work. Furthermore, the establishment of measurement standards may prove crucial for enhancing our understanding and promoting deeper collaboration among key stakeholders. In summary, while there are challenges to overcome, the potential benefits of focusing on financial health metrics are significant and merit careful attention.

input: The relationship between the independence of central banks and the reduction of inflation, as well as the volatility associated with inflation, is, therefore, evident. However, the connection between central bank independence and accelerated economic growth remains less clear. On one hand, it is worth noting that the primary rationale for maintaining central bank independence in the majority of nations with a singular mandate is to ensure price stability, which makes the absence of a correlation between the independence of monetary policy and negative economic outcomes unsurprising. Conversely, it can often be observed that the indices used to measure central bank independence may possess inherent biases. Most of these indices tend to impose penalties on central banks that have additional mandates or responsibilities extending beyond the pursuit of price stability. However, it is important to recognize that a mandate which excludes the objective of full employment does not appear to be optimal, particularly since central bankers should concentrate on the long-term implications of their actions for economic growth and overall economic activity. Furthermore, research has highlighted the interdependencies that exist among price stability, economic stability, and financial stability, thereby offering a justification for the overlapping objectives pursued by many central banks. Additionally, in practical terms, despite the recent surge in inflation that underscored the commitment of numerous central banks to combat inflation, it also seems that they have demonstrated a willingness to provide some degree of accommodation once they attained greater confidence that inflationary pressures had subsided. In fact, a majority of central banks have embarked on a cycle of easing, even while inflation rates remain somewhat above their designated targets, regardless of whether or not an employment goal is included in their mandates. In conclusion, the dynamics surrounding central bank independence and its implications for economic outcomes warrant further examination and consideration.
output: The relationship between central bank independence and lower inflation and inflation volatility is therefore clear. But the connection to faster growth in economic activity is not. On the one hand, the primary reason for central bank independence in most countries with a single mandate is to provide price stability, so the lack of association between monetary policy independence and adverse economic consequences is not surprising. On the other hand, indexes of central bank independence may be biased. Most indexes of central bank independence tend to penalize the presence of additional mandates or responsibilities beyond price stability. However, a mandate that excludes full employment does not seem optimal, given that a central banker should focus on the consequences of its actions on long-term growth and economic activity. Research has emphasized complementarities between price stability, economic stability, and financial stability, providing a rationale for these overlapping objectives at many central banks. Also, in practice, although the recent inflation run-up showcased the commitment of most central banks to fight inflation, it also appears that they have been willing to provide some accommodation after having gained greater confidence that inflationary pressures have dissipated. In fact, most central banks have initiated an easing cycle even with inflation still somewhat above their respective targets and regardless of the presence or not of an employment goal in their mandates.

The EGRPRA review process necessitates that federal banking agencies identify regulations that may be outdated, unnecessary, or excessively burdensome. Furthermore, this process involves the elimination of such regulations and the implementation of steps to address the regulatory burdens associated with those that are outdated or overly stringent. Notably, previous iterations of the EGRPRA process have often fallen short in their capacity to yield significant change. However, it is my expectation that the current review, along with the resultant report to Congress, will facilitate a productive engagement for stakeholders and the public with banking agencies regarding regulations that may no longer be necessary or may impose excessive burdens. Additionally, it is my hope that regulators will demonstrate responsiveness to public concerns raised during this process.

It is worth noting that many of the regulations established by the Board have not undergone comprehensive review or updates in over two decades. Given the evolving nature of the banking system, alongside the developments within the economy and financial services industry during this time, there is a clear need to revise and simplify numerous regulations issued by the Board, including those concerning applicability thresholds and benchmarks.

First, there should be transparency regarding the information required in the application and the criteria used for approval. Ultimately, these measures are aimed at enhancing the overall efficiency and clarity of the regulatory approval process.

The EGRPRA review process requires the federal banking agencies to identify any outdated, unnecessary, or overly burdensome regulations, eliminate unnecessary regulations, and take other steps to address the regulatory burdens associated with outdated or overly burdensome regulations. It is also my expectation that regulators will be responsive to concerns raised by the public.

Hauling these money bags around New York posed obvious risks, and these risks multiplied by the mid-19th century when the number of banks in New York grew rapidly. As this audience is well aware, the New York Clearing House Association (NYCH) was founded in 1853 and served as a central location for the clearing process, which soon evolved, with certificates replacing coins. Furthermore, by being part of a common infrastructure, all members had a reasonably good idea of the quality of each other's balance sheets. In modern economic language, the NYCH became a coordination mechanism that improved clearing by getting banks to clear and settle payments in a well-organized manner. It also reduced asymmetric information about the quality of member balance sheets. By performing this function for New York banks, which constituted a relatively large share of the U.S. financial system, the clearing and settling of payments improved nationally. In this sense, the NYCH was the closest thing the United States had at that time to a central bank.

While this was an improvement, not all important financial intermediaries were members of the NYCH or other such private arrangements. That is, there were gaps. And financial panics, sometimes driven by gaps and problems in check clearing, were a regular feature of the latter 19th and early 20th century.

It will continue to take time for tariff increases to work their way through supply chains and distribution networks. Around that time, I engaged with Alberto Alesina's paper on the topic of "partisan business cycles." In this influential work, Alesina posited that political parties possess varying preferences regarding inflation and unemployment. One political party, for instance, prioritized price stability while showing less concern for output stability in comparison to its counterpart. Furthermore, he suggested that the outcomes of monetary policy and inflation were contingent upon the political party victorious in a national election. Consequently, when power transitioned following an election, the resulting monetary policy diverged from previously anticipated policy based on the election results. These unexpected electoral outcomes were posited to generate volatility in monetary policy, which in turn affected inflation and output levels. In essence, Alesina argued that elections could induce partisan business cycles. Notably, his model proposed that monetary policy remained fully accountable to the electorate, a desirable quality that unfortunately resulted in increased economic instability.

This paper was intellectually stimulating, yet it provoked a significant inquiry within me: Why would society opt for complete electoral accountability while simultaneously accepting heightened volatility in monetary policy? Economists generally assert that trade-offs exist at the margins, suggesting that extreme solutions, or "corner solutions," are typically not optimal. It appeared to me that an improved institutional framework for the central bank could enhance overall welfare. In my examination of the structure of the Federal Reserve's Board of Governors, I concluded that electoral accountability could indeed be established through the appointment process. However, I also believed that economic instability could be mitigated by forming a monetary policy board comprised of current and former appointees who would establish policy based on a majority rule. This line of reasoning inspired me to adapt Alesina's model and investigate how the implementation of a policy board would alter his findings.
output:
It was around that time that I read Alberto Alesina's paper on "partisan business cycles."7 In that paper, he assumed there were different political parties, each having different preferences about inflation and unemployment. One party was more concerned with price stability and less concerned about output stability than the other. Monetary policy and inflation outcomes were determined by the party that won a national election. As power changed hands after an election, monetary policy would differ from expected policy depending on who won the election. These election surprises would create volatility in monetary policy and thus inflation and output. In other words, elections would lead to partisan business cycles. In Alesina's model, monetary policy was fully accountable to the electorate, which is desirable, but it came at the cost of causing greater economic instability.

This was a brilliant paper, but, again, it raised a serious question for me: Why would society choose full electoral accountability and maximum volatility in monetary policy? Economists usually think there are tradeoffs on the margin such that "corner solutions" like these aren't optimal. It seemed to me that there could be a welfare-improving institutional design for the central bank. I looked at the Federal Reserve's Board of Governors structure, and I felt that electoral accountability could be achieved through the appointment process, but economic instability would be reduced by having a monetary policy board composed of current and past appointees who set policy according to majority rule. This thinking led me to taking a variant of Alesina's model and studying how a policy board would change his results.

We know well that cyber threats pose real risks to the banking system. We also recognize that community banks may have unique needs in preventing, remediating, and responding to cyber threats. Therefore, regulators should ensure that a range of resources are available to support community banks and seek further opportunities to help build community bank resilience against these threats.

Third-Party Risk Management Third-party risk management can pose an additional challenge for community banks. Due to their size and scale, community banks often leverage centralized resources—technical experts who have greater expertise than the bank could fully maintain on staff—to advise and assist on a range of issues. Often these third-party service providers are significantly larger, and their bank clients—including smaller banks—may lack leverage in conducting due diligence and negotiating the terms of the relationship.

In 2023, the federal banking agencies published supervisory guidance addressing third-party risk management, which was expressly applicable to community banks. As I noted at the time it was issued, the guidance included shortcomings that were known and identified but not addressed in advance.

What many of you may not know is that after nearly a year from the original publication, the regulators published a guide to assist community banks interpret and apply the guidance to their third-party risk management activities. The guide was intended to provide additional context for the guidance—including step-by-step examples of how to address third-party risk management—making the guidance more useful. While I am pleased that the community bank implementation guide was eventually published, the delays in its publication suggest a shortcoming in our regulatory approach. We must ensure new guidance provides clarity to regulated firms on its own, or that we provide additional resources at the time the guidance is published.

To improve the model further, it would be useful to include additional explanatory variables that could better capture the overheating of the economy. In what follows, I include variables that might account for factors experienced in the most recent bout of inflation, such as a very tight labor market and supply chain snarls.

Third Result: Alternative Measure of Slack As I mentioned before, the very tight labor market was an important contributor to inflation in recent years, especially to services inflation, yet the weight on the unemployment gap in the Phillips curve for the more recent period is very small. This measure of slack has become less and less important over time in explaining inflation, except during selected episodes such as in the aftermath of the Global Financial Crisis, which was characterized by a very sluggish recovery. Outside of that episode, and very few others, the Phillips curve places little weight on that measure of slack in explaining inflation over the Great Moderation, including during the recent run-up. This is also a reflection of training the model over the Great Moderation, in which inflation moved fairly tightly around a very flat trend. Notice that this would suggest a "flat Phillips curve" or a big penalty in terms of unemployment needed to reduce inflation. Instead, I focus on another very promising alternative measure that I have paid a lot of attention to since I was chief economist at the Department of Labor—and again since I joined the Board of Governors—and that I am very familiar with as a scholar of labor markets. The measure is the ratio of vacancies to the level of unemployment. In effect, this ratio measures how much competition there is for a given job, or the "tightness" of the labor market. Labor is an important input into most production processes, and, thus, tightness in the labor market is closely related to price pressures. I use the standard version of this ratio that measures job openings from the Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey as the numerator and the unemployment level from the Current Population Survey as the denominator. This allows me to use data back to the 1960s. The vacancy-to-unemployment ratio as a measure of slack is more effective at explaining inflation than the unemployment gap. This represents an interesting result because it offers a larger role to heated labor markets in explaining the run-up in inflation. My results echo research that finds the vacancy-to-unemployment ratio is a helpful measure of slack to consider in out-of-sample forecasting exercises.

I feel a profound sense of honor in being invited to speak today regarding the significant legacy of George Shultz. It is important to clarify that my remarks will not encompass the present economic landscape or monetary policy.

Additionally, my admiration for George Shultz has been longstanding, dating back to my college years. I regarded him as an exemplary role model, a sentiment I expressed a few months ago during the Baccalaureate address to the class of 2025 at Princeton, which occurred fifty years after my own graduation.

Furthermore, I conveyed to the graduates that upon completing my college education, I lacked a concrete plan; however, I was determined to integrate a private-sector career with public service. In my mind, I envisioned several prominent figures from that era, particularly George Shultz, whose image adorned the wall of the Princeton eating club where both of us were members. It is worth noting that my interest in George may have been heightened by the fact that my father was a labor attorney representing a major steel company in collective bargaining. Like George, my father possessed a strong belief in the collective bargaining process and held a deep-seated respect for workers.

Moreover, I diligently followed George’s career over the years, never imagining that I would eventually have the privilege of meeting him. However, this opportunity arose after I joined the Federal Reserve in 2012, as I made occasional visits to Stanford. I recall engaging in stimulating economic discussions during group lunches held in his conference room at Hoover. Additionally, George graciously invited John Taylor, Michael, and myself for a memorable round of golf on a chilly, rainy March day.

Ultimately, today’s discussion centers on George’s remarkably extensive economic achievements. I also aim to honor the outstanding individual and policymaker that he was, as several aspects of his legacy continue to resonate with me.
output:
I am deeply honored to have been asked to speak here today about the remarkable legacy of George Shultz. Just to be clear, I will not address current economic conditions or monetary policy.

I have been an admirer of George Shultz since my college years. I saw him then and now as a great role model, as I mentioned a few months ago when delivering the Baccalaureate address to Princeton's class of 2025, 50 years after my own graduation.

As I told the graduates, when I faced the world after college, I had no real plan, but knew that I wanted to combine a private-sector career with public service. I had in mind a few well-known public figures of the era, especially George Shultz, whose picture was on the wall of the Princeton eating club of which both of us were members. George may also have caught my attention because my dad was a labor lawyer who represented one of the major steel companies in collective bargaining. Like George, my father had both a belief in the collective bargaining process and a deep respect for workers.

I followed George's career with interest through the years. It didn't occur to me that I would ever have the honor of meeting him. But I did meet him after I joined the Fed in 2012, as I visited Stanford from time to time. I remember energetic economic discussions at group lunches in his conference room at Hoover. George was also kind enough to host John Taylor, Michael, and me for a chilly round of golf on a rainy March day.

Today, our focus is on George's extraordinarily broad economic accomplishments. I also want to celebrate the remarkable man and policymaker that he was. Several things stand out for me.

While monetary policy is undeniably significant, various other factors must align to create viable job opportunities. It can often be the case that businesses require access to credit in order to expand operations and hire additional workers, and in numerous communities, this access is contingent upon the Community Reinvestment Act, community development financial institutions, and an array of related public policies. Additionally, businesses may depend on a skilled workforce, which is often reliant on workforce development initiatives supported by community development organizations. Businesses that are committed to job creation must possess confidence in both the future and the prospects of the communities they serve. output:
Let me spend just a moment on the U.S. economy and the outlook. The economy is currently on a sound footing, with low and steady unemployment, and disinflation having continued at a gradual, albeit uneven, pace toward our 2 percent target. Low-income households can ill afford increases in prices, and that's why it is so important that we bring inflation back down to our target. Looking forward, however, I expect tariffs will put upward pressure on inflation. Higher short-term inflation expectations, supply chain adjustments, and second-round effects may cause some inflation persistence. At the same time, tariffs may cause the economy to slow and unemployment to rise. Low-income workers are often hit the hardest when the job market weakens. There is still considerable uncertainty about tariff policies and their effects. Monetary policy is well positioned to allow us to wait and see how economic conditions unfold.

Turning from monetary policy to community development, let me explain how community development also serves the goals of supporting a healthy economy that works for all Americans. While monetary policy matters a lot, other factors have to come together for people to have good job opportunities. Businesses need access to credit to expand and hire, and in many communities that credit depends on the CRA, community development financial institutions, and a range of other public policies. Businesses need qualified workers, and in many places that depends on workforce development that is supported by community development organizations. Businesses that invest to create jobs need to believe in the future and believe in the future of the communities they serve. Thriving businesses and productive workers need safe, healthy, strong, and sustainable communities. These conditions are fundamental to achieving the Federal Reserve's goals that Congress has established.

This proactive approach can help ensure that they are not caught unprepared as this technology integrates into the banking system.

Furthermore, there exists a collective responsibility to establish an incentive structure that effectively manages associated risks. To the extent that banks utilize generative artificial intelligence or provide related products and services, they may bear the responsibility for managing their own risk. They should also leverage their relationships to encourage sound risk management practices among fintech partners. This responsibility necessitates selecting fintech collaborators who prioritize transparency and provide clear insights into the development of their artificial intelligence tools, while also demonstrating appropriate control in their deployment. 

Additionally, there may be an inherent tension in this dynamic; banks must strive to comprehend the tools offered by their fintech partners to enhance their own risk management capabilities, while fintech companies may be reluctant to disclose proprietary information, which can be considered their competitive advantage. With regard to generative artificial intelligence, it becomes essential for both fintechs and banks to address critical questions, such as the ownership of customer data, as well as potential conflicts that could arise if a bank's customer data is used within a fintech's generative artificial intelligence model. 

In summary, the evolving relationship between banks and fintechs necessitates careful management of risks and transparency in order to navigate the complexities associated with generative artificial intelligence.

One of the most difficult challenges on the regulatory front tends to be prioritization, both for banks managing their businesses and for regulators deciding how to fulfill their responsibilities. It is worth noting that, at a basic level, the role of regulators may be dictated by statute. Congress granted the Federal Reserve and other banking agencies broad statutory powers, but it has constrained how those powers may be directed through the use of statutory mandates, including the promotion of a safe and sound banking system and broader U.S. financial stability. In the execution of these responsibilities, the Federal Reserve must also balance the need to act in a way that enables the banking system to serve the U.S. economy and promote economic growth. While these objectives are not incompatible, they do require us to consider tradeoffs when establishing policy.

Additionally, how can regulators best meet these responsibilities? As many of you may already know, I strongly believe in a pragmatic approach to policymaking. This requires us to identify the problem we are trying to solve, determine whether we are the appropriate regulator to address the problem based on our statutory mandates and authorities, and explore options for addressing the identified issue.

Furthermore, as a first step, we must be attuned to the banking system and how regulatory actions affect that system. Notably, we oversee a wide range of banks of varying sizes, activities, affiliates, and complexity. These banks interact with a range of service providers, financial market utilities, payments providers, and non-bank partners, and they regularly compete with non-bank financial intermediaries. In essence, the banking system can often be a key driver of business formation, economic expansion, and opportunity. Ultimately, regulators may need to weigh these considerations carefully when determining how best to prioritize their responsibilities.

At the same time, the hiring rate has continued to fall and, outside of the pandemic recession, is at its lowest level since 2012. Additionally, it is worth noting that a common method for quantifying the effects of regulations may involve counting the number of pages of new regulations, although this approach tends to overlook the varying economic significance that can exist across pages. Furthermore, another approach can often entail counting the number of work hours required to comply, as reported under the Paperwork Reduction Act, which may provide some insight into the regulatory burden. Notably, the production of these cost estimates by different regulatory agencies may experience a significant degree of variation, and even within agencies, there can be variation, which may lead to inconsistencies. Ultimately, the counting of work hours related to the Paperwork Reduction Act appears to capture only a portion of the full opportunity cost of the regulations, including the potential for lost productivity and the impact on firms and industries that may not exist due to the regulation. 

In essence, when a firm needs to allocate resources to comply with new regulations, it may reach a decision to hire a person, which can result in a foregone opportunity that can be substantially larger than the wage for compliance hours, as the firm may be unable to engage in other productive activities. It is worth noting that the opportunity cost can often be significant, and the impact on firms and industries can be substantial. Additionally, there has been some progress in measuring regulation through advances in natural language processing and artificial intelligence, which may lead to more accurate estimates. Furthermore, projects such as Patrick McLaughlin's QuantGov project at Stanford University's Hoover Institution have made efforts to move beyond regulation page counts by utilizing computational tools to quantify regulations by industry, which can provide a more comprehensive understanding of the regulatory landscape. 

Ultimately, the use of machine learning methods, such as those employed by Joseph Kalmenovitz, can often facilitate the separation of regulations that are relevant to a firm's core businesses from those that are not, which may lead to a more nuanced understanding of the regulatory environment. In summary, the measurement of regulations is a complex issue that may involve various approaches, and while there has been some progress in this area, it is likely that further advancements will be made, and a more accurate understanding of the effects of regulations can be reached.

A common approach to quantifying the effects of regulations is to count the number of pages of new regulations, though this does not account for varying economic significance across pages. Another approach is to count the number of work hours required to comply, as reported under the Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA). However, there is wide variation in how different regulatory agencies produce these costs estimates, even sometimes variation within agencies, and more importantly, the counting of work hours related to the PRA does not capture the full opportunity cost of the regulations—that is, how that lost hour of work could have been used more productively—or the firms and industries that don't exist because of the regulation. If a firm needs to hire a person to comply with some new regulation and can't hire a sales associate who could generate new business or can't engage in a productive activity at all, then the foregone opportunity can be significantly larger than the wage for compliance hours.

There has been some progress in measuring regulation through advances in natural language processing and artificial intelligence, and I expect more of this to come. For instance, Patrick McLaughlin's QuantGov project at Stanford University's Hoover Institution uses computational tools to move beyond regulation page counts toward counting restrictions and obligations imposed by the text and quantifying regulations by industry. In other work, Joseph Kalmenovitz uses machine learning methods to count and separate regulations that are relevant for a firm's core businesses from those that are not relevant. These measures show a substantial drop in the number of rules in 2025.10

input: Additionally, it is worth noting that a substantial body of research, based on foundational findings related to the Great Depression authored by Ben Bernanke, tends to indicate that disruptions in financial intermediation can generate severe and prolonged economic harm. Furthermore, this harm is often characterized by restricted access to credit for many borrowers, which may have a negative impact on economic growth. Notably, numerous studies have reached a conclusion that financial crises are frequently followed by large and highly persistent declines in GDP, which can often be a prolonged and severe phenomenon. In essence, the findings of Christina and David Romer, who sampled 24 advanced economies that experienced such crises, suggest that the GDP decline related to these events may peak at 6 percent after three and a half years. Ultimately, the magnitude of these declines can be even larger following periods of extreme and persistently elevated financial distress, which appears to be a critical factor in determining the severity of the economic harm. It is also worth noting that an official study supporting the design of Basel III found that the persistent effects of a financial crisis can result in cumulative output losses that are substantially higher, with estimates on the order of 20 to 60 percent of GDP. Additionally, in the context of the Global Financial Crisis, these losses may have been equivalent to between $2.9 and $8.7 trillion in pre-crisis dollars in terms of a hit to U.S. GDP, which is a significant amount. Furthermore, the lengthy periods when economic activity falls short of its potential can be attributed to the fact that the balance sheets of banks, businesses, and households take a long time to repair, which may lead to constrained investment and innovation. In summary, it appears that impaired bank balance sheets can have a profoundly negative impact on economic growth, and this harm can often be severe and prolonged.
output: Impaired Bank Balance Sheets Harm Growth A long line of research, based on seminal findings related to the Great Depression authored by Ben Bernanke, shows how disruptions in financial intermediation generate severe and prolonged economic harm by restricting many borrowers' access to credit. Many studies have found that financial crises are followed by large and highly persistent declines in GDP. For example, Christina and David Romer sampled 24 advanced economies that experienced such crises and found that the GDP decline related to these events peaks at 6 percent after three and a half years, with larger declines following periods of extreme and persistently elevated financial distress. An official study supporting the design of Basel III found that persistent effects of a financial crisis resulted in cumulative output losses that were much higher, with estimates on the order of 20 to 60 percent of GDP.15 For the Global Financial Crisis, this would be between $2.9 and $8.7 trillion in pre-crisis dollars in terms of a hit to U.S. GDP. The lengthy periods when economic activity falls short of its potential occur because the balance sheets of banks, businesses, and households take a long time to repair. With impaired bank balance sheets, credit becomes harder to obtain for many creditworthy borrowers, leading to constrained investment and innovation.

Additionally, it is reasonable to anticipate that inventors and innovators will continue to bring forward new products and services that are enabled by AI. Furthermore, the companies that are subsequently formed in order to deliver these new products and services can often be expected to raise aggregate employment.

It is worth noting that, in light of the uncertainty regarding AI's implications for the labor market, I want to highlight the important role that decisions by firms and, to a lesser extent, workers can have for determining how AI will affect the labor market.

Additionally, if incumbent firms are able to adjust their processes in order to capture productivity benefits from AI, then these firms could help mitigate some of AI's potential for job displacement by internally reallocating affected workers to new roles and providing necessary training. Furthermore, if some job tasks can be replaced with AI, especially those that are mundane and repetitive, workers may be freed up to focus on other tasks or new activities they find more rewarding.

Notably, individual workers tend to play a limited role in determining how AI will affect their earnings and employment. In essence, workers in jobs that will be complemented by AI might benefit from familiarizing themselves with how to effectively use AI. Furthermore, workers in jobs where AI will be able to perform a substantial share of their tasks will tend to face greater challenges. Additionally, some of these workers may seek to develop expertise in the aspects of their jobs for which AI is particularly ill-suited. Ultimately, many of these more-exposed workers may need to invest in training in alternative occupations that are less exposed to AI, similar to some of the skill-retraining efforts for manufacturing workers over the past 50 years.

In essence, the overall effect of AI on the labor market tends to depend on a combination of firm-level adjustments, worker-level responses, and the pace at which new products and services are brought forward.

In the 1980s, it is worth noting that the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis emerged as a significant influence in the field of monetary policy research, largely due to its introduction of innovative economic theories and policy frameworks. Additionally, in collaboration with economists from the University of Minnesota and the University of Chicago, researchers at the Minneapolis Fed began to investigate how rational expectations could potentially impact the transmission mechanism of monetary policy. Prior to this research, forecasting models utilized by the Federal Reserve tended to operate under the assumption that individuals held adaptive expectations, which were characterized by a focus on past data. This approach implied that the econometric models employed by the Board failed to incorporate policy actions that had been publicly announced but were not yet in effect. Consequently, if households and firms were to comprehend how current policy actions and announcements might influence future outcomes, their reactions could diverge significantly from the predictions generated by the Board's forecasting models. Such discrepancies could result in considerable inaccuracies in the guidance provided by the staff to policymakers.

Furthermore, a vital finding of this research suggested that the inflation expectations of private agents tended to be forward-looking; they appeared to adjust in response to the commitments and failures of central bankers in maintaining low and stable inflation. If individuals were to doubt a central bank's assurances regarding low inflation, it could be concluded that the institution would lack credibility. This situation could subsequently lead to a rise in inflation expectations, which might incite demands for higher nominal wages, thus contributing to future inflation. It is now generally accepted that this represented a significant challenge faced by Volcker, as his assurances to reduce inflation lacked complete credibility, particularly following the Federal Reserve's inconsistent approaches to combating inflation in the preceding decade. Research in monetary policy, along with the lessons learned during the Volcker era, contributed to the emergence of the concepts of "credibility" and "stable inflation expectations," which have become essential elements in the policy decisions of contemporary central banks. In summary, the work conducted during this period has had a lasting impact on the foundations of monetary policy.
output:
In the 1980s, the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis became a dominant force in monetary policy research by proposing new economic theories and policy frameworks. In association with economists at the University of Minnesota and the University of Chicago, researchers at the Minneapolis Fed explored how rational expectations would affect the transmission channel of monetary policy. Up until then, Fed forecasting models assumed that individuals had adaptive expectations, meaning they were purely backward looking. This meant that the Board's econometric models didn't account for policy actions that were announced in advance but hadn't taken effect yet. If households and firms did understand how current policy actions and announcements would affect future outcomes, they would react in ways that didn't match the predictions of the Board's forecasting models. This would lead to significant errors in the guidance that the staff provided to policymakers.

A critical finding of all this research was that private agents' inflation expectations were forward looking—they would adjust to promises, and failures, of central bankers to keep inflation low and stable. If people didn't believe a central bank's promise to keep inflation low, then the central bank lacked credibility. This would cause inflation expectations to increase, which would lead to demands for higher nominal wages, thereby feeding future inflation. It is now widely believed that this was a key problem that Volcker faced: His promises to bring inflation down were not fully credible, as they came after the Fed's uneven efforts at fighting inflation over the previous decade. Research on monetary policy, along with the experience of the Volcker years, led to the concepts of "credibility" and "stable inflation expectations" becoming central parts of how every central bank enacts policy.

input: It is worth noting that I can provide two examples from my personal experiences to illustrate this particular point. Firstly, during the year 2022, the Federal Reserve was actively addressing persistent inflationary pressures, which necessitated substantial and rapid increases in the policy interest rate. Standard models based on the Phillips curve suggested that such actions would likely lead to a significant slowdown in economic growth coupled with elevated unemployment levels. However, I chose to place greater trust in the Beveridge curve, which establishes a relationship between the unemployment rate and the job vacancy rate, as my framework for understanding how the labor market may react to these considerable rate increases. I posited that we were situated on the steep portion of the Beveridge curve, indicating that it was feasible for us to tighten monetary policy, with the primary impact being a reduction in job vacancies rather than the heightened unemployment that many experts had anticipated. A pivotal assumption underlying my argument was that a surge in layoffs would not materialize. This assumption was somewhat contentious, as historical data suggested that such an outcome was not unusual. However, all my business contacts during that period reported their challenges in recruiting and retaining employees following the COVID-19 pandemic, indicating that they had no intentions of dismissing workers even if aggregate demand were to decline. This anecdotal evidence contributed to my conviction regarding the accuracy of my perceptions of the labor market, and subsequent empirical data corroborated my theoretical predictions. In summary, my experiences reflect the complexities involved in policy-making and highlight the importance of integrating both qualitative and quantitative data in economic forecasting.
output: Let me cite two examples of my own experience to illustrate this point. First, back in 2022, the Fed was combating rampant inflation, and this required large and rapid increases in our policy rate. Standard Phillips curve models predicted that this would cause a sharp slowdown in economic growth and high unemployment. However, I had more trust in the Beveridge curve, which relates the unemployment rate to the job vacancy rate, as my guide to thinking about how the labor market would respond to these large rate hikes. I argued that we were on the steep part of the Beveridge curve, which meant that we could tighten policy and that the brunt of the effect would be borne by a decline in job vacancies, and crucially, not by the higher unemployment many predicted. A critical assumption I made was that a spike in layoffs would not occur. This assumption was controversial, since previous hard data showed that this was not the typical outcome. But all of my business contacts at that time were telling me about their struggles to find and keep workers since the COVID-19 pandemic and that they had no intention of letting workers go if aggregate demand eased. This "soft" data helped convince me that my view of the labor market was correct, and subsequent "hard" data confirmed my theoretical prediction.

The recent increase in investment in artificial intelligence may present challenges for monetary policy. This surge in investment is expected to enhance productivity and potentially reduce inflation in the medium term. Furthermore, while this additional investment tends to elevate demand, the anticipated benefits on productivity and supply are likely to manifest relatively quickly. As a result, it appears that the economy may not experience significant tightening in the near future. In this context, it is advisable for monetary policy to avoid actions that would restrict aggregate demand, as any deviation from maximum employment is likely to be temporary.

It is worth noting that there exists a risk that expectations regarding returns on high-tech investments may be overly optimistic, which could raise concerns about financial stability. Although technology companies generally have the capacity to finance these investments independently or gain access to bond and equity markets, a failure for projected future revenues to materialize may result in significant corrections in equity markets. Such corrections can lead to a decline in investment spending due to over-capacity, which would subsequently contribute to a contraction in aggregate demand through diminished household wealth and lower anticipated profits.

Additionally, some of the factors previously mentioned may serve as significant influences on the neutral interest rate, often referred to as r*. The two primary factors that warrant attention are the slower growth of the population and the associated risks to fiscal sustainability. While these factors tend to exert opposing effects on the interplay between savings and investment, it is my assessment that slower population growth, along with an aging demographic, are more impactful in exerting downward pressure on the neutral interest rate. Ultimately, if concerns regarding fiscal sustainability are not adequately addressed in the coming years—specifically through efforts to stabilize or reduce the increasing trajectory of the federal debt-to-GDP ratio—there is a possibility that r* and interest rates could rise. This rise may, in turn, crowd out private investment.
output:
Artificial Intelligence Finally, the surge in AI investment could also be challenging for monetary policy. Investment in new technologies is likely to raise productivity and lower inflation in the medium term. Although the additional investment also boosts demand, the effects on productivity and supply are likely to occur relatively quickly, and the economy is less likely to tighten appreciably in the near term. In this case, monetary policy should refrain from restraining aggregate demand, as any deviation from maximum employment is likely to be temporary.

There is a risk that expectations of returns on these high-tech investments may be too optimistic and raise financial stability concerns. Although tech companies can largely self finance these investments, or easily access bond and equity markets, if expectations of future revenues do not materialize, we may see a large correction in equity markets and a slump in investment spending due to over-capacity. Such a correction would lead to a contraction in aggregate demand through lower household wealth and lower expected profits.

Neutral Rate of Interest Some of the factors discussed here may be key influences on the neutral interest rate, or r*. The two factors that I am more attentive to are slower population growth and fiscal sustainability risks. Although these factors have opposite effects on the balance between savings and investment and r*, I see slower population growth and the aging of the population as more prominent factors in pulling down the neutral interest rate. If fiscal sustainability concerns are not addressed in the years ahead, by stabilizing or reversing the upward trajectory of the federal debt-to-GDP ratio, I am afraid that r* and interest rates could rise and crowd out private investment.

Two additional factors contributing to productivity enhancement appear to be associated with transformations in the U.S. economy during and following the pandemic. Additionally, there was a significant increase in worker reallocation across various jobs and geographic locations at the onset of the pandemic, which persisted for an extended period. Research indicates that this reallocation may have resulted in improved and more effective matches between certain workers and job positions, thereby potentially enhancing labor productivity. Simultaneously, the pronounced labor shortages experienced during the post-pandemic recovery prompted numerous businesses to make investments in labor-saving technologies and to reorganize production processes more efficiently, which may have also provided a temporary increase in productivity.

Furthermore, the ongoing substantial investment in new technologies may foster sustained growth in productivity. A significant proportion of this investment has been directed towards artificial intelligence (AI), which possesses the potential to significantly alter various facets of the economy and the job market, as discussed in speeches earlier this fall.

In terms of international comparisons, recent productivity growth in the U.S. appears to be particularly outstanding when contrasted with productivity trends abroad. Prior to the pandemic, the U.S. exhibited relatively rapid productivity growth, as evidenced by the green segments of the bars in figure 1, compared to other advanced economies, although the differences were minor. However, since the pandemic, U.S. productivity growth has greatly surpassed that of Europe, Canada, and Australia, as illustrated in figure 2. To account for this remarkable outperformance, some observers have highlighted the relative flexibility of the U.S. labor market and its higher levels of business dynamism in comparison to these other nations. Moreover, considering that investment in technology has played a role in driving disparities across countries, it is noteworthy that private investment in AI has been significantly greater in the U.S. than in other regions. Ultimately, these factors collectively suggest a robust framework for understanding the dynamics of productivity growth in the contemporary economic landscape.
output:
Two other factors boosting productivity relate in part to changes in the U.S. economy during and after the pandemic. Worker reallocation across jobs and locations surged early in the pandemic and remained high for some time. There is some research suggesting that such reallocation resulted in better and more productive matches between some workers and jobs, thus raising labor productivity. At the same time, severe labor shortages during the post-pandemic recovery spurred many businesses to invest in labor-saving technologies and to restructure aspects of production more efficiently, which may also have given at least a one-time boost to productivity.

More broadly, the continued sizable investment in new technologies may promote ongoing strength in productivity growth. Much of this investment has gone toward artificial intelligence (AI), which has the potential to transform many aspects of the economy and job market, as I discussed in speeches earlier this fall.6,7

The Sharswood neighborhood of North Philadelphia experienced decades of redlining before the CRA and remains one of the poorest in the city. For years, Sharswood was a federally designated "food desert," medically underserved area, and "severely distressed community." Led by the Philadelphia Housing Authority, the $50 million Sharswood Ridge project includes workforce housing, green space, and retail, including a grocery store, bank branch, and urgent care medical clinic. The project has been financed with a New Markets Tax Credit, loans from the housing authority and Philadelphia Industrial Development Corp, and redevelopment assistance from the State of Pennsylvania. In addition to local crowdfunding from private investors, a critical role is being played by banks that purchased NMTC equity and provided additional CRA-aligned capital. In examining the subcomponents of the core Consumer Price Index, as illustrated in Figure 6, it is evident that the deceleration in the pace of disinflation may be attributed to various factors. Over the past year, notable decreases in services inflation have occurred, particularly in the areas of rent for shelter and other non-energy services; however, these declines appear to have been counterbalanced by an increase in the inflation of core goods prices. When analyzing the three categories individually, it is worth noting that the inflation associated with shelter, represented by the black dot-dashed line, has shown a continuous decline. Additionally, core services inflation, excluding shelter and indicated by the red dashed line, has also exhibited a downward trend, although it has experienced a somewhat more volatile trajectory. These observations are consistent with the overall inflation rate moving back toward the targeted level. Conversely, the rise in core goods prices presents a challenge to the expectation of a return to 2 percent inflation. Following extraordinarily high inflation rates during the pandemic, goods inflation experienced a significant decrease, returning to its pre-pandemic range by 2023 and fluctuating within that range until 2025. However, last year saw a notable increase in core goods price inflation, reaching 1.4 percent over the twelve months ending in December 2025, which can be attributed in part to the impact of increased tariffs affecting certain goods prices.

While some potential upward risks to inflation persist, I maintain the expectation that inflation will revert to a sustainable trajectory aligned with our 2 percent target. It is a plausible baseline assumption that the influence of tariffs on inflation may not be enduring, representing essentially a singular adjustment in the price level. My perspective that inflation will again trend toward our designated goal is supported by the recent decline in near-term inflation expectations from their historical peaks observed last year, as indicated by both market- and survey-based metrics. Moreover, most indicators of longer-term inflation expectations continue to align with our 2 percent inflation goal.

By the definition of a balance sheet, it is important to note that liabilities must be corresponded with assets held by the Federal Reserve. Furthermore, when considering the assets that correspond to our currency liability, it appears that currency does not generate interest and does not have a maturity date. Consequently, it may be possible to maintain assets of various maturity lengths to offset our currency liability. Since currency does not yield interest, it can often be the case that any interest accrued from these assets may be viewed as profit. Given that assets with longer maturities tend to offer higher interest rates and exhibit reduced volatility, it seems reasonable to consider holding longer-maturity assets against our currency liability.

Additionally, when examining the Treasury General Account (TGA) liability, it is worth noting that this account also does not accrue interest. However, unlike currency, the TGA can fluctuate significantly, which may result in greater volatility in the overall reserves within the system. This connection to reserves arises from the process in which tax payments are made to the Treasury, leading to a debit of the payer's bank reserves and a corresponding credit to the Treasury's TGA account. Subsequently, when the Treasury disburses payments, the TGA is debited, and the reserve account of the recipient bank is credited. Therefore, it can often be the case that fluctuations in the TGA influence the Federal Reserve's reserve management strategy. 

In essence, there are two potential approaches to address this issue. One strategy may involve maintaining a reserve buffer to ensure that fluctuations in the TGA do not disrupt market liquidity. Alternatively, another approach may consist of holding short-maturity assets that can be adjusted to counterbalance the movements in the TGA, thereby keeping total reserves in the banking system stable. Ultimately, the first strategy suggests that the buffer stock of assets might include somewhat longer-maturity assets, while the second strategy may necessitate the retention of short-term assets that can be easily traded with minimal interest rate risk.

For instance, over the past few years we have seen dramatic advances in generative AI technologies, which synthesize massive quantities of data to create models that can produce high-quality text, images, and video. Building upon these recent advances, a wide variety of new AI assistants have been deployed to help workers in a broad range of jobs. If AI can improve our ability to generate new ideas, then it could provide a long-term boost to labor productivity growth, as each newly discovered idea will itself provide an incremental boost to labor productivity.

After accounting for these special factors, it seems that payroll employment continued to increase in October at a pace close to the average monthly gain seen in the second and third quarters. It is worth noting that maximum employment is not something that can be measured directly. Furthermore, the natural rate of unemployment, often referred to as u*, cannot be observed directly either, which necessitates the use of statistical methods for inference. One common element across various approaches to estimating maximum employment is the reliance on multiple labor market indicators, which supplement the unemployment rate. Additionally, some methods strive to differentiate between temporary factors and more enduring economic characteristics that can be viewed as u*.

In examining the historical context, it is notable that during the 1960s, economists commonly assumed that the natural rate of unemployment, u*, was fixed at 4 percent. Although this figure may have represented a reasonable approximation during that time, it failed to account for the potential for significant changes in that value, particularly related to the surge in labor supply resulting from the post–World War II baby boomers entering the labor force. Given that younger workers generally experience higher unemployment rates, it can be inferred that the actual u* during the 1970s was likely above the 4 percent figure. 

The Federal Reserve's slow response in adjusting its estimate of u* contributed to an inaccurate perception of economic slack. This, combined with the high unemployment rate and the underestimation of the minimum unemployment rate, as well as the failure to acknowledge a deceleration in trend productivity, resulted in an overly loose monetary policy. This policy approach, among other contributing factors, led to persistently elevated inflation rates throughout that decade. Ultimately, this experience prompted the Federal Reserve to recognize that relying on a fixed 4 percent benchmark for u* was inadequate for accurately assessing the cyclical dynamics of the economy.
output:
As I have noted, maximum employment is not directly measurable. Likewise, we cannot observe u* directly, and it has to be inferred by statistical techniques, which I'll review. One element common to all the approaches that I review is that they use a number of labor market indicators in addition to the unemployment rate in forming their estimates of maximum employment. Another element in common to some of the approaches is that they try to separate transient factors, or higher-frequency variation, from a more permanent, long-run feature of the economy that can be interpreted as u*.

Case Study: The Assumption of a Fixed Maximum Employment in the 1970s A common assumption in the economics profession during the 1960s was that u* was 4 percent.

While this number might have been a decent approximation of u* during that period, it did not consider the possibility of meaningful changes in that value and, specifically, changes due to the rapid growth in labor supply from the post–World War II baby boomers entering the workforce. Especially because younger workers have higher levels of unemployment, the advent of the baby boomers meant that u* in the 1970s was surely higher than 4 percent. The Federal Reserve was slow in revising its estimate of u*. The high unemployment rate and too low fixed estimate of u* minimum unemployment, in conjunction with the failure to recognize the slowdown in trend productivity, led the Federal Reserve to exaggerate the estimate of slack in the economy and maintain monetary policy that was too loose, adding to other factors driving persistently high inflation over that decade. This experience led the Federal Reserve to recognize that a fixed 4 percent value for u* was a poor basis for understanding the cyclical position of the economy.

Finally, and turning our focus to monetary policy, this stronger economic performance, with falling inflation, has allowed the FOMC to be patient about the timing in reducing our policy rate. This performance gave us time to strongly focus on the inflation side of our mandate. And this, together with the bump in inflation early this year, helps explain why we began to ease monetary policy to less-restrictive levels only after other central banks of advanced economies had done so. But now, the combination of significant ongoing progress in reducing inflation and a cooling in the labor market means that the time has come to begin easing monetary policy, and I strongly supported the decision by the FOMC in our September meeting to cut the federal funds rate by 50 basis points.

Looking ahead, while I believe the focus should remain on continuing to bring inflation to 2 percent, I support shifting attention to the maximum-employment side of the FOMC's dual mandate as well. Monitoring Financial Stability Central banks around the world routinely monitor the financial system for risks, because financial crises can lead to severe recessions. A cornerstone of the Fed's work in this area is our framework for monitoring and assessing vulnerabilities. The most recent version of our semiannual Financial Stability Report (FSR) was released last month. Our framework distinguishes between two fundamental elements: shocks and vulnerabilities. Shocks are adverse events that by their nature are difficult to predict and, unfortunately, are all too frequent. Recent examples include the pandemic, Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank, and many geopolitical events that still warrant headlines. Vulnerabilities, which are aspects of the financial system that would amplify stress, tend to build up over time and can be identified and assessed. We monitor vulnerabilities in four key categories: asset valuation pressures, household and business borrowing, financial-sector leverage, and liquidity and maturity transformation, or funding risks. Policies to build resilience in the financial system are appropriately targeted at reducing vulnerabilities, because they do not require foreknowledge of any particular shocks.

The financial cycle is recognized as being lower in frequency than the business cycle, with vulnerabilities building over years and typically only to be crystallizing in a short-lived stress event—the classic dynamic of going up by the stairs but down by the elevator. Further, as I mentioned earlier, vulnerabilities often build during prolonged expansions as, for example, investor optimism leads to greater tolerance of risk, excess borrowing, and increased leverage. The realization of stress and associated contraction can put these forces into reverse, resulting in decreased vulnerabilities. But the economic and human costs of such an adjustment can be significant.

input: Additionally, it is worth noting that understanding the evolution of central banks can provide insight into their current independence. Furthermore, the development of central banks may be traced back to the 17th century, when institutions such as Sweden's Riksbank were established. Notably, the Riksbank was created in 1688 to provide funds to the government, and the Bank of England followed in 1694 with a similar purpose. In essence, other European central banks experienced a period of growth in the 19th and 20th centuries, including the establishment of the Federal Reserve. Ultimately, these institutions underwent a transition from private to public entities and became accountable to governments, which tends to result in a more practical and effective central bank. It is worth noting that this recognition of the importance of independence appeared to gain momentum by the mid-20th century. Furthermore, a significant event in the history of central bank independence occurred in the United States in 1951, when the Federal Reserve and the Treasury reached an agreement that allowed the Fed to pursue national economic goals independently. Additionally, this agreement was preceded by a series of high-level meetings and may be seen as a response to the economic conditions of the time, including soaring inflation. In essence, the Federal Reserve had previously agreed to peg interest rates on Treasury securities during World War II, and this agreement was continued after the war, which can often lead to a loss of independence for the central bank. Ultimately, the 1951 agreement appears to have marked a significant turning point in the history of central bank independence, and it may be summarized that the evolution of central banks has been shaped by a variety of factors, including their origins, development, and experiences over time.
output: To understand how governments have come to embrace the independence of central banks, it is helpful to review how they have evolved from their origins in the 17th century. Sweden's Riksbank was established by the private sector in 1688 to lend the government funds, and the Bank of England followed in 1694, with a similar structure and purpose. Other European central banks followed in the 19th century and a wave of many more in the 20th, including the Federal Reserve. At different times, these central banks made the transition from wholly private to wholly public institutions and became accountable to government, and by the mid-20th century, there was a growing recognition that independence made for a more practical and, ultimately, more effective central bank. In the United States, the moment of truth came in 1951. During World War II, the Federal Reserve had agreed to peg interest rates on Treasury securities in order to ensure smooth funding of the war effort, and after the war, it continued to peg the longer-term Treasury rate. In the early 1950s, inflation soared, but Treasury favored continuing a cap on longer-term interest rates so that debt management costs could continue to be low during the Korean War. After a series of high-level meetings, the Federal Reserve and the Treasury reached an agreement in 1951 that freed the Fed from the obligation to fix interest rates and allowed it to use monetary policy independently to pursue national economic goals.

Ultimately, the work of maintaining an effective bank regulatory framework is never really complete. If regulators do not consistently reassess what is already in place, it can prevent the meeting of the statutory obligation to promote a safe and sound banking system that enables banks to serve their customers effectively and efficiently.
