It is worth noting that throughout this year, the U.S. economy has exhibited resilience amid significant changes in economic policy. In relation to the Federal Reserve's dual-mandate objectives, the labor market tends to remain close to maximum employment, and while inflation levels may still be somewhat high, they have decreased considerably from the peaks observed after the pandemic. In the comments I will provide today, I will first examine the current economic conditions and the short-term outlook for monetary policy. Additionally, I will discuss the findings from our recent public review of the monetary policy framework, which are reflected in the revised Statement on Longer-Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy that we have released today.

Regarding the current economic conditions and the near-term outlook, when I addressed this audience one year ago, the economy appeared to be at a crucial turning point. Our policy rate had remained within the range of 5-1/4 to 5-1/2 percent for an extended period exceeding one year. This restrictive policy approach was generally seen as necessary to aid in reducing inflation and to promote a sustainable equilibrium between aggregate demand and supply. Inflation levels had moved significantly closer to our target, while the labor market had shown signs of cooling from its previously overheated condition. Risks associated with rising inflation seemed to have lessened. However, it is notable that the unemployment rate had risen by nearly a full percentage point, a shift that can often be associated with recessionary periods. Over the following three Federal Open Market Committee meetings, our policy stance was recalibrated, which set the groundwork for the labor market to maintain balance near maximum employment throughout the past year. In summary, the ongoing economic developments indicate a complex yet adaptive landscape for both the labor market and monetary policy.

At “Labor Markets in Transition: Demographics, Productivity, and Macroeconomic Policy,” an economic symposium sponsored by the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City, Jackson Hole, Wyoming

Over the course of this year, the U.S. economy has shown resilience in a context of sweeping changes in economic policy. In terms of the Fed's dual-mandate goals, the labor market remains near maximum employment, and inflation, though still somewhat elevated, has come down a great deal from its post-pandemic highs. At the same time, the balance of risks appears to be shifting.

In my remarks today, I will first address the current economic situation and the near-term outlook for monetary policy. I will then turn to the results of our second public review of our monetary policy framework, as captured in the revised Statement on Longer-Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy that we released today.

Current Economic Conditions and Near-Term Outlook When I appeared at this podium one year ago, the economy was at an inflection point. Our policy rate had stood at 5-1/4 to 5-1/2 percent for more than a year. That restrictive policy stance was appropriate to help bring down inflation and to foster a sustainable balance between aggregate demand and supply. Inflation had moved much closer to our objective, and the labor market had cooled from its formerly overheated state. Upside risks to inflation had diminished. But the unemployment rate had increased by almost a full percentage point, a development that historically has not occurred outside of recessions. Over the subsequent three Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meetings, we recalibrated our policy stance, setting the stage for the labor market to remain in balance near maximum employment over the past year (figure 1).

Examining Productivity Since the high-tech boom ended in the early 2000s, smoothing through recession-driven swings, growth in output per hour worked has been relatively modest, roughly 1.5 percent per year, on average, though it has picked up some over the past two years. In fact, the latest estimate for productivity would not have looked out of place in the high-tech boom: it grew 2.7 percent over the year ending in the second quarter. The emergence of generative AI has raised hopes for a technology-fueled revival of strong growth in labor productivity, which could support rising real earnings for workers and purchasing power for households. Like many of the most significant innovations of the past few centuries—such as the steam engine, electricity, computers, and the internet—AI has the potential to affect labor productivity in a wide swath of economic activities across many industries and occupations.

Although I share the view that AI could lift productivity out of this period of low growth, it bears emphasis that recent productivity gains have been modest despite rather impressive changes in information technology. For example, we live much of our lives on our smartphones, devices that almost no one used 20 years ago. Moreover, the generative AI models that have captured our attention since 2022 were preceded by other forms of AI that have already been integrated into e-commerce and other business operations. In other words, the modest productivity growth seen of late already incorporates gains from some types of AI. In contrast, numerous analyses concerning the potential impact of tariffs on inflation have been based on empirical studies related to the U.S.–China trade conflict prior to the pandemic. It is important to note that these studies often exhibit biases arising from trade rerouting and minimal exemptions. When a Chinese exporter manages to avoid bearing the incidence of tariffs through costly transshipment or by taking advantage of the minimal exemption loophole, the motivation to do so tends to be closely linked to the incidence absorbed. Consequently, goods that would require China to absorb a higher proportion of the tariff cost are likely to be excluded from the sample, while those goods for which China can transfer tariff costs to importers remain included, leading to violations of identification restrictions. Jackson Mejia has conducted a study on this bias within pass-through estimates and has found evidence indicating that as much as 40 percent of product categories subject to tariffs may be influenced by transshipment, with trade volumes approaching 25 percent for intermediate and capital goods. The minimal exemption introduces similar identification challenges, suggesting that the effects of transshipment may represent lower bounds on the identification problem present in this body of literature. Furthermore, these studies tend to focus on short-term effects, while incidence analyses are typically concerned with long-term outcomes; the distinction between short-run and long-run elasticities is generally accepted.

Additionally, any assertion that tariffs currently contribute to inflation must be supported by a clear counterfactual description. Several analyses utilize the two decades preceding the pandemic as the relevant counterfactual; however, I argue that these time periods may not be reasonable due to significant concurrent shocks that could distort the analysis. Attributing all excess inflation above the pre-trend level to tariffs is a methodology that could be applied to numerous recent policies or shocks, including the emphasis on supply chain resilience after the pandemic, which is unrelated to tariffs. Ultimately, this discussion underscores the complexity of isolating the effects of tariffs on inflation amidst various influencing factors.

Following the Global Financial Crisis (GFC), bank regulators established and implemented regulations that mandate the largest banking institutions to maintain a portfolio of High-Quality Liquid Assets (HQLA) in quantities that are calibrated to their anticipated requirements during stressful scenarios. This regulatory framework, in conjunction with capital requirements, aims to bolster the resilience of these significant banks in the face of stress events. Rather than permitting these institutions to jeopardize the stability of the financial system, which would necessitate government bailouts, the regulatory approach requires them to essentially self-insure by holding a sufficient quantity of HQLA. It is worth noting that as conditions evolve, there exists a reasonable basis for the consideration of recalibrating these regulations. However, the banking stresses experienced in 2023 may indicate that liquidity requirements should be increased rather than decreased, a position I have articulated in several prior speeches. Furthermore, following the aforementioned events, banks demonstrated a notable increase in the collateral pledged at the discount window, exceeding $1 trillion. This enhanced state of operational readiness is crucial to maintain, particularly as the memories of this occurrence tend to fade over time, as historical patterns indicate.

In addition, the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) treats reserves and Treasury securities equivalently while also necessitating that banks prove their capacity to access private markets. This requirement serves to ensure that banks possess the operational experience essential for raising liquidity when necessary. The provision of liquidity by the Federal Reserve is also incorporated into these regulatory frameworks. For instance, at present, banks have the ability to utilize term primary credit to enhance their LCR if required; however, this action entails actual borrowing rather than merely the potential to borrow. Furthermore, High-Quality Liquid Assets that are pre-positioned at the discount window are fully recognized in fulfilling liquidity requirements. The implication of these factors is that the provision of liquidity by the Federal Reserve is already deeply integrated with the existing liquidity requirements. In summary, the relationship between liquidity regulation and the practices of banks is complex and critical for maintaining financial stability.

output:

I assess that current policy is only moderately constraining aggregate demand, suggesting that even a slight uptick in inflation might prompt me to back a tighter policy stance. output:

If there is evidence that progress toward 2 percent inflation reversed in August, a small adjustment in our stance would help ensure that it resumes.

If inflation expectations risk becoming unanchored, then a stronger reaction to the inflation side of the mandate may be warranted, as this can help to mitigate the potential risks. Conversely, if inflationary pressures do not intensify and inflation expectations remain well anchored, then it may be prudent to prioritize the downside risks to output and employment, as this can help to minimize the potential costs.

It is worth noting that another consideration is whether the shock is expected to be short lived or persistent, keeping in mind that monetary policy actions tend to work with a lag. Furthermore, this consideration is important when deciding whether to respond to the shock or to allow it to pass without a policy response. In essence, if a shock is expected to reverse before monetary policy can take effect, looking through it may be the appropriate approach, as this can help to avoid unnecessary interventions. However, it may be challenging to predict how long a shock may last, and therefore the appropriate monetary policy response requires weighing the risks to both sides of the mandate from various actions. Ultimately, a careful evaluation of the potential risks and costs is necessary to determine the most effective response. In summary, the monetary policymaker must reach a decision based on a thorough analysis of the economic situation and the potential consequences of different policy actions.

It is worth noting that the relationship between a 4 percent wage growth and a 2 percent inflation rate may be influenced by productivity trends, which have demonstrated an annual growth rate of approximately 2 percent since the onset of the pandemic. Furthermore, this productivity growth appears to have accelerated slightly in 2023 and 2024. Unless there is a significant alteration in this productivity trajectory, it may be possible for wage growth to align with the goal of reducing inflation to 2 percent.

Additionally, last week’s inflation data, when considered comprehensively, revealed a mildly disappointing trend; however, this disappointment was not as severe as one might conclude from an exclusive focus on the consumer price index (CPI). Specifically, the total CPI inflation for January registered at a notably high 0.5 percent, while core inflation reached 0.4 percent. This resulted in year-over-year changes of 3.0 percent and 3.3 percent, respectively. Although these 12-month figures indicate some progress compared to January 2024, they still remain elevated.

Moreover, the producer price data released last week provided additional context, and when analyzed in conjunction with the CPI data, the forecasts for January personal consumption expenditures (PCE) inflation appear less alarming. Estimates suggest that total PCE inflation may be around 0.3 percent, while core PCE inflation is approximately 0.25 percent. These figures indicate a potential increase in the monthly core inflation rate by about one-tenth of one percentage point, following readings below 0.2 percent in November and December. Consequently, the 12-month and 6-month average core PCE inflation rates may settle around 2.6 percent and 2.4 percent, respectively. Although these rates are lower than those observed in January 2024, the pace of progress toward achieving our 2 percent inflation target has been slower than anticipated. In summary, while there are signs of improvement, challenges remain in addressing inflation effectively.
output:
As for whether 4 percent wage growth is consistent with 2 percent inflation, I will note, as I have before, that productivity has grown at roughly a 2 percent annual rate since the advent of the pandemic—and slightly faster than that in 2023 and 2024. Unless that productivity trend changes a lot, wage growth is consistent with bringing inflation down to 2 percent.

Turning to inflation, last week's data taken as a whole were mildly disappointing but not nearly so disappointing as a focus on the consumer price index (CPI) alone would have indicated. Total CPI inflation for January came in hot at 0.5 percent, and core was 0.4 percent, which brings the 12-month changes to 3.0 percent and 3.3 percent, respectively. These 12-month readings are lower than we had in January 2024, so we have made some progress over the past year, but they are still too high.

However, we also received producer price data last week, and, combining that information with the CPI data, forecasts for January PCE inflation aren't as alarming as the CPI inflation data. Estimates for total PCE inflation, the FOMC's preferred measure, are about 0.3 percent and that for core PCE inflation was around 0.25 percent. These numbers will mean a bump-up in the monthly pace of core inflation of about one-tenth of 1 percentage point from readings of under 0.2 percent in November and December. And this would leave the 12-month and 6-month average core PCE inflation around 2.6 percent and 2.4 percent, respectively. These rates are lower than where they stood in January 2024, which is good, but progress has been slower than I expected on reducing inflation to our 2 percent target.

output:

Additionally, it is essential to emphasize that central banks, including the Federal Reserve, must enhance their pace of adoption of artificial intelligence in order to optimize their operations. The fundamental nature of central banking work is characterized by careful analysis, thoughtful consideration, and measured responses when evaluating novel technologies. This cautious approach is particularly relevant in the context of emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence. 

Furthermore, it is increasingly evident that the numerous advantages presented by artificial intelligence may facilitate central banks in improving various aspects of their operational processes. The rapid advancement of this technology underscores the necessity for proactive engagement in its application within our operations. Consequently, the Federal Reserve is actively utilizing artificial intelligence, where appropriate, to bolster staff efficiency and effectiveness. It is worth noting that generative artificial intelligence represents a transformative technological advancement with which central banks must remain actively engaged to ensure their adaptability as technology evolves.

Moreover, as we advance toward achieving greater efficiency, it is crucial to utilize the appropriate tools for specific tasks, acknowledging that generative artificial intelligence may not always represent the optimal solution. Certain challenges we encounter can often be effectively addressed through robotic process automation or traditional artificial intelligence methodologies. These considerations are consistent with the evaluation process that every organization contemplating the integration of artificial intelligence ought to undertake.

In essence, at the Federal Reserve, we have concentrated our efforts on ensuring that we can effectively leverage artificial intelligence capabilities through the establishment of a dedicated artificial intelligence program and governance framework. We are adopting an enterprise-wide strategy that promotes a learn-by-doing approach, systematically integrating high-value applications of generative artificial intelligence, including writing, coding, and research activities. We have adopted a proactive engagement strategy for our staff members to interact directly with this technology. Furthermore, we are in the process of identifying business processes that may be enhanced and transformed through the application of these advanced technologies. Ultimately, our commitment to innovation and improvement in operations will position us favorably for the future.
output:
AI and Central Banking A third and final point I would like to leave you with is that central banks, including the Fed, need to keep up with AI by increasing our speed of adoption for our own operations.

The nature of central banking work is inherently careful, considered, and measured when evaluating anything new. This is particularly true for any new technologies. But it seems clear already that the many advantages offered by AI could assist central banks in at least some of their operations, and the speed at which this technology is moving makes it appropriate to proactively engage in using AI for our own operations. That is why the Federal Reserve is using AI, where appropriate, to increase staff efficiency and effectiveness. My view is that GenAI is a transformative technology that central banks need to remain engaged with to ensure an ability to execute as technology evolves.

As we push ahead on efficiency gains, it is important that we leverage the right tools for the task at hand, recognizing that GenAI is not always the best choice. Some of the challenges that we face can be addressed by robotic process automation or traditional AI methods. These are the same kinds of questions that every business and organization considering AI should be weighing.

At the Federal Reserve, we have focused on ensuring we can leverage AI capabilities by establishing an AI program and governance framework for the use of AI technologies. We are taking an enterprise-wide approach of learning-by-doing and broadly adopting high-value uses of GenAI, such as writing, coding, and research activities. We have taken a "hands on keys" approach to having staff engage with it. We are identifying the business processes that can be improved and transformed with the technology.

In its current manifestation, the Standing Repo Facility (SRF) has established a minimum bid rate that corresponds directly to the primary credit rate of the discount window. This rate is also aligned with the upper boundary of the target range for the federal funds rate. Consequently, the SRF, by its inherent design, is not optimally configured to function solely as a backstop during instances of market dysfunction and stress. It is worth noting that I advocate for a minimum bid rate that exceeds the upper limit of the federal funds rate target range, as this adjustment would underscore that the primary objective of the SRF is to act exclusively as a backstop. A rate that surpasses the peak of the target range would likely serve to dissuade utilization of this facility except during exceptional market-wide episodes characterized by acute stress. Moreover, it appears that a rate which is not established at a sufficiently elevated level may still be perceived as an option for primary dealers facing idiosyncratic pressures that are not linked to broader market disruptions. In my opinion, facilitating an outlet for dealers encountering such pressures should not constitute the intended purpose of this facility.

Furthermore, while the aspiration to create a "release valve" in order to enhance market liquidity has been a goal of the SRF, I harbor concerns that one of its unintended consequences may be the distortion of market signals through an artificial influence on repo rate dynamics. It is essential to recognize that it is not the role of the Federal Reserve to supplant or engage in arbitrage of private market activities.

In addition, having a minimum bid rate on the SRF that is not sufficiently elevated in relation to prevailing market rates poses a risk of suppressing or distorting critical signals that arise from overnight money markets. As the balance sheet runoff transitions into a new phase, it becomes increasingly important to maintain the ability to observe the underlying conditions of reserves and money markets clearly. Ultimately, ensuring the integrity of market signals is vital to the effective functioning of financial systems.
output:
In its current form, the SRF has a minimum bid rate set equal to the discount window primary credit rate, which is also equal to the top of the target range for the federal funds rate. As a result, the SRF, by design, is not fully positioned to serve only as a backstop during times of market dysfunction and stress. My preference would be for a minimum bid rate higher than the top of the federal funds rate target range in order to emphasize that the SRF's purpose is to serve only as a backstop. A rate above the top of the target range would be more likely to discourage use of the facility outside of exceptional market-wide episodes of acute stress. It seems likely that a rate that's not set at a sufficiently high level might still be considered an option for primary dealers experiencing idiosyncratic pressures outside of market-wide disruption. In my view, providing an outlet for dealers that experience these kinds of pressures should not be the intended purpose of this facility.

While creating a "release valve" to provide greater market liquidity has been a goal of the SRF, I remain concerned that one of its unintended consequences is to distort market signals by artificially affecting repo rate dynamics. It is not the Fed's role to replace or arbitrage private-market activities.

Having a minimum bid rate on the SRF that is not sufficiently elevated relative to market rates risks suppressing or distorting valuable signals stemming from overnight money markets. While balance sheet runoff is entering a new phase, it is especially important to be able to observe underlying reserve and money market conditions.

Given the substantial volume of commercial real estate assets that are reaching maturity and will require refinancing, I will continue to monitor this market closely. output:
Allow me to discuss our view of valuation pressures in property markets and come back shortly to the imprint of the April volatility on stock and bond prices. The significant rise in house prices during and after the pandemic has slowed substantially over the past couple of years, but price-to-rent ratios and model-based valuation measures are around the record levels last seen in 2005. Two key differences are that lax underwriting standards do not appear to have driven the increase in house prices and owners' equity appears to be more solid, using both price- and model-based measures.

We also noted that commercial real estate (CRE) valuations had been elevated going into 2022 but declined significantly through the period of higher interest rates and deteriorating CRE fundamentals. Prices and fundamentals appear to have moderated, and valuations are closer to historical norms. Given the significant volume of CRE that is maturing and will need to be refinanced, I am continuing to watch this market closely.

I express my gratitude to Francisco for the gracious introduction and extend my appreciation to the Economic Club of Miami for facilitating this opportunity to address you today. It is worth noting that the South Florida economy exhibits considerable vibrancy and growth. The unemployment rate in the Miami region is currently below the national average, and consumers in Florida appear to demonstrate resilience that is notable compared to the rest of the country. I welcome the chance to engage with all of you who play a vital role in this economic dynamism.

Furthermore, I am particularly pleased to provide an update on my economic outlook shortly after the initial meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) for this year. My focus remains on fulfilling the dual mandate of achieving maximum employment and maintaining stable prices, as assigned by Congress. In this discussion, I will address both aspects of that mandate and share my perspective on the evolving economic landscape. Additionally, I will offer insights into the apparent disconnect between sentiment and activity indicators, followed by a consideration of the implications for monetary policy.

In a broad sense, I perceive the U.S. economy as exhibiting continued resilience, with recent data suggesting that growth during the second half of 2025 was stronger than earlier projections indicated. Inflation appears to have stagnated persistently above our target of 2 percent, while simultaneously, the labor market shows signs of stabilization in recent months. Although the overall economic condition remains robust, I am closely monitoring sentiment, delinquencies, and other indicators that may highlight a deteriorating outlook for low- and moderate-income households. Ultimately, this ongoing observation underscores the complexity of the current economic environment and its varying impacts across different demographic groups.
output:
Thank you, Francisco, for the kind introduction, and many thanks to the Economic Club of Miami for the opportunity to speak with you today. It is wonderful to see firsthand the vibrant and growing South Florida economy. The Miami region's unemployment rate is below the national average, and consumers in Florida have been among the country's most resilient. I am happy to have the opportunity to engage with all of you who are central to that dynamism.

I am especially glad to have the chance to update you on my economic outlook shortly after the Federal Open Market Committee's (FOMC's) first meeting of the year. As always, I am focused on achieving the dual mandate of maximum employment and stable prices given to us by Congress. This evening, I will discuss both parts of that mandate and give you my view of how the economy is evolving. I will then share some thoughts about the apparent disconnect between sentiment and activity readings before discussing implications for monetary policy.

Economic Outlook Broadly, I see the U.S. economy as continuing to be resilient, with recent data indicating that growth in the second half of 2025 was even stronger than previously forecast. Inflation appears to have stalled stubbornly above our 2 percent goal, while at the same time the labor market appears to have stabilized in recent months. While the overall condition of the economy is solid, I am carefully watching sentiment, delinquencies, and other indicators that show a worsening outlook for low- and moderate-income households.

Additionally, the surge in business creation during and after the pandemic may be attributed to various factors, which economists will likely debate for years to come. Furthermore, it is worth noting that strong monetary and fiscal policy, pandemic social safety net policies, and accommodative financial conditions may have played a role in this phenomenon. Notably, the need for further research has been reached, and this topic will likely be the subject of numerous dissertations in the near future. Ultimately, this highlights the complexity of the issue, which can often be influenced by multiple factors.

In essence, the response of American entrepreneurs to the pandemic appears to be a significant aspect of the story, as they tended to adapt to the changing needs of households and businesses. This suggests that entrepreneurship can often facilitate the economy's ability to respond to significant shocks, such as the COVID-19 pandemic, which experienced a substantial impact. It is worth noting that research has reached a conclusion that entrepreneurs and their businesses are highly responsive to major economic disruptions. Furthermore, the pandemic has resulted in a considerable amount of uncertainty, particularly with regard to the potential productivity effects of the surge in new businesses, especially in the high-tech sector.

Ultimately, the future trajectory of new business creation remains uncertain, as the pre-pandemic period was characterized by a decline in new business formation rates, and the pandemic-induced surge may be experiencing a decline. Additionally, the possibility of continued growth in this area is an open question, which may be influenced by various factors. In summary, the surge in business creation during and after the pandemic is a complex phenomenon that may be attributed to various factors, and its long-term effects on the economy are still uncertain, but it appears to be an important aspect of the economy's ability to adapt to change.
output:
Economists will spend years debating the various causes of the surge in business creation during and soon after the pandemic. Perhaps strong monetary and fiscal policy backstopping aggregate demand played some role, or pandemic social safety net policies, or simply the accommodative financial conditions of 2020 and 2021.18 Indeed, more research is needed and will be the subject of many dissertations in the near future.

I do think a large part of the story is ultimately a case of resourceful and determined American entrepreneurs, perhaps including some of you, responding to the tumultuous shocks of the pandemic. They, like some of you, stepped in to meet the rapidly changing needs of households and businesses. This points to a fourth way economists like to think about entrepreneurship, which is that entrepreneurship plays a big role in helping the economy adapt to change. Research suggests that entrepreneurs and the businesses they create are highly responsive to big economic shocks, and the COVID-19 pandemic was certainly a seismic shock. To be sure, the future is uncertain. It is unclear what the productivity effects of the pandemic surge of new businesses, particularly in high tech, will be. And whether that surge will continue is an open question; after all, the pre-pandemic period was a period of declining rates of new business creation, and the pandemic surge itself does appear to be cooling off recently.

Conclusion For now, let me say that I am grateful that entrepreneurs continue to give us a hand in meeting our employment mandate, and whatever productivity gains we may reap in coming years as a result may help ease tradeoffs with inflation as well.

Let's turn to the inflation data. In the past two days, we received June consumer and producer price data that give us a good idea of the inflation rate based on PCE, the FOMC's benchmark for monetary policy. After several months of readings that moved the 12-month inflation rate closer to the FOMC's target, the consumer price index and the producer price index suggest that total PCE inflation moved up to around 2.5 percent in June, and core inflation likewise rose to roughly 2.7 percent. I believe these data reflect some modest effect from tariff increases, which began in February, and I believe there are further tariff-induced increases to inflation to come later this year, with the asterisk that there remains a lot of uncertainty about how trade agreements or escalations in trade conflicts may affect that outcome.

To understand how tariffs are affecting prices, I have been following not only the Bureau of Labor Statistics monthly data, but also studies of high frequency price data. For example, some researchers this year are tracking the short-run price impact of tariffs on goods prices in real time by examining product-level price data from online stores of large U.S. retailers. Using data through mid-July, they find that, on net, imported goods prices have increased modestly while domestic goods prices are little changed. Looking across country of origin, Chinese goods imports have seen the most persistent and steady price increases. That said, to date, the data point to very small goods price increases relative to the size of the tariff rates.

input: Additionally, it is worth noting that a potential solution to address the loss in risk sensitivity may involve the Board reaching a decision to utilize its capital directive authority in exceptional circumstances. Furthermore, this approach can often entail imposing individualized capital requirements on specific firms, taking into account a firm's particular circumstances, including its capital structure and risk-related factors. Notably, this method tends to be similar to the requirements implemented in other jurisdictions, such as the United Kingdom's Pillar II-B requirements. In essence, these individualized requirements would be informed by stress test results, as well as qualitative factors and supervisory judgment, and would be adjusted to reflect a specific firm's risk profile. Ultimately, this approach appears to preserve the benefits of tailoring capital requirements to a firm's specific risks, while also allowing the Board to address significant deficiencies in capital adequacy. It is worth noting that this type of exercise may not be suitable as a default manner for setting capital requirements, but in exceptional cases, it can often provide a means of preserving the benefits of the current regime. Furthermore, this approach tends to maintain the flexibility and adaptability of stress testing, thereby retaining its value as a tool for identifying idiosyncratic risk and ensuring sufficient capital. In addition, this method can often allow for continued innovation in stress testing, which is vital as the finance sector evolves and banks seek to reduce supervisory requirements. Ultimately, this approach may provide a means of advancing scenario design and modeling, unencumbered by the limitations imposed by the notice-and-comment process, and in summary, it appears to offer a potential solution for addressing the loss in risk sensitivity while preserving the benefits of stress testing.
output:
To address this loss in risk sensitivity, I would propose that, in exceptional circumstances, the Board could use its capital directive authority to impose individualized capital requirements on specific firms to account for a firm's particular circumstances, including its capital structure, riskiness, complexity, financial activities, and other appropriate risk-related factors. This would be similar to the United Kingdom's Pillar II-B requirements and those of other jurisdictions. While these requirements could be informed by the stress test results in part, they would also take into account qualitative factors and supervisory judgment. Because these individualized requirements would consider the specific risks of a firm, they would be adjusted to reflect a specific firm's risk profile. While I don't believe it would be advisable for this type of exercise to become the default manner for setting capital requirements, in exceptional cases, it would preserve some of the tailoring benefits of the current SCB regime in a manner that comports with the changes I have discussed. Furthermore, it would preserve the ability for the Board to address stress results that demonstrate significant deficiencies in capital adequacy under a stressed scenario, when the firms are otherwise in compliance with regulatory capital requirements.

With these changes, stress testing could maintain its flexibility and adaptability and therefore could retain its value as an effective tool for identifying idiosyncratic risk in a major bank and ensuring that capital is sufficient to address the risk. Among the benefits would be the space this approach would allow for continued innovation in stress testing. Such innovation is vital as finance evolves and banks continue to seek ways to reduce supervisory and regulatory requirements. This approach could allow for scenario design and modeling advancements unencumbered by the limitations I've spoken of imposed by the notice-and-comment process.

input:
Many of the subjects that Stan emphasized and discussed during his tenure at the Board continue to hold significant relevance for policymakers even a decade later. For example, Stan articulated in numerous speeches that although regulatory measures enacted in the aftermath of the financial crisis have considerably enhanced the resilience of banks, certain activities are likely to transition to nonbank intermediaries that lack the same regulatory protections. He remarked in his aptly titled address, "Financial Stability and Shadow Banks: What We Do Not Know May Injure Us," that the absence of data and the limited visibility regarding some of these activities constitute a distinct source of systemic risk. Furthermore, we are currently engaged in efforts to deepen our understanding of these matters, with the objective of enhancing our monitoring of financial stability, and I will persist in collaborating with my colleagues on the Board to identify tangible approaches for achieving this goal.

Additionally, Stan recognized the importance of providing policymakers with a platform to engage in discussions about tail risks and long-term questions pertaining to the evolution of the financial system. These considerations may not always exert immediate influence on the short-term macroeconomic forecast; however, it is essential to remain cognizant of them. Consequently, staff briefings to the financial stability committee examine the plausible range of severe shocks that could potentially impact the economy, as well as the mechanisms through which such shocks may propagate through financial markets and institutions, with the aim of comprehending the ultimate ramifications for the broader macroeconomy.

Moreover, in the event of a negative shock, financial conditions tend to tighten. One perspective on the work related to financial stability can often be viewed as the pursuit of understanding the extent to which, or the speed at which, this tightening may take place. Addressing that inquiry necessitates consideration of the plausible range of shocks that could affect the economy, alongside an assessment of the resilience of critical financial markets and institutions. In conclusion, these ongoing evaluations are vital for maintaining and enhancing the stability of the financial system.
output:
Many of the topics that Stan focused on and spoke about during his time at the Board remain highly relevant to policymakers a decade later. For instance, Stan pointed out in several speeches that while post-crisis regulatory measures had significantly bolstered bank resilience, certain activities were going to migrate to nonbank intermediaries that were not subject to the same regulatory safeguards. He noted in his aptly named speech "Financial Stability and Shadow Banks: What We Don't Know Could Hurt Us" that the data gaps and limited visibility into some of these activities were their own source of systemic risk. We are working to better understand these issues with an eye toward improving our financial stability monitoring, and I will continue to work with my Board colleagues to find concrete ways to do so.

Stan also appreciated the value of giving policymakers a venue in which to discuss tail risks and longer-horizon questions related to the evolution of the financial system. These considerations do not always have immediate bearing on the near-term macro forecast, but you do not want to lose sight of them. When I decide to maintain interest rates at their current levels, I provide an explanation of how prevailing economic conditions have influenced this policy decision. When contemplating future economic data, I express that if the data manifests in a specific manner, then I will advocate for a particular policy response. It is worth noting that this statement does not constitute a commitment to a specific policy action; rather, it represents a conditional policy declaration. A different economic outcome may prompt me to advocate for an alternative policy action. In my remarks today, I have delineated the conditions that would lead me to support a continued pause, as well as those that would compel me to endorse a more restrictive policy stance. By way of wrapping up, I want to speak about central bank communication, which I consider an essential part of the monetary policy process. I distinguish between three types of communication that matter for monetary policy and how I try to communicate my views to the public.

First, I try to communicate why I have taken my current policy position. If I vote to hold rates steady, I explain how current economic conditions affected my policy decision. I was comfortable supporting the FOMC's decision in late July to hold rates steady because the data at that time led me to view the real side of the economy as solid and we finally saw hints that disinflation may be starting. So I was willing to be patient and see if the disinflation would continue.

The second way in which I communicate is to explain how future economic data will shape my future monetary policy decisions—in short, I try to describe my "reaction function." When thinking about future data, I communicate that IF the data comes in a particular way, THEN I will advocate for policy to be set a particular way. The key point here is that this it is not a commitment to a policy action—it is a conditional policy statement. A different economic outcome would lead me to advocate for a different policy action. In my remarks today, I have outlined what it would take for me to support a continued pause as well as what would cause me to support tighter policy. By communicating my reaction function, consumers, businesses, and investors can better understand how I will vote on policy given the range of outcomes and then factor that into their planning for the future.

Additionally, the next challenge for central bankers that I would like to address contains both shorter and longer-term dimensions, and it may be referred to as a rethink of globalization. For close to a decade, many countries have been engaged in a reexamination of the costs and benefits associated with the steadily freer global movement of capital, labor, and goods that tended to be the norm over previous decades. Although global trade has not experienced a decline over the last decade, changes in trade patterns have clearly been observed, with more countries and firms placing greater emphasis on the rerouting of trade flows and the shortening of supply chains to avoid geopolitical risk and tariffs. This situation is not simply the result of a failed ministerial meeting or a bilateral conflict, but rather it appears to be a persistent and widespread trend that has been under way for some time. The presumption that the increasingly tighter global integration of our economies and financial markets would inevitably continue can no longer be considered as safe as it long was.

At the same time, I have refrained from calling this development, as some have done, the end of globalization, because I do not believe that this will be the outcome. As I think about the 38 governments represented by the OECD and consider how this organization has grown in size and in the depth of its engagement on different issues, I would say that globalization is not going away. What I do expect, however, is that there will be more thought and consideration among our leaders regarding how globalization affects the people we serve, with a more careful weighing of both the potential costs of closer integration and the potential benefits. As these decisions by governments are reached, central bankers will need to be prepared to respond appropriately in the setting of monetary policy and the promotion of financial stability.

Our overarching goal has consistently been to restore price stability without incurring the painful rise in unemployment that has often accompanied efforts to reduce high inflation levels. In discussing inflation, it is worth noting that the increases in prices may have caused significant challenges for American families. Accordingly, I have supported various policies that aim to bring inflation sustainably back to our targeted level of 2 percent. This collective effort appears to have yielded some positive outcomes. Specifically, inflation has experienced a notable decline from its peak of over 7 percent recorded in June 2022. Furthermore, based on the consumer price index and producer price index data for February, the estimated 12-month change in the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index was approximately 2.5 percent last month. While this represents welcome progress, it is important to acknowledge that the rate of improvement may have slowed since last summer. 

Additionally, in certain subcategories, there appears to be evidence that inflation may have reaccelerated in recent months. Importantly, although goods inflation was negative in 2024—a trend that was common prior to the pandemic—it has recently turned positive. This shift may be problematic, as goods inflation has often played a role in restraining total inflation and influencing inflation expectations. Beyond the price increases already documented in official data, surveys indicate that consumers are anticipating further rises in prices in the near future. For instance, both short-term and long-term inflation expectations reported in the Michigan survey have increased in recent months. According to feedback from survey respondents, a considerable portion of this uncertainty may be linked to trade policy. 

I am closely monitoring the acceleration of price increases and the rise in inflation expectations, particularly in light of the recent bout of inflation experienced over the past few years. Given the overall solid position of the economy and the elevated level of uncertainty, I have expressed my support for the Federal Open Market Committee's (FOMC) decision last week to maintain the policy rate at its current level. I perceive current policy as continuing to be restrictive, and I assess that the FOMC's approach is well positioned for the circumstances at hand. The committee may have the flexibility to respond to new developments by holding the current rate steady for some time, as we continue to closely monitor incoming data and the cumulative effects of new policies. Ultimately, I remain dedicated to the goal of reducing inflation back to our target of 2 percent while simultaneously supporting a strong labor market. As always, I will carefully evaluate the incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks when determining the appropriate policy rate.

Good morning, and I would like to express my gratitude for the invitation to join you today. It is a distinct pleasure to be present for the 161st Assembly for Bank Directors of the Southwestern Graduate School of Banking. Additionally, prior to initiating our fireside chat, it appears to be beneficial to summarize my views regarding the recent policy decision made by the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), which concluded its January meeting earlier this week. Following this summary, I will proceed to offer remarks concerning the current state of the economy while also sharing my perspective on the future trajectory of monetary policy.

Furthermore, as we approach the year 2026, the economy has shown a tendency to continue growing, and I observe that inflation is moving closer to our established target. However, it is worth noting that, beneath the surface of these encouraging indicators, the labor market may be experiencing fragility. I will provide insights into why I consider this fragility to represent a significant risk and what implications this may have for the future direction of policy.

In regard to the most recent FOMC meeting, my colleagues and I reached a decision to maintain the federal funds rate target range at 3.5 to 3.75 percent. Let me elucidate my rationale for supporting this decision. I continue to perceive the current policy stance as moderately restrictive, and, when considering the outlook for 2026, my Summary of Economic Projections anticipates three rate cuts for this year. In my assessment, the central question at this meeting revolved around the timeline for executing these cuts, essentially requiring a choice between persistently removing policy restraint to achieve my estimate of neutral policy by the upcoming April meeting or opting to transition to a neutral stance at a more measured pace throughout the course of this year. In conclusion, the path forward appears to involve careful consideration of these dynamics as we navigate the evolving economic landscape.
output:
Good morning, and thank you for the invitation to join you today. It is a pleasure to be with you for the Southwestern Graduate School of Banking's 161st Assembly for Bank Directors. Before we get started on the fireside chat, since the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) concluded its January meeting earlier this week, I think it would be helpful to summarize my views on the recent policy decision. I will then offer some remarks on the economy and also share my perspective on the outlook for monetary policy.

As we enter 2026, the economy has continued to grow, and I see inflation moving closer to our goal. But beneath the surface, the labor market is fragile. I will provide some perspective on why I think that fragility poses the greater risk and what that means for the path of policy.

Update on the Most Recent FOMC Meeting At our FOMC meeting this week, my colleagues and I voted to hold the federal funds rate target range at 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent. Let me explain why I agreed to support this decision. I continue to see policy as moderately restrictive, and, looking ahead to 2026, my Summary of Economic Projections includes three cuts for this year. In my mind, the question at this meeting was about the timeline for implementing these cuts, essentially choosing between continuing to remove policy restraint and arriving at my estimate of neutral by the April meeting, or moving policy to neutral at a more measured pace throughout this year.

Additionally, it is worth noting that this decentralized approach appeared to be more sensible during a period when both the economy and the banking system tended to exhibit a predominantly regional character, although the subsequent expansion of finance and the economy toward a national scope can often be seen as having necessitated certain adjustments. Furthermore, statutory modifications were introduced by Congress to the Federal Reserve Act in 1935, under which the presidents of the Reserve Banks assumed a national role in the formulation of monetary policy through the FOMC. Moreover, the discount rate may be described as having been nationalized in such a manner that all Banks tended to charge an identical rate for lending to local banks. In essence, despite these changes, most Reserve Bank operations continued to remain local in character. It is worth noting that, while monetary policy was conducted at the national level, bank supervision, payment system activities, and most other functions at Reserve Banks appeared to remain focused on serving their respective Districts.

Additionally, a characteristic feature of the early years can be observed in the fact that Reserve Banks tended to employ large numbers of workers engaged in processes that were, at that time, highly manual and labor-intensive in nature. Furthermore, such work may be said to have included the processing of paper checks, the managing of the distribution of coins and currency, the discounting or provision of liquidity to commercial banks against a variety of instruments, often involving the taking of physical custody of this collateral to assure a security interest, and the managing of U.S. Treasury securities. Ultimately, these arrangements illustrate the manner in which the early Reserve Banks combined localized operations with labor-intensive functions.
output:
This decentralized approach made more sense when the economy and the banking system were much more regional in nature, but as finance and the economy became more national in scope, changes were needed. Statutory changes were made by Congress to the Federal Reserve Act in 1935 under which the presidents of the Reserve Banks took on a national role in setting monetary policy via the FOMC. The discount rate was also "nationalized" so that all Banks charged the same rate for lending to local banks. But after these changes, most Reserve Bank operations remained local. While monetary policy was conducted at the national level, bank supervision, payment system activities, and most other functions at Reserve Banks remained focused on serving its District.

Also characteristic of the early years were Reserve Banks that had large numbers of workers engaged in what were at that time highly manual and labor-intensive processes. Such work included processing paper checks, managing distribution of coins and currency, "discounting" or providing commercial banks liquidity against a variety of instruments—often taking physical custody of this collateral to assure a security interest—and managing U.S. Treasury securities.

Good morning. It is a pleasure to be present with you today as we commence our discussion regarding the bank liquidity framework. Additionally, Hal and his team have organized a series of panels that can often enhance our understanding while we contemplate potential adjustments to this framework. The insights provided by the panelists, which include academics, market participants, and fellow policymakers, are expected to enrich our comprehension of these intricate issues and, importantly, prompt us to critically evaluate the effectiveness of the existing framework.

Furthermore, bank liquidity plays a crucial role in ensuring the resilience of the banking system. Specifically, regulatory requirements such as the liquidity coverage ratio (LCR) and the net stable funding ratio (NSFR) were established to guarantee that banks could meet potential cash withdrawal and repayment obligations through their on-balance-sheet holdings. In addition, internal liquidity stress testing and resolution planning were implemented to require banks to evaluate their liquidity positions, particularly in preparation for converting assets under adverse conditions. In theory, these regulatory measures are intended to work in concert to mitigate the risk of bank failure stemming from an inability to fulfill ongoing payment obligations and anticipated cash outflows.

Notably, fifteen years after the global financial crisis, it is imperative to assess whether these regulatory tools achieve the resilience they promise or whether we have established a framework that appears robust in theory but fails to address the vulnerabilities that may arise during times of stress. It is essential to advance our inquiry beyond simply determining whether banks are compliant and to examine whether such compliance genuinely translates into resilience. In summary, this discussion will seek to clarify the effectiveness of our current liquidity framework in fostering a stable banking environment.
output:
Good morning. It's a pleasure to be with you this morning to open our discussion on the bank liquidity framework. Hal and his team have assembled a series of excellent panels that will further inform our approach as we consider adjusting this framework. The panelists' perspectives—including academics, market participants, and fellow policymakers—will enrich our understanding of these complex issues and, importantly, challenge us to think critically about whether the framework we have in place works as intended.

Bank liquidity ensures that the banking system remains resilient. Regulatory requirements including the liquidity coverage ratio (LCR) and the net stable funding ratio (NSFR) were designed to ensure that potential cash withdrawal and repayment obligations could be met with on balance sheet holdings. Internal liquidity stress testing and resolution planning were also designed to require banks to assess liquidity positions, in preparation for monetizing assets under stressed conditions. In theory, these requirements should work together to mitigate the risk of a bank failure resulting from a lack of liquidity to meet its ongoing payment obligations and foreseeable cash outflows.

Fifteen years post-GFC, we need to know whether these tools deliver the promised resilience or whether we have created a framework that looks impressive on paper but fails to capture the vulnerabilities that emerge in times of stress. It is time to move beyond asking whether banks are compliant and ask whether compliance actually translates into resilience.

Let me now turn to the economic outlook. Economic activity continues to be solid. While high energy prices were likely a drag on consumer spending in the second quarter, spending appears to have held up reasonably well. At the same time, businesses continued to make investments related to artificial intelligence (AI). Together, private domestic final purchases, a good indicator of the underlying momentum of real GDP, likely rose strongly.

A consistent feature of the U.S. economy over the past several years has been the resilience of consumers. Starting with high inflation in 2021, followed by high interest rates from 2022 through 2024, the shock of import tariffs in 2025, and higher energy prices from the Middle East conflict, consumers have powered through and have continued spending at a solid pace. With a nod to that resilience, I expect solid consumer spending growth to continue, helped by energy prices that have recently fallen from their April highs. input: It is worth noting that certain tasks traditionally performed by various Districts in diverse manners continue to retain their locally oriented approach and substance in contemporary practice. Furthermore, there appears to be no justification for diminishing the number of Reserve Banks or altering their defined geographic boundaries. Each president of the Banks continues to possess an independent voice within the Federal Open Market Committee regarding the appropriate direction of monetary policy, and this practice should remain intact. The perspectives of each president are influenced by the research conducted by the economists at their respective Banks, insights from regional experts, contributions from the Bank's board of directors, as well as the president's interactions with business leaders within the District. In essence, each Bank president adds a unique viewpoint to the discussions held in Washington with fellow colleagues, thereby fostering a comprehensive understanding of the national economy and informing the trajectory of policy decisions. Additionally, beyond their contributions to monetary policy formulation, each president actively engages with the business, financial, and nonprofit sectors to gain insights into local economic challenges, positioning the Bank to facilitate collaboration among various interest groups to tackle such issues as labor force development, financial inclusion, and concerns affecting rural areas. The significance of these endeavors is immense, as they are vital to the fulfillment of the Federal Reserve's mission, and they should be sustained. Moreover, each Reserve Bank continues to oversee the supervision of state member banks and bank holding companies, drawing upon the regional knowledge and expertise of supervisors situated within the District, as well as on local industries and economic trends. It is essential to recognize that local presence will remain a critical component of this oversight function. This regional expertise also proves to be crucial when the Reserve Bank acts as a lender to depository institutions. Ultimately, let us now shift our focus to a distinctly different category of activities that are integral to the overall operations of the System, in which geographical considerations are less significant.
output:
Clearly, some of the work that has always been carried out by different Districts in different ways remains appropriately local in approach and substance today. I see no reason to reduce the number of Reserve Banks or alter their geographic boundaries. Each Bank president still has an independent voice at the FOMC on the appropriate course of monetary policy and that should continue. Each president's views are shaped by the research of the Bank's economists, its regional experts, the input from the Bank's board of directors, and the president's interactions with business leaders in the District. Each Bank president contributes that perspective to the discussion in Washington with his or her colleagues, which generates a view of the economy as a whole at the national level and thus what direction policy should take. In addition to contributing to the development of monetary policy, each president engages with the business, financial, and nonprofit communities to understand local economic issues, and to position the Bank to serve as a convener of various interest groups to address local economic issues, such as labor force development, financial inclusion, and issues related to rural areas. These activities are enormously valuable to carrying out the Fed's mission, and they should continue. Each Reserve Bank also still conducts supervision of state member banks and bank holding companies, relying on the regional knowledge and expertise of supervisors based in the District and on regional industries and economic trends. Local presence will continue to be important. This local expertise is also important when the Reserve Bank serves as a lender to depository institutions.

Now let's turn to a very different class of activities that are important to the System's overall operations and for which geography does not matter.

Before I proceed, I want to be clear: I am not attempting to provide an impossible degree of precision, but a general ballpark. Based on this analysis, I believe the appropriate fed funds rate is in the mid-2 percent area, almost 2 percentage points lower than current policy. The Federal Reserve has been entrusted with the important goal of promoting price stability for the good of all American households and businesses, and I am committed to bringing inflation sustainably back to 2 percent. However, leaving policy restrictive by such a large degree brings significant risks for the Fed's employment mandate.

Policies Impacting Inflation Rents I'll start with inflation. The general approach I take is to assume all components of inflation that I'm not explicitly addressing will continue at their current run rates. I look forward to breaking down my expectations for other components of inflation in the future, but today I'll focus on what I consider to be first-order changes to the inflation forecast.

Housing represents nearly 16 percent of the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, and more than double that in the consumer price index (CPI). Housing affordability is highly influential for Americans' perception of, and experience of, the economy.

Because measured inflation incorporates rental inflation with a lag, it has remained elevated above market rents for several years, infamously "catching up." While an index of all-tenant rents took time to incorporate the spike in new rents in 2021 and 2022, that gap subsequently closed, indicating the catch-up is complete. Now, new rent indices show this inflation is well below all-tenant inflation, around 1 percent annualized.

output:
Thank you for inviting me to speak here today. The theme for Sibos this year, "the next frontiers of global finance" is a fitting one. We are indeed witnessing a new frontier of innovation in payments and the broader financial system. New technologies like distributed ledgers, tokenized assets, smart contracts, and artificial intelligence (AI) have the potential to make payments smarter, faster, and more efficient. I know many of you in the audience today represent firms that are using the latest cutting-edge advances to bring new global solutions to the market.

This surge in demand coincided with disruptions in supply chains related to food processing and grocery distribution. Beyond the direct impact of rising costs, grocery prices tend to serve as a significant factor influencing consumers' inflation expectations, given the frequency with which food purchases are made. 

Notably, another wave of inflation originated from categories other than food and energy, commonly referred to by economists as "core goods." In the years leading up to the pandemic, goods prices did not appear to be a major contributor to inflationary pressures. During the economic expansion from 2009 to 2020, core goods inflation experienced a decline of 0.5 percent annually, on average. However, once the pandemic took hold, consumer demand began to shift from services towards goods. Simultaneously, additional supply chain challenges arose, including factory closures and disruptions at ports. As consumption rapidly transitioned towards goods, their prices experienced a significant increase. Core goods inflation notably accelerated in the spring of 2021, ultimately reaching a peak of 7.6 percent on a twelve-month basis in February 2022. This development stands out as significant, particularly because, throughout much of the current century, deflation in goods prices has generally counterbalanced price increases in other categories, thereby helping to moderate overall inflation. In summary, these various waves of inflation highlight the intricate dynamics between consumer behavior, supply chain issues, and market expectations.

Ultimately, history illustrates that advancements in technology tend to enhance productivity and improve the overall standard of living. Additionally, there is often a preliminary discussion regarding the idea that technology will act as a substitute for human labor. This notion aligns with the basic premise of Marx's theory of capitalism, which posits that machines would ultimately replace human workers in production, resulting in significant unemployment levels that could incite social revolution, potentially leading to the dissolution of capitalism and the emergence of a socialist utopia. However, this theory appears to overlook a critical aspect: capital and labor are more accurately viewed as complements rather than substitutes. 

Notably, increased machinery permits firms to produce a greater output, which, in turn, necessitates a corresponding increase in labor. This relationship can be clearly observed by examining economic data. For instance, the capital stock of the United States, when measured at constant prices, has expanded to seven times its size since 1950. Furthermore, the unemployment rate recorded in September 1950 was 4.4 percent, while the rate stood at 4.3 percent in August 2025. This data highlights why many economists tend to adopt a techno-optimistic perspective; historical evidence has consistently demonstrated that the integration of new technologies tends to foster economic growth and enhance employment opportunities.

In addition, technological disruption represents a facet of a concept that has been the subject of economic inquiry since Joseph Schumpeter introduced the term "creative destruction" in 1942. This theme has gained increasing relevance in recent discussions. It is worth noting that just last week, two economists received a share of the Nobel Prize in Economics for their research on how productivity-enhancing disruptions can lead to elevated living standards.

Furthermore, while it is likely that artificial intelligence will generate both winners and losers, there remains a fundamental question concerning the distribution of gains from AI, as well as how these gains will be measured, particularly at a macroeconomic level. Firms are currently leveraging AI technologies to boost productivity, which facilitates an increase in output using the same level of inputs. This increase is reflected in key economic indicators such as gross domestic product (GDP) and its related measure, gross national income. In conclusion, the implications of AI on productivity and economic metrics are significant and warrant careful examination.
output:
Returning to my final point, history has shown us that technology improves productivity and our standard of living. We initially always talk about how it will be a substitute for labor. This was the basic premise behind Marx's theory of capitalism—machines would replace humans in production, which would raise unemployment so high that social revolution would occur, leading to the end of capitalism and the rise of a socialist utopia. Yet this theory makes the fundamental mistake of failing to see that capital and labor are complements, not substitutes. More machines mean a firm can produce more output, but that also requires more labor as well. This is obvious just looking at economic data. The U.S. capital stock, measured in constant prices, is seven times larger than it was in 1950. Yet the unemployment rate in September 1950 was 4.4 percent, and it is 4.3 percent as of August 2025. This is why economists are typically techno-optimists—history has repeatedly shown that adopting new technologies leads to economic growth and greater employment, not less. Technological disruption is one form of a concept that economists have studied since Joseph Schumpeter named it in 1942: creative destruction. This topic has never been more relevant, and I note that just last week a share of the Nobel Prize in Economics was awarded to two economists who explored how productivity-enhancing disruption raises living standards.

There will surely be losers and winners from AI, but aside from questions about how AI's gains will be distributed, there is the more fundamental matter of how they will be measured, even at a macro level. Firms are using AI to increase productivity, which allows for greater output based on the same level of inputs. This gain is counted in gross domestic product (GDP) and its corollary, gross national income.

Observations from the stress experienced in 2023 indicate that banks did utilize their liquidity. Furthermore, there may be technical adjustments that could alleviate concerns among banks regarding the usage of their liquidity buffers. It is also worth noting that an examination of the Federal Reserve's daylight overdraft policies may reveal potential improvements that could encourage greater usage. Additionally, investments in payment infrastructure, such as the proposed liquidity savings mechanism, may reduce the demand for reserves but could also introduce other costs. These factors should be carefully balanced against other priorities for system improvements, including the transition toward near-continuous availability for Fedwire® Funds and the expanded implementation of FedNow, both of which I would prioritize.

Ultimately, the Federal Reserve plays a crucial role in the financial system, yet its influence in financial markets is not solely determined by the size of its balance sheet. Some proposals aimed at reducing the balance sheet may inadvertently increase the Fed's influence in other ways, and all such proposals are likely to involve significant trade-offs. Notably, initiatives such as decreasing liquidity requirements could compromise financial stability. Allowing banks to treat certain assets pledged at the discount window as equivalent to Treasury securities or reserves, as some have suggested, may diminish self-insurance and weaken the resilience of the banking system. In any discussion regarding alterations in the Federal Reserve's strategy for managing its balance sheet, it is essential to revisit fundamental questions about the problems we are attempting to address. In summary, the objective of reducing the Fed's balance sheet appears misguided, and compromising the resilience of the banking system as a means to that end is similarly inappropriate.

We should take steps to make sure banks understand that required liquidity is usable. My experience during the stress of 2023 was that banks in fact did use their liquidity, and there may be technical adjustments that would ease banks' fears about using their liquidity buffers. It is also worth taking a look at the Fed's daylight overdraft policies to see if they can be improved, encouraging usage. In addition, investments in our payment infrastructure—such as through a liquidity savings mechanism that some have suggested—might reduce reserve demand but might have other downside costs and should be weighed against other priorities for system improvement, including movement to a near continuous availability for Fedwire® Funds and expanded use of FedNow, both of which I'd prioritize.

Conclusion The Federal Reserve has an important role in the financial system, but its footprint in financial markets is not well defined by the size of its balance sheet. Some proposals to shrink the balance sheet increase the Fed's footprint in other ways, and all of them would entail significant tradeoffs. Some of the most prominent ideas, such as reducing liquidity requirements, would undermine financial stability. Letting banks treat some amount of assets because these assets are pledged at the discount window—as though they are the same as Treasury securities or reserves—as some have proposed, would, as I said, just reduce self-insurance and decrease the resilience of the banking system. In any consideration of a change in the Federal Reserve's approach to managing its balance sheet, we ought to go back to basics and ask what problem we are trying to solve. In sum, shrinking the Fed's balance sheet is the wrong goal, and reducing the resilience of the banking system is the wrong means.

Furthermore, over the past ten years, a notable decline has been experienced in the bank share of corporate lending, which decreased from 48 percent to 29 percent between 2015 and 2025. Moreover, the private credit market appears to be a significant driver of this shift, and it has grown substantially, currently accounting for approximately $1.4 trillion, a size comparable to that of the leveraged loan market and the high-yield bond market. Ultimately, the private credit market tends to be a relatively small fraction of overall corporate borrowing in the United States, making up only about 10 percent.

In essence, the private credit market has reached a significant level of growth, and its impact on corporate lending is becoming increasingly apparent. Notably, the growth of the private credit market can be attributed to the unintended consequences of post-2008 financial crisis reforms, which strengthened bank capital and liquidity, thereby promoting the safety and soundness of banks and U.S. financial stability. However, it is worth noting that these reforms may have resulted in some requirements becoming excessive relative to underlying risk, leading banks to reach a decision to pare back on some corporate lending activities or to increase the cost of credit to borrowers. Furthermore, the effects of the current framework can be observed in the incentive structure that it creates, which may encourage banks to finance intermediaries rather than directly serve end-borrowers.

Additionally, the current capital rules tend to create a perverse incentive, whereby banks receive a more favorable treatment for lending to private credit funds than for lending directly to creditworthy corporations. It is worth noting that this treatment appears to encourage banks to prioritize financing intermediaries over directly serving end-borrowers, which can have significant implications for the corporate lending landscape. Ultimately, a thorough examination of the current framework and its effects on corporate lending is necessary to understand the underlying dynamics at play, and it can be concluded that the recent growth of nondepository financial institution corporate lending is a complex phenomenon that is influenced by a variety of factors, including regulatory reforms and market developments.
output:
The Recent Growth of Nondepository Financial Institution Corporate Lending Over the past ten years, we have seen a shift in how credit reaches businesses in the real economy. Since 2015, the bank share of corporate lending decreased from 48 percent to 29 percent in 2025. The private credit market is a significant driver of this shift. In the United States, the private credit market has grown significantly and currently accounts for about $1.4 trillion, similar in size to both the leveraged loan market and the high-yield bond market. But despite its recent rapid growth, private credit is still a small fraction of overall corporate borrowing in the U.S.—making up only about 10 percent.

There is no mystery about what drove the shift in corporate lending away from banks. While post-2008 financial crisis reforms strengthened bank capital and liquidity—which were necessary to promote the safety and soundness of banks and U.S. financial stability—they did so with unintended consequences. Attempts to address legitimate gaps resulted in some requirements becoming excessive relative to underlying risk, forcing banks to pare back on some corporate lending activities or to raise the cost of credit to borrowers.

The effects of the current framework become clear when we examine the incentive structure that it creates. Current capital rules create a perverse incentive—ironically, banks receive a more favorable treatment for lending to private credit funds than for lending directly to creditworthy corporations. This treatment encourages banks to finance intermediaries rather than directly serve end-borrowers.
