Additionally, the primary challenge in analyzing the economic effects of the tariff increases is the considerable uncertainty that remains regarding their magnitude and permanence. Furthermore, it is worth noting that this uncertainty has led to the formulation of various scenarios for tariff policy, which can often inform the economic response. Notably, a decision has been reached to focus on two possible scenarios for tariff policy, which may yield distinct outcomes for the economy and monetary policy. In essence, one possibility is that the tariffs will experience a prolonged duration and remain at a relatively high level, approaching the current average of 25 percent or more, as part of a broader effort by the Administration to engineer a significant shift in the U.S. economy toward increased domestic production and reduced trade deficits. Moreover, this scenario tends to be characterized by a commitment to maintaining high tariffs as a means of achieving these objectives. 

Ultimately, the second scenario appears to involve a concerted effort to negotiate reductions in foreign barriers faced by U.S. exporters, which may result in the removal of most of the announced import tariffs, thereby reducing the average tariff rate to approximately 10 percent. It is worth noting that this latter scenario had previously been considered the base case, although this assessment was revised after March 1. Additionally, a range of possibilities can often be identified that may combine these objectives for tariff policy, although the two approaches outlined above tend to yield significantly different outcomes for the economy and monetary policy. In essence, the discussion of these two scenarios is intended to provide a framework for understanding the potential implications of different tariff policy approaches. Furthermore, it is worth noting that the objectives for the tariff increases are not being evaluated, as the role of a central banker involves taking fiscal and other policy decisions made by others as a given when formulating monetary policy, which tends to involve a focus on the economic effects of these decisions rather than their underlying motivations. Ultimately, the analysis of the economic effects of the tariff increases is facilitated by the consideration of these two scenarios, which can often provide a useful framework for understanding the potential implications of different policy approaches.
output:
The primary challenge in analyzing the economic effects of the tariff increases is the considerable uncertainty that remains about their size and permanence. So I have decided to focus on two scenarios for tariff policy when thinking about the economic response. One possibility is that they will remain very high and be long-lasting, near the current average of 25 percent or more, as part of a committed effort by the Administration to engineer a fundamental shift in the U.S. economy toward producing more goods domestically and reducing trade deficits. The second scenario is that the suspensions are the beginning of a concerted effort to negotiate reductions in foreign barriers faced by U.S. exporters that will result in the removal of most of the announced import tariffs, which would reduce the average tariff rate to around 10 percent. This latter scenario had been my base case up until March 1. While there is a range of possibilities that could combine these objectives for tariff policy, these two approaches would yield significantly different outcomes for the economy and monetary policy, so I would like to discuss them today as two separate scenarios.

In doing so, I am not here to judge the objectives for the tariff increases. I am a central banker, and, as I said earlier, that means I take fiscal and other policy decisions made by others as a given when setting monetary policy.

Additionally, in order to prevent this change from causing a reduction in the overall level of capital within the system, supervisory capital buffers could instead be established entirely through regulatory means. Furthermore, for the majority of non-globally systemically important banks that are subject to the supervisory capital buffer requirement, the existing buffer floor of 2.5 percent appears to remain an appropriate level. It is worth noting that for globally systemically important banks with substantial trading operations, past stress tests have routinely indicated that supervisory capital buffers should likely be set at a level higher than the 2.5 percent floor, and any regulatory capital measure designed to replace the current framework would need to take this gap into account. While additional analytical work is required, the shortfall that is generated by decoupling the stress tests from the supervisory capital buffer may be largely addressed through a regulatory capital requirement that is linked to the risks present in the trading book, with perhaps some other adjustments as necessary to maintain appropriate capital levels. Ultimately, if over time the results of stress testing indicate that this replacement regulatory capital measure routinely exceeds or falls short of the capital levels that are required to provide adequate resilience to stress conditions, the Board could undertake a revision of the regulatory measure through a notice-and-comment process, informed by data that is gathered during the stress testing process.

In essence, this proposed approach of decoupling the stress tests from regulatory capital and increasing regulatory capital in order to make up for the shortfall in the supervisory capital buffer appears to be the most effective way to retain the value of stress testing as a supervisory exercise while maintaining appropriate levels of capital within the system. However, the replacement of the current framework of individualized supervisory capital buffers, which are informed by firm-specific stress test results, with broadly applicable and formulaic regulatory capital requirements would result in a diminution of the risk sensitivity that is reflected in supervisory capital buffer requirements. Notably, this means that capital levels for firms that are subject to the stress tests would be relatively less tailored than they currently are and would be less reflective of the unique business models, exposures, and risk profiles of a particular firm.

So that this change does not reduce overall capital in the system, SCBs could instead be set entirely by regulation. For most non-G-SIBs subject to the SCB requirement, the current 2.5 percent buffer floor likely remains an appropriate level. For G-SIBs with a lot of trading, past stress tests have routinely indicated that SCBs should likely be set higher than the 2.5 percent floor, and any regulatory capital measure designed to replace the current SCB framework would need to account for this gap. While further analytical work is required, the shortfall generated by decoupling the stress tests from the SCB may be largely addressed by a regulatory capital requirement linked to the risks in the trading book, with perhaps some other adjustments as required to maintain appropriate capital levels. If, over time, stress testing results indicate that this replacement regulatory capital measure routinely exceeds or falls short of the capital levels required to provide adequate resilience to stress conditions, the Board could revise the regulatory measure through a notice-and-comment process, informed by data gathered in the stress testing process.

This proposed approach of decoupling the stress tests from regulatory capital and increasing regulatory capital to make up the shortfall in the SCB appears to me to be the best way to retain the value of stress testing as a supervisory exercise while maintaining appropriate levels of capital in the system. However, replacing the current framework of individualized SCBs—informed by firm-specific stress test results—with broadly applicable, formulaic regulatory capital requirements would result in a diminution of the risk sensitivity reflected in SCB requirements. That is, capital levels for firms that are subject to the stress tests would be relatively less tailored than they currently are and less reflective of the unique business models, exposures, and risk profiles of a particular firm.

output: Given this benign view of inflation, I believe the ultimate disposition of the labor market will be the more salient factor affecting monetary policy. I wish to express my appreciation for the invitation to participate in this gathering in Phoenix at the Conference for Community Bankers organized by the American Bankers Association. Additionally, it is worth noting that over the course of the past seven years, this conference has provided an excellent forum in which I and other bankers have had the opportunity to meet and interact with a diverse range of state and federal regulators, policymakers, service providers, and other relevant stakeholders. Moreover, I would like to take this opportunity today to share a brief update regarding my views on monetary policy and the economy before I turn my attention to matters of bank regulation, and to describe how I believe regulators should approach the important work of maintaining the regulatory framework.

Furthermore, with respect to the economic outlook and monetary policy, it is worth noting that toward the end of last year the Federal Open Market Committee began the process of moving the target range for the federal funds rate toward a more neutral setting in order to reflect the progress that has been made since 2023 in lowering inflation and cooling the labor market. Additionally, at our September meeting, the Committee voted to lower the target range for the first time since we began tightening monetary policy to combat inflation, reducing it by 50 basis points to a range of 4-3/4 to 5 percent.

Moreover, you may recall that I dissented from that decision, which represented the first instance in nearly 20 years in which a Fed Governor dissented from a rate decision of the Committee. In essence, I preferred a smaller initial reduction as a means of beginning the policy recalibration phase. Furthermore, I explained my reasoning in a statement published after the meeting, noting that the strong economy and a healthy labor market did not appear to warrant a larger reduction. Additionally, moving the policy rate downward too quickly could unnecessarily risk stoking demand, potentially reigniting inflationary pressures, and could be interpreted as a premature declaration of victory with respect to our price-stability mandate. Ultimately, these considerations continue to shape my perspective on the appropriate path of monetary policy.
output:
Thank you for the invitation to join you here in Phoenix at the ABA's Conference for Community Bankers. For the past seven years, this conference provided an excellent forum for me and bankers to meet and interact with a range of state and federal regulators, policymakers, service providers, and other stakeholders. Today I would like to share a brief update on my views on monetary policy and the economy, before I turn to bank regulatory issues, and describe how I think that regulators should approach the important work of "maintenance" of the regulatory framework.

Economic Outlook and Monetary Policy Toward the end of last year, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) began the process of moving the target range for the federal funds rate to a more neutral setting to reflect the progress made since 2023 on lowering inflation and cooling the labor market. At our September meeting, the FOMC voted to lower the target range, for the first time since we began tightening monetary policy to combat inflation, by 50 basis points to 4-3/4 to 5 percent.

You may remember that I dissented from that decision, the first time a Fed Governor dissented from an FOMC rate decision in nearly 20 years. I preferred a smaller initial cut to begin the policy recalibration phase. I explained my reasoning in a statement published after the meeting noting that the strong economy and a healthy labor market did not warrant a larger cut. In addition, moving the policy rate down too quickly could unnecessarily risk stoking demand, potentially reigniting inflationary pressures, and could be interpreted as a premature "declaration of victory" on our price-stability mandate.

output:
The softening of labor market activity comes as overall economic activity has moderated this year. In the first half of 2025, U.S. GDP grew at about a 1.5 percent annual rate, which reflects a marked cooling from last year's 2.5 percent growth rate. The slowdown in economic activity in the first half of this year was primarily driven by weaker consumer spending. That said, U.S. retail spending picked up over the summer. Overall, I expect the U.S. economy to maintain the first half's rate of growth through the remainder of the year.

In terms of the labor market, there has been notable slowing in both labor supply and labor demand. Net immigration into the U.S., an important contributor to workforce growth, has dropped sharply. At the same time, total employment growth has slowed. Over the past three months, American employers have added just 29,000 jobs to payrolls a month on average. The recent pace of employment growth has been the slowest since the U.S. economy recovered from the COVID-19 pandemic recession, which is largely explained by the slower growth in the labor force. Over time, various criticisms regarding the approach taken by the Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR) have emerged. It is worth noting that one significant concern was the perception that CCAR operated independently from the processes employed to establish a bank's fundamental, risk-based capital requirements. Furthermore, large banks have often expressed dissatisfaction with CCAR due to its perceived lack of transparency and predictability, which may have compelled them to commit to lower capital distributions and maintain elevated levels of capital.

In 2020, the Federal Reserve Board took steps to address these concerns raised by the banks by introducing the stress capital buffer (SCB). To respond to the critique that CCAR functioned as an additive measure and was not sufficiently integrated into capital planning, the SCB merged the basic capital requirement for banks with an additional requirement. This additional component was intended to correspond to a bank's anticipated decline in capital ratio during the stress test, along with a year’s worth of planned dividends, thereby linking the various elements of the capital framework. Additionally, to mitigate the criticism regarding the transparency and predictability of CCAR, the SCB established a requirement for each participating bank that mirrored its losses during the stress test while allowing for flexibility in adjusting dividends in real time.

Another notable criticism from banks was that the qualitative assessment used by CCAR was subjective. In response to this feedback, the SCB eliminated the qualitative aspect and reformulated the evaluation of capital planning practices as a more traditional supervisory examination.

By integrating stress testing more directly into capital regulation, the SCB appears to have shifted the focus of stress testing from supervision to the regulatory domain, which is a significant development. While this modification was designed to enhance consistency and predictability, it may have inadvertently diminished some value of the exercise. This reduction in value stems from the limited range of factors and circumstances that the Board appears to consider when assessing the capital adequacy of individual firms. Consequently, the Board's capacity to adjust determinations regarding capital adequacy based on the unique characteristics of different firms, encompassing various business models and risk profiles, may have been restricted. In summary, the changes introduced by the SCB have sought to address banks' concerns while also presenting new challenges in capital regulation.

The Great Depression significantly disrupted the prevailing economic understanding and initiated extensive research aimed at comprehending the causes of economic fluctuations and the appropriate policy responses. It is noteworthy that financial factors gained prominence in economic theory for the first time as a result of this crisis. In direct reaction to the deficiencies in economic theory exposed by the Depression, John Maynard Keynes introduced the concept of a "liquidity trap," which describes a situation where fear elevates the demand for money to such an extent that conventional corrective strategies become ineffective. Furthermore, Friedrich Hayek and the Austrian school of economics highlighted the impact of unsustainable credit booms, asserting that these booms generate "malinvestment" leading to significant mismatches that necessitate intervention. Despite the initial focus on financial panics, credit booms, and extreme economic dynamics, macroeconomic research developed in a manner that downplayed the significance of the financial system. This evolution likely stemmed from technical limitations and a broader need to establish policy frameworks relevant to the post-World War II economy, where the Great Depression's relevance appeared diminished. 

Modeling financial crises necessitates grappling with complex nonlinear dynamics, feedback loops, and sudden changes, such as defaults and bank runs. These elements proved to be analytically challenging and computationally unmanageable given the limitations of contemporary tools. Consequently, the macroeconomic framework influenced by Keynes's concepts generally operated under the assumption of stable and frictionless financial markets. Ultimately, the IS-LM, or Investment-Saving Liquidity Preference-Money Supply framework, emerged as the primary analytical instrument used to understand the interactions between the goods market and the money market, which collectively determine aggregate output and interest rates within the economy.

The supply side of the economy encompasses the structure of production processes and markets. Furthermore, supply shocks may affect the productive capacity of the economy, which is often referred to as potential output. This productive capacity captures the available supply of labor and capital, in addition to the productivity of those inputs. It is worth noting that potential output represents the hypothetical level of production that the economy can sustain over the long run while maintaining price stability and achieving maximum employment.

Notably, both demand and supply shocks can vary in their duration. They may be temporary, which causes short-term fluctuations, or they may be persistent, resulting in more enduring changes within the economy. The nature and duration of these shocks can significantly influence the approach to monetary policymaking, a topic that warrants further discussion.

A key concept for the analysis of an economic shock is the output gap, which serves as a valuable tool for monetary policymakers in assessing economic conditions as it summarizes the strength of demand in comparison to supply. The output gap represents the relationship between the actual output of the economy, typically measured by gross domestic product, and an estimate of its potential output. When gross domestic product exceeds potential output, the output gap is positive and the economy is characterized by excess demand. In this scenario, employment levels may be above their maximum sustainable level, resulting in upward pressure on inflation. Conversely, when gross domestic product falls below potential output, the output gap is negative and the economy experiences excess supply. During such periods of negative output gaps, employment levels typically fall below their maximum sustainable point, leading to downward pressure on inflation. This comprehensive examination of the output gap highlights its significance in understanding the relationships between demand, supply, and inflationary pressures within the economy.

One notable shift in the current financial landscape is that the supplementary leverage ratio has increasingly become the binding capital constraint for the largest banks in the United States. Within the United States banking system, there are generally two basic types of capital requirements that tend to operate in tandem. The first category consists of risk-based requirements, which impose a capital charge that is based on the underlying risk of a particular activity. The second category consists of leverage-based requirements, which do not differentiate based on the risk characteristics of the underlying assets. Furthermore, while leverage-based capital requirements are generally intended to function as a backstop to risk-based requirements, changes in the financial system and the broader economy can often alter this relationship between the two sets of requirements. Ultimately, this shift in the nature of leverage-based capital requirements, from a backstop to a binding constraint, was not driven by a deliberate policymaking process. Instead, it appears to have been driven by the maintenance of a high level of reserves in the banking system, as well as by the introduction of liquidity requirements that compelled banks to replace loans with high-quality liquid assets.

Turning to monetary policy and the economic outlook, I would like to provide a brief update on my outlook for the economy and for monetary policy before I turn to the main theme of my remarks. At the meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee last week, the Committee voted to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent. In addition, the Committee voted to continue to reduce the Federal Reserve's securities holdings. I supported this decision because the data shows a solid labor market, and I would like to see further confirmation that inflation is close to our 2 percent target on a sustained basis. If inflation remains near its current level, or if it continues to move closer to our target, or if the data show signs of weakening in labor market conditions, it would be appropriate to consider lowering the policy rate and moving it closer to a neutral setting.

One shift in particular is that of the supplementary leverage ratio increasingly becoming the binding capital constraint for the largest banks in the United States. The U.S. banking system includes two basic types of capital requirements: risk-based requirements that impose a capital "charge" based on the underlying risk of a particular activity, and leverage-based requirements that do not differentiate based on the risk characteristics of underlying assets. And while leverage-based capital requirements are generally intended to operate as a backstop to risk-based requirements, changes in the financial system and the broader economy can alter this relationship between capital requirements. This shift in the nature of leverage-based capital requirements, from backstop to binding constraint, was not driven by a deliberate policymaking process, but rather by the maintenance of a high level of reserves in the banking system, as well as the introduction of liquidity requirements that compelled banks to replace loans with high-quality liquid assets.

Monetary Policy and Economic Outlook Before turning to the main theme of my remarks, I would like to give a brief update on my outlook for the economy and monetary policy.

At the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting last week, the Committee voted to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 4-1/4 to 4‑1/2 percent and to continue to reduce the Federal Reserve's securities holdings. I supported this decision because the data shows a solid labor market and I would like to see further confirmation that inflation is close to our 2 percent target on a sustained basis.

If inflation remains near its current level or continues to move closer to our target, or if the data show signs of weakening in labor market conditions, it would be appropriate to consider lowering the policy rate, moving it closer to a neutral setting.

output: Another recent challenge for OECD economies is the widespread weakness in manufacturing. input: Thank you for the invitation to speak with you today, and before I turn to my main topic, I would like to offer my current views on the economy and on monetary policy. Last week, we received the latest report on employment, and it provided further evidence that, while the labor market experienced a slowing through last summer, it now appears to be stabilizing. Notably, this stabilization is occurring at an unemployment rate that is broadly consistent with what many estimates suggest is its long-run level, which is the level associated with an economy that is in balance. That said, it is worth noting that job creation has been near zero over the course of the past year, and labor force growth has likewise been near zero. In essence, with very low levels of job creation and also a low rate of firing, there appears to be a tentative balance between labor supply and labor demand. Furthermore, this is a delicate balance, and that means the labor market may be especially vulnerable to negative shocks. Turning to the other component of our mandate, inflation as measured by personal consumption expenditures remains elevated at 3 percent, which is about where it stood a year ago. Additionally, disinflation, which began in mid-2022, experienced a slowing last year, as goods price inflation picked up, in large part because of tariffs. It is worth noting that this pattern appeared to continue in the inflation data that were released last week. Looking ahead, it is reasonable to forecast that the effects of tariffs on inflation will begin to abate later this year, but there are many reasons to be concerned that inflation will remain elevated. In my assessment, the risk of persistent inflation above our 2 percent target appears to be significant, which means we need to remain vigilant. Ultimately, the labor market appears to be in a tentative and delicate balance while inflation remains elevated, so continued vigilance in our policy approach seems warranted.
output:
Thank you for the invitation to speak to you today. Before I get into my main topic, I wanted to share my current views on the economy and monetary policy.

Last week, we received the latest report on employment, and it provided further evidence that while the labor market slowed through last summer, it is now stabilizing. This stabilization is occurring with an unemployment rate that is broadly consistent with what many estimate is its long-run level, when the economy is in balance. That said, job creation has been near zero over the course of last year, as has labor force growth. With very low levels of job creation and also a low firing rate, there seems to be a tentative balance in labor supply and demand. But it is a delicate balance, and that means that the labor market could be especially vulnerable to negative shocks.

Turning to the other component of our mandate, inflation based on personal consumption expenditures remains elevated at 3 percent, about where it was a year ago. Disinflation, which started in mid-2022, slowed last year, as goods price inflation picked up, in large part due to tariffs. That pattern appeared to continue in the inflation data released last week. Looking ahead, it is reasonable to forecast that tariff effects on inflation will begin to abate later this year, but there are many reasons to be concerned that inflation will remain elevated. I see the risk of persistent inflation above our 2 percent target as significant, which means we need to remain vigilant.

Emerging types of "agentic" AI have the ability to perform complex, multistep tasks, such as guiding a customer through a transaction and subsequently placing an automated order. This characterization encompasses widespread adoption, complementary advancements in various downstream applications, and consistent improvements in the foundational technology. Historical instances of general purpose technologies have led to significant productivity gains. Ultimately, this context raises the pertinent question regarding the potential impact of AI on productivity and the labor market.

Speech and facial recognition are already ubiquitous. These more long-standing forms of AI are continuing to improve, driving progress in domains ranging from finance to medical diagnosis, and becoming so deeply embedded in our daily lives that we scarcely notice them anymore.

Unlike traditional machine learning techniques, which often focus on relatively simple prediction and classification tasks, the large language models that have emerged in recent years can generate new content—anything from news articles to computer code to images and video to customer service dialogue. Growing evidence indicates that AI will be a "general purpose technology"—such as railroads, electricity, or computers—which is characterized by widespread adoption, complementary progress in many downstream applications, and ongoing improvement in the core technology. Past general purpose technologies have dramatically improved productivity. So, against this background, the natural question is, what about AI?

input: The research literature highlights several strategies that may prevent adverse economic effects. Specifically, the implementation of bank capital and liquidity requirements appears to reduce both the likelihood and intensity of financial crises. Additionally, economies that exhibit higher bank capital ratios prior to a crisis tend to experience more rapid recoveries following such events, which is often due to a more robust recovery in credit growth. Furthermore, increases in bank capital ratios can reduce the probability of experiencing extreme negative outcomes related to gross domestic product. It is worth noting that evidence suggests U.S. states that engaged in less deregulation during the 1980s may have experienced smaller credit expansions during economic growth, while also facing reduced declines in economic activity and employment during subsequent recessions. This suggests that the immediate benefits associated with credit booms resulting from deregulation may be overshadowed by longer-term losses in output, employment, and income. Ultimately, these findings underscore the importance of maintaining stringent financial regulations to mitigate potential economic downturns.
output: How These Ill Effects Can Be Prevented The research literature also shows how these bad effects can be prevented: bank capital and liquidity requirements reduce the probability and severity of financial crises. Increases in bank capital ratios reduce the likelihood of the worst GDP outcomes. There is also evidence that U.S. states that deregulated less in the 1980s experienced smaller credit booms during the expansion but smaller declines in activity and employment in the subsequent recession. In other words, the short-term "sugar high" of a credit boom from deregulation is outweighed by longer-term loss of output, employment, and income.

output:

Estimates based on the consumer price index and other data released last week indicate that total PCE prices rose 2.3 percent over the 12 months ending in October. Core PCE prices—which exclude the volatile food and energy categories—increased 2.8 percent, down from a peak of 5.6 percent in February 2022.

Despite this significant progress on disinflation, the elevated core figure suggests that we have further to go before credibly achieving our inflation target of 2 percent. Although most price indicators suggest that progress is ongoing, I anticipate bumps along the road. For instance, when measured on a monthly basis, estimated core PCE inflation stepped up in September and October after four months of lower readings. Even so, I still see headline and core inflation falling to 2.2 percent next year and to lower levels after that. Moreover, disinflation has been widespread across a broad range of goods and services. Taken together, recent data support my view that the disinflationary process is continuing.

The first is that today's labor market isn't nearly as tight. When the FOMC started raising rates in 2022, there were two job vacancies for every unemployed person, and now the ratio is nearly one to one. While the main effect of higher rates then was to reduce vacancies—rather than employment—there is a much greater risk now that tighter monetary policy could drive up unemployment and even risk a recession. Another sign that the labor market isn't as tight is provided by data on nominal wage growth. Average hourly earnings grew at an annual rate of between 5 percent and 6 percent in 2022 but are only growing around 3.5 percent this year, a pace that is consistent with 2 percent inflation, given solid trend labor productivity growth.

However, I would be remiss if I did not highlight an additional challenge facing community banks within the current regulatory landscape, namely the deregulation of large banks.

It is important to recognize that community banks were not the entities that contributed to the 2008 financial crisis; rather, it was the largest and most complex financial firms whose excessive risk-taking almost led to systemic collapse. In the aftermath of that crisis, substantial reforms, including increased capital requirements, stricter liquidity mandates, and thorough stress testing, have been implemented to help protect our economy. Nonetheless, recent proposals aimed at rolling back capital standards for the largest banks, altering the supervisory framework for large financial institutions, and reducing the rigor of stress testing for these entities pose a risk of undermining those essential protections. These changes are unlikely to enhance the safety of the financial system; instead, they may leave community banks vulnerable to the negative consequences should the largest institutions experience difficulties. Given that we cannot afford to repeat past mistakes, I have expressed my opposition to any weakening of standards for large banks, and I intend to maintain this position moving forward. In summary, the ongoing challenges faced by community banks in the context of regulatory changes warrant careful attention and proactive advocacy.

The objective of this address is to articulate the rationale behind my assertion that the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) should implement a reduction in the policy rate by 25 basis points during our upcoming meeting. Furthermore, I have previously advised my junior research colleagues that presentations should not resemble murder mysteries; rather, it is more effective to disclose the main point to the audience at the outset. Therefore, I will adhere to my own guidance and clearly outline the reasons supporting the proposed policy rate reduction in two weeks.

Additionally, it is important to note that tariffs represent one-time increases in the price level and do not typically generate inflation beyond a fleeting spike. Standard practices in central banking dictate a tendency to "look through" such price-level impacts, particularly in circumstances where inflation expectations remain stable, which they currently do.

Furthermore, a significant array of data suggests that the monetary policy stance should align closely with neutrality, rather than adopting a restrictive position. It appears that real gross domestic product (GDP) growth was approximately 1 percent during the first half of this year and is projected to remain subdued throughout the remainder of 2025, a figure that is notably lower than the median estimates of longer-run GDP growth provided by FOMC participants. Concurrently, the unemployment rate stands at 4.1 percent, which is in proximity to the Committee's longer-run estimate. Additionally, headline inflation is slightly above our target at just over 2 percent when excluding the temporary effects of tariffs, which I believe will not persist. Collectively, this data suggests that the appropriate policy rate should be neutral, which is estimated by the median of FOMC participants to be around 3 percent, rather than the current level, which is 1.25 to 1.50 percentage points above that neutral rate. In summary, this analysis supports the conclusion that a policy rate reduction is warranted.

My purpose this evening is to explain why I believe that the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) should reduce our policy rate by 25 basis points at our next meeting. I used to tell my junior research colleagues that presentations are not murder mysteries—just tell the audience up front "who did it" by telling them the main point. So let me follow my own advice and state up front the reasons I believe we should cut the policy rate at our meeting in two weeks.

First, tariffs are one-off increases in the price level and do not cause inflation beyond a temporary surge. Standard central banking practice is to "look through" such price-level effects as long as inflation expectations are anchored, which they are.

Second, a host of data argues that monetary policy should be close to neutral, not restrictive. Real gross domestic product (GDP) growth was likely around 1 percent in the first half of this year and is expected to remain soft for the rest of 2025, much lower than the median of FOMC participants' estimates of longer-run GDP growth. Meanwhile, the unemployment rate is 4.1 percent, near the Committee's longer-run estimate, and headline inflation is close to our target at just slightly above 2 percent if we put aside tariff effects that I believe will be temporary. Taken together, the data imply the policy rate should be around neutral, which the median of FOMC participants estimates is 3 percent, and not where we are—1.25 to 1.50 percentage points above 3 percent.

input: Additionally, it is worth noting that economic research has played a role in shaping monetary policy at the Federal Reserve since its earliest days, though the form and application of that research have experienced considerable variation over time. Furthermore, a full treatment of this topic would require more time than is available today, so the discussion here will instead touch on a few historical highlights. During the early decades of the Federal Reserve System, research activities at the Fed tended to be largely confined to the collection of statistics, and only a portion of these was published by the Fed or by other government agencies. Additionally, at the Reserve Banks, the focus was often placed on the measurement and reporting of regional economies or sectors. Notably, decisions regarding monetary policy were reached through the use of policy frameworks that were often not subjected to the rigorous and scientific testing associated with economic research today. For instance, during the 1920s, the Federal Reserve adhered to the real bills doctrine, which called for the provision of liquidity to businesses when it was demanded during expansions and for the contraction of credit when demand for it experienced a decline during periods of slowing growth. Furthermore, this approach can often be exactly the opposite of what monetary policy should do, whether the goal is the control of inflation in an overheating economy or the support of economic activity during a slowdown. In essence, the history of research at the Federal Reserve illustrates a gradual evolution from limited statistical collection toward the more rigorous analytical foundations that tend to inform monetary policy decisions today.
output: History of Research at the Federal Reserve Economic research has shaped monetary policy at the Federal Reserve from its very beginnings, but the form and use of that research has varied considerably over time. I do not have the time today to give this topic the justice it deserves. But I will touch on a few historical highlights. During the early decades of the Federal Reserve System, "research" at the Fed was largely limited to the collection of statistics, only some of which were published by the Fed and other government agencies. At the Reserve Banks, the focus was often on measuring and reporting on regional economies or sectors. Monetary policy decisions were made using policy frameworks that were often not tested in the rigorous and scientific ways associated with economic research today. For example, in the 1920s, the Federal Reserve adhered to the "real bills" doctrine that called for providing liquidity to businesses when it was demanded during expansions and contracting credit when demand for it fell during times of slowing growth. This, of course, is often exactly the opposite of what monetary policy should do to either control inflation in an overheating economy or support economic activity in a slowdown.

The authors suggest that one potential explanation for the resilience of real activity amidst rising interest rates may be the robust financial positions of households and businesses at the onset of the tightening cycle. It is worth noting that during the pandemic, households accumulated significant excess savings, a phenomenon attributed to increased fiscal stimulus as well as decreased consumption resulting from social distancing measures and supply chain disruptions. Specifically, data from the Financial Accounts of the U.S. reveal that household bank deposits experienced an increase of nearly $4 trillion in the two-year period from the end of 2019 to the end of 2021.

Furthermore, many households and nonfinancial businesses took advantage of the opportunity to refinance their mortgages and corporate bonds at notably low interest rates during the pandemic. Although the rise in interest rates likely constrained further consumption expenditures and investment activities, the impact on the net cash flows of households and nonfinancial businesses appears to have been mitigated, as the average interest rates on outstanding household mortgages and business debt remained comparatively low.

Additionally, the historically low borrowing costs during the pandemic led to exceptionally high levels of mortgage originations and refinancing activities. Consequently, by 2022, the proportion of outstanding mortgages with interest rates below 4 percent rose to nearly 70 percent, remaining significantly above the levels observed prior to the pandemic. Similarly, nonfinancial businesses issued an unprecedented volume of corporate bonds and extended the maturities of their existing debt to avoid the need for new debt issuance during the subsequent rate hiking cycle. Between 2020 and 2021, the proportion of triple-B corporate bonds maturing within three years decreased to its lowest level in nearly 20 years. Ultimately, these factors collectively illustrate the financial resilience experienced by households and businesses during this period of economic adjustment.

As the authors argue, another reason why real activity was more resilient in the face of higher interest rates may have been the healthy balance sheets of households and businesses at the start of the tightening cycle. Households had accumulated excess savings during the pandemic, reflecting both increased fiscal stimulus and reduced consumption due to social distancing and supply bottlenecks. In fact, data from the Financial Accounts of the U.S. indicate that in the two years between the end of 2019 and the end of 2021, household bank deposits rose by nearly $4 trillion.

In addition, many households and nonfinancial businesses were able to refinance their mortgages and corporate bonds at very low rates during the pandemic. Although higher interest rates likely held back additional consumption expenditures and investment spending, they had less of an effect on households' and nonfinancial businesses' net cash flows as the average interest rates on household mortgages and business debt remained low.

With historically low borrowing costs during the pandemic era, mortgage originations and refinancing activity reached very high levels. As a result, the share of outstanding mortgages with an interest rate below 4 percent increased to nearly 70 percent by 2022 and it remains well above pre-pandemic levels today. Similarly, nonfinancial businesses issued record amounts of corporate bonds and extended the maturity of their debt to avoid new debt issuance earlier in the subsequent rate hiking cycle. Between 2020 and 2021, the fraction of triple-B corporate bonds maturing within three years fell to its lowest levels in nearly 20 years.

The motivation for continuing to cut the policy rate at the next FOMC meeting begins with an assessment of how restrictive the current setting appears to be. After the Committee cut by 75 basis points, the evidence tends to suggest that policy remains significantly restrictive. Furthermore, an additional cut would simply mean that policymakers are not pressing on the brake pedal quite as hard. Although monthly core inflation has flattened out in recent months, there is no indication that the pace of price increases for key service categories such as housing and nonmarket services should remain at their current levels or increase.

Additionally, another factor that supports a further rate cut is that the labor market appears to finally be in balance, and policymakers should aim to keep it that way. Conversely, based on what is known today, one could argue that there is a case for skipping a rate cut at the next meeting. Notably, monthly readings on inflation have moved up noticeably in recent months, and it is unclear whether this uptick in inflation will persist or reverse, as was seen a year ago. Due to strikes and hurricanes, recent labor market data are giving a cloudy view of the true state of the labor market that will not be clearer for a couple of months.

As a result, one could advocate for not changing the policy rate at the upcoming meeting and for adjusting the policy stance in a measured way going forward. In fact, if policymakers' estimates of the target range at the end of next year are close to correct, then the Committee will most likely be skipping rate cuts multiple times on the way to that destination. Ultimately, the decision at the next meeting appears to rest on a balance between the case for further easing and the case for patience.

Since my previous address regarding the economy and monetary policy on July 17, recent economic data have further corroborated my perspective on the economic outlook. Additionally, my assessment suggests that the time has arrived to implement a more accommodative monetary policy, transitioning it toward a more neutral stance.

In July, I contended that, when considering the impact of tariffs, the current underlying inflation rate is near the established target, and the potential upside risks to inflation appear to be limited. Therefore, I posited that the Federal Open Market Committee should not delay a reduction in the policy rate until signs of deterioration in the labor market are evident. Based on the comprehensive data now available, I maintain that this argument has gained additional strength, particularly as the downside risks to the labor market may have intensified.

In July, I cautioned that the rate of job creation was weaker than it initially appeared in the payroll figures. I indicated that forthcoming data, expected in early September, would likely show a significant downward adjustment in payroll growth following the annual revisions scheduled for next spring. However, prior to that point, the employment report for July revealed that job creation was notably subdued, and the figures for May and June were revised downward sharply, resulting in a three-month average growth rate for total nonfarm payrolls of merely 35,000. After taking these revisions into account, along with the information we will receive in the coming weeks, the data may suggest that overall employment actually experienced a decline during those three months. I intend to provide further insights regarding the revisions to labor market data and their implications for evaluating the monthly jobs report, which serves as one of the most essential tools for assessing economic conditions.
output:
Since I last spoke on the economy and monetary policy on July 17, economic data have reinforced my view of the outlook and my judgment that the time has come to ease monetary policy and move it to a more neutral stance.

In July, I argued that, looking through tariff effects, with underlying inflation near target and the upside risks to inflation limited, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) should not wait until the labor market deteriorates before we cut the policy rate. Based on all the data in hand, I believe this argument is even stronger today, and that the downside risks to the labor market have increased.

In July, I warned that job creation was weaker than it seemed in the payroll numbers and that data due in early September would indicate that payroll growth will be significantly lowered when annual revisions are made next spring. But even before then, job creation came in soft in the employment report for July, and May and June were revised down sharply, for a three-month average pace for total nonfarm payroll growth of only 35,000. After accounting for these revisions and what we will learn in a couple of weeks, the data are likely to indicate that employment actually shrank over those three months. I will have more to say about labor market data revisions and how they should be treated in evaluating the monthly jobs report, one of the most valuable tools we have for judging economic conditions.

When we consider the benefits and the costs, we can institute greater efficiencies in both banking regulation and in the banking industry itself. The bank regulatory framework is complex, and the various elements of this framework are intended to work in a complementary way. As banks evolve—by growing larger, or by engaging in new activities—tailoring can help us to quickly recalibrate requirements in light of the new risks posed by the firm.

But the regulatory framework, especially how supervisors prioritize its application to the banking industry, can pose a serious threat to a bank's viability. For example, imposing the same regulatory requirements on banks with assets of $2 billion to $2 trillion under the new rules implementing the Community Reinvestment Act demonstrated a missed opportunity to promote greater effectiveness and efficiency. In the previous year, Congress enacted the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins (GENIUS) Act, which offers essential clarity to stablecoin issuers regarding their integration within the regulatory framework. Furthermore, although significant efforts remain for the relevant agencies to delineate specific details during the rule-making process, the enhancement of regulatory certainty can potentially accelerate the development of stablecoins.

Currently, stablecoins are predominantly employed to facilitate activities related to cryptocurrency trading, while they are secondarily utilized as a dollar-denominated store of value in certain foreign jurisdictions. Moreover, stablecoins may serve to decrease the costs associated with remittances between various countries, enhance the efficiency of managing the paperwork and processes intrinsic to global trade and trade finance, or assist multinational corporations in optimizing their treasury operations. Additionally, innovations in payment systems could emerge through the utilization of stablecoins, tokenized deposits, or alternative frameworks.

It is worth noting that a significant area of concern pertains to the potential use of stablecoins in activities associated with money laundering or terrorist financing, as malicious entities can acquire stablecoins in secondary markets that may lack stringent customer identification requirements. In order to mitigate these risks, both regulatory measures and technological solutions will be necessary.

Another critical concern is the issue of financial stability. While individuals acquiring something designated as a "stablecoin" may reasonably anticipate the ability to redeem it at par on demand, the quality and liquidity of the reserve assets that support the stablecoins could render them susceptible to fluctuations. Stablecoins can only maintain their stability if they can be consistently and promptly redeemed at par across various conditions, including periods of market stress that exert pressure on the value of otherwise liquid government debt, as well as during episodes of strain affecting the individual issuer or its associated entities. Ultimately, these multifaceted considerations underscore the complexities and challenges inherent in the stablecoin ecosystem.

It is worth noting that the terms and conditions of the BTFP directly addressed the underlying source of uncertainty within the banking sector, specifically regarding the capacity of various banks to maintain their high-quality securities that had experienced a decline in value due to rising interest rates. The provision of BTFP advances instilled confidence in the banking system, assuring that banks would possess adequate funding to retain these securities on their balance sheets. Ultimately, the program fostered confidence among depositors, ensuring that banks would have prompt access to sufficient cash to meet their needs, thereby reducing the likelihood that a self-fulfilling panic could trigger additional bank runs.

However, there are other uses emerging from these technologies that look more like complements to centralized finance. For example, distributed ledger technology, or DLT, may be an efficient and faster way to do recordkeeping in a 24/7 trading world. We already see several financial institutions experimenting with DLT for traditional repo trading that occurs 24/7. But before these ledgers can be used to facilitate transactions in traditional assets—like debt, equity, and real estate—these assets must be tokenized. Undertaking the process to tokenize assets and use distributed ledgers like blockchain can speed up transfers of assets and take advantage of another innovation: smart contracts.

Rather than relying on each party to separately carry out the transaction, smart contracts can effectively combine multiple legs of a transaction into a single unified act executed by a smart contract. This can provide value as it can mitigate risks associated with settlement and counterparty risks by ensuring the buyer will not pay if the seller does not deliver. While these efforts are still in early stages, the functionality could expand to a broad set of financial activities. The bottom line is that things like DLT, tokenization, and smart contracts are just technologies for trading that can be used in defi or also to improve efficiency in centralized finance. That is why I see them as complements.

In October of the previous year, the Board released a proposal aimed at enhancing public accountability while ensuring robust outcomes within the stress testing framework and its associated practices. This proposal encompasses the disclosure of stress test models, the framework for designing stress test scenarios, and the specific scenarios intended for the 2026 stress tests. Additionally, the proposed modifications to the models are designed to reduce volatility in capital requirements, addressing certain deficiencies present in existing models and promoting full transparency. Furthermore, the proposal guarantees that any significant future changes to these models will incorporate public input prior to their implementation. Earlier this month, following a comprehensive review of the comments regarding the 2026 scenarios, the Board published the finalized scenarios for the upcoming stress test.

In addition, the banking agencies finalized modifications to the enhanced Supplementary Leverage Ratio (SLR) proposal that is applicable to U.S. global systemically important banking organizations, commonly referred to as G-SIBs. These modifications are intended to ensure that leverage capital requirements primarily function as a backstop to risk-based capital requirements, aligning with their original purpose. It is worth noting that when the leverage ratio becomes the predominant constraint, it can often discourage banks and dealers from participating in low-risk activities, such as holding Treasury securities, due to the uniform capital requirement imposed on both safe and risky assets. Overall, these developments reflect ongoing efforts to strengthen the financial system’s resilience and accountability.
output:
Stress Testing The Board released a proposal in October of last year to enhance public accountability and ensure robust outcomes of our stress testing framework and practices. The proposal includes disclosure of the stress test models, the framework for designing stress test scenarios, and the scenarios for the 2026 stress tests. The proposed model changes reduce volatility in capital requirements by addressing some shortcomings in our models and by providing full transparency. The proposal also ensures that any future significant changes to these models will benefit from public input prior to implementation. Earlier this month, after reviewing the comments on the 2026 scenarios, the Board published the final scenarios for the 2026 stress test.

Supplementary Leverage Ratio (SLR) The banking agencies also finalized changes to the enhanced SLR proposal for U.S. global systemically important banking organizations (G-SIBs). These changes help ensure that leverage capital requirements serve primarily as a backstop to risk-based capital requirements, as originally intended. When the leverage ratio generally becomes the binding constraint, it discourages banks and dealers from engaging in low-risk activities, including holding Treasury securities, because the leverage ratio assigns the same capital requirement across both safe and risky assets.

Ultimately, preventing Treasury market dysfunction in the first place appears to be a desirable outcome, as it may help to limit the Fed's footprint. In essence, providing relief in a proactive manner can often be more effective than reacting to problems after they have occurred. It is worth noting that delaying relief until after a problem has arisen may lead to the perception that the Federal Reserve is providing undue assistance to specific entities. Moreover, this approach is not entirely new, as banking regulators have previously reached a decision to exclude certain assets from the leverage ratio denominator in response to changing circumstances. While this intervention was largely successful, it did result in some unintended consequences, including a decline in bank deposits and a subsequent increase in usage of certain financial facilities. Notably, bank and depositor behavior experienced a decline in stability, as some banks were forced to reverse course and compete for deposits in response to rising interest rates. Ultimately, it appears that excluding certain instruments from the leverage ratio denominator can often be a relatively straightforward process, as evidenced by the fact that certain instruments are already excluded without causing disruption, and in summary, this approach may be a useful way to promote stability in the Treasury market.
output:
Removing these securities from the leverage ratio, as was suggested as an alternative in the proposed rule, would help insulate the Treasury market from stressful episodes when liquidity is in short supply. Due to heightened uncertainty accompanying extreme volatility, policymakers tend to "overdo it" when overreacting to dysfunction. Instead of being forced to react to Treasury market dysfunction after it has occurred, I think excluding those assets now is a small price to pay to deter that potential dysfunction.

Preventing Treasury market dysfunction in the first place may be the best way to limit the Fed's footprint. Moreover, providing this relief ex post instead of ex ante may lead to the unfortunate perception that the Federal Reserve is bailing out specific entities for poor investment decisions.

While I have noted my openness to new ideas, this one is not novel. The banking regulators excluded Treasurys and reserves from the leverage ratio denominator in response to the increase in bank deposits during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. The only observable downside from that intervention came from the transition back to including them in the denominator. Conferences of this nature tend to concentrate on the ways in which technology is transforming the future landscape. Furthermore, I have endeavored to illustrate how the Federal Reserve is addressing this challenge by delivering our mission through innovation enabled by technology, placing significant emphasis on execution and efficiency. In pursuing this approach, we exemplify the capacity of a public institution to adopt artificial intelligence in a responsible manner, thereby reinforcing public trust.

Moreover, as we observe the emergence of technologies such as tokenization and agentic artificial intelligence, it is worth noting that this is not the first instance in which our industry has navigated substantial shifts. For example, the introduction of automated teller machines initially did not lead to the eradication of bank tellers; rather, it transformed the operational dynamics of banking. Routine transactions became more cost-effective, expeditious, and accessible, while human resources transitioned toward higher-value tasks. The fundamental effect was not merely automation; instead, it was the manner in which institutions restructured themselves in response to technological advancements.

Artificial intelligence presents a comparable situation. The most significant benefits may not arise from the mere integration of AI into existing processes. Rather, they are likely to emerge from a comprehensive reevaluation of workflows, roles, and systems to leverage the potential that this technology offers.

In essence, what remains uncertain—and may always remain uncertain—is the precise timing of when these technologies will reach their full inflection point. There will likely be no definitive indication signaling the transition of artificial intelligence from a phase of rapid advancement to one of truly systemic influence. However, it is important to recognize that waiting for a moment of absolute clarity does not constitute a viable strategy. If we aspire to be adequately prepared for when that pivotal moment arrives, it is imperative that our efforts commence without delay.
output:
Conferences like this one focus on how technology is reshaping the future. What I've tried to show today is how we're approaching that challenge at the Federal Reserve—delivering our mission through technology-enabled innovation, with a clear focus on execution and efficiency. And in doing so, we demonstrate how a public institution can adopt AI responsibly and in a way that strengths public trust.

As we see technologies like tokenization and agentic AI coming into view, it's worth remembering that this isn't the first time our industry has navigated shifts like this. When ATMs were first introduced, they didn't eliminate bank tellers. Instead, they changed how banking worked. Routine transactions became cheaper, faster, and more accessible, while human effort shifted toward higher-value activities. The real impact wasn't automation alone—it was how institutions reorganized around technology.

AI is similar. The biggest gains won't come from simply adding AI to existing processes. They'll come from rethinking workflows, roles, and systems to take advantage of what this technology makes possible.

What we don't know—and can't know—is exactly when these technologies will hit their full inflection point. We won't get a clear signal when AI moves from rapid progress to truly systemic impact. But waiting for perfect clarity isn't a strategy. If we want to be ready when that moment comes, the work has to start now.

Despite these policies to discourage use of the discount window, slide 9 shows that discount window borrowing, adjusted for the size of the Federal Reserve's balance sheet, was notable in the 1970s and 1980s, suggesting that the discount window was an important marginal source of funding for banks during that period.

That changed in the 1980s and early 1990s, when there were notable solvency problems in the banking industry. During this period, the discount window provided support to troubled institutions, while the FDIC sought to find merger partners or otherwise manage the failure of these institutions in an orderly manner. The discount window activity that took place while FDIC resolutions proceeded increased the association between use of the discount window and being a troubled institution. As a result, banks became more reluctant to borrow from the discount window. The greater reluctance to borrow from the discount window made it less effective, both as a monetary policy tool and as a crisis-fighting tool. That resulted in a series of efforts by the Fed in the early 2000s to change how the discount window operates. Tomorrow, I will discuss those efforts when I speak at the Charlotte Economics Club.

Furthermore, it is worth noting that depositors and investors experienced a decline in confidence in certain New York banks that had undergone a process of consolidation into large, complex, and opaque trust companies that were not members of the New York Clearing House. Ultimately, this resulted in the occurrence of runs on those trusts, which tended to lead to broader liquidity problems. Notably, the New York Clearing House had the capacity to provide liquidity to those trusts, but the provision of that liquidity was subject to a delay. It is worth noting that, at the time, the New York Clearing House appears to have been guided by a particular principle, namely Bagehot's dictum, when reaching a decision regarding the provision of liquidity. In essence, this dictum dictates that the institution providing liquidity should have a thorough understanding of the solvency of the recipient institution, as the extension of liquidity to an insolvent institution may be akin to a futile expenditure of resources. Moreover, the trust companies in question were not member institutions, which hindered the clearinghouse's ability to acquire a comprehensive understanding of their balance sheets and determine their solvency. Additionally, some banks refused to engage in the clearance of checks from other institutions, which led to a further erosion of depositor confidence and an increase in the number of failures. Furthermore, this historical example tends to highlight the importance of a particular aspect of a payment system, namely its resilience. Ultimately, the problems that arose during the 1907 panic, including coordination failures and a lack of resilience, may have been mitigated with the assistance of a central bank. Notably, Paul Warburg, a prominent banker at the time, argued that a central bank could facilitate the establishment and maintenance of a robust system of credit, enabling general banks to transform cash credits into actual cash with a high degree of ease and certainty. In essence, the creation of such a system would tend to ensure that the use of cash credit, instead of actual cash, would continue uninterrupted, regardless of any potential disruptions. Ultimately, the implementation of a central bank may have played a crucial role in mitigating the problems that arose during the 1907 panic, and it is worth noting that this historical example may provide valuable insights into the importance of a resilient payment system.

The Panic of 1907 was a classic example of that. But because the trust companies at the time weren't member institutions, the clearinghouse didn't have a good enough understanding of their balance sheets to know whether they were solvent. Additionally, one easily identifiable way to achieve this is the use of the Economic Growth and Regulatory Paperwork Reduction Act (EGRPRA) review process, which the agencies initiated in February last year.

The Labor Market 

In this analysis, it is necessary to examine the labor market's performance in 2025 before interpreting the most recent data. Throughout much of the previous year, the labor market appeared to experience a gradual cooling. Both the supply of workers and the demand for labor may have eased during 2025, with a more pronounced pullback on the demand side. On the supply side, the growth of the labor force exhibited a slowdown, which was primarily driven by a significant decline in net migration. Furthermore, on the demand side, firms appeared to be hesitant to hire, partially due to heightened uncertainty surrounding the economic outlook. As a result, the pace of job creation may have cooled in 2025 compared to previous years, with job growth becoming more concentrated within a limited number of industries, such as health care and social assistance. Notably, the unemployment rate increased, rising from 4.0 percent in January 2025 to 4.5 percent by November 2025.

In more recent months, the labor market seems to have shown signs of stabilization. The unemployment rate decreased slightly in March to 4.3 percent, which is similar to the level recorded at the end of the previous summer. This unemployment rate may be close to a level that many forecasters estimate as the natural rate, which represents the level of unemployment that persists when the economy is functioning at full strength. In summary, the labor market has undergone significant changes, and the current trends indicate a potential stabilization phase.
output:
The Labor Market Now, let me turn to the labor market. To set up this discussion, I will first review how the labor market performed in 2025. Then, I will discuss how I interpret the most recent data.

For much of last year, the labor market exhibited a gradual cooling. Both the supply of workers and the demand for labor eased in 2025, with the pullback on the demand side more pronounced. On the supply side, labor force growth slowed, mostly driven by a sharp decline in net migration. On the demand side, firms were reluctant to hire in part because of elevated uncertainty around the economic outlook. The pace of job creation cooled in 2025 compared to the previous few years, and job growth became more concentrated in a handful of industries, such as health care and social assistance. The unemployment rate, shown in figure 4, crept up from 4.0 percent in January 2025 to 4.5 percent in November 2025.

In more recent months, the labor market has shown signs of stabilization. The unemployment rate edged lower in March to 4.3 percent, similar to its level at the end of last summer. The unemployment rate is near a level many forecasters estimate as its natural rate, or the level of unemployment that persists when the economy is at full strength.

The NMTC was conceived with the belief that there were also significant investment opportunities within underserved domestic communities.

During one visit to Clarksdale, Mississippi, we encountered an energetic atmosphere in a hot furniture factory, where we listened to entrepreneurs seeking new funding, community development financial institutions in search of capital to support these entrepreneurs, and local lenders aiming to stimulate their regional economies. Ultimately, this experience underscores the continuing importance of the NMTC in fostering economic opportunity.
output:

I consider the credit a great achievement for communities all across the United States. Artificial intelligence has the potential to enhance productivity growth by accelerating the generation of ideas, which is a fundamental aspect of Paul Romer's endogenous growth theory. This capability stems from AI's proficiency in rapidly processing and synthesizing knowledge. Furthermore, by making powerful analytical tools accessible to a wider audience, rather than limiting them to experts, AI promotes a more inclusive environment for innovation. This inclusivity enables a greater number of individuals to engage as inventors, innovators, and entrepreneurs, thereby creating a self-reinforcing cycle in which ideas generate additional ideas. This democratization of innovation aligns with Romer's assertion that ideas can be shared repeatedly without being depleted, which may fundamentally alter the landscape of innovation by facilitating broader contributions to economic advancement. 

Additionally, it is important to recognize that AI is likely to introduce new tasks and professions, many of which are difficult to envision at present. This observation is underscored by the fact that approximately 60 percent of today’s jobs did not exist in 1940, illustrating the dynamic nature of the labor market. Professions such as airplane designer, computer application engineer, and cybersecurity analyst have emerged as recognized occupations since the conclusion of World War II. 

While the potential of AI is significant, a cautious perspective regarding its widespread implementation is warranted. AI's rise appears to represent the latest instance of the concept of creative destruction, as articulated by economist Joseph Schumpeter nearly a century ago. We seem to be on the cusp of a profound reorganization of work that may yield new opportunities alongside potential challenges. 

Ultimately, this transition may lead to job displacement occurring prior to job creation, raising the possibility that the unemployment rate could increase and labor force participation might decrease during the economic adjustment. Such developments could result in significant difficulties for many workers and their families. This complex interplay of opportunity and risk underscores the importance of careful consideration as society navigates the implications of AI integration into the workforce.

Life on Earth can be broadly categorized into two main groups: prokaryotes and eukaryotes. Prokaryotes are defined as single-celled organisms that lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles within their cellular structure. This lack of complexity suggests that they possess relatively fewer cellular components that could be damaged by extreme conditions, such as high temperatures, low temperatures, acidic environments, or harmful radiation.

Furthermore, organisms that thrive in high-temperature environments are referred to as thermophiles. To accurately classify as a true thermophile, an organism must demonstrate the ability to replicate, move, consume nutrients, and survive in temperatures exceeding 113 degrees Fahrenheit (45 degrees Celsius).

Notably, prokaryotes encompass two distinct domains: bacteria and archaea, with the latter showcasing remarkable resilience in extreme conditions. Given their relatively simple structure, scientists posit that prokaryotes were among the earliest forms of life to emerge on Earth, billions of years ago, during a time when the planet's environment was significantly more hostile than it is at present.

In contrast, eukaryotes represent more complex organisms that are believed to have evolved later in the timeline of life on Earth. These organisms are characterized by the presence of a defined cell nucleus, which houses delicate genetic material. Additionally, eukaryotic cells contain membrane-bound organelles, including mitochondria and the endoplasmic reticulum, which function similarly to specialized cellular machines performing distinct tasks. Eukaryotes encompass a diverse range of life forms, including both single-celled algae and multicellular entities such as plants and humans.

Ultimately, high temperatures can lead to the degradation of essential proteins and biomolecules necessary for cellular function. In addition, heat has the potential to disrupt cellular membranes, thus resulting in cell destruction. It has been suggested that the membranes of organelles within eukaryotic cells may not remain stable at temperatures above 144 degrees Fahrenheit (62 degrees Celsius). However, the discovery of I. cascadensis challenges this assumption, indicating that there may be exceptions to previously held beliefs regarding the stability of organelle membranes in extreme conditions.

The apparent position of continents in imagery from a NASA camera located in deep space experiences a shift with the seasons, and this phenomenon is caused by the tilt in the axis of Earth's rotation.

Most children learn during their elementary school years that the seasons are caused by Earth rotating on a tilted axis as it completes its yearly orbit around the Sun. The substantial tilt of approximately 23.5 degrees is thought to be the result of an ancient planetary body known as Theia, which smashed into Earth about 4.5 billion years ago in the same cataclysmic collision that formed the Moon.

To visualize why Earth has seasons, one can imagine the planet as a spinning top that is tilted to one side. Around the June solstice, the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun, which brings more direct sunlight and longer days. Around the December solstice, the Southern Hemisphere does the same. That is why June ushers in summer and warm weather in the Northern Hemisphere, while December does so in the Southern Hemisphere.

The March and September equinoxes serve as the midpoints between these two seasonal extremes. On those days, the terminator, which is the boundary between the sunlit and dark sides of Earth, runs directly through both poles. As a result, the Northern and Southern Hemispheres receive almost the same amount of sunlight, and day and night are nearly equal in length.

What do the seasons look like from about one million miles away? That is the view provided by NASA's EPIC, or Earth Polychromatic Imaging Camera, aboard the NOAA mission DSCOVR, or Deep Space Climate Observatory. By maintaining an orbit that puts the spacecraft between the Sun and Earth at roughly 1.6 million kilometers, or 1 million miles, from Earth, the camera has a nearly continuous view of the sunlit hemisphere. As Earth spins during the course of a day, EPIC captures a full-disk image of the planet's sunlit face every few hours.

The crew’s work aboard the space station helps improve life on Earth and prepare for future human missions to the Moon and Mars.

On the day of an equinox, individuals observing from the equator will experience the Sun directly overhead at noon. After the March equinox, observers across the Earth may notice that the Sun’s path in the sky progressively shifts further north each day until the June solstice, at which point it begins its southward journey. The Sun crosses the equatorial plane once more during the September equinox and continues its southward motion until the December solstice, when it will start to head north again. This cyclical movement is why some individuals refer to the March equinox as the northward equinox and the September equinox as the southward equinox.
