input: During the equinoxes, the Sun provides illumination equally to both the Northern and Southern Hemispheres, which is why these periods represent the only occasions in the year when the North and South Poles are simultaneously lit by sunlight. It is worth noting, however, that the duration of day and night on the equinox is not precisely equal, as the exact date of this balance depends on latitude and may occur a few days earlier or later than the equinox itself. This highlights the complicating influence of the Sun and the atmosphere. Additionally, because the Sun is a sphere rather than a point light source, its edge undergoes refraction by the atmosphere as it rises and sets, which adds several minutes of light to each day. Furthermore, the Sun does not neatly switch on and off at sunrise and sunset like a light bulb, and so a perfect split of day and night on the equinox does not occur, although it is very close. Equinoxes are also associated with the changing seasons. In March, Northern Hemisphere observers welcome the longer, warmer days heralded by their vernal, or spring, equinox, while Southern Hemisphere observers note the shorter days and longer, cooler nights signaled by their autumnal, or fall, equinox. Ultimately, come September, the reverse is true.

However, LINK will still endeavor to perform rendezvous and proximity operations with NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, which may serve to demonstrate essential capabilities for the future of space exploration.

output:
Due to an ongoing commercial spacecraft attitude control issue, NASA and Katalyst Space announced Wednesday the LINK spacecraft will not capture or boost an agency satellite to a higher altitude to extend its science mission as planned. However, LINK still will attempt to conduct rendezvous and proximity operations with NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory to demonstrate key capabilities for the future of space exploration.

“NASA should be willing to move quickly and take smart risks when the potential return is worth it, and that is exactly what we did with this mission,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “This is not the outcome we were working toward, but it does not change why this mission was worth attempting. The team moved with extraordinary speed to give Swift a chance to carry out more science while advancing capabilities America will need for satellite servicing in the future. We are going to learn everything we can from LINK’s rendezvous attempt and put those lessons to work on the missions that follow.”

NASA and Katalyst are working closely to assess next steps for rendezvous and gather as much data as possible to inform future satellite servicing operations.

“We knew this was a high-risk, high-reward mission – a first-of-its kind attempt, developed on an unprecedented timeline driven by the Sun’s activity,” said Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director, Astrophysics Division, NASA Headquarters in Washington. “We were all hoping for more science from Swift. But we knew the takeaways from this mission would be worthwhile either way, and we have gained so much through the series of accomplishments up to this point.”

Planning crewed missions to celestial bodies such as the Moon and Mars necessitates thorough preparation for the medical realities associated with long-duration space travel. Factors such as cosmic radiation exposure, the effects of microgravity, and the considerable distance from Earth contribute to a set of unique health considerations that astronauts may encounter. To proactively address these potential challenges, NASA has developed the Integrated Medical Model, often referred to as the IMM.

Utilizing Monte Carlo simulations, this tool facilitates the modeling of thousands of potential mission trajectories. Each simulation run incorporates specific mission parameters, including crew size, flight duration, planned extravehicular activities, and the environmental conditions of the spacecraft. This comprehensive approach enables mission planners to evaluate the risks associated with new mission profiles that may lack historical data.

Given that spacecraft are subject to stringent mass and volume limitations, the outputs generated by the IMM play a crucial role in determining the composition of onboard medical kits, which are designated as MedCap. Consequently, mission planners can effectively balance the requirement for adequate medical coverage with the constraints of available cargo space, armed with clear and reliable data.

On the International Space Station, it may be possible for emergency medical evacuations back to Earth to occur within a matter of hours. However, deep-space exploration significantly alters this timeline, as it introduces communication delays and eliminates the possibility of a swift return to Earth. In summary, the complexities of long-duration space travel necessitate meticulous planning to ensure astronaut health and safety.
output:
Planning crewed missions to the Moon and Mars involves preparing for the medical realities of long-duration space travel. Factors like cosmic radiation, microgravity, and distance from Earth create unique health considerations for astronauts. To anticipate these needs ahead of time, NASA developed the Integrated Medical Model (IMM).

Using Monte Carlo simulations, the tool models thousands of potential mission paths. Each run accounts for specific mission parameters, such as crew size, flight duration, planned spacewalks, and the spacecraft environment. This approach allows planners to evaluate risks for new mission profiles that lack historical precedents.

Because spacecraft carry strict mass and volume constraints, these outputs guide the composition of onboard medical kits (MedCap). Mission planners can balance necessary medical coverage against available cargo space with clear data in hand.

On the International Space Station, emergency medical evacuation back to Earth can happen within hours. Deep-space exploration changes that timeline significantly, introducing communication delays and eliminating the option for a rapid return.

Life on Earth can be categorized into two main groups: prokaryotes and eukaryotes. Prokaryotes are defined as single-celled organisms that lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, which suggests they possess fewer cellular components that may be vulnerable to extreme conditions such as high temperatures, low temperatures, strong acidity, or hazardous radiation.

Furthermore, organisms that thrive in extreme heat are referred to as thermophiles. To qualify as a true thermophile, an organism must demonstrate the capability to replicate, move, consume nutrients, and endure environments exceeding 113 degrees Fahrenheit (45 degrees Celsius).

Notably, prokaryotes encompass both bacteria and archaea, with archaea displaying significant resilience in extreme environments. This simplicity in structure leads scientists to propose that prokaryotes were likely the earliest forms of life to emerge on Earth, billions of years ago, during a time when the planet’s conditions were far more hostile than those experienced today.

In contrast, eukaryotes are described as more complex organisms, which are believed to have evolved at a later stage in the development of life on Earth. These organisms are characterized by the presence of a distinct cell nucleus that houses delicate genetic material. Additionally, eukaryotes contain membrane-bound organelles, such as mitochondria and the endoplasmic reticulum, which function as specialized cellular components. The eukaryotic group includes a diverse range of life forms, from unicellular algae to multicellular species like plants and humans.

Ultimately, high temperatures can lead to the degradation of proteins and other essential biomolecules required for cellular functions. Heat exposure may also result in the disintegration of cellular membranes, which can cause cell death. It has been indicated that the membranes of organelles in eukaryotes are unable to maintain stability at temperatures exceeding 144 degrees Fahrenheit (62 degrees Celsius). However, the discovery of I. cascadensis challenges this assumption, suggesting the need for a reevaluation of temperature limits for eukaryotic membranes.

These drugs, which usually take the form of large protein molecules, are manufactured by growing living cells that are genetically engineered to produce the proteins. These large protein molecules, however, can stick together during the manufacturing process to form particles that can cause an unwanted immune response in patients.

A new standard reference material (SRM) from the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) will help them do that. The new material, SRM 1989: Monodisperse Irregularly Shaped Epoxy-Based Particles, consists of three vials containing particles of different sizes: 220 micrometers, 150 micrometers and 100 micrometers. (For comparison, a sheet of regular printer paper is roughly 100 micrometers thick.)

“This material will be the first publicly available visible particle standard for protein-based particles in biotherapeutic drugs,” said NIST research chemist Srivalli Telikepalli. “This will help drug manufacturers monitor particles in their products so that they can ensure that those products are safe and effective.”

Protein-based particles, which are small but sometimes visible to the naked eye, form because proteins can be unstable. Any stress, like a temperature change or sudden shaking of a drug vial, can cause proteins to clump together into particles. This can happen when the drug products are being purified, packaged, shipped or stored for long periods of time.

At biopharmaceutical manufacturing plants, trained analysts visually inspect each vial of drug product. If the vial contains visible particles, it is removed from the batch. If a certain number of vials fail, the entire batch will be discarded. Each failed batch can cost the manufacturer millions of dollars.

Actinium-225 represents one of several radioisotopes, which are radioactive manifestations of stable elements, that release a significant amount of energy in the form of alpha particles within a remarkably short distance in the human body. Alpha particles, which consist of two protons and two neutrons, exhibit a relatively substantial mass and density, thereby limiting their range before they deposit all their energy.

Furthermore, by capitalizing on this short-range emission of energy, medical practitioners have developed therapeutic agents that function as anticancer missiles. These agents bind actinium-225 or another alpha-emitting radioisotope to molecules that specifically target and attach to cancer cells. Once the radioactive source reaches a tumor, it is the alpha particles that effectively destroy the DNA of the cancer cells while leaving the surrounding healthy cells largely unaffected.

In order to deliver the appropriate dosage to the tumor, it is essential for clinicians to ascertain the number of alpha particles emitted at the tumor site. However, the process of counting radioactive decays may not be as straightforward as it initially appears.

When actinium-225 undergoes radioactive decay, it successively transitions into a series of smaller, unstable atoms that also emit their own alpha particles, in addition to gamma rays, which represent a form of high-energy electromagnetic radiation, and beta particles, which are electrons. Consequently, in order to accurately measure radioactivity, researchers must take into consideration all decay products resulting from the transformation process.

To establish the new standard, Bergeron and his colleagues at the National Institute of Standards and Technology employed a well-known method for measuring radioactivity, referred to as the triple-to-double coincidence ratio (TDCR). They introduced a small quantity of actinium-225 into a vial containing a liquid that emits flashes of light when it is struck by radioactive particles. Subsequently, they converted these flashes into electrical signals for analysis. In summary, this meticulous approach allows for a more accurate assessment of radioactivity, crucial for the effective application of actinium-225 in medical treatments.

Sirens blared across Joplin, Missouri, on a spring afternoon in 2011, just 23 minutes before the tip of the deadliest tornado on official records descended from the clouds and touched the ground.

Directly in the path of the vortex was St. John’s Regional Medical Center, a huge hospital complex that employed more than 1,000 people. The staff had done tornado drills before and quickly jumped into action, ushering patients and visitors away from the windows as dark clouds blotted out the sun. Then the lights went out. Ventilators stopped working. The storm had torn apart an electrical substation and the hospital’s emergency generator building, causing a total loss of power. The occupants were in complete darkness when the doors and windows blasted open, shooting broken glass and furniture through the hallways.

It took less than a minute for the mile-wide tornado to pass through St. John’s before moving on to tear through public schools, retirement homes, grocery stores, and suburban neighborhoods. The entire tornado lasted about 30 minutes, but by the end of it, a quarter of Joplin was destroyed and 161 people had lost their lives.

Just hours after the tornado hit Joplin, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) began a long-term study of what went wrong that day. After more than a decade of work, that research is making its way into standards and codes to make new buildings safer.

Because of its unique geography, the United States has more tornadoes, and more intense tornadoes, than any other country. Cool, dry air from the Rocky Mountains collides with warm, moist air from the Gulf of Mexico to twist up into more than 1,200 tornadoes per year.

However, it is crucial to ensure that the utilization of UV light is both safe and effective. To facilitate this assurance, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has undertaken the reconstruction of its specialized calibration laboratory, known as the Ultraviolet Spectral Comparator Facility (UVSCF). This facility enables industry customers to send their UV detection equipment for precise measurement and calibration, thereby enhancing the accuracy of UV applications.

UV light is employed across a broad spectrum of applications due to its germicidal properties, making it an essential tool for sanitization and disinfection, particularly within health-care environments. Furthermore, it is an effective means of addressing microbial contamination in various types of water, including drinking water, wastewater, and surface water disinfection. Additionally, homeowners often apply UV-cured epoxy for the installation of new kitchen countertops, while the nail salon industry utilizes UV light boxes to cure gel nail products. In recent years, there has also been an increase in consumer products designed to provide UV protection, including clothing that safeguards against unwanted UV exposure. This underscores the need for carefully calibrated UV light sources to ensure that these products perform as intended.

It is worth noting that ultraviolet light is not visible to the human eye, as it possesses shorter wavelengths than visible light. UV light can be categorized into three distinct types based on wavelength: UVA, UVB, and UVC. Wavelength pertains to the distance between the peaks of light waves, which can be observed in different colors of visible light. While NIST’s new calibration system is designed to accommodate all three categories, it is particularly adept at accurately measuring UVC light, which is characterized by wavelengths ranging from 200 to 300 nanometers. Ultimately, this enhancement is significant for maintaining the efficacy and safety of UV applications across various fields.

Older approaches to network security rely on the idea of a perimeter, where once a device gains entry it can then freely access the network’s internal data, applications and other resources. This perimeter idea, developed when many networks were limited to a single location such as a building or campus, is growing obsolete. Nowadays a single organization may operate several internal networks, use cloud services, and allow for remote work — meaning there is no single perimeter.

This complexity has led to the development of the zero trust concept. ZTA implements a risk-based approach to cybersecurity — continuously evaluating and verifying conditions and requests to decide which access requests should be permitted, then ensuring that each access is properly safeguarded. Zero trust also prevents attackers who have gained access from roaming freely within the network and wreaking havoc as they go. Because of its effectiveness against both internal and external threats, ZTA adoption is increasing, and some organizations are required to use a ZTA.

“This guidance gives you examples of how to deploy ZTAs and emphasizes the different technologies you need to implement them,” Kerman said. “It can be a foundational starting point for any organization constructing its own ZTA.”

The new guidance augments NIST’s 2020 publication Zero Trust Architecture (NIST SP 800-207), a high-level document that describes zero trust at the conceptual level. While the earlier publication discussed how to deploy a ZTA and offered models, the new publication gives users more help addressing their own needs, which can be a substantial task when implementing ZTA.

Quantum computers, which are still at a nascent stage of development, would harness the bizarre properties of quantum mechanics to do jobs that even our most powerful classical computers find intractable, such as aiding in the development of new drugs by performing sophisticated simulations of chemical interactions. However, quantum computer designers still confront many problems. One of these is that quantum circuits are kicked around by external or even internal noise, which arises from defects in the materials used to make the computers. This noise is essentially random behavior that can create errors in qubit calculations. It is worth noting that this noise tends to undermine the reliability of qubit operations.

Present-day qubits are inherently noisy by themselves, but that's not the only problem. Many quantum computer designs have what is called a static architecture, where each qubit in the processor is physically connected to its neighbors and to its readout resonator. The fabricated wiring that connects qubits together and to their readout can expose them to even more noise. Ultimately, this configuration appears to compound the noise-related challenges that designers already face.

Such static architectures have another disadvantage: They cannot be reprogrammed easily. A static architecture's qubits could do a few related jobs, but for the computer to perform a wider range of tasks, it would need to swap in a different processor design with a different qubit organization or layout. (Imagine changing the chip in your laptop every time you needed to use a different piece of software, and then consider that the chip needs to be kept a smidgen above absolute zero, and you get why this might prove inconvenient.) In essence, the inflexibility of static architectures tends to limit the range of tasks that a given quantum processor can perform.

This technique, identified as hydroxide catalysis bonding (HCB), establishes an inorganic, glasslike chemical bond between the optical fiber and the photonic chip. Rather than depending on glue, this process utilizes a small quantity of sodium hydroxide solution to fuse the surfaces at the molecular level, which results in a rigid and stable connection.

This allowed the researchers to confirm that the chip itself continued to operate normally, indicating the effectiveness of the HCB technique in extreme conditions.

Researchers at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) have achieved a significant increase in the sensitivity of their atomic radio receiver, improving it by a factor of one hundred. This enhancement was accomplished by enclosing a small glass cylinder filled with cesium atoms within a specially designed structure resembling copper headphones.

This structure consists of a square loop positioned overhead, which connects two square panels. It serves to amplify the incoming radio signal, or electric field, directed at the gaseous atoms contained in the flask, referred to as a vapor cell, situated between the panels. This amplification allows the radio receiver to identify signals that are considerably weaker than previously detectable levels. The findings are detailed in a recent publication.

The headphone-like structure is technically described as a split-ring resonator, which functions similarly to a metamaterial. Metamaterials are engineered materials designed with unique structures that yield unconventional properties. “We can call it a metamaterials-inspired structure,” stated Chris Holloway, the project leader at NIST.

It is important to note that NIST researchers had previously demonstrated the functioning of the atom-based radio receiver. An atomic sensor is expected to offer advantages, including a smaller physical footprint and superior performance in environments with high levels of noise, among other potential benefits.

The dimensions of the vapor cell measure approximately 14 millimeters (mm) in length and 10 mm in diameter, making it comparable to the size of a fingernail or a computer chip, though slightly thicker. The overhead loop of the resonator measures about 16 mm per side, while the ear covers are approximately 12 mm on each side.

The operation of the NIST radio receiver is dependent on a specific state of the cesium atoms. Researchers utilize two distinct colors of lasers to excite the atoms within the vapor cell into high-energy states, known as "Rydberg" states. These states exhibit unique properties, including heightened sensitivity to electromagnetic fields. The frequency and intensity of an applied electric field influence the colors of light absorbed by the atoms, effectively transforming the signal strength into an optical frequency that can be measured with high accuracy. Ultimately, this development underscores the potential advancements in atomic radio technology.

Small devices typically possess limited resources, which necessitates the need for security solutions with compact implementations. It is essential that algorithms designed for these environments address the resource constraints commonly encountered by such devices, as highlighted by NIST computer scientist Kerry McKay.

Additionally, McKay indicated that a range of criteria was evaluated during the selection process. The primary focus was on the ability to provide effective security, but considerations also extended to the associated performance and flexibility of candidate algorithms in relation to speed, size, and energy consumption. Ultimately, the selection made appeared to represent a well-rounded option.

Ascon was introduced in 2014 by a collaborative team of cryptographers from Graz University of Technology, Infineon Technologies, Lamarr Security Research, and Radboud University. The algorithm was chosen in 2019 as the preferred option for lightweight authenticated encryption within the final portfolio of the CAESAR competition. This selection signifies that Ascon had endured extensive scrutiny by cryptography experts over several years, a quality that McKay noted was highly regarded by the NIST team.

Currently, there are seven variants within the Ascon family, and it is possible that some or all of these will form part of NIST’s forthcoming lightweight cryptography standard. In this context, the variants collectively offer a diverse range of functionalities, which can provide designers with options tailored to various tasks. Notably, two critical tasks in lightweight cryptography identified by McKay are authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD) and hashing.

AEAD serves to safeguard the confidentiality of messages while simultaneously permitting the inclusion of additional information, such as message headers or device IP addresses, without encryption. This algorithm ensures the authenticity of all protected data and verifies that it has remained unaltered during transmission. AEAD has potential applications in vehicle-to-vehicle communications and can assist in preventing message counterfeiting associated with radio frequency identification (RFID) tags, which are frequently used for package tracking in warehouse environments. Ultimately, the development and implementation of Ascon and its variants may significantly contribute to advancing lightweight cryptography standards.

Although awareness of the disinfection capabilities of ultraviolet (UV) light has existed for over a century, there has been a significant increase in research related to UV disinfection during the last ten years. One contributing factor to this surge in interest is the presence of toxic substances, such as mercury, in traditional UV light sources. Recently, the adoption of nontoxic light-emitting diode (LED) lamps as an alternative UV light source has alleviated some of these environmental and health concerns.

In this particular study, the collaborators from the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) partnered with biologists at the National Biodefense Analysis and Countermeasures Center (NBACC). The research conducted at NBACC plays a critical role in informing biodefense strategies against biological threats, including anthrax and the Ebola virus.

Miller noted that the capabilities of NBACC allowed researchers to cultivate the virus, concentrate it, and eliminate extraneous materials. The objective was to determine the specific amount of UV light necessary to inactivate the SARS-CoV-2 virus effectively.

In the course of the study, the research team examined the virus in various suspensions. Alongside using a saliva mimic, scientists also introduced the virus into water to evaluate its behavior in a more controlled environment that lacked other components that could potentially obstruct the disinfection process. The virus suspensions were assessed in both liquid form and as dried droplets on steel surfaces, simulating conditions that may arise when an infected individual sneezes or coughs.

The role of NIST involved directing the UV light produced by a laser onto the virus samples. The researchers aimed to ascertain the UV dose needed to achieve a 90% inactivation rate of the virus.

Through this experimental arrangement, the collaborative team was able to analyze the virus's response to 16 distinct wavelengths, which ranged from the lower end of the UVC spectrum at 222 nanometers to the middle range of visible wavelengths at 488 nanometers. Researchers incorporated longer wavelengths into their analysis because it is suggested that certain blue light wavelengths may exhibit disinfecting properties. This research contributes to a deeper understanding of UV light's capabilities in viral inactivation.

The Organization of Scientific Area Committees (OSAC) for Forensic Science has recently added two new standards related to firearm and toolmark analysis to its Registry of Approved Standards. This inclusion represents a significant endorsement from OSAC, which is under the auspices of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), indicating that these standards possess technical validity and may assist forensic laboratories in enhancing their operational processes and methodologies.

These newly approved standards are the 100th and 101st entries on the OSAC registry, which aims to bolster forensic science in the United States by promoting the establishment and adoption of high-quality standards. The organization was initiated in 2014 in response to a fragmented landscape of standards that lacked a unified strategy for advancing and refining standards across various forensic science areas.

Forensic professionals may often establish a connection between a bullet or cartridge case and the firearm that discharged it by examining the microscopic marks that are left on the bullet during its passage through the barrel or on the cartridge case upon its ejection from the firearm. For instance, to ascertain whether a bullet retrieved from a crime scene was discharged from a particular gun, experts typically perform a test-firing procedure to create a second bullet, which is then compared with the original bullet to analyze the congruity of the microscopic marks present on both.

Examiners generally utilize a split screen comparison microscope to conduct their evaluations, wherein they rotate and manipulate the bullets to determine if the markings correspond. This traditional technique has been employed for over a century. However, researchers are actively exploring innovative methodologies that incorporate three-dimensional surface scanning microscopes, which generate three-dimensional models, or virtual representations, of the bullets. Subsequently, computer algorithms analyze the microscopic characteristics of the two virtual bullets to quantify their similarity. This development underscores the ongoing evolution of forensic science methodologies aimed at improving accuracy and reliability in analysis.

This stamp of approval from OSAC, which is administered by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), indicates that these standards are technically sound and will help forensic laboratories improve their processes and methods.

These are the 100th and 101st standards to be placed on the registry by OSAC, which works to strengthen forensic science in the U.S. by facilitating the development and adoption of high-quality standards. When the organization launched in 2014, there was a patchwork of standards but no coordinated effort to develop and improve standards across multiple forensic science disciplines.

Forensic experts can often link a bullet or cartridge case to the gun that fired it based on microscopic marks left on the bullet as it exits the barrel, or on the cartridge case as it is ejected from the firearm. For instance, to test whether a bullet found at a crime scene was fired from a specific gun, experts test-fire that gun to produce a second bullet. They then compare the microscopic marks on the pair of bullets to see how similar they are.

Examiners usually compare the bullets under a split screen comparison microscope, rotating and moving them to see if the markings line up — a method that has been in use for more than 100 years. However, researchers have been developing new methods that use 3D surface scanning microscopes to produce 3D models, or virtual copies, of the bullets. Computer algorithms then compare the microscopic features of the two virtual bullets to measure how similar they are.

Furthermore, a study conducted last year by researchers at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in collaboration with the University of Colorado Boulder suggested that a single breath test may not be a reliable indicator of recent cannabis use. This is primarily because the effects of cannabis may persist in the body for weeks, which complicates the ability to differentiate between prior and current usage.

In light of these findings, the researchers are now exploring a novel methodology that involves administering two breath tests within approximately an hour of each other. If their research proves to be fruitful, this approach could potentially facilitate the development of a roadside testing procedure for cannabis that incorporates two breath analyses taken at a predetermined interval. 

Kavita Jeerage, a materials research engineer at NIST, emphasized the significance of this development by stating, “This is potentially paradigm-changing.” Should this endeavor succeed, it might provide law enforcement with the means to detect recent cannabis use promptly and effectively.

It is worth noting that breath tests for alcohol have existed for nearly a century, effectively measuring ethanol that can be exhaled as a gaseous vapor, correlating well with the ethanol levels found in blood. 

In contrast, tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the primary psychoactive component in cannabis, exists in the breath at a significantly lower concentration than ethanol. Tara Lovestead, a chemical engineer at NIST, has described the challenge of detecting THC as akin to “looking for a needle in a haystack.” 

Additionally, the metabolic processes involved in the breakdown and elimination of cannabis occur at a much slower rate compared to ethanol. NIST and University of Colorado researchers have observed that regular users of cannabis may exhibit THC levels in their breath on days when they do not consume the substance that can be similar to the levels present just an hour after usage. This phenomenon underscores the difficulties in distinguishing between recent and past cannabis consumption among habitual users. 

In summary, the pursuit of an effective breath test for cannabis use presents several complexities, yet ongoing research may offer promising advancements in this area.

The newly developed JILA clock employs a network of light, referred to as an "optical lattice," to simultaneously trap and measure tens of thousands of individual atoms. The inclusion of such a substantial ensemble of atoms offers a considerable advantage in terms of precision. In essence, the greater the number of atoms that are measured, the more extensive the data available for generating an accurate measurement of the second.

Furthermore, in order to achieve performance that breaks previous records, the researchers at JILA implemented a shallower and gentler configuration of laser light to trap the atoms, in contrast to previous optical lattice clocks. This innovative approach significantly mitigated two primary sources of error, which include the effects generated by the laser light used to trap the atoms and the interactions that occur when atoms collide with one another due to tight packing.

Notably, NIST and JILA physicist Jun Ye has remarked that this clock exhibits such precision that it can detect minute effects predicted by theoretical frameworks such as general relativity, even at a microscopic level. This development appears to be advancing the limits of what is achievable in the field of timekeeping.

In summary, general relativity represents Einstein's theoretical framework that explains how gravity results from the curvature of space and time. A fundamental prediction of general relativity indicates that time is influenced by gravitational forces, with stronger gravitational fields resulting in slower passage of time.

This novel clock design enables the detection of relativistic effects on timekeeping at a submillimeter scale, which is approximately equivalent to the thickness of a single human hair. Adjusting the clock’s position by such a minute distance is sufficient for researchers to identify a slight alteration in the flow of time, attributable to the effects of gravity.

Ultimately, this capability to observe the implications of general relativity at the microscopic scale can serve to significantly bridge the existing divide between the quantum realm and the large-scale phenomena that are explained by general relativity.

input: UV-C has been used for decades to rid air, water and surfaces of bacteria and viruses, with the applications backed by scientific research. However, with its sudden widespread application toward N95 masks, the technology was catapulted into uncharted territory, where little was known about how to apply it effectively. To better understand how UV-C could be used to disinfect N95 masks, NIST partnered with UV-Concepts, a manufacturer of UV-C systems not currently marketed for N95 disinfection, and ResInnova Laboratories, an antimicrobial testing company. The authors of the new study fastened N95 masks to racks within a UV-Concepts system, an enclosure lined with 19 UV-C lamps and coated in a reflective surface, and blasted them with UV light for three minutes, 10 times each. The team doused some of the masks with a solution laden with OC43, a human coronavirus and close relative of the COVID-19-causing virus. After the irradiation, they summed up the number of remaining active OC43 viruses and found that the method adequately disinfected the N95 masks throughout their three layers, even inactivating up to 100% of viral particles in some areas. "The wavelength of UV-C used for inactivation of a virus is not known to produce chemicals, such as ozone, that could damage the plastic in the N95 masks. But it is still important to check," said NIST researcher John Wright, a co-author of the study.

According to Helgeson, the researchers managed to separate the cumulative effects of belonging to the HUGO group from other associated factors, yet they acknowledged that the current dataset did not allow for a definitive identification of the mechanism through which HUGO affiliation heightens relative impacts. This comprehensive study highlights the complex interactions between trees, seasons, and signal attenuation, providing valuable insights into the factors influencing wireless communication.

Additionally, the lasers that generate these colors tend to be large, expensive, and energy-intensive, which effectively restricts the application of these quantum technologies to a limited number of specialized laboratories.

Furthermore, by integrating lasers into circuits on microchips, researchers aim to make quantum technologies more affordable and portable, which can facilitate the realization of their significant potential.

The new photonics chip developed by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) can be likened to a layered structure. NIST physicists Papp and Grant Brodnik, along with their collaborators, began with a standard silicon wafer that was coated with silicon dioxide, a glass-like substance, and lithium niobate, which is recognized as a nonlinear material capable of altering the color of incoming light.

In addition, the researchers incorporated metal components to enable electrical control of the circuits, facilitating the conversion of one color of light into others. They also established other interfaces between metal and lithium niobate that permitted the rapid modulation of light within the circuits, a critical functionality for efficient data processing and high-speed signal routing.

Ultimately, a second nonlinear material known as tantalum pentoxide, or tantala, served as an advanced enhancement to the chip. Tantalum pentoxide can modify light in remarkable ways, accepting a single color from a laser and producing a spectrum of visible colors along with a broad array of infrared wavelengths. Papp and his team have dedicated years to devising methods for fabricating circuits from tantala without applying heat, which enables the deposition of this material onto other surfaces without causing damage. This innovative approach indicates a significant advancement in the development of portable quantum technologies.

Theorists have predicted three distinct possibilities, or phases, that may occur when the superconductor experiences a quench. To illustrate this concept, Thompson compares the system to a large group of square dancers. Initially, everyone remains in sync and keeps to the beat of the music. Subsequently, some individuals may become tired while others begin to move too quickly, which causes collisions and results in a mosh pit. This scenario represents Phase I, in which superconductivity appears to collapse. During Phase II, the dancers lose the beat but still manage to remain in sync, and superconductivity tends to survive the quench. Scientists have been able to observe and study these two phases.

Furthermore, researchers have never observed a long-predicted third phase in which the superconductivity of the system oscillates over time. In this phase, the dancers may move somewhat faster or slower at various moments, but no collisions occur. Consequently, the system can often function as a weaker superconductor at certain times and a stronger superconductor at others. Until now, no one had been able to observe that third phase.

Additionally, in collaboration with Rey's theory group, Thompson's team at JILA laser-cooled and loaded strontium atoms into an optical cavity, which is a space featuring highly reflective mirrors at either end. Laser light tends to bounce back and forth millions of times before some light leaks out at one end.

Notably, the light within the cavity mediated interactions between the atoms, which caused them to align into a superposition state, meaning they exist in both the excited and ground state simultaneously, and to lock in phase, similar to the behavior of Cooper pairs, as Rey explains.

Ultimately, scientists can quench the system using lasers, and by measuring the light that leaks out, they may learn how the energy gap has changed over time. Through this quantum superconductor simulation, they were able to observe all three dynamic phases for the first time. In essence, this experiment provided the first observation of all three predicted phases.

It is worth noting that laser systems referred to as frequency combs are capable of identifying specific molecules with exceptional accuracy and sensitivity. This capability extends from the monitoring of greenhouse gas concentrations to the detection of COVID in breath samples. Furthermore, these systems appear to handle targets as simple as carbon dioxide and as complex as monoclonal antibodies. This highlights the broad analytical potential of frequency comb technology across diverse scientific applications.

Additionally, frequency combs have generally been subject to limitations regarding the speed at which they can capture high-speed processes. Such processes may include hypersonic propulsion or the folding of proteins into their final three-dimensional shapes. This suggests that the temporal resolution of conventional frequency comb systems has tended to constrain their application to rapid dynamic phenomena.

Notably, researchers at the National Institute of Standards and Technology, Toptica Photonics AG and the University of Colorado Boulder have reached a significant development. They have produced a frequency comb system that can detect the presence of specific molecules in a sample every 20 nanoseconds, which is equivalent to billionths of a second. Ultimately, this represents a substantial improvement in the temporal capabilities of frequency comb detection.

Furthermore, this new capability may allow researchers to use frequency combs for a better understanding of split-second intermediate steps in fast-moving processes. Such processes can range from the workings of hypersonic jet engines to the chemical reactions between enzymes that regulate cell growth. The research team announced its results in a paper published in Nature Photonics, according to the available information.

In their experiment, the researchers made use of the now-common dual-frequency comb setup, which contains two laser beams that work together. This configuration serves to detect the spectrum of colors that a molecule absorbs. It is worth noting that most dual-frequency comb setups involve two femtosecond lasers, which send out a pair of ultrafast pulses in lockstep.

Additionally, in this new experiment, the researchers employed a simpler and cheaper setup known as electro-optic combs. In this arrangement, a single continuous beam of light first undergoes a splitting into two separate beams. Then, an electronic modulator produces electric fields that alter each light beam, shaping them into the individual teeth of a frequency comb. Each tooth is a specific color or frequency of light that can then be absorbed by a molecule of interest. Ultimately, this approach appears to offer a more accessible means of achieving high-speed molecular detection.

The recently reported research signifies an initial phase within a broader initiative known as the True Becquerel (TrueBq) project, which aims to revolutionize the monitoring and characterization of radioactivity. The designation of the project is derived from the unit employed for measuring radioactive decay, thereby paying homage to the French physicist Henri Becquerel, recognized for his discovery of radioactivity.

Furthermore, the overarching objective of the TrueBq project is to create a measurement system that can accommodate an extensive variety of radioactive materials, including intricate mixtures. This system will integrate a precision mass balance mechanism with the TES device to assess the massic activity of radioactive substances with a level of accuracy that has not been previously achieved.

Notably, this innovative approach signifies a considerable advancement over conventional workflows, which may frequently involve multiple methodologies, chemical processing, and the utilization of chemical tracers and standards. By refining the measurement process, the TrueBq project is anticipated to diminish the duration necessary for analysis while concurrently enhancing accuracy.

The advancements fostered by the TrueBq project have the potential to significantly improve the ability of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to effectively serve its clientele. NIST provides a diverse array of measurement services that are customer-focused, which encompass calibrations, standard reference materials (SRMs), and proficiency testing. Each of these services may benefit from the more efficient workflow, additional data, and reduced uncertainties that the TrueBq technology is expected to provide.

While the current emphasis of TrueBq is on enhancing measurements within NIST, the researchers maintain long-term aspirations for the technology’s applications. In the future, they envision the development of more portable and user-friendly iterations of the system that could be utilized beyond NIST for critical needs in various fields, including medicine, environmental remediation, and nuclear waste management. Ultimately, these innovations could lead to transformative changes in how radioactivity is monitored and managed.

Directly printing these patterns on such surfaces is tricky, so scientists transfer prints. There are flexible tapes and plastics that can do the job (like using putty to pick up newsprint), but these solids can still have trouble conforming to sharp curves and corners when the print is laid back down. They could also leave behind plastics or other chemicals that could be hard to remove or be unsafe for biomedical uses.

There are liquid techniques, where the transfer material is floated on the surface of water and the target surface is pushed through it. But that can be tricky too; with a freely flowing liquid it can be hard to place the print precisely where you want it on a new surface.

When dissolved in a small amount of water, this sugar mixture can be poured over micropatterns on a flat surface. Once the water evaporates, the candy hardens and can be lifted away with the pattern embedded. The candy with the print is then placed over the new surface and melted. The sugar/corn syrup combination maintains a high viscosity as it melts, letting the pattern maintain its arrangement as it flows over curves and edges. Then, using water, the sugar can be washed away, leaving just the pattern behind.

Using this technique, called REFLEX (REflow-driven FLExible Xfer), microcircuit patterns could be transferred like a stencil to allow scientists or manufacturers to etch and fill the materials they need in the right places. Or, patterned materials could be transferred from their original chip onto fibers or microbeads for potential biomedical or microrobotics studies, or over sharp or curved surfaces within new devices.

Recent interviews, along with analyses of test results and physical evidence conducted by the National Institute of Standards and Technology, appear to reinforce the preliminary findings that the 2021 failure of the Champlain Towers South building may have originated in its pool deck rather than within the tower itself. Furthermore, the investigation has identified various indications of the building’s distress that could be observed in the weeks leading up to the partial collapse in Surfside, Florida.

Notably, investigative lead Judith Mitrani-Reiser and co-lead Glenn Bell provided an update on the NIST investigation during a virtual meeting of the National Construction Safety Team Advisory Committee. Their presentation summarized the ongoing activities of the investigation and reiterated preliminary findings that had been shared in earlier updates. This included an extensive video that was released in June 2025 and emphasized substantial progress in the failure analysis since the previous update in June.

In addition, Bell described the team’s current efforts to enhance its evaluations of potential failure initiation scenarios by utilizing computer simulations, which are supported by large-scale structural testing and the documented evidence of the building’s distress observed in the weeks preceding the collapse. The team has also been refining its analysis regarding the impacts of steel reinforcement corrosion, concrete shrinkage, and inadequately constructed construction joints within the pool deck slab.

Moreover, Bell elaborated on how the results obtained from large-scale structural testing, in conjunction with computer analyses of video footage recorded at the time of the collapse, can often illuminate the progression of the collapse as it transitioned from the pool deck into and throughout the tower. In summary, the NIST investigation is making significant strides in understanding the factors that contributed to the collapse of the Champlain Towers South building.

Many of the most innovative and beneficial inventions can often find their inspiration in nature. For example, the aerodynamic design of the Shinkansen bullet train in Japan is modeled after the kingfisher bird, illustrating how natural forms can lead to technological advancements. Similarly, the creation of Velcro by a Swiss engineer stemmed from the observation of burrs that attach to a dog's fur, which exhibit tiny hooks.

Furthermore, scientists have recently turned their attention to a small underwater predator known as the mantis shrimp for additional inspiration. This colorful invertebrate possesses remarkable strength, capable of cracking clamshells with a force comparable to that of a .22 caliber bullet, largely due to its unique exoskeletal structures which contribute to its surprising durability.

Researchers at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) have created synthetic versions of these structures and conducted experiments to assess their performance under impact conditions by using microprojectiles. They found that modifications to specific characteristics of these structures influenced their capacity to absorb and dissipate impact energy effectively.

This research represents a significant advancement in the field of bioinspired materials design, with potential applications in aerospace. As NIST materials research engineer Edwin Chan stated, the insights gained may assist in improving spacecraft resilience against micrometeoroid impacts and in protecting orbiting satellites from debris collisions.

The idea for this research originated from Sujin Lee, who joined NIST as a National Research Council (NRC) postdoctoral fellow. Lee sought to understand the mechanisms preventing the mantis shrimp's appendage from breaking as it exerted force to smash the shells of other organisms. Chan shared this interest, leading them to collaboratively develop a research project focused on this phenomenon.

It is worth noting that while it appears the mantis shrimp does not experience injury when striking, this observation is closely tied to the microscopic "Bouligand structures" present in the shrimp's exoskeleton, which may play a crucial role in its remarkable impact resistance.

The National Institute of Standards and Technology, alongside its collaborators, has achieved a significant advancement in timing technology through the development of compact chips that effectively convert light into microwaves. This innovative chip has the potential to enhance various applications, including Global Positioning System accuracy, the quality of telephone and internet connections, the precision of radar and sensing systems, as well as other technologies that rely on high-precision timing and communication.

Furthermore, this technology addresses an issue known as timing jitter, which refers to slight, random fluctuations in the timing of microwave signals. This phenomenon can be likened to a musician striving to maintain a consistent beat; similarly, the timing of these signals may occasionally deviate. The researchers have succeeded in minimizing these variations to an extraordinarily small interval of 15 femtoseconds, which represents a substantial improvement over conventional microwave sources. This enhancement results in significantly more stable and precise signals, potentially augmenting radar sensitivity, increasing the accuracy of analog-to-digital converters, and improving the clarity of astronomical images acquired through coordinated telescopes.

Moreover, what distinguishes this demonstration is the compact design of the components that generate these signals. For the first time, researchers have succeeded in miniaturizing a system that previously occupied a tabletop into a compact chip comparable in size to a digital camera memory card. The reduction of timing jitter at this smaller scale not only diminishes power consumption but also enhances usability in everyday devices.

At present, several components essential to this technology remain external to the chip while researchers assess their effectiveness. Ultimately, the overarching objective of this project is to achieve the integration of all necessary components—such as lasers, modulators, detectors, and optical amplifiers—onto a single chip, which would represent a significant milestone in the advancement of timing technology.

Researchers at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) have identified a potential source of error that may arise when utilizing acoustic waves to measure the properties of fluids, including blood. This discovery raises the possibility of achieving more accurate diagnostic tests for specific types of blood cancer, as well as enhancing the precision of blood cell sorting techniques.

Acoustic waves, which encompass ultrasound, generate regions characterized by alternating high and low pressure within various media, including air, water, and fluids such as blood. Researchers frequently employ these waves to investigate the properties of small volumes of “microfluids,” which are typically confined within vessels no wider than the thickness of a credit card.

In order to assess the properties of a microfluid blood sample, researchers utilize ultrasound waves that possess a known frequency and energy. These waves are generated just beneath the bottom wall of the vessel by a piezoelectric crystal, which is a material capable of converting electrical flow into acoustic waves. The waves that successfully penetrate the fluid predominantly travel along the bottom surface, situated between the liquid and the wall. Upon exiting the fluid, scientists are able to detect any loss of energy or frequency shift in the waves. Such measurements can provide insights that are vital for evaluating blood flow, which may become dangerously slow in some patients suffering from blood cancer. Furthermore, acoustic waves can also be employed to sort cells within whole blood samples.

Biomedical researchers and oncologists exhibit a particular interest in quantifying the viscosity of a microfluid. Viscosity, which is sometimes described as a fluid’s thickness, is more accurately defined as the measure of a fluid's resistance to shear. For instance, molasses demonstrates a significantly greater resistance to shear compared to water, being approximately 5,000 times more viscous, which accounts for its notably slow-pouring behavior. Ultimately, these findings may lead to improved understanding and applications in the diagnosis and treatment of blood-related conditions.

These devices, developed by Qunnect, sent beams of “reference” light through the fiber and, at the other end, measured how their polarization states had been transformed. The exact inverse of these transformations were then applied to the experimental photons, keeping them entangled.

The scientists managed to transmit 1,500 entangled photons per second, a respectable rate though one that would need to improve for quantum networks to become practical. Over a 24-hour period, the researchers were able to distribute entangled photons 92.8% of the time, needing only 7.2% of the time for correcting polarizations. A statistical test confirmed that the photons detected at each end of the fiber had indeed remained entangled.

The experiment did not break a record for long-distance entanglement; a European group in 2022 distributed entangled photons over 248 kilometers of underground fiber. But the new study stands out for how much fiber was above ground and exposed to influences that real-world quantum networks will have to contend with.

“I would call this a stress test of quantum networking systems,” says Yicheng Shi, a physicist at NIST and the study’s lead author. “We put this to an extreme test in an environment that’s really noisy. Amazingly, it turned out it still worked. It’s a demonstration that quantum networking protocols can work in real-world environments.”

For airliners, cargo ships, nuclear power plants, and other critical technologies, strength and durability are essential requirements. This highlights why many of these systems contain a remarkably strong and corrosion-resistant alloy known as 17-4 precipitation hardening (PH) stainless steel. Now, for the first time ever, it appears that 17-4 PH steel can be consistently 3D-printed while still retaining its favorable characteristics.

Additionally, a team of researchers from the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), the University of Wisconsin-Madison, and Argonne National Laboratory has identified particular 17-4 steel compositions that, when printed, match the properties of the conventionally manufactured version. Furthermore, the researchers’ strategy, described in the journal Additive Manufacturing, is based on high-speed data about the printing process that they obtained using high-energy X-rays from a particle accelerator.

Notably, the new findings could help producers of 17-4 PH parts use 3D printing to reduce costs and increase their manufacturing flexibility. In essence, the approach used to examine the material in this study may also set the table for a better understanding of how to print other types of materials and predict their properties and performance. Ultimately, despite its advantages over conventional manufacturing, 3D-printing of some materials can produce results that are too inconsistent for certain applications. It is worth noting that printing metal is particularly complex, in part because of how quickly temperatures shift during the process.

“When you think about additive manufacturing of metals, we are essentially welding millions of tiny, powdered particles into one piece with a high-powered source such as a laser, melting them into a liquid and cooling them into a solid,” said NIST physicist Fan Zhang, a study co-author. “But the cooling rate is high, sometimes higher than one million degrees Celsius per second, and this extreme nonequilibrium condition creates a set of extraordinary measurement challenges.” Ultimately, these findings suggest that 3D printing of 17-4 PH steel can be made more reliable, which may help manufacturers adopt the technique more widely.

His research team focuses on the utilization of optical tweezers to create precisely controlled quantum systems, specifically those consisting of ordered arrays of single alkaline-earth atoms. One notable project for which Kaufman is recognized involves enhancing the effectiveness of optical atomic clocks through the application of optical tweezers. Optical atomic clocks measure time based on the movement of electrons within an atom. It is worth noting that the accuracy of these clocks relies on the precise arrangement and preparation of the atoms to prevent interference that could disrupt time measurement. This process often requires significant time and effort, and the coherence duration during which the atoms can effectively function as a clock is typically limited to a few seconds before a reset is necessary.

Kaufman and his research team employ optical tweezers to trap strontium atoms quickly and efficiently, facilitating the construction of an optical atomic clock. Furthermore, the tweezers enable the team to manage interactions between atoms, allowing for the preparation of entangled atomic states, a quantum phenomenon that permits individual atoms to behave collectively. Through this innovative approach, Kaufman’s group has achieved extended coherence times, enabling the clock to operate continuously for durations between 30 and 50 seconds. Additionally, they successfully prepared the first entangled "Bell states" within a neutral-atom optical clock, a development that may enhance the tick rate of the clock and, consequently, improve its precision. This highlights the researchers' goal of transitioning their experimental findings from a laboratory setting into a practical public service initiative.

To achieve this objective, researchers at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), in collaboration with colleagues at the University of Colorado Boulder, developed the Colorado University Randomness Beacon, known as CURBy. This innovative system produces random numbers automatically and disseminates them daily through a publicly accessible website, allowing universal access.

At the core of this service lies the NIST-operated Bell test, which generates results that are genuinely random. This randomness serves as a foundational element that the researchers then process and enhance into the random numbers released by the beacon.

The Bell test involves measuring pairs of entangled photons, which exhibit correlated properties regardless of the distances separating them. While the measurement of an individual particle yields a random outcome, the correlation of the paired properties exceeds the limitations established by classical physics, thus providing a method for researchers to validate the randomness of the results. This phenomenon, described by Einstein as “spooky action at a distance,” exemplifies quantum nonlocality.

This initiative represents the first random number generator service that derives its numbers from quantum nonlocality, and it also stands as the most transparent source of random numbers to date. The results produced by CURBy are certifiable and traceable to a degree that surpasses existing conventional random number generators.

Shalm further elaborated that CURBy is among the first publicly accessible services that demonstrates a provable quantum advantage, marking a significant milestone in the field. He emphasized that the quality and origin of the random bits generated can be certified in a manner that is not achievable with traditional random number generators. Ultimately, this advancement indicates a promising development in the reliability and accessibility of random number generation.

Each year, it is estimated that hundreds of meteorites, which are rocky remnants from the initial formation of the solar system, may strike Earth, bringing with them minerals, metals, and water. The analysis of the mineral-rich deposits and crevices within these meteorites not only appears to unveil the early history of planet formation but also may offer insights into how the young Earth acquired water and other vital components necessary for sustaining life.

Furthermore, researchers at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) have recently combined two complementary imaging techniques, specifically X-ray imaging and neutron imaging, allowing for an in-depth examination of these geological remnants. Neutron imaging tends to be particularly effective for detecting water and other compounds that contain hydrogen, as neutrons can readily bounce off hydrogen atoms. In contrast, X-ray imaging is generally more adept at identifying deposits of heavier elements, such as iron and nickel, because X-rays primarily interact with the numerous electrons present in heavier atoms.

Importantly, neither of these imaging techniques tends to cause significant harm or alteration to the meteorites, which sets them apart from other chemical analysis methods that often necessitate cutting thin slices from the rocks. Although each imaging method has been utilized individually in previous studies, this research team appears to be among the first to employ both techniques concurrently, enabling the creation of combined X-ray and neutron-beam images. In summary, the integration of these imaging methods represents a promising advancement in the study of meteorites and their potential contributions to our understanding of Earth’s history.

A Josephson junction consists of layers of superconducting materials divided by a slender insulating film.

These hazard maps were the first to account for the size of the building. The bigger a building is, the more likely it is to be struck by a tornado, and so including building size significantly improves the accuracy of the tornado risk assessment.

The process of updating a building code takes four main steps: research the issue, develop a standard, update the model building code, and pass local laws.

To perform the research step, NIST and its collaborators used wind tunnels, historical tornado data, and carefully examined debris to figure out how to design buildings to resist tornadoes. One thing they discovered is that not all wind is the same. “Tornadic winds are very different from straight-line winds,” explains Levitan.

For one thing, tornadic winds have higher windspeeds close to the ground and rapidly change direction. These winds can pull and push on a building in ways it wasn’t designed for. For example, wind flowing quickly over a building can decrease the air pressure above the roof and create a strong upward force.

It’s the same principle that lifts airplanes into the air. At high wind speeds, aerodynamics are as important for buildings as they are for airplane wings.

That uplift force can be made even stronger by updrafts. Near the center of a tornado, winds blow at an upward angle. A NIST-funded team simulated updrafts using a wind tunnel to blow air over miniature houses and found that updrafts tend to suck roofs upwards with more force than straight winds.

“Normally, buildings are designed to keep the roof from falling down due to gravity,” said Levitan. “Engineers designing for tornadoes should also keep the roof from ‘falling up.’” If a roof peels off, it could cause the entire structure to collapse.

input: Since the 1990s, individuals who create content for the web have made use of HTML, which enables the adjustment of the appearance, behavior, and arrangement of displayed text in accordance with its surrounding context. If you have ever altered the dimensions of a webpage and observed its text repositioning itself smoothly to fit within the boundaries of the new rectangle, you are witnessing a capability that readers with visual impairments desire. Modern HTML contains extensions that not only permit this capacity for text to re-flow but also allow mathematical formulas to be read aloud by machine for those who cannot read the text themselves. These characteristics make HTML well suited to the creation of accessible text, but for many years there was no effective method for converting LaTeX into HTML. This situation presented a difficulty for Miller when he required a means of bringing the more than 1,000 pages of NIST's venerable Handbook of Mathematical Functions into the digital realm. At the time, certain programs purported to convert LaTeX to webpages, but none of them worked well enough, according to his statement. He figured that they should attempt to make their own. The resulting NIST tool was LaTeXML, which reads a LaTeX source file and constructs a representation of the document that it can then turn into HTML. LaTeXML was the key to creating the online Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, and several years later the managers of a major online resource realized that it could be of assistance to them as well.

Aiming to enhance the technology for first responders to track their locations, the First Responder Smart Tracking Challenge (FRST) has successfully concluded its final phase.

Led by Indiana University and funded by an $8 million cooperative agreement from the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), FRST addresses the crucial need for improved tracking capabilities in complex indoor environments where GPS often falls short.

Six teams vied for top ranking in the development of 3D tracking technology, a critical innovation aimed at improving the safety and efficiency of emergency response operations.

“Emergency response organizations across the country are begging and budgeting for this type of technology and are just waiting to get their hands on it,” said Gary Howarth, program officer for NIST’s Public Safety Communications Research Division, which oversees the FRST challenge.

The competition, which started in March 2022, included five phases, culminating in a final live testing phase at the Muscatatuck Urban Training Center in south-central Indiana. There, first responders from across Indiana, including the Columbus Fire Department, Indianapolis Fire Department and Bedford Police Department, faced various challenging scenarios, including smoke-filled rooms, darkness, stairs, ladders and tunnels, replicating real-world emergency conditions.

“All six of the finalist teams did well, and they each have unique offerings for the public safety community,” said Sonny Kirkley, director of the FRST Challenge at Indiana University. “While the judges did rate the teams, in many ways all six finalists were successful and have a real ability to bring a product to market from this competition.”

In the ongoing evolution of wireless communications, researchers at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) have made significant strides in resolving a critical dispute regarding transmission performance across various bands of the millimeter-wave (mmWave) spectrum, which is increasingly targeted for high-speed, data-intensive 5G systems. 

Furthermore, as wireless systems transition to the mmWave spectrum that operates within the range of 10-100 gigahertz (GHz), operators are often drawn to lower bands, particularly those around 3 GHz, which are already utilized by earlier 5G systems and are less congested. It may be the case that system operators are influenced by a conventional understanding that suggests higher frequencies may experience greater signal loss due to their smaller wavelengths, leading to reduced effective antenna sizes. However, previous measurements conducted by various organizations have shown discrepancies regarding the validity of this assertion.

In response to this uncertainty, NIST researchers developed an innovative methodology aimed at measuring frequency effects, selecting the 26.5-40 GHz band as a representative example for their investigations. After conducting extensive laboratory studies and examining two real-world environments, the results acquired by NIST provided confirmation that the primary signal path, characterized by a clear “line of sight” between the transmitter and receiver, does not appear to vary by frequency. This finding aligns with a generally accepted principle in traditional wireless systems, yet it had not been substantiated for the mmWave spectrum until now. The team's findings are detailed in a newly published paper.

In addition, the researchers observed that signal losses in secondary paths, which occur when transmissions are reflected, bent, or diffused into clusters of reflections, can exhibit some degree of variation by frequency, depending on the nature of the path. Notably, reflective paths, which are identified as the second strongest and play a crucial role in sustaining connectivity, experienced only minor reductions in signal strength at higher frequencies. Conversely, weaker bent and diffuse paths tended to experience slightly greater losses. Until this point, the influence of frequency on such multipath effects had not been clearly understood. 

In summary, this research contributes valuable insights into the performance characteristics of mmWave systems, potentially guiding future developments in wireless communication technologies.

Ozone and formaldehyde have the capacity to absorb ultraviolet light. In this context, researchers ascertain the concentration of these chemicals by directing ultraviolet light through a sample and quantifying the extent of light absorption at designated wavelengths.

Furthermore, the measurement of ultrafine particles is conducted through a technique known as scanning mobility particle sizing. Initially, the air sample is passed through an X-ray field, which imparts a predictable electric charge to the particles present in the air. This charge facilitates the manipulation of the particles using electric fields, with larger particles experiencing a stronger charge and consequently being propelled more vigorously. Subsequently, electric fields are employed to eliminate the larger particles from the air, isolating the smaller particles of interest. At this stage, the particles are often too diminutive to count effectively, necessitating their passage through a cool steam bath. This process allows the particles to absorb moisture and expand to a size sufficient to scatter laser light. By quantifying the frequency of laser light scattering, researchers can estimate the number of ultrafine particles present in the sample.

It is important to note that a new testing method was published by ASTM International, which is an organization focused on the development of standards. The National Institute of Standards and Technology played a significant role in the formulation of the new standard, which involved the collaboration of various stakeholders and the execution of fundamental research over a four-year period. The newly established testing method is characterized as a consensus standard, indicating that it was developed with the contributions of air quality researchers, manufacturers of air cleaning devices, testing laboratories, and the general public. This approach reflects a proactive effort to leverage existing technologies for innovative solutions in critical situations.

NISTCHO represents a groundbreaking development as a first-of-its-kind living reference material created by NIST, which will be accessible to researchers globally. It is worth noting that, according to NIST biologist Brad O’Dell, the majority of antibody-producing cell lines that closely resemble those utilized in large-scale clinical manufacturing are often unavailable for open-access research due to significant investments in intellectual property. This limitation may restrict many researchers from obtaining a cell line that accurately represents those employed by the industry. The introduction of NISTCHO intends to address this issue, with the collaboration of MilliporeSigma and NIIMBL assisting NIST in making industry-grade monoclonal antibody-producing cells publicly available.

Furthermore, the subsequent phase of this project involves the development of a NISTCHO reference material (RM). This process will draw on the insights gained from the NISTCHO research-grade transfectant material (RGTM) alongside NIST’s expertise in measurement science. In essence, creating a NISTCHO RM will necessitate meticulous measurement of NISTCHO itself, as well as the determination of specific properties or values, such as DNA sequences or the concentration of molecules. These measurements will enable NIST to provide accurate reports, including descriptions of potential sources of error or uncertainty. With these additional measurements, the NISTCHO RM may facilitate calibration and standardization, thereby supporting both basic and applied research and development.

Ultimately, while the release of the reference material is still a few years away, individuals interested in studying the NISTCHO RGTM or seeking further information are encouraged to visit the NISTCHO project page for more details.

Manufacturers producing new foams may also find it beneficial to utilize the reference materials when verifying that their products are free from PFAS.

Wildfires move fast. They can reduce communities to ash in a matter of hours. To save as many lives as possible, officials must have an evacuation and shelter plan in place before an actual wildfire threatens their community.

To support planning efforts, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has just updated its guidance on preparing for wildfires based on the latest research and community feedback. Called Wildland-Urban Interface Fire Evacuation and Sheltering Considerations: Assessment, Planning, and Execution (ESCAPE), the report is now available on the NIST website.

This report is especially relevant to the estimated 115 million people in the U.S. who live in areas of high wildfire risk. Many wildfires do not stay confined in remote forests. They can invade neighborhoods and destroy homes, sometimes with only minutes of advance warning. Traditional approaches to evacuation are less effective during such aggressive fires, which can outrun emergency notifications and cut off roads before residents can escape.

“This report can save thousands of lives because it offers a science-backed approach to planning for worst-case scenarios,” said lead author Alexander Maranghides, a fire protection engineer at NIST. “We need a rigorous approach because we have seen, time and time again, that these fires are unforgiving.”

For more than 120 years, NIST has performed research in fire safety and fire science, including many studies of fires at the wildland-urban interface. NIST frequently investigates past fires to learn lessons that will help save lives in future fires.
