One of the initial steps in addressing health concerns involves the careful measurement of relevant substances. For firefighters, a notable health concern arises from the presence of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), commonly referred to as “forever chemicals” due to their resistance to natural degradation in the environment. Since the year 2021, researchers at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) have engaged in a systematic examination of PFAS concentrations within firefighter equipment. In their most recent report, which was published this week, they investigated the impact of wear and tear on PFAS levels in firefighting hoods and gloves utilized in structural fire situations, as well as in gear designed for forest or “wildland” fires. The findings indicated that wear and tear significantly increased PFAS levels in hoods and gloves, while a decrease was observed in wildland gear.

Firefighters don special protective clothing to ensure their safety while performing their duties. Given that water is a conductor of heat, it becomes essential for these garments to maintain dryness for firefighters. PFAS, which have also found applications in nonstick cookware and rain-resistant garments, are known for their remarkable ability to repel liquids, which is why they are sometimes employed to treat firefighter clothing for enhanced moisture resistance.

Furthermore, exposure to elevated concentrations of PFAS has been associated with an increased risk of cancer, and awareness regarding these hazards appears to be on the rise. Research studies suggest that firefighters may experience higher rates of cancer compared to the general population, although it is important to note that this correlation may not solely be attributed to PFAS exposure.

In addition, Congress mandated NIST to conduct measurements of PFAS levels in firefighter gear through the provisions of the 2021 National Defense Authorization Act. Rick Davis, the project leader responsible for NIST’s reports on PFAS in firefighter gear, stated, “At that time, there were no measurements of how much PFAS was in this equipment. Making those measurements is a crucial starting point for understanding and addressing the problem.” In conclusion, the ongoing research and measurement efforts are essential for addressing the health implications associated with PFAS in firefighter equipment.

The effectiveness of a powerful computer is diminished if its output cannot be interpreted or if it cannot be reprogrammed for various tasks. Individuals involved in the design of quantum computers encounter these obstacles, and a newly developed device may offer solutions.

This device, presented by researchers at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), comprises two superconducting quantum bits, or qubits, which serve as the equivalent of logic bits in a classical computer's processing unit. The core of this innovative approach is a "toggle switch" mechanism that links the qubits to a component known as a "readout resonator," which is capable of interpreting the output generated from the qubits' computations.

This toggle switch can transition between different states, thereby modifying the strength of the connections between the qubits and the readout resonator. When the switch is in the off position, the three components remain isolated from one another. Conversely, when the switch is activated to connect the two qubits, they are able to interact and execute calculations. Upon completion of these calculations, the toggle switch can facilitate the connection of either qubit to the readout resonator in order to obtain the results.

The introduction of a programmable toggle switch significantly contributes to the reduction of noise, which is a prevalent issue in quantum computer circuits that complicates the ability of qubits to perform calculations and present results with clarity. 

Ray Simmonds, a physicist at NIST and one of the authors of the research, explained that the objective is to maintain optimal conditions for the qubits so that they can calculate without interference, while also ensuring that their outputs can be accessed when needed. This device architecture is designed to safeguard the qubits and holds the potential to enhance the precision of measurements that are essential for the construction of quantum information processors utilizing qubits. Ultimately, these developments may lead to significant advancements in the field of quantum computing.

What good is a powerful computer if you can’t read its output? Or readily reprogram it to do different jobs? People who design quantum computers face these challenges, and a new device may make them easier to solve.

The device, introduced by a team of scientists at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), includes two superconducting quantum bits, or qubits, which are a quantum computer’s analogue to the logic bits in a classical computer’s processing chip. The heart of this new strategy relies on a “toggle switch” device that connects the qubits to a circuit called a “readout resonator” that can read the output of the qubits’ calculations.

This toggle switch can be flipped into different states to adjust the strength of the connections between the qubits and the readout resonator. When toggled off, all three elements are isolated from each other. When the switch is toggled on to connect the two qubits, they can interact and perform calculations. Once the calculations are complete, the toggle switch can connect either of the qubits and the readout resonator to retrieve the results.

Having a programmable toggle switch goes a long way toward reducing noise, a common problem in quantum computer circuits that makes it difficult for qubits to make calculations and show their results clearly.

“The goal is to keep the qubits happy so that they can calculate without distractions, while still being able to read them out when we want to,” said Ray Simmonds, a NIST physicist and one of the paper’s authors. “This device architecture helps protect the qubits and promises to improve our ability to make the high-fidelity measurements required to build quantum information processors out of qubits.”

input: The National Institute of Standards and Technology, which operates within the United States Department of Commerce, has released the Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework, also known as AI RMF 1.0. It is worth noting that this document is intended for voluntary use by organizations that are involved in designing, developing, deploying, or using artificial intelligence systems. Furthermore, its purpose is to assist such organizations in managing the numerous risks that are associated with artificial intelligence technologies. The framework was developed following a directive from Congress, which asked the National Institute of Standards and Technology to create it. Additionally, it was produced through close collaboration with both the private sector and the public sector. In essence, the framework is designed to adapt to the evolving artificial intelligence landscape as technologies continue to develop over time. It can often be applied by organizations in varying degrees and capacities, so that society may benefit from artificial intelligence technologies while also being protected from potential harms. Don Graves, who serves as the Deputy Secretary of Commerce, stated that this voluntary framework will help develop and deploy artificial intelligence technologies in ways that enable the United States, other nations, and organizations to enhance trustworthiness. Furthermore, it will help them manage risks based on democratic values, according to his statement. He also noted that it should accelerate innovation and growth in artificial intelligence while advancing civil rights, civil liberties, and equity for all, rather than restricting or damaging them. When compared with traditional software, artificial intelligence tends to pose a number of different risks. Notably, artificial intelligence systems are trained on data that can change over time, sometimes significantly and unexpectedly, which can affect the systems in ways that may be difficult to understand. Additionally, these systems are socio-technical in nature, which means they are influenced by societal dynamics and human behavior. Ultimately, artificial intelligence risks can emerge from the complex interplay of these technical and societal factors, and they can affect people's lives in situations ranging from experiences with online chatbots to the results of job and loan applications.

Throughout the 1990s, engineers acquired substantial insight into the manner in which structures respond to actual earthquakes, and the 1994 Northridge earthquake, which caused devastation across the greater Los Angeles area, serves as a notable example of this phenomenon. Consequently, building codes began to impose stringent requirements regarding the degree to which buildings may sway during seismic events, and this measure is commonly known as story drift.

Steel columns in multistory buildings, which possess cross sections shaped like a capital "I," tend to perform well when supporting the downward forces created by the weight of the floors and roof resting upon them. However, a shaking ground can often introduce additional forces in all directions, and this may potentially cause columns to sway laterally, thereby contributing to story drift. Before 1994, the middle part of columns' I-shaped cross sections, which is known as the web, was often relatively short in buildings with steel frames. Since that time, however, building designers have satisfied story drift requirements by selecting columns with longer, or deeper, and typically more slender webs in order to boost their lateral stiffness.

According to the current building standards, these deep columns were acceptable for use as long as their web dimensions did not surpass certain depth-to-width ratios, which are known as a slenderness limit and are intended to reduce the risk of columns losing their capability to carry weight during earthquakes, according to Harris. Nevertheless, some engineers were uncertain of how these columns would hold up against real earthquake motions.

When the slenderness limits were developed decades ago, engineers did not possess the capability of testing the seismic performance of full-scale columns like those actually used in buildings. Instead, they based the limits on reduced-scale model columns, which created some uncertainty about their effectiveness in reality. However, full-scale tests have since become possible with the availability of very powerful facilities, which are known as shake tables and are designed to put full-scale structural components through the seismic gauntlet.

Ultimately, the evolution of building codes and testing capabilities has progressively improved the understanding of how steel columns behave under seismic conditions.

While various research teams have successfully generated Airy beams using particles such as photons or electrons, the manipulation of neutrons into Airy beams presents a more significant challenge. Additionally, conventional lenses lack the capability to bend neutrons, and due to the absence of an electric charge, neutrons are unaffected by electric fields. Consequently, the research team recognized the necessity for an innovative approach.

To address this challenge, the researchers custom-designed a diffraction grating array, which consists of a silicon square approximately the size of the head of a pencil eraser, meticulously marked with fine lines. Furthermore, these lines are arranged into over six million squares measuring one micrometer each, with precise separations between them, allowing for the transformation of a standard beam of neutrons into an Airy beam.

In essence, although the concept of etching a silicon surface may appear straightforward, the process of determining the optimal arrangement of these etchings to create the Airy beam proved to be highly complex.

“It required years of effort to ascertain the precise dimensions necessary for the array,” remarked coauthor Dmitry Pushin, a faculty member at the Institute for Quantum Computing and a professor at the University of Waterloo. “While the actual carving of the grating at the University of Waterloo’s nanofabrication facility took only about 48 hours, the preparatory phase demanded several years of work by a postdoctoral fellow.”

Moreover, neutron Airy beams possess the potential to enhance the capabilities of neutron imaging facilities, as indicated by Huber. These beams may improve the resolution of scans or facilitate the creation of distinct focal points for closer examination of specific regions within objects, thereby advancing commonly utilized imaging methodologies such as neutron scattering and neutron diffraction.

Ultimately, one of the most intriguing prospects, according to Huber, involves the exploration of methods to integrate a neutron Airy beam with an alternative form of neutron beam.

While other research teams have created Airy beams out of other particles — such as photons or electrons — wrangling neutrons into Airy beams is more difficult. Lenses are powerless to bend them, and because neutrons have no charge, electric fields do not affect them. The team needed a new approach.

So the researchers custom-built a diffraction grating array — a square of silicon about the size of a pencil eraser’s head and scored with tiny lines. These lines, arranged into more than six million squares one micrometer across and separated at precise distances from one another, can split an ordinary beam of neutrons into an Airy beam.

While the idea of scratching up a piece of silicon is simple in principle, figuring out just how to arrange the scratches to produce the Airy beam was anything but.

“It took us years of work to figure out the correct dimensions for the array,” said coauthor Dmitry Pushin, IQC faculty and professor at the University of Waterloo. “We only needed about 48 hours to carve the grating at the University of Waterloo’s nanofabrication facility, but before that it took years of a postdoctoral fellow’s time to prepare.”

Neutron Airy beams could help neutron imaging facilities see better, Huber said. They would help increase the resolution of a scan or create different focal spots to look more closely at particular parts of objects, improving commonly used imaging techniques such as neutron scattering and neutron diffraction.

One of the most tantalizing possibilities, Huber said, would be to find ways to combine a neutron Airy beam with another type of neutron beam.

When measurements are taken, atoms may occupy one energy state at one moment and a different state at another, creating variability in results. Nevertheless, by utilizing entanglement, researchers can effectively manage and reduce this noise.

Moreover, when atoms become entangled, the state of one atom influences the states of all other atoms to which it is entangled. Consequently, the collaboration of dozens, or ideally hundreds, of entangled atoms serves to diminish noise levels, resulting in clearer and more reliable measurement signals. The remaining 11 qPCR methods assist in identifying fecal sources from humans, cattle, dogs, pigs, and birds. Ultimately, this comprehensive approach may enhance the accuracy of pollution source identification and fecal contamination assessment.

Color these scientists happy. An exotic gel they studied at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has an unexpected property: The material’s temperature determines which color of light can pass through it.

The material, which the research team calls “SeedGel,” already has shown promise as a multipurpose tool, with applications ranging from batteries to water filters to tissue engineering. The team’s new paper, appearing in Nature Communications, highlights the gel’s newfound capability as a temperature-sensitive light filter. Shine white light at the gel, and depending on the gel’s temperature, only a specific wavelength, or color, will pass through it. A temperature change of less than a tenth of a degree Celsius can be enough to alter the permitted wavelength, which can be any color in the visible range as well as parts of the ultraviolet and infrared.

“Our previous work showed that the SeedGel can transform from clear to opaque and back again, but we did not explore what it can do with color,” said Yun Liu, who is both a scientist at the NIST Center for Neutron Research (NCNR) and a professor at the University of Delaware. “Its ability to control color precisely was a new discovery.”

The team’s creation is distinct from others that may be familiar from the marketplace. Don’t confuse it with a mood ring, whose thermochromic liquid crystals change color with temperature. Neither is it a variation on photochromic sunglass lenses, which darken when exposed to ultraviolet rays. Instead, the gel functions as a temperature-sensitive gate for a particular wavelength of light.

Currently, the prevailing economic model is often described as “linear”; this refers to the process where plastics are manufactured from petroleum, utilized, and subsequently discarded in landfills or the environment. However, in a circular economy, it is suggested that plastics should be engineered to maintain their value through processes of repeated reuse, repair, and recycling, with disposal ideally being a last resort. Achieving a circular economy may necessitate the introduction of innovative manufacturing techniques, advanced chemical processes, and efficient plastic separation capabilities, in addition to fresh strategies for optimizing the design of plastic products and the cycling of plastics throughout the value chain.

Ultimately, Kathryn Beers, who leads NIST’s Circular Economy Program, has emphasized the pressing need for the workforce to consider materials, particularly plastics, and to design them for multiple uses rather than for single use. She has indicated that the goal is to enable these materials to have an extended lifespan, ideally leading to infinite reuse. Additionally, she has pointed out the necessity of educating various disciplines, highlighting a significant unmet demand at the undergraduate level. output:

input: In efforts to limit the transmission of disease while simultaneously preserving individual privacy, an interdisciplinary research team at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has designed and tested low-cost devices and methods that can detect when people or animals come into close contact with each other. Additionally, the wearable devices combine commercial Bluetooth radio hardware with cryptographic features developed by NIST. Furthermore, while the system may not always be reliable in estimating the distance between wearers, it is worth noting that the NIST system may be useful for research on how people and animals move through spaces and interact with one another. Moreover, the system may offer certain advantages over contact tracing that relies on smartphones, which tend to be used inconsistently in certain settings and may be less private. In essence, seventeen volunteers across ten households participated in the NIST study of system performance during normal activities. Additionally, the devices were either worn or placed within the house to collect data for at least one hour per day. Furthermore, researchers measured the strength of the radio signals received by the devices in order to estimate the distance between the volunteers. It is worth noting that they defined an encounter as occurring when device wearers came within two meters of each other for at least fifteen minutes, based on the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention definition of close contact. Moreover, participants were also asked to manually log when and for how long they thought they had experienced an encounter. Ultimately, the results showed some correlation between the strength of the radio signal received and the distance between wearers, but estimates were unreliable due to the effects of variables such as the direction the user was facing. Furthermore, there was also uncertainty about how to process trade-offs, such as how much of an error in distance was acceptable or whether close encounters were properly defined in terms of their possible effect on disease transmission. In essence, while the NIST system demonstrates potential, further refinement may be necessary to address the limitations identified in this study.

Ultimately, superconductivity represents a remarkable phenomenon with wide-ranging potential applications.

These solid materials often comprise multiple kinds of atoms in complicated structures that tend to be difficult to manipulate in the laboratory. Furthermore, it is even harder to study what happens when there is a sudden change, such as a spike in temperature or pressure, that throws the superconductor out of equilibrium. Notably, such perturbations can often lead to complex and unpredictable behavior.

Quantum theory has predicted intriguing behaviors when a superconductor is driven out of equilibrium. However, it has been challenging to perturb these materials in the laboratory without disrupting their delicate superconducting properties, which has left these predictions untested. In essence, the gap between theoretical prediction and experimental verification remains significant.

However, scientists can obtain surprisingly deep insights into superconductivity by studying it with fully controllable arrays of atoms in a gas. That is the approach of a research collaboration at JILA, a joint institute of the National Institute of Standards and Technology and the University of Colorado Boulder. Additionally, this method appears to offer a promising avenue for exploring superconducting behavior.

In their latest work, JILA researchers caused a gas of strontium atoms to act like a superconductor. Even though the strontium atoms themselves are not superconducting, they follow the same rules of quantum physics. Furthermore, the researchers could make atoms in a gas interact in a way that preserves the sorts of interactions responsible for superconductivity while suppressing other competing, complex interactions. By throwing the atoms out of equilibrium, the researchers saw changes in atomic interactions that would affect the properties of actual superconductors. When this mixture is subjected to heating within a specific temperature range, it undergoes a transformation into a physical gel that retains its transparency while acquiring a distinct internal structure. In this state, the previously formless fluid forms intricate interlocking microscopic channels, within which the nanoparticles are confined.

Furthermore, as the temperature continues to rise, an interesting phenomenon is observed: the gel starts to become opaque to most wavelengths of light while selectively allowing certain colors to pass through. Initially, it permits shorter, bluer wavelengths, and progressively becomes more opaque to longer, redder wavelengths. Ultimately, when the temperature surpasses a certain threshold, the gel becomes opaque to all visible light.

It is worth noting that Yun Liu, a scientist at NCNR and a professor at the University of Delaware, remarked on previous findings, stating, "Our previous work showed that the SeedGel can transform from clear to opaque and back again, but its ability to control color precisely was a new discovery.”

In addition, neutron scattering experiments conducted at NCNR provide insights into this peculiar behavior. The alterations in temperature instigate a movement of liquid molecules between the microscopic channels, which, in turn, modifies the overall refractive index of these channels. As a result, one specific wavelength of light can pass through, while other colors are scattered. This analysis suggests that the unique characteristics of the gel are influenced by both its structural composition and thermal conditions.

Buildings in the United States are typically engineered to endure common environmental challenges, including precipitation, strong winds, snowfall, and the occasional seismic activity. However, atypical occurrences such as gas explosions, vehicular impacts, or uncontrolled structural fires are often not included in initial design considerations. When vulnerable structures encounter any of these unexpected events, the consequences can be severe and tragic. Nonetheless, recent advancements in building standards have the potential to assist engineers in mitigating the most detrimental outcomes.

The American Society of Civil Engineers (ASCE) has introduced the ASCE/SEI 76-23 Standard for Mitigation of Disproportionate Collapse Potential in Buildings and Other Structures, marking the first national building standard specifically addressing this issue. This standard, developed over a decade and in collaboration with research conducted by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), establishes design requirements and provides guidance aimed at preventing small, localized failures within a structure from escalating into a total collapse of the entire building or a significant portion thereof, a scenario defined by the standard as disproportionate collapse.

It is worth noting that various loads are considered during the design phase of a building; however, if an unforeseen load occurs that was not specifically accounted for in the design process, it should not result in the complete failure of the structure. This observation was articulated by NIST research engineer Joseph Main, who has contributed to the development of the standard as a member of the ASCE committee.

Although the risk of disproportionate collapse has historically been associated with large structures, such incidents are relatively infrequent. For many years, the necessity for a dedicated standard addressing disproportionate collapse within the United States has been a topic of considerable debate among experts in the field. In summary, the introduction of this new standard represents a significant step forward in safeguarding buildings against these unforeseen risks.

Notably, abuse attacks involve the introduction of incorrect information into a source, such as a webpage or online document, which is subsequently absorbed by the artificial intelligence. Unlike the previously mentioned poisoning attacks, abuse attacks typically aim to provide the artificial intelligence with incorrect data from a legitimate yet compromised source, thereby repurposing the intended function of the artificial intelligence system.

In essence, “Most of these attacks may be relatively simple to execute and can require only minimal knowledge of the artificial intelligence system along with limited adversarial capabilities,” stated co-author Alina Oprea, a professor at Northeastern University. “For instance, poisoning attacks can often be conducted by controlling a small number of training samples, which may represent a very minor percentage of the entire training set.” Ultimately, it can be observed that an understanding of these various attack methods is essential for developing more robust artificial intelligence systems.

Abuse attacks involve the insertion of incorrect information into a source, such as a webpage or online document, that an AI then absorbs. Unlike the aforementioned poisoning attacks, abuse attacks attempt to give the AI incorrect pieces of information from a legitimate but compromised source to repurpose the AI system’s intended use.

“Most of these attacks are fairly easy to mount and require minimum knowledge of the AI system and limited adversarial capabilities,” said co-author Alina Oprea, a professor at Northeastern University. “Poisoning attacks, for example, can be mounted by controlling a few dozen training samples, which would be a very small percentage of the entire training set.”

Furthermore, the study, which involved an examination of emissions from two primary sources, namely agriculture and oil and gas production, led to two unexpected findings. Notably, methane emissions from concentrated animal feeding operations, or CAFOs, appeared to be greater than had been predicted. In essence, total emissions from oil and gas production within the study area appear to have reached a plateau over the last several years, despite the fact that production has been rising.

Kevin Cossel, who is a NIST researcher and a co-author of the study, stated that the collection of this type of data is what tends to be useful for policymakers, so that they can see how emissions are changing over time and can adjust regulations accordingly.

Furthermore, methane has approximately 30 times greater global warming potential than carbon dioxide does over a 100-year period. It is worth noting that a substantial reduction of methane emissions can help to reduce the risks associated with climate change. However, in order to manage methane emissions, there is a need to measure them, which tends to present many technical challenges.

Additionally, traditional methods for the tracking of methane emissions are based on economic activity. For instance, one might calculate the emissions from a CAFO by multiplying the number of animals present there by an estimate of how much methane each animal emits. On the other hand, the NIST method makes an estimate of emissions by directly measuring the variation of methane and other gases within the atmosphere. Ultimately, the upgraded NIST technology appears to offer a more direct means of estimating emissions, and the findings from Northern Colorado may help policymakers to adjust regulations as emissions continue to change over time.

For the first time in the report's history, which spans several decades, it includes chapters dedicated to social equity and environmental justice. Ultimately, this shift towards inclusivity may enhance the effectiveness of future climate initiatives.

In contrast, additive manufacturing involves the creation of products layer by layer, as printers sequentially produce each layer and bond them to form a specific shape, which can only be defined by a three-dimensional model.

In addition to generating less waste compared to subtractive methods, additive manufacturing can provide opportunities for the realization of more complex designs, including structures that may not be entirely solid but rather partially hollow with intricate meshwork that can assume various configurations.

It is worth noting that, according to NIST mechanical engineer Paul Witherell, additive manufacturing has introduced numerous unique design possibilities for engineers; however, this increased freedom may also present difficulties in effectively communicating complex designs. 

The absence of a standardized method for conveying characteristics of products related to the distinct capabilities of 3D printing has complicated communication among various organizations and resulted in obstacles to the broader adoption of this technology.

Witherell stated that the committee was not seeking temporary or makeshift solutions; rather, it was focused on identifying approaches that could be standardized and embraced by the community to resolve the communication challenges. He further emphasized that while the ability to produce high-quality parts using additive manufacturing is already established, the objective is to scale up production, making it a crucial step in the process. This initiative underscores the importance of developing a uniform communication strategy within the realm of additive manufacturing.

The question of whether artificial intelligence can be made entirely resistant to adversaries aiming to misuse it is significant and has a historical context that dates back nearly a century. Despite ongoing efforts, it is important to recognize that achieving complete security for AI systems through conventional security models may not be feasible. 

Notably, a mathematical proof published in the peer-reviewed journal IEEE Security and Privacy by Apostol Vassilev, a senior scientist at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), reinforces this assertion. This proof builds upon foundational work by the renowned logician Kurt Gödel, whose incompleteness theorems demonstrated intrinsic limits to what can be established within systems governed by a finite set of rules.

Furthermore, the constraints that dictate an AI's operations are representative of such systems, and an implication of Vassilev's proof is that there will invariably exist methods to encourage an AI to bypass its established regulations; the challenge lies in identifying these methods. Vassilev emphasized that a key principle of responsible AI development is ensuring that the technology remains secure. He articulated the need for AI systems to resist adversarial attacks while performing intended functions, rather than acting according to the wishes of malicious actors. The proof indicates that no finite collection of guidelines can provide universal protection against adversarial inputs.

In addition, organizations engaged in AI development frequently recognize the inherent risks that their technologies present in real-world applications. To mitigate potential harm, they incorporate constraints designed to prevent AI from producing forbidden content, such as deepfakes, malware, or instructions for creating biological weapons or illegal drugs. When an AI system is prompted to generate such content, the intention is for the built-in limitations to detect the request and decline to comply with it. Ultimately, this highlights the ongoing challenge of balancing innovation with safety in the realm of artificial intelligence.
output:
Can we make artificial intelligence impervious to adversaries who want to twist the technology to nefarious ends? Though AI is among the newest of technologies, the question’s answer is nearly a century old.

Try as we might, we can never render AI completely unassailable using conventional security models. In the peer-reviewed journal IEEE Security and Privacy, Apostol Vassilev, a senior scientist at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), has published a mathematical proof of this statement building on work published in 1931 by famed logician Kurt Gödel. His incompleteness theorems showed that there are limits to what can be proved within a system built on a finite number of rules.

The guardrails that govern an AI’s behavior are just such a system, and one of the proof’s implications is that there will always be a way to prompt an AI system to disregard its rules — it’s just a matter of finding it.

“One of the pillars of responsible AI is that you want the technology to be secure,” said Vassilev, the proof’s author and an expert in adversarial machine learning. “You want it to withstand adversarial attacks and perform only what you want it to do, not what an attacker might want. What this proof shows is that there is no finite set of guardrails that is universally robust against adversarial prompts.”

Companies that develop AI often acknowledge that the tools they are creating have the potential to cause harm in the physical world, so they build in constraints intended to stop AI from generating prohibited content such as deepfakes, malware or instructions for making biological weapons or illicit drugs. If the system is prompted to generate such content, the guardrails should flag the issue and refuse to comply.

It is worth noting that a single-atom-thick sheet of carbon, referred to as graphene, possesses exceptional attributes on its own; however, the situation may become even more intriguing when multiple sheets are stacked. When two or more superimposed sheets of graphene are slightly misaligned, twisted at specific angles in relation to one another, they tend to acquire a wide range of exotic characteristics. Depending on the angle of twisting, these materials, which are known as moiré quantum matter, may unexpectedly generate their own magnetic fields, exhibit superconductivity with no electrical resistance, or, alternatively, function as perfect insulators.

Furthermore, Joseph A. Stroscio and his colleagues at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), in collaboration with an international team, have developed what they describe as a “quantum ruler” to measure and investigate the unusual properties of these twisted materials. This research may also pave the way for the establishment of a new, miniaturized standard for electrical resistance, which could facilitate the calibration of electronic devices directly on the factory floor, thereby eliminating the necessity of transporting them to an off-site standards laboratory.

In addition, collaborator Fereshte Ghahari, a physicist from George Mason University located in Fairfax, Virginia, utilized two layers of graphene, known as bilayer graphene, which are approximately 20 micrometers in size, and twisted them in relation to another two layers to construct a moiré quantum matter device. Ghahari created this device within the nanofabrication facility at NIST's Center for Nanoscale Science and Technology. NIST researchers Marlou Slot and Yulia Maximenko subsequently cooled this twisted material device to one-hundredth of a degree above absolute zero, which reduced the random motions of atoms and electrons, thereby enhancing the potential for electron interactions within the material. After achieving ultralow temperatures, they conducted examinations regarding how the energy levels of electrons within the layers of graphene changed in response to variations in the strength of an external magnetic field. Measuring and manipulating these energy levels is essential for the design and manufacture of semiconductor devices. In summary, the exploration of moiré quantum matter may significantly influence future advancements in electronic device technology.

It is worth noting that the local building code can often be the determining factor between survival and fatality.

Furthermore, as recently as 2011, it was relatively uncommon for engineers to incorporate tornado resiliency into their building designs. In Joplin, there were no regulations in place that were designed to help hospitals resist the effects of tornadoes. In the aftermath of the disaster, it was observed that some buildings remained standing while others were completely demolished. It became important to determine the reasons behind these differing outcomes.

Making a breathalyzer for cannabis is harder than making a breathalyzer for alcohol. Alcohol is a relatively simple and highly volatile molecule: It easily travels through the lungs and evaporates when it contacts air. But THC is a larger, more complicated molecule with very low volatility, and consumption is typically hundreds of times less than alcohol. It shows up in very small concentrations in breath, making THC detection much more challenging. Regular users of cannabis can have THC in their breath for at least eight hours and in their blood for potentially weeks after stopping use, meaning that a single measurement is insufficient to learn when a person last used it.

In the new study, NIST’s partners at the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus observed 29 participants who each brought a cannabis-infused gummy to the lab with them. The edibles contained anywhere from 5 to 100 milligrams of THC. Researchers first took a breath sample from the participants before they ingested the product. Then they observed each participant for three hours, obtaining breath samples approximately every hour.

NIST researchers measured the concentration of THC and other cannabinoids in breath at those intervals. They detected THC in most of the participants before they took the edible, even though they had been asked to abstain for eight hours before the study. That wasn’t surprising. Our bodies process cannabinoids slowly, taking weeks to get them out of our systems compared with hours for alcohol.

Legionella pneumophila is known to flourish at temperatures ranging from 20 to 45 degrees Celsius, which is equivalent to 68 to 113 degrees Fahrenheit. These reference materials are utilized by laboratories to ensure accuracy, precision, and effective quality control in their testing processes. For instance, NIST's cholesterol reference material serves to enhance the reliability of cholesterol test results, thereby ensuring that both physicians and patients can place their trust in these outcomes.

Furthermore, Scott Jackson, a molecular geneticist at NIST, articulates the current advancements in the field, stating, “We are at the beginning of a new era of live microbial therapies. This is not merely wishful thinking. It is already occurring.” 

In order to procure fecal material, NIST engaged a medical services company that was responsible for recruiting healthy adult individuals and collecting stool samples. The recruited individuals comprised both men and women, with approximately half adhering to a vegetarian diet while the other half followed an omnivorous diet. Given that dietary habits can significantly influence the composition of the gut microbiome, this dual cohort approach was instrumental in achieving a comprehensive representation of microbial variability. It is important to note that NIST does not possess information regarding the specific identities of the individual donors.

Moreover, the analysis of the fecal material presented considerable challenges due to the presence of trillions of microorganisms across hundreds of species, in addition to food particles, human cells, and myriad proteins, enzymes, and metabolites. This complexity renders fecal matter one of the most intricate biological materials known.

Additionally, a team of over a dozen scientists dedicated six years to transforming these samples into NIST's microbiome reference material. Through their efforts, they successfully identified more than 150 metabolites utilizing advanced chemical analysis techniques and documented over 150 species of microbes by analyzing their genetic signatures.

It is also essential to highlight that the reference material has been developed with stability in mind, designed to maintain a shelf life of no less than five years, and to ensure homogeneity, meaning that each sample is consistent within the parameters of stated measurement uncertainties.

In conclusion, Jackson asserts, “Through a lot of trial and error, brainstorming, and collaboration with the scientific community, we were able to create a reference material that fulfills the needs of our stakeholders.” This collaborative effort underscores the importance of rigorous scientific inquiry in developing reliable reference materials.

U.S. for-profit organizations, nonprofit organizations, accredited institutions of higher education, federally funded research and development centers (FFRDCs), and federal entities are encouraged to submit applications. It is important to highlight that all applicants must present a white paper to be considered for funding, and those selected to advance to the next stage will be required to provide a pre-negotiation package. Superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (SNSPDs) typically incorporate a wire that is 100 nanometers in width, constructed from superconducting material, which connects to a readout circuit. The flow of electric current through the wire resembles the flow of water in a river. When a photon strikes the wire, it creates a disruption in the current, akin to a rock striking the water, leading to the formation of a hot spot. This hot spot generates a voltage pulse that is subsequently detected by the readout electronics.

Additionally, researchers have posited that superconducting wires in SNSPDs are required to be at a nanoscale to optimize the minimal "splash" produced by photons across the wire, as noted by NIST postdoctoral researcher Eli Mueller. He indicated that the energy of the photon must effectively disrupt superconductivity throughout the entire width of the wire. It is challenging to maintain a device within a functional range that allows for effective disruption over a width of 100 microns, which necessitates that devices be designed with widths on the order of hundreds of nanometers.

Furthermore, this nanoscale construction results in the necessity for SNSPDs to function at lower current levels. Consequently, lower-energy photons produce a reduced disruption and are more difficult to detect, resulting in less pronounced readout signals. The behavior of electric current is also imperfect; it does not flow uniformly throughout the wire, and defects can cause current accumulation at the edges, producing false signals known as dark counts, as explained by Parzuchowski.

Ultimately, Mueller elaborated that if it is possible to enhance the current flow in the central region of the device beyond previously achievable levels, it may be possible to generate a hot spot over a wire of arbitrary width. This hot spot is responsible for producing the detectable pulse. He further suggested that operating closer to the transition point between the superconducting and normal states can maintain sensitivity to very low-energy photons. This information highlights the complexities involved in enhancing the detection capabilities of SNSPDs.

SNSPDs typically use a 100-nanometer-wide wire made of superconducting material connected to a readout circuit. Electric current flows through the wire like water through a river. When a photon hits the wire, like a rock hitting the river, it creates a hot spot disrupting the current. That hot spot creates a voltage pulse, which is picked up by the readout electronics.

Scientists believed that superconducting wires in SNSPDs needed to be nanoscale to maximize the photon’s minuscule “splash” across the wire, points out NIST postdoctoral researcher Eli Mueller.

“Your photon energy needs to break superconductivity over the entire width of the wire,” he said. “It's very difficult to have your device in a regime where the photon could break superconductivity over 100 microns wide, so devices needed to be on the order of hundreds of nanometers wide.”

Due to that nanoscale size, SNSPDs have to operate at lower currents, which means that lower-energy photons don’t make as much of a splash and are harder to detect. Readouts are fainter blips. The electric current doesn’t behave perfectly, either: It doesn’t flow evenly across the wire. Defects can also cause current to build up along the edges, like whirlpools or eddies along a river, leading to false signals called dark counts, Parzuchowski added.

“If we can get the middle of our device to flow more current than what was previously accessible, then we can generate a hot spot over an arbitrarily wide wire. And that hot spot is what's giving you the pulse out,” Mueller explained. “If you're operating even closer to that transition between the superconducting state and the normal state, then you're still sensitive to the very low energy photons.”

This system includes optical fibers, electrical contacts and other components. Ultimately, good packaging allows the chips to be used in compact, reliable devices without damage or misalignment.

Furthermore, photonic integrated chips have a particular advantage because they transmit data at high speeds while consuming far less power than conventional chips. This advantage, however, can often be realized only if the packaging is able to keep delicate optical connections perfectly aligned.

Notably, photonic integrated chips already play a central role in telecommunications, medical diagnostics and advanced sensing. Nevertheless, their use in demanding environments has remained limited. Additionally, industrial and energy applications demand sensors that can withstand heat, pressure and corrosive environments. Ultimately, the development of packaging that can endure such conditions appears to be a significant factor in expanding the use of photonic integrated circuits.

Furthermore, this innovative technique, known as cryogenic decay energy spectrometry, may have far-reaching implications, potentially improving cancer treatments and ensuring the safety of nuclear waste cleanup procedures. 

Notably, the key to this novel technique is a transition-edge sensor, a device that provides a capability to record individual radioactive decay events, in which an unstable atom releases particles. Moreover, the device operates at extremely low temperatures, near absolute zero, and absorbs energy released during radioactive decay, causing a change in electrical resistance. Additionally, researchers precisely measure this change, which provides a high-resolution energy signature of the decay event, enabling them to identify the specific radioactive atom undergoing decay.

Furthermore, earlier methods may be effective at either measuring radioactivity or identifying radioactive atoms, but they tend to require multiple techniques to fully characterize a sample.

Researchers at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) have demonstrated a new and faster method for detecting and measuring the radioactivity of minuscule amounts of radioactive material. The innovative technique, known as cryogenic decay energy spectrometry (DES), could have far-reaching impacts, from improving cancer treatments to ensuring the safety of nuclear waste cleanup.

The key to this novel technique is a transition-edge sensor (TES), a high-tech device widely used to measure radiation signatures. TES provides a revolutionary capability to record individual radioactive decay events, in which an unstable atom releases one or more particles. By building up data from many individual decays, researchers can then identify which unstable atoms, known as radionuclides, produce the events.

“The TES is much more advanced than a familiar Geiger counter or other detectors used today,” said NIST physicist Ryan Fitzgerald. “Instead of just clicking to indicate radiation, or giving a blurry indication of the decay energy, it gives us a detailed fingerprint of what’s there.”

The TES device operates at extremely low temperatures, near absolute zero. When a radioactive decay occurs in a sample, the energy released is absorbed by the TES. This absorbed energy causes a tiny change in the electrical resistance of the TES. The researchers precisely measure this change in resistance, which provides a high-resolution “energy signature” of the decay event. By analyzing the detailed energy spectrum from multiple events, the researchers can identify the specific radioactive atom undergoing decay. This is possible because different radioactive atoms release unique energy signatures when they decay.

Earlier methods are good at either measuring the amount of radioactivity or identifying which radioactive atoms are present — not both. Fully characterizing a sample once required the use of multiple techniques. In contrast, DES both identifies radioactive elements and quantifies their level of radioactivity.

Harris stated that they noticed that as the columns became stockier and less slender, they can more easily go through the entire loading protocol without losing a significant amount of their capability to withstand the earthquake motions. The experiments, described in the Feb. 17 issue of Nature, suggest how to make atomic clocks 50 times more precise than today’s best designs and offer a route to perhaps revealing how relativity and gravity interact with quantum mechanics, a major quandary in physics.

Einstein’s 1915 theory of general relativity explains large-scale effects such as the gravitational effect on time and has important practical applications such as correcting GPS satellite measurements. Although the theory is more than a century old, physicists remain fascinated by it. NIST scientists have used atomic clocks as sensors to measure relativity more and more precisely, which may help finally explain how its effects interact with quantum mechanics, the rulebook for the subatomic world.

The U.S. Department of Commerce’s National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has initiated a collaborative project aimed at adapting digital identity guidelines to enhance public benefits programs. These programs are intended to assist beneficiaries in meeting basic living expenses, which include food, housing, and medical costs. Through a cooperative research and development agreement, NIST will collaborate with the Digital Benefits Network (DBN), part of Georgetown University’s Beeck Center for Social Impact + Innovation, along with the nonprofit Center for Democracy & Technology (CDT). This partnership aims to create resources that assist providers in achieving a balance among security, privacy, equity, and usability.

It is worth noting that Laurie E. Locascio, the Under Secretary of Commerce for Standards and Technology and NIST Director, emphasized the importance of balancing access and security to enhance the delivery of benefits to the U.S. public. She indicated that diverse populations possess varying needs, barriers, and circumstances that require consideration, and this collaboration is designed to unite a wide range of communities to address these factors.

Furthermore, in response to increased fraud and related cybersecurity threats that emerged during the COVID-19 pandemic, several agencies responsible for administering benefits have begun to implement new safeguards. These safeguards include the introduction of individual digital accounts and identity verification, also referred to as identity proofing, in online applications. However, the adoption of certain methods, such as those that depend on facial recognition technology or data brokers, has raised concerns regarding privacy and data security, due process, and potential biases that may disproportionately affect communities of color and marginalized groups. Additionally, the implementation of more effective, evidence-based identity verification methods has been slow, despite recommendations from both NIST and the Government Accountability Office. Ultimately, this situation highlights the challenges faced in improving the effectiveness and fairness of identity verification processes within public benefits programs.

Locascio. “Different populations have different needs, barriers and circumstances that must be considered, and this collaboration will bring together a diverse set of communities to do just that.”

In response to heightened fraud and related cybersecurity threats during the COVID-19 pandemic, some benefits-administering agencies began to integrate new safeguards such as individual digital accounts and identity verification, also known as identity proofing, into online applications. Simultaneously, adoption of more effective, evidence-based methods of identity verification has lagged, despite recommendations from NIST (Question A4) and the Government Accountability Office.

These new curricula will encompass diverse fields, including chemistry, economics, business management, entrepreneurship, and related subjects.

Furthermore, the Training for Improving Plastics Circularity Grant Program intends to cultivate the future workforce necessary for the advancement of a circular economy pertaining to plastics. A circular economy can be described as a system in which materials maintain their value through methods of repeated reuse, repair, and recycling, with disposal occurring only as a last resort.

Moreover, the establishment of a circular economy necessitates the development of innovative manufacturing techniques, chemical processes, and separation capabilities, along with novel methodologies for optimizing the lifecycle of plastics within the industrial supply chain.

It is worth noting that Kathryn Beers, who leads NIST’s Circular Economy Program, emphasized the need for a proficient workforce capable of adopting a holistic perspective on plastics, which would facilitate the creation of new business opportunities while simultaneously addressing a significant environmental challenge. She stated that the five institutions awarded TIPC grants adopt various approaches, yet all are committed to formulating innovative programs that concentrate on this critical issue.

In addition, NIST’s Circular Economy Program is dedicated to aiding U.S. industry in implementing strategies that extend the useful lifespan of plastics. Among other initiatives, NIST scientists are engaged in the development of measurements, models, and data that will enhance the understanding of the chemical processes involved when utilized plastics are decomposed and transformed into new products.

Arizona State University is set to develop seven curriculum modules designed to support a certificate or degree in sustainable macromolecular materials and manufacturing. Concurrently, Pittsburg State University, located in Pittsburg, Kansas, plans to enhance and refine its plastics engineering technology degree program by incorporating lecture-based and hands-on laboratory learning modules that emphasize plastics circularity during the phases of materials, design, and processing involved in production.

The authors of the report have compiled a range of methods aimed at protecting structures against the two primary dangers posed by wildfires: flames and airborne burning debris referred to as embers. 

In order for a residence to be rendered fire resistant, or hardened, it may be necessary to upgrade as many as forty different components, including windows, gutters, and decks, either through the addition of new elements or the replacement of existing ones with materials that exhibit lower flammability. Furthermore, due to the pervasive nature of embers, it is essential that all forty considerations be addressed comprehensively for a homeowner to achieve significant protective benefits. 

Alexander Maranghides, a fire protection engineer at NIST and the lead author of the report, stated that if a homeowner is faced with an overwhelming number of embers, estimated to be in the millions, any vulnerabilities present are likely to be exploited. He emphasized that hardening only a portion of a home will not yield proportional improvements in safety, asserting that a selective approach is not feasible. 

In contrast to embers, flames generally possess a more limited reach, and the strategies for mitigating their threats tend to be more specific to the unique circumstances surrounding each home. The authors recommend conducting an assessment of the types and proximity of combustible features both on a property and in adjacent areas to ascertain where potential flames may pose a threat and to identify suitable mitigation actions. 

Ultimately, the primary defense against flames involves either the removal of combustible items, such as wooden furniture or storage sheds, or positioning them at a safe distance from the home, as determined by the authors' guidelines. This comprehensive approach underscores the importance of addressing both flames and embers in fire prevention strategies.

When contemplating soaps, one may initially envision the liquid foams or solid bars that are intended to eliminate dirt, grime, and bacteria from surfaces. However, it is important to recognize that not all soaps function as cleansers. In the realm of art conservation, metal carboxylates, which are commonly referred to as "metal soaps," tend to be viewed as problematic; they arise from ongoing chemical reactions that may harm both the structural integrity of the paint and the visual appeal of paintings over time. 

Additionally, despite the long-standing presence of these compounds in oil paintings, surprisingly limited information is available regarding their formation and their subsequent impact on these artistic works. Recently, researchers from the National Institute of Standards and Technology, in collaboration with the National Gallery of Art and other institutions, have employed innovative infrared-light-based techniques that can identify the composition and distribution of these metal soaps with enhanced precision. Their discoveries may ultimately assist art conservators in more effectively preserving oil paintings for future generations.

It is worth noting that oil paintings do not typically exhibit visible changes to the unaided eye. Nevertheless, once the paint dries, it is not permanently fixed. Influenced by environmental factors such as humidity and temperature, ongoing chemical reactions at a microscopic level continually take place among the oils and pigments. Over time, whether this period encompasses several years or spans centuries, the resulting metal soaps can lead to degradation of the paint, manifesting as issues such as cracking or peeling layers.

Furthermore, similar to bath soaps, which consist of fatty acid molecules linked to sodium ions, metal soaps comprise fatty acid molecules that form when the oils in paint react with water and oxygen, thus bonding to metal ions that are leached from the pigments. Specifically, paints containing zinc and lead pigments commonly develop metal soaps, while various other metal-containing paints, including aluminum, calcium, and manganese, have also been reported to produce such soaps. In summary, understanding the formation and effects of metal soaps can be critical for the preservation of oil paintings.

Now, researchers from the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) have collaborated with the National Gallery of Art and other institutions to use novel infrared-light-based methods that identify the composition and distribution of these metal soaps at multiple levels of detail. Oil paintings don’t appear to change in front of the naked eye. However, once the paint dries, it’s not set in stone. Driven by environmental factors such as humidity and temperature, chemical reactions at the microscopic level constantly occur among the oils and pigments. Over time, whether a few years or centuries, the resulting metal soaps can cause paint degradation, such as cracking or peeling of paint layers.

Like bath soaps, which are composed of fatty acid molecules bonded to sodium ions, metal soaps are composed of fatty acid molecules, formed when the oils in paint react with water and oxygen, and bond to metal ions leached out from the pigments. Paints with zinc and lead pigments frequently form metal soaps, while many other metal-containing paints (such as aluminum, calcium and manganese) have been reported to form soaps as well.

The innovative method utilizes acoustic waves to ascertain the average gas temperature within large vessels. However, it is worth noting that there exists a significant downside to these substances, as researchers have discovered evidence suggesting that certain PFAS may be linked to cancer and other serious health complications.

Furthermore, governmental agencies and environmental organizations are increasingly engaged in the monitoring of PFAS. Nonetheless, the situation is complicated by the existence of thousands of distinct chemical structures within the PFAS category, with only a limited fraction being measurable with high confidence.

Notably, biologist Jared Ragland from the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) emphasizes the absence of a definitive authority regarding the definition and composition of PFAS. He states that, while the structural characteristics of a few hundred PFAS are known, there may be as many as 9,000 or more possible PFAS structures, indicating that this is not a trivial issue.

For instance, a community may seek to determine whether significant levels of PFAS are present in a local lake utilized for fishing purposes. In such cases, local officials typically collect samples and send them to a laboratory for testing. However, it is important to recognize that most PFAS are not included in the suite of chemicals analyzed quantitatively, resulting in potential omissions of these substances in laboratory tests. Additionally, laboratories may possess incomplete or outdated chemical data regarding PFAS. Given the ongoing discovery of new PFAS, maintaining a comprehensive central database that consolidates the scientific community's understanding of both known and unknown PFAS chemical structures proves to be a considerable challenge.

To address this pressing issue, researchers at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) have successfully developed a pioneering database that assists users in identifying and categorizing PFAS within chemical analysis data. This database includes "untargeted" chemical analysis data, which encompasses information on both known PFAS and unidentified PFAS that may be present in a sample. Ultimately, this database represents the first of its kind and has the potential to be valuable for monitoring environmental pollution and various other applications.

They do not construct houses, especially in rural areas, nor do they farm the land. They rarely manage to survive by stealing until they reach six years of age, unless they are exceptionally gifted. I acknowledge that they learn the basics of survival earlier, but during this formative period, they should be seen only as learners. A prominent gentleman from the county of Cavan informed me that he has never encountered more than one or two cases of children under six who were adept at this skill, even in a region noted for its rapid learning.
output: The number of souls in this kingdom being usually reckoned one million and a half, of these I calculate there may be about two hundred thousand couple, whose wives are breeders; from which number I subtract thirty thousand couple, who are able to maintain their own children, (although I apprehend there cannot be so many under the present distresses of the kingdom) but this being granted, there will remain a hundred and seventy thousand breeders. I again subtract fifty thousand, for those women who miscarry, or whose children die by accident or disease within the year. There only remain a hundred and twenty thousand children of poor parents annually born. The question therefore is, How this number shall be reared and provided for? which, as I have already said, under the present situation of affairs, is utterly impossible by all the methods hitherto proposed. For we can neither employ them in handicraft or agriculture; they neither build houses, (I mean in the country) nor cultivate land: they can very seldom pick up a livelihood by stealing till they arrive at six years old; except where they are of towardly parts, although I confess they learn the rudiments much earlier; during which time they can however be properly looked upon only as probationers; as I have been informed by a principal gentleman in the county of Cavan, who protested to me, that he never knew above one or two instances under the age of six, even in a part of the kingdom so renowned for the quickest proficiency in that art.

input: Some people of a despondent disposition are deeply concerned about the large number of poor people who are aged, diseased, or maimed, and I have been asked to consider what measures might be taken to relieve the nation of such a burdensome problem. However, I feel no unease about the matter, since it is well known that these people are dying and decaying every day from cold, famine, filth, and vermin as quickly as could reasonably be expected. This suggests that the problem is, in practice, resolving itself. As for the young laborers, they are now in an almost equally promising condition. They cannot find work, and consequently waste away from lack of nourishment to such a degree that if they are ever accidentally hired for common labor, they lack the strength to perform it. Ultimately, in this way both the country and themselves are conveniently delivered from the evils to come.
output: Some persons of a desponding spirit are in great concern about that vast number of poor people, who are aged, diseased, or maimed; and I have been desired to employ my thoughts what course may be taken, to ease the nation of so grievous an incumbrance. But I am not in the least pain upon that matter, because it is very well known, that they are every day dying, and rotting, by cold and famine, and filth, and vermin, as fast as can be reasonably expected. And as to the young labourers, they are now in almost as hopeful a condition. They cannot get work, and consequently pine away from want of nourishment, to a degree, that if at any time they are accidentally hired to common labour, they have not strength to perform it, and thus the country and themselves are happily delivered from the evils to come.

input: In essence, I do not hold my own opinion with such fervor as to dismiss any proposal put forth by wise individuals, provided that such proposals are found to be equally innocent, economical, straightforward, and effective. However, before any alternative to my scheme is presented, along with an assertion of superiority, I request that the author or authors carefully consider two critical points. First, given the current circumstances, I would like to know how they plan to secure food and clothing for a hundred thousand individuals who contribute little to society. Furthermore, considering that there exists a total of one million individuals in human form within this kingdom, if their collective means of subsistence were to be pooled together, they would find themselves in debt to the tune of two million pounds sterling. This figure includes not only professional beggars but also those who, though engaged in farming, cottage industries, or labor, find themselves in a state of perpetual need alongside their families. I urge those politicians who oppose my proposal and may dare to respond to first consult with the parents of these individuals. They should inquire whether, at this moment, those parents would perceive it as a significant fortune to have been sold for sustenance at the tender age of one, as I suggest, thereby escaping the relentless cycle of misfortune that they have endured due to the tyranny of landlords, the inability to pay rent in the absence of money or trade, the lack of basic necessities, and the absence of shelter or clothing to protect them from the harshness of the elements. Additionally, they should consider the grim prospect of perpetuating similar, if not greater, miseries for future generations.
output: After all, I am not so violently bent upon my own opinion, as to reject any offer, proposed by wise men, which shall be found equally innocent, cheap, easy, and effectual. But before something of that kind shall be advanced in contradiction to my scheme, and offering a better, I desire the author or authors will be pleased maturely to consider two points. First, As things now stand, how they will be able to find food and raiment for a hundred thousand useless mouths and backs. And secondly, There being a round million of creatures in humane figure throughout this kingdom, whose whole subsistence put into a common stock, would leave them in debt two million of pounds sterling, adding those who are beggars by profession, to the bulk of farmers, cottagers and labourers, with their wives and children, who are beggars in effect; I desire those politicians who dislike my overture, and may perhaps be so bold to attempt an answer, that they will first ask the parents of these mortals, whether they would not at this day think it a great happiness to have been sold for food at a year old, in the manner I prescribe, and thereby have avoided such a perpetual scene of misfortunes, as they have since gone through, by the oppression of landlords, the impossibility of paying rent without money or trade, the want of common sustenance, with neither house nor clothes to cover them from the inclemencies of the weather, and the most inevitable prospect of intailing the like, or greater miseries, upon their breed for ever.
title: A Modest Proposal
author: Jonathan Swift

input:
My intention may not be limited to assisting only the children of known beggars; it can often extend to include all infants of a certain age who are born to parents who may be equally unable to support them, much like those who seek our help on the streets. 

Reflecting on this important issue over many years and carefully considering various proposals, I have found that many of these ideas may be fundamentally flawed in their calculations. It is true that a newborn may survive on its mother's milk for about a year with minimal additional nourishment, typically costing around two shillings, which the mother can often earn through her legal begging activities. It is precisely at the age of one year that I plan to ensure their care in a way that not only relieves their parents and the community from financial burden but also enables these children to eventually contribute to the sustenance and clothing of many others. In summary, my aim is to create a system that benefits both the children in need and the wider community.
output:
But my intention is very far from being confined to provide only for the children of professed beggars: it is of a much greater extent, and shall take in the whole number of infants at a certain age, who are born of parents in effect as little able to support them, as those who demand our charity in the streets.

As to my own part, having turned my thoughts for many years upon this important subject, and maturely weighed the several schemes of our projectors, I have always found them grossly mistaken in their computation. It is true, a child just dropt from its dam, may be supported by her milk, for a solar year, with little other nourishment: at most not above the value of two shillings, which the mother may certainly get, or the value in scraps, by her lawful occupation of begging; and it is exactly at one year old that I propose to provide for them in such a manner, as, instead of being a charge upon their parents, or the parish, or wanting food and raiment for the rest of their lives, they shall, on the contrary, contribute to the feeding, and partly to the clothing of many thousands.

input: Several additional benefits could be listed. For example, the export of barrel-cured beef would increase by thousands of carcasses. output: Many other advantages might be enumerated. For instance, the addition of some thousand carcasses in our exportation of barrel’d beef: the propagation of swine’s flesh, and improvement in the art of making good bacon, so much wanted among us by the great destruction of pigs, too frequent at our tables; which are no way comparable in taste or magnificence to a well grown, fat yearling child, which roasted whole will make a considerable figure at a Lord Mayor’s feast, or any other publick entertainment. But this, and many others, I omit, being studious of brevity.

input: I can think of no objection that might possibly be raised against this proposal, unless it should be argued that the number of people in the kingdom would be greatly reduced. This I freely admit, and indeed it was one principal design in offering it to the world. I wish the reader to observe that I calculate my remedy for this one individual Kingdom of Ireland, and for no other that ever was, is, or, I believe, ever can be upon Earth. Therefore, let no man speak to me of other expedients: of taxing our absentees at five shillings a pound; of using neither clothes nor household furniture except what is of our own growth and manufacture; of utterly rejecting the materials and instruments that promote foreign luxury; of curing the expensiveness of pride, vanity, idleness, and gaming in our women; of introducing a vein of parsimony, prudence, and temperance; of learning to love our country, in which we differ even from Laplanders and the inhabitants of Topinamboo; of quitting our animosities and factions, and no longer acting like the Jews, who were murdering one another at the very moment their city was taken; of being a little cautious not to sell our country and consciences for nothing; of teaching landlords to have at least one degree of mercy toward their tenants. Lastly, of putting a spirit of honesty, industry, and skill into our shopkeepers, who, if a resolution could now be taken to buy only our native goods, would immediately unite to cheat and exact upon us in the price, the measure, and the goodness, nor could ever yet be brought to make one fair proposal of just dealing, though often and earnestly invited to do so.

output:
The Gryphon sat up and rubbed its eyes: then it watched the Queen till she was out of sight: then it chuckled. “What fun!” said the Gryphon, half to itself, half to Alice.

They had not gone far before they saw the Mock Turtle in the distance, sitting sad and lonely on a little ledge of rock, and, as they came nearer, Alice could hear him sighing as if his heart would break. She pitied him deeply. “What is his sorrow?” she asked the Gryphon, and the Gryphon answered, very nearly in the same words as before, “It’s all his fancy, that: he hasn’t got no sorrow, you know. Subsequently, it became clear that the squire and I shared similar sentiments, and we both harbored strong negative feelings towards the captain. 

Throughout the night, the crew was extremely busy, as we worked to store items in their designated locations. Furthermore, numerous boatloads of the squire's acquaintances, such as Mr. Blandly, arrived to extend their well wishes for a successful voyage and a safe return. Notably, the level of activity on this occasion surpassed that of any night I had previously experienced at the Admiral Benbow, and I was thoroughly exhausted by the time the boatswain sounded his pipe, shortly before dawn, and the crew began to prepare the capstan-bars. Nevertheless, despite my fatigue, I remained on deck, as every aspect of the scene was novel and fascinating to me, including the concise commands, the high-pitched sound of the whistle, and the men rapidly taking their positions in the faint light of the ship's lanterns.
output:
We were all hard at work, changing the powder and the berths, when the last man or two, and Long John along with them, came off in a shore-boat.

“Aye, aye, sir,” answered the cook, and touching his forelock, he disappeared at once in the direction of his galley.

I assure you I was quite of the squire’s way of thinking, and hated the captain deeply.

All that night we were in a great bustle getting things stowed in their place, and boatfuls of the squire’s friends, Mr. Blandly and the like, coming off to wish him a good voyage and a safe return. We never had a night at the Admiral Benbow when I had half the work; and I was dog-tired when, a little before dawn, the boatswain sounded his pipe and the crew began to man the capstan-bars. I might have been twice as weary, yet I would not have left the deck, all was so new and interesting to me - the brief commands, the shrill note of the whistle, the men bustling to their places in the glimmer of the ship’s lanterns.
