Moreover, our systems of classification will ultimately become, to the extent that this is feasible, genealogical in nature; and will thereby provide a genuine representation of the underlying plan of creation. It is worth noting that the principles governing classification will likely become more straightforward once a clear objective has been established. Moreover, in the absence of explicit records of ancestry or lineage, we must endeavour to identify and trace the numerous diverging lines of descent in our natural genealogies, utilizing characteristics of any kind that have been inherited over an extended period. Additionally, rudimentary organs will provide unequivocal evidence regarding the nature of structures that have been lost over time. In addition, species and groups of species that are considered aberrant, and which may be figuratively referred to as living relics of the past, will assist us in forming a conception of the ancient forms of life. Furthermore, the study of embryology will reveal to us the structure, to some extent obscured, of the prototypical forms of each major class.
output: A grand and almost untrodden field of inquiry will be opened, on the causes and laws of variation, on correlation of growth, on the effects of use and disuse, on the direct action of external conditions, and so forth. The significance of minor characteristics in classification largely stems from their correlation with other characters of varying importance. This highlights the value of considering an aggregate of characteristics in natural history. A species can differ from its allies in several key characteristics, yet its classification remains clear. This suggests that classification based on a single characteristic, regardless of its importance, is inherently flawed, as no aspect of an organism's structure is universally constant. The importance of aggregate characteristics, even when individually insignificant, explains the observation made by Linnæus that the genus determines the characters, rather than the characters defining the genus. This implies an appreciation for numerous subtle similarities that are difficult to define. 

Certain plants within the Malpighiaceæ family exhibit both perfect and degraded flowers, with the latter lacking many characteristic features of the species, genus, family, and class. However, when Aspicarpa, a genus within this family, produced only degraded flowers in France over several years, displaying significant deviations from the typical structure of the order, M. Richard nonetheless recognized that it should still be classified amongst the Malpighiaceæ. This case illustrates the nuanced approach sometimes necessary in classification. Ultimately, it demonstrates the need to consider the aggregate of characteristics rather than relying on individual traits, which can be misleading or inconsistent.
output: The importance, for classification, of trifling characters, mainly depends on their being correlated with several other characters of more or less importance. The value indeed of an aggregate of characters is very evident in natural history. Hence, as has often been remarked, a species may depart from its allies in several characters, both of high physiological importance and of almost universal prevalence, and yet leave us in no doubt where it should be ranked. Hence, also, it has been found, that a classification founded on any single character, however important that may be, has always failed; for no part of the organisation is universally constant. The importance of an aggregate of characters, even when none are important, alone explains, I think, that saying of Linnæus, that the characters do not give the genus, but the genus gives the characters; for this saying seems founded on an appreciation of many trifling points of resemblance, too slight to be defined. Certain plants, belonging to the Malpighiaceæ, bear perfect and degraded flowers; in the latter, as A. de Jussieu has remarked, “the greater number of the characters proper to the species, to the genus, to the family, to the class, disappear, and thus laugh at our classification.” But when Aspicarpa produced in France, during several years, only degraded flowers, departing so wonderfully in a number of the most important points of structure from the proper type of the order, yet M. Richard sagaciously saw, as Jussieu observes, that this genus should still be retained amongst the Malpighiaceæ. This case seems to me well to illustrate the spirit with which our classifications are sometimes necessarily founded.

On the Affinities of Extinct Species to Each Other and to Living Forms

Let us now consider the mutual affinities of extinct and living species. They all fall into one grand natural system, and this fact is at once explained on the principle of descent. As a general rule, the more ancient a form is, the more it differs from living forms. However, as Buckland long ago remarked, all fossils can be classed either within still existing groups or between them. It cannot be disputed that extinct forms of life help to fill up the wide intervals between existing genera, families, and orders. This highlights that if we confine our attention either to the living or to the extinct alone, the series is far less perfect than if we combine both into one general system. With respect to the Vertebrata, whole pages could be filled with striking illustrations from our great palaeontologist, Owen, showing how extinct animals fall in between existing groups. Cuvier ranked the Ruminants and Pachyderms as the two most distinct orders of mammals, but Owen has discovered so many fossil links that he has had to alter the whole classification of these two orders, and has placed certain pachyderms in the same sub-order with ruminants; for example, he dissolves by fine gradations the apparently wide difference between the pig and the camel. In regard to the Invertebrata, Barrande, and a higher authority could not be named, asserts that he is every day taught that palaeozoic animals, though belonging to the same orders, families, or genera as those living at the present day, were not at this early epoch limited in such distinct groups as they now are. This suggests that the affinities between extinct and living species are best understood when both are considered together within a single natural system.

Domestic instincts are often regarded as actions that have become inherited solely due to long-continued and compulsory habit. However, this explanation is not entirely accurate. The ability of the tumbler-pigeon to tumble, for instance, is not a trait that can be taught. In fact, young birds that have never seen a pigeon tumble are still able to perform this action. Therefore, it is likely that some pigeons initially exhibited a slight tendency to tumble, and subsequent generations of selective breeding resulted in the development of this trait.

Additionally, the process of selection has played a crucial role in the development of certain traits in other animals. For example, dogs that point may have originated from individuals that naturally exhibited this tendency. Once this tendency was observed, breeders could selectively breed for this trait, resulting in the development of dogs that are skilled at pointing. Similarly, unconscious selection is still occurring, as breeders seek to acquire dogs that are well-suited for hunting and standing. 

In some cases, however, habit alone has been sufficient to bring about significant changes in animals. The domestic rabbit, for instance, is a prime example of an animal that has undergone a substantial transformation from being extremely wild to extremely tame. Nevertheless, it is unlikely that domestic rabbits were selectively bred for tameness. Instead, it is probable that the inherited change in temperament can be attributed to habit and long-continued close confinement.
output: Domestic instincts are sometimes spoken of as actions which have become inherited solely from long-continued and compulsory habit, but this, I think, is not true. No one would ever have thought of teaching, or probably could have taught, the tumbler-pigeon to tumble, - an action which, as I have witnessed, is performed by young birds, that have never seen a pigeon tumble. We may believe that some one pigeon showed a slight tendency to this strange habit, and that the long-continued selection of the best individuals in successive generations made tumblers what they now are; and near Glasgow there are house-tumblers, as I hear from Mr. Brent, which cannot fly eighteen inches high without going head over heels. It may be doubted whether any one would have thought of training a dog to point, had not some one dog naturally shown a tendency in this line; and this is known occasionally to happen, as I once saw in a pure terrier. When the first tendency was once displayed, methodical selection and the inherited effects of compulsory training in each successive generation would soon complete the work; and unconscious selection is still at work, as each man tries to procure, without intending to improve the breed, dogs which will stand and hunt best. On the other hand, habit alone in some cases has sufficed; no animal is more difficult to tame than the young of the wild rabbit; scarcely any animal is tamer than the young of the tame rabbit; but I do not suppose that domestic rabbits have ever been selected for tameness; and I presume that we must attribute the whole of the inherited change from extreme wildness to extreme tameness, simply to habit and long-continued close confinement.

The observation that forms of life change simultaneously in different parts of the world has had a significant impact on notable observers such as MM. de Verneuil and d'Archiac. They have noted the parallelism of palaeozoic forms of life in various European regions. Additionally, they have observed that similar phenomena occur in North America, leading them to conclude that modifications of species, extinctions, and introductions of new species cannot be attributed to local or temporary factors such as changes in marine currents. 

Furthermore, these events must be governed by general laws that apply to the entire animal kingdom. Similarly, M. Barrande has made similar comments, emphasizing the same point. It is clear that changes in currents, climate, or other physical conditions cannot be the primary cause of these significant changes in forms of life worldwide, regardless of the climate. As Barrande has noted, it is necessary to consider a special law that governs these phenomena. Moreover, this will become more apparent when we examine the current distribution of organic beings and observe the limited relationship between the physical conditions of various countries and the nature of their inhabitants.
output: The fact of the forms of life changing simultaneously, in the above large sense, at distant parts of the world, has greatly struck those admirable observers, MM. de Verneuil and d’Archiac. After referring to the parallelism of the palæozoic forms of life in various parts of Europe, they add, “If struck by this strange sequence, we turn our attention to North America, and there discover a series of analogous phenomena, it will appear certain that all these modifications of species, their extinction, and the introduction of new ones, cannot be owing to mere changes in marine currents or other causes more or less local and temporary, but depend on general laws which govern the whole animal kingdom.” M. Barrande has made forcible remarks to precisely the same effect. It is, indeed, quite futile to look to changes of currents, climate, or other physical conditions, as the cause of these great mutations in the forms of life throughout the world, under the most different climates. We must, as Barrande has remarked, look to some special law. We shall see this more clearly when we treat of the present distribution of organic beings, and find how slight is the relation between the physical conditions of various countries, and the nature of their inhabitants.

It seems that young women often have a subtle way of indicating their disapproval without directly stating it. output: Both ladies, as I advanced, rose to welcome me, and both addressed me by the name of “Miss Eyre.” Eliza’s greeting was delivered in a short, abrupt voice, without a smile; and then she sat down again, fixed her eyes on the fire, and seemed to forget me. Georgiana added to her “How d’ye do?” several commonplaces about my journey, the weather, and so on, uttered in rather a drawling tone: and accompanied by sundry side-glances that measured me from head to foot - now traversing the folds of my drab merino pelisse, and now lingering on the plain trimming of my cottage bonnet. Young ladies have a remarkable way of letting you know that they think you a “quiz” without actually saying the words. A certain superciliousness of look, coolness of manner, nonchalance of tone, express fully their sentiments on the point, without committing them by any positive rudeness in word or deed.

output: “You should hear himself on the subject. He has again and again explained that it is not himself, but his office he wishes to mate. “That you may, my good little girl: there is not another being in the world has the same pure love for me as yourself - for I lay that pleasant unction to my soul, Jane, a belief in your affection.”

input: Eliza spoke very little, as she appeared to have no time for conversation. This highlights the busy nature of her daily routine. Despite her constant activity, it was not immediately clear what she accomplished or what the end result of her efforts was. She woke up early to an alarm and allocated her time into specific tasks after breakfast. Each hour had a designated activity, which she followed diligently. This suggests that she valued structure and organization in her daily life. Three times a day, she would study a Common Prayer Book, which she found particularly interesting due to the Rubric. She also spent three hours stitching a square crimson cloth with gold thread, which was intended to be an altar covering for a newly built church near Gateshead. Additionally, she devoted time to writing in her diary, working in the kitchen-garden, and managing her accounts. Ultimately, Eliza seemed content with her solitary and routine-driven lifestyle, preferring not to have her schedule disrupted by unexpected events or social interactions. This routine appeared to bring her happiness, and she was most annoyed when anything forced her to deviate from it.
output: Eliza still spoke little: she had evidently no time to talk. I never saw a busier person than she seemed to be; yet it was difficult to say what she did: or rather, to discover any result of her diligence. She had an alarm to call her up early. I know not how she occupied herself before breakfast, but after that meal she divided her time into regular portions, and each hour had its allotted task. Three times a day she studied a little book, which I found, on inspection, was a Common Prayer Book. I asked her once what was the great attraction of that volume, and she said, “the Rubric.” Three hours she gave to stitching, with gold thread, the border of a square crimson cloth, almost large enough for a carpet. In answer to my inquiries after the use of this article, she informed me it was a covering for the altar of a new church lately erected near Gateshead. Two hours she devoted to her diary; two to working by herself in the kitchen-garden; and one to the regulation of her accounts. She seemed to want no company; no conversation. I believe she was happy in her way: this routine sufficed for her; and nothing annoyed her so much as the occurrence of any incident which forced her to vary its clockwork regularity.

input: I approached John's chair, as was my usual practice of obedience. He spent about three minutes extending his tongue toward me, seemingly testing his limits. I anticipated that he would soon strike me, and I found myself contemplating his unpleasant appearance. It is uncertain whether he sensed my thoughts, but suddenly and without warning, he struck me with considerable force. I staggered backward and, after regaining my balance, stepped back a few paces from his chair.
output: Habitually obedient to John, I came up to his chair: he spent some three minutes in thrusting out his tongue at me as far as he could without damaging the roots: I knew he would soon strike, and while dreading the blow, I mused on the disgusting and ugly appearance of him who would presently deal it. I wonder if he read that notion in my face; for, all at once, without speaking, he struck suddenly and strongly. I tottered, and on regaining my equilibrium retired back a step or two from his chair.

This highlights the importance of maintaining a sense of dignity and respectability, even in difficult circumstances. Ultimately, I was able to present myself in a clean and respectable manner, with no remaining signs of the dirt and disorder that I found so degrading. With the aid of the banisters, I made my way down a stone staircase to a narrow, low passage, and from there, I found my way to the kitchen. output: On a chair by the bedside were all my own things, clean and dry. My black silk frock hung against the wall. The traces of the bog were removed from it; the creases left by the wet smoothed out: it was quite decent. My very shoes and stockings were purified and rendered presentable. There were the means of washing in the room, and a comb and brush to smooth my hair. After a weary process, and resting every five minutes, I succeeded in dressing myself. My clothes hung loose on me; for I was much wasted, but I covered deficiencies with a shawl, and once more, clean and respectable looking - no speck of the dirt, no trace of the disorder I so hated, and which seemed so to degrade me, left - I crept down a stone staircase with the aid of the banisters, to a narrow low passage, and found my way presently to the kitchen.

The other members of the household—namely, John and his wife, Leah the housemaid, and Sophie the French nurse—were decent people, though not particularly remarkable in any way. input:
As the half-hour drew to a close, the five o'clock bell struck, signaling the end of the school day. Consequently, the students proceeded to the refectory for tea, and the room was soon empty. At this point, I decided to go downstairs, and as I did, I noticed that it was already quite dark. I then sat down on the floor in a corner, seeking some solitude. Meanwhile, the emotional strength that had sustained me thus far began to wane, and a strong sense of grief took its place. Additionally, this feeling became so intense that I eventually lay down on the ground, overcome with emotion. Now, I gave in to my tears, and I wept openly, as there was no one present to offer me comfort or support, particularly Helen Burns, whose presence I misses deeply.

Previously, I had envisioned a successful and happy experience at Lowood, where I would make many friends and earn the respect and affection of my peers. Furthermore, I had made significant progress towards achieving these goals, as evidenced by my promotion to the head of my class that very morning. Moreover, I had received praise from Miss Miller and approval from Miss Temple, who had also offered to teach me drawing and French if I continued to perform well for the next two months. Nevertheless, despite these accomplishments, I was now lying on the ground, feeling defeated and wondering if I would ever be able to regain my composure and rise above my current difficulties.
output: Ere the half-hour ended, five o’clock struck; school was dismissed, and all were gone into the refectory to tea. I now ventured to descend: it was deep dusk; I retired into a corner and sat down on the floor. The spell by which I had been so far supported began to dissolve; reaction took place, and soon, so overwhelming was the grief that seized me, I sank prostrate with my face to the ground. Now I wept: Helen Burns was not here; nothing sustained me; left to myself I abandoned myself, and my tears watered the boards. I had meant to be so good, and to do so much at Lowood: to make so many friends, to earn respect and win affection. Already I had made visible progress: that very morning I had reached the head of my class; Miss Miller had praised me warmly; Miss Temple had smiled approbation; she had promised to teach me drawing, and to let me learn French, if I continued to make similar improvement two months longer: and then I was well received by my fellow-pupils; treated as an equal by those of my own age, and not molested by any; now, here I lay again crushed and trodden on; and could I ever rise more?

author: Charlotte Bronte

"I should indeed like to go to school," I concluded aloud, bringing my thoughts to an end.

At that moment, Bessie returned, and the carriage was heard coming up the gravel walk.

Bessie invited him into the breakfast room and led the way. From what happened afterward, I assume that during his meeting with Mrs. Reed, the apothecary suggested that I be sent to school, and this recommendation was likely accepted without much hesitation. This is supported by what Abbot said one night while sewing with Bessie in the nursery, after I had gone to bed and they believed I was asleep: she remarked that Mrs. Reed was probably glad to be rid of such a troublesome and difficult child, who always seemed to be watching everyone and secretly plotting something. I think Abbot regarded me as a kind of child-sized Guy Fawkes.
output:
“I should indeed like to go to school,” was the audible conclusion of my musings.

Bessie now returned; at the same moment the carriage was heard rolling up the gravel-walk.

Bessie invited him to walk into the breakfast-room, and led the way out. In the interview which followed between him and Mrs. Reed, I presume, from after-occurrences, that the apothecary ventured to recommend my being sent to school; and the recommendation was no doubt readily enough adopted; for as Abbot said, in discussing the subject with Bessie when both sat sewing in the nursery one night, after I was in bed, and, as they thought, asleep, “Missis was, she dared say, glad enough to get rid of such a tiresome, ill-conditioned child, who always looked as if she were watching everybody, and scheming plots underhand.” Abbot, I think, gave me credit for being a sort of infantine Guy Fawkes.

He has certainly consumed too much wine, I thought, and I was unsure how to respond to his strange question. How could I determine if he was capable of being re-transformed? 

"You appeared quite confused, Miss Eyre," he remarked. "While you are not beautiful, any more than I am handsome, your puzzled expression suits you. Furthermore, it is advantageous, as it distracts your probing gaze from my face and redirects it to the floral patterns of the rug. So, continue to puzzle. Young lady, I feel inclined to be sociable and talkative tonight."
output:
“Decidedly he has had too much wine,” I thought; and I did not know what answer to make to his queer question: how could I tell whether he was capable of being re-transformed?

“You looked very much puzzled, Miss Eyre; and though you are not pretty any more than I am handsome, yet a puzzled air becomes you; besides, it is convenient, for it keeps those searching eyes of yours away from my physiognomy, and busies them with the worsted flowers of the rug; so puzzle on. Young lady, I am disposed to be gregarious and communicative to-night.”

The house's walls appeared to be in a state of disrepair, with dampness and greenery covering them. Upon entering through an unlatched portal, I found myself in a enclosed area, with the wood sweeping away in a semicircle. The space was relatively bare, with no flowers or garden beds, just a gravel walk surrounding a grassy area, set within the forest. The house had a distinctive frontage, with two pointed gables, latticed windows, and a narrow front door, which was accessible by a single step. Overall, the location tended to seem quite isolated, much like the host of the Rochester Arms had described, and the only sound that could be heard was the gentle patter of rain on the forest leaves, creating an atmosphere that was similarly quiet to a church on a weekday. In summary, the house and its surroundings appeared to be a somewhat neglected and serene spot, surrounded by the dense forest.
output:
I thought I had taken a wrong direction and lost my way. The darkness of natural as well as of sylvan dusk gathered over me. I looked round in search of another road. There was none: all was interwoven stem, columnar trunk, dense summer foliage - no opening anywhere.

I proceeded: at last my way opened, the trees thinned a little; presently I beheld a railing, then the house - scarce, by this dim light, distinguishable from the trees; so dank and green were its decaying walls. Entering a portal, fastened only by a latch, I stood amidst a space of enclosed ground, from which the wood swept away in a semicircle. There were no flowers, no garden-beds; only a broad gravel-walk girdling a grass-plat, and this set in the heavy frame of the forest. The house presented two pointed gables in its front; the windows were latticed and narrow: the front door was narrow too, one step led up to it. The whole looked, as the host of the Rochester Arms had said, “quite a desolate spot.” It was as still as a church on a week-day: the pattering rain on the forest leaves was the only sound audible in its vicinage.

author: Charlotte Bronte

input: The hour I spent at Millcote was somewhat trying for me. Mr. Rochester insisted that I go to a certain silk warehouse, where I was asked to choose half a dozen dresses. I disliked the task and begged to put it off, but he would not hear of it; it had to be done now. By pleading in urgent whispers, I managed to reduce the half-dozen to two, though he declared he would choose them himself. I watched with some unease as his eye wandered over the bright displays, and he settled on a rich silk in a vivid amethyst shade and a splendid pink satin. I whispered again that he might as well buy me a gold gown and a silver bonnet at once, since I could never bring myself to wear his choices. Since he could be quite stubborn, it took a great deal of effort to persuade him to exchange them for a sober black satin and a pearl-grey silk. He remarked that it might do for now, but that he would still see me glittering like a flower bed someday.

input:
As evening approaches, I think I may soon see Mr. Rochester, since I have not heard his voice or step in the house today. Earlier I was somewhat afraid of meeting him, but now I would welcome it, as my long wait has made me rather impatient.

When dusk finally fell and Adèle went to play in the nursery with Sophie, I wanted to see him even more. I listened for the bell downstairs and for Leah bringing a message. Sometimes I thought I heard Mr. Rochester’s step and turned toward the door, expecting him to enter, but the door stayed shut and only darkness came through the window. It was still early, since he often sent for me at seven or eight, and it was only six. I felt I should not be entirely disappointed tonight, as I had many things to say to him. I wanted to bring up Grace Poole again and hear his answer, and to ask him directly whether he truly believed she had made the dreadful attempt the night before, and if so, why he kept her wrongdoing secret. It mattered little whether my curiosity annoyed him, since I knew the pleasure of irritating and calming him in turn and took special delight in it. A sure instinct usually kept me from going too far; I never ventured beyond the verge of provocation but liked to test my skill at the very brink. While keeping every small form of respect and propriety of my station, I could still argue with him without fear or uneasy restraint, which suited us both.
output:
“Evening approaches,” said I, as I looked towards the window. “I have never heard Mr. Rochester’s voice or step in the house to-day; but surely I shall see him before night: I feared the meeting in the morning; now I desire it, because expectation has been so long baffled that it is grown impatient.”

When dusk actually closed, and when Adèle left me to go and play in the nursery with Sophie, I did most keenly desire it. I listened for the bell to ring below; I listened for Leah coming up with a message; I fancied sometimes I heard Mr. Rochester’s own tread, and I turned to the door, expecting it to open and admit him. The door remained shut; darkness only came in through the window. Still it was not late; he often sent for me at seven and eight o’clock, and it was yet but six. Surely I should not be wholly disappointed to-night, when I had so many things to say to him! I wanted again to introduce the subject of Grace Poole, and to hear what he would answer; I wanted to ask him plainly if he really believed it was she who had made last night’s hideous attempt; and if so, why he kept her wickedness a secret. It little mattered whether my curiosity irritated him; I knew the pleasure of vexing and soothing him by turns; it was one I chiefly delighted in, and a sure instinct always prevented me from going too far; beyond the verge of provocation I never ventured; on the extreme brink I liked well to try my skill. Retaining every minute form of respect, every propriety of my station, I could still meet him in argument without fear or uneasy restraint; this suited both him and me.

input: And, Miss Eyre, I was so flattered by this preference of the French sylph for her British gnome that I set her up in a hotel and gave her a complete household of servants, a carriage, cashmere shawls, diamonds, lace, and so on. In short, I began to ruin myself in the accepted style, like any other sentimental fool. It seems I did not have the originality to mark out a new road to shame and destruction, but instead trod the old track with a stupid exactness, never deviating an inch from the beaten centre. I had, as I deserved to have, the fate of all other such fools. Happening to call one evening when Céline did not expect me, I found her out; but it was a warm night, and I was tired from strolling through Paris, so I sat down in her boudoir, happy to breathe the air she had so lately occupied. No—I exaggerate; I never thought there was any sacred quality about her. It was rather a sort of pastille perfume she had left, a scent of musk and amber, than an odour of sanctity. I was just beginning to stifle in the fumes of hothouse flowers and sprinkled essences when I thought to open the window and step out onto the balcony. It was moonlight and gaslight besides, and very still and serene. The balcony had a chair or two; I sat down and took out a cigar—I will take one now, if you will excuse me.

A group of ladies stood at the entrance; they proceeded to enter, and the curtain fell behind them.

Although there were only eight, their collective presence created an illusion of a significantly larger assembly. Some were notably tall, many wore white garments, and all possessed a flowing elegance in their attire that seemed to enhance their figures, much like a mist amplifies the appearance of the moon. I rose and performed a courteous curtsey to them; one or two inclined their heads in acknowledgment, while the others regarded me with mere curiosity.
output:

There were but eight; yet, somehow, as they flocked in, they gave the impression of a much larger number. Some of them were very tall; many were dressed in white; and all had a sweeping amplitude of array that seemed to magnify their persons as a mist magnifies the moon. I rose and curtseyed to them: one or two bent their heads in return, the others only stared at me.

It is unpleasant and yet, I find myself drawn to you once more. I believe I will continue to feel this way, and I will compel you to admit that my feelings extend beyond mere liking; I truly love you with sincerity, intensity, and unwavering devotion.

I become quite discontented with women who only appeal to me based on their appearances. When I discover they lack depth, emotional richness, and intellect, I see only a landscape of dullness, superficiality, and perhaps ignorance, rudeness, and a lack of kindness. In contrast, I am always nurturing and loyal to those with clarity of thought and the ability to communicate well. I admire a soul that is passionate and a character that is both flexible and resilient—one that is adaptable yet steadfast, compliant yet reliable.
output:
“Distasteful! and like you again! I think I shall like you again, and yet again: and I will make you confess I do not only like, but love you - with truth, fervour, constancy.”

“To women who please me only by their faces, I am the very devil when I find out they have neither souls nor hearts - when they open to me a perspective of flatness, triviality, and perhaps imbecility, coarseness, and ill-temper: but to the clear eye and eloquent tongue, to the soul made of fire, and the character that bends but does not break - at once supple and stable, tractable and consistent - I am ever tender and true.”

input: Additionally, it is essential to address the central issue regarding your departure from England and your collaboration with me in my future endeavors. You must maintain a singular focus on how best to accomplish the work you have undertaken. It is advisable to simplify your complex array of interests, emotions, thoughts, desires, and objectives, consolidating all considerations into one overarching aim: to effectively and powerfully fulfill the mission of your esteemed Master. To accomplish this, it is imperative that you have a partner—not merely a brother, as that relationship is too tenuous—but rather a husband. Furthermore, I too do not seek a sister, as such a bond could be severed at any moment. I desire a wife, the sole companion whom I can influence effectively throughout my life and retain unconditionally until death.
output: “Well - well. To the main point - the departure with me from England, the co-operation with me in my future labours - you do not object. You have already as good as put your hand to the plough: you are too consistent to withdraw it. You have but one end to keep in view - how the work you have undertaken can best be done. Simplify your complicated interests, feelings, thoughts, wishes, aims; merge all considerations in one purpose: that of fulfilling with effect - with power - the mission of your great Master. To do so, you must have a coadjutor: not a brother - that is a loose tie - but a husband. I, too, do not want a sister: a sister might any day be taken from me. I want a wife: the sole helpmeet I can influence efficiently in life, and retain absolutely till death.”

The letters did not contain any explicit complaints, nor did they revisit past issues or describe current difficulties. However, it can often be observed that Jane's usual cheerfulness was somewhat lacking in her writing, which tended to be characterized by a serene and kindly tone. As Elizabeth re-read the letters, she noticed that many of the sentences conveyed a sense of uneasiness, which may not have been as apparent on her initial reading. The knowledge of Mr. Darcy's role in her sister's distress may have made Elizabeth more aware of Jane's struggles. It was somewhat comforting for Elizabeth to think that Mr. Darcy's visit to Rosings would soon be coming to an end, and it was even more reassuring that she would be reunited with Jane in less than a fortnight, at which point she could try to help her sister recover her spirits through their affection for each other. In summary, Elizabeth's review of Jane's letters gave her a deeper understanding of her sister's situation and reinforced her desire to support Jane during a difficult time.
output: When they were gone, Elizabeth, as if intending to exasperate herself as much as possible against Mr. Darcy, chose for her employment the examination of all the letters which Jane had written to her since her being in Kent. They contained no actual complaint, nor was there any revival of past occurrences, or any communication of present suffering. But in all, and in almost every line of each, there was a want of that cheerfulness which had been used to characterize her style, and which, proceeding from the serenity of a mind at ease with itself, and kindly disposed towards everyone, had been scarcely ever clouded. Elizabeth noticed every sentence conveying the idea of uneasiness, with an attention which it had hardly received on the first perusal. Mr. Darcy’s shameful boast of what misery he had been able to inflict gave her a keener sense of her sister’s sufferings. It was some consolation to think that his visit to Rosings was to end on the day after the next, and a still greater that in less than a fortnight she should herself be with Jane again, and enabled to contribute to the recovery of her spirits, by all that affection could do.

Herbert, without realizing it, took the chair, but quickly stood up, pushed it away, and chose a different one. There was no need for either of us to express our mutual dislike for my patron; we shared that understanding without needing to say a word.
output:
Herbert received me with open arms, and I had never felt before so blessedly what it is to have a friend. When he had spoken some sound words of sympathy and encouragement, we sat down to consider the question, What was to be done?

The chair that Provis had occupied still remaining where it had stood, - for he had a barrack way with him of hanging about one spot, in one unsettled manner, and going through one round of observances with his pipe and his negro-head and his jackknife and his pack of cards, and what not, as if it were all put down for him on a slate, - I say his chair remaining where it had stood, Herbert unconsciously took it, but next moment started out of it, pushed it away, and took another. He had no occasion to say after that that he had conceived an aversion for my patron, neither had I occasion to confess my own. We interchanged that confidence without shaping a syllable.

A helpful stranger might pretend to fold up my bank-notes for safety and then take the notes and give me nutshells; but his trick is nothing compared with mine, when I fold up my own nutshells and pass them off to myself as notes.

An obliging stranger, under pretence of compactly folding up my bank-notes for security’s sake, abstracts the notes and gives me nutshells; but what is his sleight of hand to mine, when I fold up my own nutshells and pass them on myself as notes!

input: I lived what was, in many ways, an unhappy life, and one dominant anxiety tended to overshadow all my other worries, much like a high mountain rising above a range of mountains, and it rarely left my thoughts. I might start up from my bed with the fresh terror that he had been discovered; I might sit listening with dread for Herbert's returning step at night, in case it should be quicker than usual and seem to bring bad news—yet despite all that, and much more of the same kind, the ordinary course of things tended to go on. Condemned to inaction and to a state of constant restlessness and suspense, I would row about in my boat and wait, and wait, and wait, as best I could. Overall, my life at that time was marked by persistent anxiety and a wearying, uncertain waiting.
output: It was an unhappy life that I lived; and its one dominant anxiety, towering over all its other anxieties, like a high mountain above a range of mountains, never disappeared from my view. Still, no new cause for fear arose. Let me start from my bed as I would, with the terror fresh upon me that he was discovered; let me sit listening, as I would with dread, for Herbert’s returning step at night, lest it should be fleeter than ordinary, and winged with evil news, - for all that, and much more to like purpose, the round of things went on. Condemned to inaction and a state of constant restlessness and suspense, I rowed about in my boat, and waited, waited, waited, as I best could.

“Yes,” said I. “Estella waved a blue flag, and I waved a red one, and Miss Havisham waved one sprinkled all over with little gold stars, out at the coach-window. And then we all waved our swords and hurrahed.”

“That’s true, Mum,” said Mr. Pumblechook, with a grave nod. “That’s the state of the case, for that much I’ve seen myself.” And then they both stared at me, and I, with an obtrusive show of artlessness on my countenance, stared at them, and plaited the right leg of my trousers with my right hand.

I approached the forge with a hint of apprehension, unsure of the reason, and eventually caught sight of it, only to find it closed. There was no flicker of fire, no bright sparks flying, and no sound of bellows; everything was quiet and still.

However, the house was not unoccupied, as the best parlor appeared to be in use. I noticed white curtains gently moving in the open window, which was adorned with cheerful flowers. As I quietly approached, intending to peek over the flowers, I found Joe and Biddy standing together, arm in arm, greeting me.
output:
Almost fearing, without knowing why, to come in view of the forge, I saw it at last, and saw that it was closed. No gleam of fire, no glittering shower of sparks, no roar of bellows; all shut up, and still.

But the house was not deserted, and the best parlour seemed to be in use, for there were white curtains fluttering in its window, and the window was open and gay with flowers. I went softly towards it, meaning to peep over the flowers, when Joe and Biddy stood before me, arm in arm.

output: My young conductress locked the gate, and we went across the courtyard. It was paved and clean, but grass was growing in every crevice. I aimed to share what I learned with Joe. This reflects my intention to help him become less ignorant and more sophisticated, thereby making him more suitable for my company and less susceptible to Estella's criticism. 

Our learning took place at the old Battery on the marshes, where our tools consisted of a broken slate and a small piece of slate-pencil, complemented by Joe’s customary pipe of tobacco. Despite my efforts, Joe did not seem to retain any knowledge from one Sunday to the next, nor did he gain any significant information under my guidance. However, he would smoke his pipe at the Battery with a demeanor that suggested he felt more knowledgeable there than in any other setting, almost as if he believed he was making considerable progress. Ultimately, I hope that he felt he was.
output:
Whatever I acquired, I tried to impart to Joe. This statement sounds so well, that I cannot in my conscience let it pass unexplained. I wanted to make Joe less ignorant and common, that he might be worthier of my society and less open to Estella’s reproach.

The old Battery out on the marshes was our place of study, and a broken slate and a short piece of slate-pencil were our educational implements: to which Joe always added a pipe of tobacco. I never knew Joe to remember anything from one Sunday to another, or to acquire, under my tuition, any piece of information whatever. Yet he would smoke his pipe at the Battery with a far more sagacious air than anywhere else, - even with a learned air, - as if he considered himself to be advancing immensely. Dear fellow, I hope he did.

author: Charles Dickens

input: Additionally, it is worth noting that approximately a month subsequent to my sister's reappearance in the kitchen, Biddy arrived at our residence with a small, speckled box containing all of her personal belongings, and her presence proved to be a significant benefit to the household. Furthermore, she was particularly advantageous to Joe, as the poor man had been deeply distressed by the constant contemplation of his wife's deteriorated condition, and had developed a habit of occasionally turning to me in the evening, while attending to her, and remarking, with his eyes moistened, that she had once been a woman of considerable physical attractiveness. Moreover, Biddy immediately assumed a highly competent and nurturing role in relation to her, as if she had been familiar with her needs since childhood; consequently, Joe was able to appreciate the greater tranquility that characterized his life, and to periodically visit the Jolly Bargemen, which provided him with a beneficial change of environment. In essence, it is notable that the individuals associated with the police had, to some extent, harbored suspicions regarding Joe's character, albeit without his knowledge, and had unanimously regarded him as a person of remarkable intelligence and depth.
output: It may have been about a month after my sister’s reappearance in the kitchen, when Biddy came to us with a small speckled box containing the whole of her worldly effects, and became a blessing to the household. Above all, she was a blessing to Joe, for the dear old fellow was sadly cut up by the constant contemplation of the wreck of his wife, and had been accustomed, while attending on her of an evening, to turn to me every now and then and say, with his blue eyes moistened, “Such a fine figure of a woman as she once were, Pip!” Biddy instantly taking the cleverest charge of her as though she had studied her from infancy; Joe became able in some sort to appreciate the greater quiet of his life, and to get down to the Jolly Bargemen now and then for a change that did him good. It was characteristic of the police people that they had all more or less suspected poor Joe (though he never knew it), and that they had to a man concurred in regarding him as one of the deepest spirits they had ever encountered.

“Well,” Joe said thoughtfully, not that it was really necessary to think about it, but because it was customary at the Jolly Bargemen to appear as though one was deeply considering every topic discussed over drinks, “well - no. No, he isn’t.” 

“What on earth is he?” the stranger asked, which seemed to me to be an unnecessarily forceful question.

Mr. Wopsle then chimed in, as someone who often discussed relationships and was mindful of which female relatives a man could not marry. He elaborated on the connections between Joe and me. After sharing his insights, Mr. Wopsle concluded with a rather dramatic quote from Richard the Third, appearing to believe that this was sufficient explanation when he added, “- as the poet says.” 

In summary, the conversation involved some thoughtful considerations and a touch of theatrical flair from Mr. Wopsle.
output:
“Well,” said Joe, meditatively, not, of course, that it could be in anywise necessary to consider about it, but because it was the way at the Jolly Bargemen to seem to consider deeply about everything that was discussed over pipes, - “well - no. No, he ain’t.”

“What the Blue Blazes is he?” asked the stranger. Which appeared to me to be an inquiry of unnecessary strength.

Mr. Wopsle struck in upon that; as one who knew all about relationships, having professional occasion to bear in mind what female relations a man might not marry; and expounded the ties between me and Joe. Having his hand in, Mr. Wopsle finished off with a most terrifically snarling passage from Richard the Third, and seemed to think he had done quite enough to account for it when he added, “ - as the poet says.”

input: At the far end of the brewery, there was a neglected garden enclosed by an old wall. It was not too high, allowing me to climb up and catch a glimpse of the garden, which was filled with overgrown weeds. However, there was a visible path winding through the greenery, suggesting that someone had walked there recently. I noticed Estella walking away from me at that moment. Her presence felt pervasive. When I succumbed to the temptation to walk along the casks, I saw her again at the end of the yard, facing away from me. She held her brown hair in both hands and did not turn around before disappearing from my sight. Inside the brewery, a large, high-paved area where beer was once made, I initially felt overwhelmed by its somber atmosphere as I stood near the entrance. I then saw her moving among the extinguished fires and ascending a set of light iron stairs, exiting through a gallery above, which gave the impression she was stepping into the sky.
output: Behind the furthest end of the brewery, was a rank garden with an old wall; not so high but that I could struggle up and hold on long enough to look over it, and see that the rank garden was the garden of the house, and that it was overgrown with tangled weeds, but that there was a track upon the green and yellow paths, as if some one sometimes walked there, and that Estella was walking away from me even then. But she seemed to be everywhere. For when I yielded to the temptation presented by the casks, and began to walk on them, I saw her walking on them at the end of the yard of casks. She had her back towards me, and held her pretty brown hair spread out in her two hands, and never looked round, and passed out of my view directly. So, in the brewery itself, - by which I mean the large paved lofty place in which they used to make the beer, and where the brewing utensils still were. When I first went into it, and, rather oppressed by its gloom, stood near the door looking about me, I saw her pass among the extinguished fires, and ascend some light iron stairs, and go out by a gallery high overhead, as if she were going out into the sky.
title: Great Expectations
author: Charles Dickens

input: Miss Havisham interjected, directing Jaggers to leave me alone and accompany him to dinner, which he agreed to do. As we made our way down the dimly lit stairs together, he inquired about how often I had witnessed Miss Havisham eating and drinking, offering a wide range of possibilities from many times to just once. He then replied, with a slight frown, that she would never permit anyone to see her engage in either activity since she began her current way of living. This suggests that she prefers to roam at night and discreetly take whatever food she needs.
output:
“Jaggers,” interposed Miss Havisham, much to my relief, “leave my Pip alone, and go with him to your dinner.”

He complied, and we groped our way down the dark stairs together. While we were still on our way to those detached apartments across the paved yard at the back, he asked me how often I had seen Miss Havisham eat and drink; offering me a breadth of choice, as usual, between a hundred times and once.

“And never will, Pip,” he retorted, with a frowning smile. “She has never allowed herself to be seen doing either, since she lived this present life of hers. She wanders about in the night, and then lays hands on such food as she takes.”

input:
Additionally, it is worth noting that I was never permitted to have a candle to illuminate my path to bed, and as I ascended the stairs in darkness, with my head still reeling from the effects of Mrs. Joe's thimble being used to strike me, thereby accompanying her parting words, I was intensely aware of the considerable convenience that the prison ships posed for me. Moreover, it seemed evident that I was destined for such a fate. I had initiated a sequence of events by posing questions, and subsequently, I was progressing towards committing a serious transgression against Mrs. Joe.

Furthermore, since that period, which is now sufficiently distant, I have frequently reflected on the fact that few individuals are aware of the secrecy that exists among the young when they are subjected to intense fear. In essence, the reasonableness of the fear is of little consequence, as long as the fear itself is present. I was consumed by an overwhelming sense of dread in relation to the young man who had expressed a desire for my vital organs; I was also filled with mortal terror in response to my interlocutor with the iron leg; moreover, I was afraid of my own self, from whom a solemn promise had been extracted. It is worth noting that I had no expectation of rescue or deliverance through the agency of my sister, who consistently rejected me. Additionally, I am reluctant to contemplate the potential actions I might have taken, had I been required to do so, given the secrecy and intensity of my fear.
output:
I was never allowed a candle to light me to bed, and, as I went upstairs in the dark, with my head tingling, - from Mrs. Joe’s thimble having played the tambourine upon it, to accompany her last words, - I felt fearfully sensible of the great convenience that the hulks were handy for me. I was clearly on my way there. I had begun by asking questions, and I was going to rob Mrs. Joe.

Since that time, which is far enough away now, I have often thought that few people know what secrecy there is in the young under terror. No matter how unreasonable the terror, so that it be terror. I was in mortal terror of the young man who wanted my heart and liver; I was in mortal terror of my interlocutor with the iron leg; I was in mortal terror of myself, from whom an awful promise had been extracted; I had no hope of deliverance through my all-powerful sister, who repulsed me at every turn; I am afraid to think of what I might have done on requirement, in the secrecy of my terror.
title: Great Expectations
author: Charles Dickens

input: During this period, I was unable to reflect on my own circumstances, and this remained the case. I lacked the capacity to focus on my situation. Furthermore, I was experiencing significant emotional distress, although it was a vague and general feeling. Additionally, I was not capable of developing a plan for the future, as it was completely beyond my abilities at that time. As I opened the shutters and observed the damp and gloomy morning, which appeared dull and gray, I felt a sense of misery. Moreover, as I walked through the rooms or sat shivering by the fire, waiting for my laundress to arrive, I couldn't help but think about my unhappy state. Nevertheless, I had difficulty understanding the reasons for my misery, or even recalling the duration of my distress, the current day of the week, or my own identity at that moment.
output: All this time I had never been able to consider my own situation, nor could I do so yet. I had not the power to attend to it. I was greatly dejected and distressed, but in an incoherent wholesale sort of way. As to forming any plan for the future, I could as soon have formed an elephant. When I opened the shutters and looked out at the wet wild morning, all of a leaden hue; when I walked from room to room; when I sat down again shivering, before the fire, waiting for my laundress to appear; I thought how miserable I was, but hardly knew why, or how long I had been so, or on what day of the week I made the reflection, or even who I was that made it.
title: Great Expectations
author: Charles Dickens

input: They maintained a state of silence around me throughout the day, consistently ensuring that my arm remained properly dressed while providing me with cooling beverages. Around midnight, I rose from my bed and approached Herbert, firmly believing that I had been asleep for a full twenty-four hours and that Wednesday had already concluded. This represented the final exertion of my unease, for thereafter I fell into a deep and uninterrupted sleep.
output: They kept me very quiet all day, and kept my arm constantly dressed, and gave me cooling drinks. Whenever I fell asleep, I awoke with the notion I had had in the sluice-house, that a long time had elapsed and the opportunity to save him was gone. About midnight I got out of bed and went to Herbert, with the conviction that I had been asleep for four-and-twenty hours, and that Wednesday was past. It was the last self-exhausting effort of my fretfulness, for after that I slept soundly.

author: Charles Dickens

It started as soon as we sat down for dinner. Mr. Wopsle delivered grace with dramatic flair, resembling a blend of a ghost from Hamlet and Richard III. He concluded with a commendable wish for genuine gratitude. At that moment, my sister turned her gaze toward me and remarked in a soft, reproachful tone, "Do you hear that? Be grateful."

Mrs. Hubble shook her head and regarded me with a somber sense of foreboding about my future. She inquired, "Why is it that the young are never grateful?" This philosophical question seemed to baffle the others until Mr. Hubble succinctly provided an answer: "Naturally vicious." Everyone responded with murmurs of "True!" and directed uncomfortable and personal looks at me.
output:
It began the moment we sat down to dinner. Mr. Wopsle said grace with theatrical declamation, - as it now appears to me, something like a religious cross of the Ghost in Hamlet with Richard the Third, - and ended with the very proper aspiration that we might be truly grateful. Upon which my sister fixed me with her eye, and said, in a low reproachful voice, “Do you hear that? Be grateful.”

Mrs. Hubble shook her head, and contemplating me with a mournful presentiment that I should come to no good, asked, “Why is it that the young are never grateful?” This moral mystery seemed too much for the company until Mr. Hubble tersely solved it by saying, “Naterally wicious.” Everybody then murmured “True!” and looked at me in a particularly unpleasant and personal manner.
title: Great Expectations
author: Charles Dickens

input:
Biddy made considerable efforts to communicate to my sister some understanding of the situation. To the best of my knowledge, these attempts did not succeed. She laughed and nodded her head several times and even echoed Biddy's words, "Pip" and "Property." However, I wonder if these expressions carried any real meaning beyond mere sound, and I cannot help but think that her state of mind may have been quite perplexing. 

I would not have believed it if I had not experienced it myself, but as Joe and Biddy grew more relaxed and cheerful, I found myself becoming rather gloomy. While I certainly could not be dissatisfied with my circumstances, it is possible that I may have felt some discontent with myself, perhaps without fully realizing it. In summary, the contrasting emotions within me highlighted a complex inner struggle.
output:
Infinite pains were then taken by Biddy to convey to my sister some idea of what had happened. To the best of my belief, those efforts entirely failed. She laughed and nodded her head a great many times, and even repeated after Biddy, the words “Pip” and “Property.” But I doubt if they had more meaning in them than an election cry, and I cannot suggest a darker picture of her state of mind.

I never could have believed it without experience, but as Joe and Biddy became more at their cheerful ease again, I became quite gloomy. Dissatisfied with my fortune, of course I could not be; but it is possible that I may have been, without quite knowing it, dissatisfied with myself.
title: Great Expectations
author: Charles Dickens

input: After we had talked for a short time, Herbert showed me the basket with a compassionate and gentle smile. He explained that it contained poor Clara's supper, which was served out every night. It included her allowance of bread, her slice of cheese, and her rum, which he drank himself. He then pointed out that the basket also held Mr. Barley's breakfast for the following day, served out to be cooked. This consisted of two mutton chops, three potatoes, some split peas, a small amount of flour, two ounces of butter, a pinch of salt, and a generous amount of black pepper. Herbert noted that all of these ingredients were stewed together and taken hot, and he remarked that it seemed like a fine dish for the gout.
output: “Look here,” said Herbert, showing me the basket, with a compassionate and tender smile, after we had talked a little; “here’s poor Clara’s supper, served out every night. Here’s her allowance of bread, and here’s her slice of cheese, and here’s her rum, - which I drink. This is Mr. Barley’s breakfast for to-morrow, served out to be cooked. Two mutton-chops, three potatoes, some split peas, a little flour, two ounces of butter, a pinch of salt, and all this black pepper. It’s stewed up together, and taken hot, and it’s a nice thing for the gout, I should think!”

I told him when I had arrived, and how Miss Havisham had wished me to come and see Estella. To which he replied, “Ah! Very fine young lady!” Then he pushed Miss Havisham in her chair before him, with one of his large hands, and put the other in his trousers-pocket as if the pocket were full of secrets.

The suitor kissed the hem of the garment once more before letting it go and responded, “Habraham Latharuth, on the subject of payment.” 

“Holy father, Mister Jaggerth!” exclaimed my anxious companion, turning pale. “Do not say you are referring to Habraham Latharuth again!” 

“Mister Jaggerth! Just a moment! My own cousin has gone to Mister Wemmick at this very moment to offer him terms. Mister Jaggerth! Just a quarter of a moment! If you would consider being bought off from the other side—at any superior price!—money is no object!—Mister Jaggerth—Mister—!”
output:
The suitor, kissing the hem of the garment again before relinquishing it, replied, “Habraham Latharuth, on thuthpithion of plate.”

“Holy father, Mithter Jaggerth!” cried my excitable acquaintance, turning white, “don’t thay you’re again Habraham Latharuth!”

“Mithter Jaggerth! Half a moment! My hown cuthen’th gone to Mithter Wemmick at thith prethent minute, to hoffer him hany termth. Mithter Jaggerth! Half a quarter of a moment! If you’d have the condethenthun to be bought off from the t’other thide - at hany thuperior prithe! - money no object! - Mithter Jaggerth - Mithter -!”

author: Charles Dickens

input: Mr. Pocket guided me into the house and presented my room, which was comfortable and suitable for use as a private sitting area. output: Mr. Pocket took me into the house and showed me my room: which was a pleasant one, and so furnished as that I could use it with comfort for my own private sitting-room. Putting on the best clothes I had, I went into town as early as I could hope to find the shops open, and presented myself before Mr. Trabb, the tailor, who was having his breakfast in the parlour behind his shop, and who did not think it worth his while to come out to me, but called me in to him.

After drinking for the second time, he rose from the bench where he had been sitting and pushed the table aside. He then picked up the candle and, shading it with his murderous hand to direct its light toward me, stood before me, watching me and taking pleasure in the sight.

"Wolf, I will tell you something more. It was Old Orlick whom you tumbled over on your stairs that night."

I saw the staircase with its extinguished lamps. I saw the shadows of the heavy stair-rails, cast by the watchman's lantern upon the wall. I saw the rooms that I was never to see again; here, a door half open; there, a door closed; and all the articles of furniture around.
output:

If the villain had ceased his actions at this point, his misdeeds would have been sufficiently egregious; however, he exacerbated his culpability by proceeding to take me into custody, possessing a claim of authority that overshadowed all of his previous criminal behavior. 

“It is worth noting that we are profoundly indebted to you, Uncle Pumblechook,” remarked my sister as she grasped the money. 

The Justices were convening in the nearby Town Hall, and we immediately proceeded to arrange for my apprenticeship to Joe in the presence of the magistrates. I assert that we proceeded, but in reality, I was propelled forward by Pumblechook, as though I had just committed a theft or set a barn ablaze; indeed, the prevailing sentiment in the courtroom was that I had been apprehended in the act. As Pumblechook pushed me through the throng, I overheard various remarks, such as, “What has he done?” and others stating, “He is quite young, yet he appears to be rather sinister, does he not?” Furthermore, an individual of gentle and benevolent demeanor even presented me with a pamphlet illustrated with an engraving of a sinister young man adorned with an array of chains, entitled TO BE READ IN MY CELL.
output:
If the villain had stopped here, his case would have been sufficiently awful, but he blackened his guilt by proceeding to take me into custody, with a right of patronage that left all his former criminality far behind.

“Goodness knows, Uncle Pumblechook,” said my sister (grasping the money), “we’re deeply beholden to you.”

The Justices were sitting in the Town Hall near at hand, and we at once went over to have me bound apprentice to Joe in the Magisterial presence. I say we went over, but I was pushed over by Pumblechook, exactly as if I had that moment picked a pocket or fired a rick; indeed, it was the general impression in Court that I had been taken red-handed; for, as Pumblechook shoved me before him through the crowd, I heard some people say, “What’s he done?” and others, “He’s a young ’un, too, but looks bad, don’t he?” One person of mild and benevolent aspect even gave me a tract ornamented with a woodcut of a malevolent young man fitted up with a perfect sausage-shop of fetters, and entitled TO BE READ IN MY CELL.
title: Great Expectations
author: Charles Dickens

"You informed me, Mr. Jaggers, that it might be several years hence before that individual appeared." 

As we gazed directly at one another, I became acutely aware of my breath quickening in my intense desire to elicit a response from him. Furthermore, as I sensed this increase in my respiration, I recognized that he was also aware of my heightened state, which led me to conclude that my chances of obtaining any information from him had diminished significantly. 

Mr. Jaggers shook his head, not to refute the query, but rather to entirely dismiss the idea that he could be persuaded to respond. Moreover, the two disturbing casts of the twitching faces appeared, when my eyes wandered toward them, as though they were on the verge of reaching a climax in their suspended attention, as if they were about to sneeze.
output:
“You told me, Mr. Jaggers, that it might be years hence when that person appeared.”

As we looked full at one another, I felt my breath come quicker in my strong desire to get something out of him. And as I felt that it came quicker, and as I felt that he saw that it came quicker, I felt that I had less chance than ever of getting anything out of him.

Mr. Jaggers shook his head, - not in negativing the question, but in altogether negativing the notion that he could anyhow be got to answer it, - and the two horrible casts of the twitched faces looked, when my eyes strayed up to them, as if they had come to a crisis in their suspended attention, and were going to sneeze.
title: Great Expectations
author: Charles Dickens

input: The Temple was notably quiet, with the windows of the recently occupied rooms by Provis dark and still. The Garden Court was also devoid of people. output: All things were as quiet in the Temple as ever I had seen them. The windows of the rooms on that side, lately occupied by Provis, were dark and still, and there was no lounger in Garden Court. I walked past the fountain twice or thrice before I descended the steps that were between me and my rooms, but I was quite alone. Herbert, coming to my bedside when he came in, - for I went straight to bed, dispirited and fatigued, - made the same report. Opening one of the windows after that, he looked out into the moonlight, and told me that the pavement was as solemnly empty as the pavement of any cathedral at that same hour.

Pennsylvania and North Carolina are two states that include a cautionary statement: "As standing armies in time of peace may be a threat to liberty, they ought not to be maintained." New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Delaware, and Maryland each incorporate a similar clause in their bills of rights, suggesting that "standing armies can be dangerous to liberty and should not be established or sustained without the consent of the Legislature." This language acknowledges the power of the Legislature in this context. In contrast, New York does not include any bills of rights and does not address this issue in its constitution. Additionally, other states do not have bills of rights attached to their constitutions, aside from those mentioned; those constitutions also tend to remain silent on the matter. It has been indicated to me that one or two states may possess bills of rights not included in this collection, but these also generally affirm the legislative authority in this area. In summary, while there are various approaches to the issue of standing armies across states, the legislative authority is often recognized in the context of potential threats to liberty.
output: 1 This statement of the matter is taken from the printed collection of State constitutions. Pennsylvania and North Carolina are the two which contain the interdiction in these words: "As standing armies in time of peace are dangerous to liberty, THEY OUGHT NOT to be kept up." This is, in truth, rather a CAUTION than a PROHIBITION. New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Delaware, and Maryland have, in each of their bills of rights, a clause to this effect: "Standing armies are dangerous to liberty, and ought not to be raised or kept up WITHOUT THE CONSENT OF THE LEGISLATURE"; which is a formal admission of the authority of the Legislature. input: It is notable that not only the first Congress but every subsequent Congress, as well as the recent convention, has consistently agreed with the people that America's prosperity depended on its Union. Preserving and perpetuating that Union was the people's great purpose in forming the convention, and it is likewise the great purpose of the plan the convention has recommended they adopt. This highlights the question of why, at this particular time, some men are attempting to diminish the importance of the Union, or why it is suggested that three or four confederacies would be preferable to one. I am convinced that the people have always judged rightly on this matter, and that their universal and consistent attachment to the cause of the Union rests on great and weighty reasons, which I will endeavor to explain in the papers that follow. Those who promote the idea of replacing the convention's plan with a number of separate confederacies appear to recognize clearly that rejecting it would place the Union's continuation in the utmost jeopardy. That would certainly be the case, and I sincerely wish that every good citizen might foresee just as clearly that, whenever the dissolution of the Union comes, America will have reason to exclaim, in the poet's words: "FAREWELL! A LONG FAREWELL TO ALL MY GREATNESS."
output: It is worthy of remark that not only the first, but every succeeding Congress, as well as the late convention, have invariably joined with the people in thinking that the prosperity of America depended on its Union. To preserve and perpetuate it was the great object of the people in forming that convention, and it is also the great object of the plan which the convention has advised them to adopt. With what propriety, therefore, or for what good purposes, are attempts at this particular period made by some men to depreciate the importance of the Union? Or why is it suggested that three or four confederacies would be better than one? I am persuaded in my own mind that the people have always thought right on this subject, and that their universal and uniform attachment to the cause of the Union rests on great and weighty reasons, which I shall endeavor to develop and explain in some ensuing papers. They who promote the idea of substituting a number of distinct confederacies in the room of the plan of the convention, seem clearly to foresee that the rejection of it would put the continuance of the Union in the utmost jeopardy. That certainly would be the case, and I sincerely wish that it may be as clearly foreseen by every good citizen, that whenever the dissolution of the Union arrives, America will have reason to exclaim, in the words of the poet: "FAREWELL! input: If he were to conduct a careful and critical examination of the Articles of Confederation, his astonishment would not only grow but also include a sense of indignation. He would realize that these articles, while they had cautiously limited the authority of state legislatures, did not impose any restrictions on the federal government. If he were a person of strong emotions, he would likely begin to view the resulting outcry as the deceptive tactics of an unprincipled opposition to a plan that deserved a fair and honest assessment from all true patriots. He might question how the authors of such criticisms could be so quick to condemn a proposal that aligns with the general consensus of American governance and even introduces a powerful safeguard that was absent in previous frameworks. Conversely, if he were more composed and rational, he might simply express disappointment in human nature and lament that a matter of great significance to the happiness of millions should be clouded by tactics that hinder objective judgment. Even a person of calm disposition would likely observe that such behavior seems aimed at misleading the public by stirring their emotions instead of persuading them with reasoned arguments.
output: If he should now apply himself to a careful and critical survey of the articles of Confederation, his astonishment would not only be increased, but would acquire a mixture of indignation, at the unexpected discovery, that these articles, instead of containing the prohibition he looked for, and though they had, with jealous circumspection, restricted the authority of the State legislatures in this particular, had not imposed a single restraint on that of the United States. If he happened to be a man of quick sensibility, or ardent temper, he could now no longer refrain from regarding these clamors as the dishonest artifices of a sinister and unprincipled opposition to a plan which ought at least to receive a fair and candid examination from all sincere lovers of their country! How else, he would say, could the authors of them have been tempted to vent such loud censures upon that plan, about a point in which it seems to have conformed itself to the general sense of America as declared in its different forms of government, and in which it has even superadded a new and powerful guard unknown to any of them? If, on the contrary, he happened to be a man of calm and dispassionate feelings, he would indulge a sigh for the frailty of human nature, and would lament, that in a matter so interesting to the happiness of millions, the true merits of the question should be perplexed and entangled by expedients so unfriendly to an impartial and right determination. Even such a man could hardly forbear remarking, that a conduct of this kind has too much the appearance of an intention to mislead the people by alarming their passions, rather than to convince them by arguments addressed to their understandings.

input: In the observations I have shared so far, my fellow citizens, I have tried to help you guard against any attempts, from whatever source, to influence your decision on a matter of great importance to your welfare through impressions other than those that may arise from the evidence of truth. You will no doubt also have gathered from the general direction of these remarks that they come from a source that is not unfriendly to the new Constitution. Yes, my countrymen, I admit to you that, after giving it careful consideration, I am clearly of the view that it is in your interest to adopt it. I am convinced that this is the safest course for your liberty, your dignity, and your happiness. I do not pretend to have reservations I do not feel. I will not entertain you with an appearance of deliberation when I have already decided. I openly acknowledge my convictions to you, and I will freely lay before you the reasons on which they are based. A awareness of good intentions tends to reject ambiguity. I will not, however, multiply assurances on this point. My motives must remain within my own heart. My arguments will be open to everyone and can be judged by everyone. They will at least be offered in a spirit that will not disgrace the cause of truth, and I hope they may help you weigh this important question with the seriousness it deserves.
output: In the course of the preceding observations, I have had an eye, my fellow-citizens, to putting you upon your guard against all attempts, from whatever quarter, to influence your decision in a matter of the utmost moment to your welfare, by any impressions other than those which may result from the evidence of truth. In this case, if the particular tribunals are invested with a right of ultimate jurisdiction, besides the contradictions to be expected from difference of opinion, there will be much to fear from the bias of local views and prejudices, and from the interference of local regulations. Instead, the laws of the federal government should be applied directly to individual citizens. The existing plan of quotas and requisitions should be seen as impractical and unfair. Consequently, it is essential for the Union to be granted the full authority to raise military forces, construct and equip naval fleets, and generate the revenue needed to establish and maintain an army and navy, following the standard practices employed by other governments.
output: The experiment has, however, demonstrated that this expectation was ill-founded and illusory; and the observations, made under the last head, will, I imagine, have sufficed to convince the impartial and discerning, that there is an absolute necessity for an entire change in the first principles of the system; that if we are in earnest about giving the Union energy and duration, we must abandon the vain project of legislating upon the States in their collective capacities; we must extend the laws of the federal government to the individual citizens of America; we must discard the fallacious scheme of quotas and requisitions, as equally impracticable and unjust. The result from all this is that the Union ought to be invested with full power to levy troops; to build and equip fleets; and to raise the revenues which will be required for the formation and support of an army and navy, in the customary and ordinary modes practiced in other governments.
