Celia admitted that being addressed as "Lady" was preferable to "Mrs." and noted that Dodo was unconcerned about precedence as long as she could have her own way. Mrs. Cadwallader maintained that it provided little satisfaction to occupy a position of precedence when everyone around one was aware of the absence of noble lineage. In response, Celia paused to glance at Arthur and remarked, “It would indeed be delightful if he were a Viscount, particularly with his lordship’s first tooth emerging! He might have held that title if James had been an Earl.”
output: The ladies also talked politics, though more fitfully. Mrs. Cadwallader was strong on the intended creation of peers: she had it for certain from her cousin that Truberry had gone over to the other side entirely at the instigation of his wife, who had scented peerages in the air from the very first introduction of the Reform question, and would sign her soul away to take precedence of her younger sister, who had married a baronet. Lady Chettam thought that such conduct was very reprehensible, and remembered that Mrs. Truberry’s mother was a Miss Walsingham of Melspring. Celia confessed it was nicer to be “Lady” than “Mrs.,” and that Dodo never minded about precedence if she could have her own way. Mrs. Cadwallader held that it was a poor satisfaction to take precedence when everybody about you knew that you had not a drop of good blood in your veins; and Celia again, stopping to look at Arthur, said, “It would be very nice, though, if he were a Viscount - and his lordship’s little tooth coming through! He might have been, if James had been an Earl.”
title: Middlemarch
author: George Eliot

input: She returned home by Mr. Borthrop Trumbull’s office, intending to make a visit. It was the first occasion in her life when Rosamond contemplated engaging in any form of business, yet she regarded herself as capable of rising to the challenge. The notion that she would be compelled to undertake an activity she profoundly disliked transformed her quiet determination into active creativity. In this instance, it was insufficient merely to defy expectations and remain serenely obstinate; she felt it necessary to act in accordance with her judgment, assuring herself that her assessment was valid—indeed, had it not been so, she would not have felt the inclination to pursue it.
output: She returned home by Mr. Borthrop Trumbull’s office, meaning to call there. It was the first time in her life that Rosamond had thought of doing anything in the form of business, but she felt equal to the occasion. That she should be obliged to do what she intensely disliked, was an idea which turned her quiet tenacity into active invention. Here was a case in which it could not be enough simply to disobey and be serenely, placidly obstinate: she must act according to her judgment, and she said to herself that her judgment was right - “indeed, if it had not been, she would not have wished to act on it.”
title: Middlemarch
author: George Eliot

input: Additionally, it is worth noting that Celia remarked to Dorothea that, in the event of her eventual marriage, the presence of distinguished lineage and physical attractiveness would be a considerable advantage. Furthermore, this observation was prompted by Celia's reflection that Mr. Casaubon had not been particularly blessed with these qualities, and that it would be prudent to caution Dorothea in a timely manner. Moreover, Dorothea responded by reassuring her sister, stating that she had entirely different aspirations for her life, and that she had no intention of entering into matrimony again. In essence, Dorothea's statement was accompanied by a gentle gesture, as she touched her sister's chin and regarded her with affectionate indulgence, having come to bid her sister good-night while Celia was attending to her infant.
output:
“But you know, Dodo, if you ever did marry, it would be all the better to have blood and beauty,” said Celia, reflecting that Mr. Casaubon had not been richly endowed with those gifts, and that it would be well to caution Dorothea in time.

“Don’t be anxious, Kitty; I have quite other thoughts about my life. I shall never marry again,” said Dorothea, touching her sister’s chin, and looking at her with indulgent affection. Celia was nursing her baby, and Dorothea had come to say good-night to her.
title: Middlemarch
author: George Eliot

input: Rosamond reached for the inkstand and placed it on the table, intending to walk away when Lydgate, standing nearby, gently wrapped his arm around her and pulled her closer, saying something tender. His natural warmth may not easily be suppressed, and it tends to be a part of a husband's sense of responsibility to recognize that an inexperienced young woman might face challenges after marrying him. She accepted his kiss and responded with a slight return, creating a temporary sense of harmony between them. However, Lydgate found himself apprehensive about the upcoming conversations concerning their finances and the likely need for significant adjustments to their lifestyle. In summary, while they shared a moment of connection, underlying worries about their future added complexity to their relationship.
output:
Rosamond went to reach the inkstand, and after setting it on the table was going to turn away, when Lydgate, who was standing close by, put his arm round her and drew her towards him, saying -

His native warm-heartedness took a great deal of quenching, and it is a part of manliness for a husband to feel keenly the fact that an inexperienced girl has got into trouble by marrying him. She received his kiss and returned it faintly, and in this way an appearance of accord was recovered for the time. But Lydgate could not help looking forward with dread to the inevitable future discussions about expenditure and the necessity for a complete change in their way of living.
title: Middlemarch
author: George Eliot

input:
“You would greatly oblige me by doing so, Dorothea,” stated Mr. Casaubon, exhibiting a slight increase in meekness in his typically polite demeanor. “I find myself awake: my mind is remarkably clear.”

“I fear that the excitement may prove to be too overwhelming for you,” replied Dorothea, recalling Lydgate’s warnings.

“No, I do not perceive any undue excitement. Thought comes easily.” Dorothea hesitated to press the matter further, and she continued to read for an hour or more, adhering to the same plan as she had during the evening, albeit progressing through the pages with greater speed. Mr. Casaubon’s mind appeared more alert, and he seemed to anticipate the forthcoming content after only the slightest verbal cue, remarking, “That will suffice—mark that,” or “Proceed to the next section—I will omit the second excursus on Crete.” Dorothea was astonished to contemplate the bird-like swiftness with which his mind was traversing the terrain that had previously been so painstakingly explored over the years. Eventually, he said—
output:
“You would oblige me greatly by doing so, Dorothea,” said Mr. Casaubon, with a shade more meekness than usual in his polite manner. “I am wakeful: my mind is remarkably lucid.”

“I fear that the excitement may be too great for you,” said Dorothea, remembering Lydgate’s cautions.

“No, I am not conscious of undue excitement. Thought is easy.” Dorothea dared not insist, and she read for an hour or more on the same plan as she had done in the evening, but getting over the pages with more quickness. Mr. Casaubon’s mind was more alert, and he seemed to anticipate what was coming after a very slight verbal indication, saying, “That will do - mark that” - or “Pass on to the next head - I omit the second excursus on Crete.” Dorothea was amazed to think of the bird-like speed with which his mind was surveying the ground where it had been creeping for years. At last he said -
title: Middlemarch
author: George Eliot

input: However, the same constitution that gives the commons a power to check the king by withholding supplies also gives the king a power to check the commons by allowing him to reject their other bills. This can seem to assume that the king is wiser than those whom it has already assumed to be wiser than him, which may strike many people as rather absurd. There is something quite ridiculous in the makeup of monarchy: it tends to exclude a man from the means of information, yet it still empowers him to act in cases where the highest judgment is required. The position of a king can shut him off from the world, yet the business of a king requires him to know it thoroughly. As a result, these different parts, by working against and undermining each other, tend to show that the whole arrangement is unreasonable and impractical. Overall, monarchy tends to combine powers in a way that makes the whole system difficult to justify.
output:
But as the same constitution which gives the commons a power to check the king by withholding the supplies, gives afterwards the king a power to check the commons, by empowering him to reject their other bills; it again supposes that the king is wiser than those whom it has already supposed to be wiser than him. A mere absurdity!

There is something exceedingly ridiculous in the composition of monarchy; it first excludes a man from the means of information, yet empowers him to act in cases where the highest judgment is required. The state of a king shuts him from the world, yet the business of a king requires him to know it thoroughly; wherefore the different parts, by unnaturally opposing and destroying each other, prove the whole character to be absurd and useless.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input: However, the injuries and disadvantages we experience from that connection can often seem countless, and our duty to humanity as a whole, as well as to ourselves, may suggest that we should renounce the alliance. This is because any submission to, or dependence on, Great Britain tends to draw this continent directly into European wars and quarrels, and it can set us at odds with nations that might otherwise seek our friendship, and toward whom we feel neither anger nor complaint. Since Europe is our market for trade, it seems wise for us to avoid forming any partial connection with any part of it. It is in America's true interest to stay clear of European conflicts, which it can hardly do while, through its dependence on Britain, it is made the make-weight in the scale of British politics.
output: But the injuries and disadvantages we sustain by that connection, are without number; and our duty to mankind at large, as well as to ourselves, instruct us to renounce the alliance: Because, any submission to, or dependance on Great-Britain, tends directly to involve this continent in European wars and quarrels; and sets us at variance with nations, who would otherwise seek our friendship, and against whom, we have neither anger nor complaint. As Europe is our market for trade, we ought to form no partial connection with any part of it. It is the true interest of America to steer clear of European contentions, which she never can do, while by her dependence on Britain, she is made the make-weight in the scale of British politics.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input:
Thousands of individuals have already been devastated by British brutality, and it is likely that thousands more will suffer the same fate. Meanwhile, those who have not suffered have different feelings than those who have been affected. The latter group now possesses only their liberty, having sacrificed everything else in its service, and with nothing more to lose, they reject submission. Additionally, the overall attitude of the colonies towards a British government will be similar to that of a young person who is nearing the end of their obligation, and as a result, they will have little regard for it.

Furthermore, a government that cannot maintain peace is essentially no government at all, and in such a case, the payment of taxes is unnecessary. Moreover, it is worth considering what Britain can actually do, given that its power will be limited to theoretical authority, should a civil uprising occur immediately after reconciliation. Some individuals have expressed concerns that independence would lead to civil wars, although it is likely that many of these people spoke without fully thinking through the issue. Generally, initial thoughts are not always accurate, and this is the case here, as there are significantly more reasons to be concerned about a renewed connection with Britain than about independence.

Moreover, when considering the situation of those who have suffered, it is necessary to put oneself in their position. Therefore, if one were to be forced from their home, have their property destroyed, and have their circumstances ruined, it is unlikely that they would be able to accept the idea of reconciliation or feel bound by it. As a result, it is essential to acknowledge the depth of the injuries that have been inflicted and the lasting impact they will have on those who have been affected.
output: Thousands are already ruined by British barbarity; (thousands more will probably suffer the same fate) Those men have other feelings than us who have nothing suffered. All they now possess is liberty, what they before enjoyed is sacrificed to its service, and having nothing more to lose, they disdain submission. Besides, the general temper of the colonies, towards a British government, will be like that of a youth, who is nearly out of his time; they will care very little about her. And a government which cannot preserve the peace, is no government at all, and in that case we pay our money for nothing; and pray what is it that Britain can do, whose power will be wholly on paper, should a civil tumult break out the very day after reconciliation? I have heard some men say, many of whom I believe spoke without thinking, that they dreaded an independance, fearing that it would produce civil wars. It is but seldom that our first thoughts are truly correct, and that is the case here; for there are ten times more to dread from a patched up connexion than from independance. I make the sufferers case my own, and I protest, that were I driven from house and home, my property destroyed, and my circumstances ruined, that as man, sensible of injuries, I could never relish the doctrine of reconciliation, or consider myself bound thereby.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input:
The sentiments expressed in the following pages may not yet be widely accepted, which could limit their appeal. A longstanding habit of overlooking a particular issue can create an illusion of correctness and initially provoke a strong defense of established customs. However, this uproar tends to fade over time. Ultimately, time influences more change than reason does.

A prolonged and severe abuse of power often leads to questioning its legitimacy. Such inquiries may arise regarding matters that would not have been considered had the individuals suffering not been pushed to seek answers. The King of England has claimed the right to support the Parliament in what he refers to as their authority. Given that the citizens of this country face significant oppression from this alliance, they possess an undeniable right to scrutinize the claims of both parties and to reject the overreach of either.
output:
Perhaps the sentiments contained in the following pages, are not yet sufficiently fashionable to procure them general favor; a long habit of not thinking a thing wrong, gives it a superficial appearance of being right, and raises at first a formidable outcry in defense of custom. But the tumult soon subsides. Time makes more converts than reason.

As a long and violent abuse of power, is generally the Means of calling the right of it in question (and in Matters too which might never have been thought of, had not the Sufferers been aggravated into the inquiry) and as the King of England hath undertaken in his own Right, to support the Parliament in what he calls Theirs, and as the good people of this country are grievously oppressed by the combination, they have an undoubted privilege to inquire into the pretensions of both, and equally to reject the usurpation of either.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input:
The list of warships in England is extensive and impressive; however, at any given time, only a small portion of these ships are operational, with many either decommissioned or not in existence. Their names remain on the list even if only remnants of the ship exist. Furthermore, of the ships that are operational, only a limited number can be allocated to any single location simultaneously. The demands on the British navy are significant, covering regions such as the East and West Indies, the Mediterranean, Africa, and other territories under British claim. 

This highlights a common misconception about the strength of the English navy, which has led to the belief that it is necessary to match their entire naval force at once. This perception has been used by certain groups to discourage the development of an American navy. In reality, even a fraction of the British naval capacity would provide a strategic advantage to America, as the U.S. does not possess overseas territories and could concentrate its naval resources along its own coast. This strategic positioning would allow the U.S. to effectively defend against British forces, which would need to travel considerable distances to launch an attack and then return for resupply and maintenance. Additionally, while Britain maintains a check on American trade with Europe through its fleet, the U.S. exerts a comparable influence over British trade with the West Indies, which is vulnerable due to its proximity to the American coast.
output: The English list of ships of war, is long and formidable, but not a tenth part of them are at any one time fit for service, numbers of them not in being; yet their names are pompously continued in the list, if only a plank be left of the ship: and not a fifth part, of such as are fit for service, can be spared on any one station at one time. The East and West Indies, Mediterranean, Africa, and other parts over which Britain extends her claim, make large demands upon her navy. From a mixture of prejudice and inattention, we have contracted a false notion respecting the navy of England, and have talked as if we should have the whole of it to encounter at once, and for that reason, supposed, that we must have one as large; which not being instantly practicable, have been made use of by a set of disguised Tories to discourage our beginning thereon. Nothing can be farther from truth than this; for if America had only a twentieth part of the naval force of Britain, she would be by far an over match for her; because, as we neither have, nor claim any foreign dominion, our whole force would be employed on our own coast, where we should, in the long run, have two to one the advantage of those who had three or four thousand miles to sail over, before they could attack us, and the same distance to return in order to refit and recruit. And although Britain by her fleet, hath a check over our trade to Europe, we have as large a one over her trade to the West- Indies, which, by laying in the neighbourhood of the Continent, is entirely at its mercy.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input: The institution of monarchy is problematic, and the concept of hereditary succession further exacerbates this issue. As a result, the former is a degradation of humanity, while the latter, asserted as a right, is an affront to future generations. Naturally, all individuals are initially equal, and therefore, no one possesses the inherent right to establish their family as superior to others in perpetuity. Although a person may deserve a certain level of respect from their contemporaries, their descendants may not necessarily be worthy of inheriting such honors. Furthermore, one of the most compelling arguments against hereditary right in monarchs is that nature itself appears to reject this notion. Consequently, nature often seems to mock this idea by presenting individuals who are utterly unqualified to hold positions of power, thereby highlighting the absurdity of hereditary succession.
output: To the evil of monarchy we have added that of hereditary succession; and as the first is a degradation and lessening of ourselves, so the second, claimed as a matter of right, is an insult and an imposition on posterity. For all men being originally equals, no one by birth could have a right to set up his own family in perpetual preference to all others for ever, and though himself might deserve some decent degree of honors of his cotemporaries, yet his descendants might be far too unworthy to inherit them. One of the strongest natural proofs of the folly of hereditary right in kings, is, that nature disapproves it, otherwise she would not so frequently turn it into ridicule by giving mankind an ass for a lion.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input: Independence serves as the sole bond capable of uniting us. This highlights the importance of presenting a unified front, allowing us to focus on our objectives while legally distancing ourselves from the plans of an adversary who is both cunning and ruthless. Moreover, achieving independence would position us favorably for negotiations with Britain, as it is likely that the British government would find it less damaging to engage in discussions with the American states, rather than with what they perceive as "rebellious subjects." Delaying our pursuit of independence only fuels Britain's hopes for victory and extends the duration of the conflict. Our previous attempts to withhold trade in order to seek redress for our grievances have been ineffective, suggesting it may be time to independently address these issues and subsequently propose a reopening of trade. The mercantile and rational factions in England are likely to support us, as peace coupled with trade is preferable to ongoing warfare without it. Should our proposal not be accepted, we may consider seeking assistance from other nations.
output: In short, Independance is the only Bond that can tye and keep us together. We shall then see our object, and our ears will be legally shut against the schemes of an intriguing, as well, as a cruel enemy. We shall then too, be on a proper footing, to treat with Britain; for there is reason to conclude, that the pride of that court, will be less hurt by treating with the American states for terms of peace, than with those, whom she denominates, "rebellious subjects," for terms of accommodation. It is our delaying it that encourages her to hope for conquest, and our backwardness tends only to prolong the war. As we have, without any good effect therefrom, withheld our trade to obtain a redress of our grievances, let us now try the alternative, by independantly redressing them ourselves, and then offering to open the trade. The mercantile and reasonable part in England, will be still with us; because, peace with trade, is preferable to war without it. And if this offer be not accepted, other courts may be applied to.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input:
In short, monarchy and succession may often have plunged not just individual kingdoms but much of the world into bloodshed and ruin. It is a form of government that the word of God can be seen as testifying against, and bloodshed tends to accompany it.

If we look into what a king actually does, we may find that in some countries they have no duties at all; after spending their lives idly, without pleasure to themselves or benefit to the nation, they tend to withdraw from the scene and leave their successors to follow the same idle pattern. In absolute monarchies, the whole burden of business, both civil and military, tends to fall on the king; the children of Israel, in requesting a king, urged this point, "that he may judge us, and go out before us and fight our battles." But in countries where he is neither a judge nor a general, as in England, one might be puzzled to know what his business actually is.
output:
In short, monarchy and succession have laid (not this or that kingdom only) but the world in blood and ashes. 'Tis a form of government which the word of God bears testimony against, and blood will attend it.

If we inquire into the business of a king, we shall find that in some countries they have none; and after sauntering away their lives without pleasure to themselves or advantage to the nation, withdraw from the scene, and leave their successors to tread the same idle round. In absolute monarchies the whole weight of business, civil and military, lies on the king; the children of Israel in their request for a king, urged this plea "that he may judge us, and go out before us and fight our battles." But in countries where he is neither a judge nor a general, as in England, a man would be puzzled to know what is his business.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input: By shifting from debate to armed conflict, a new era in politics has begun, leading to a new way of thinking. Plans and proposals made before April 19, when hostilities began, are now outdated and irrelevant. Arguments presented by both sides at that time ultimately aimed for a union with Great Britain; the only distinction between them was their approach—one advocating force and the other promoting reconciliation. However, the first approach has proven ineffective, and the second has diminished in influence. This highlights a significant transformation in the political landscape.
output: By referring the matter from argument to arms, a new æra for politics is struck; a new method of thinking hath arisen. All plans, proposals, &c. prior to the nineteenth of April, i.e. to the commencement of hostilities, are like the almanacks of the last year; which, though proper then, are superseded and useless now. Whatever was advanced by the advocates on either side of the question then, terminated in one and the same point, viz. a union with Great- Britain; the only difference between the parties was the method of effecting it; the one proposing force, the other friendship; but it hath so far happened that the first hath failed, and the second hath withdrawn her influence.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input: If we were to overlook the current favorable and promising circumstances, and if independence were to be achieved through alternative means in the future, we may need to hold ourselves accountable, or perhaps more accurately, those individuals whose narrow perspectives tend to oppose this initiative without sufficient inquiry or consideration. There are reasons supporting independence that are perhaps better contemplated privately than expressed openly. Our focus should not be on whether we should pursue independence, but rather on how to achieve it in a stable, secure, and honorable manner, and it is understandable to feel apprehensive that we have not yet initiated this process. Each passing day reinforces the necessity of taking action. Even those who may still identify as Tories should, in theory, be particularly interested in supporting this cause; after all, the establishment of committees initially shielded them from public discontent, and a sound and well-organized government may be the best assurance for their continued security. Therefore, if they lack the inclination to embrace the ideals of independence, it would be prudent for them to still desire its attainment. In summary, the pursuit of independence is essential for our collective future stability and security.
output: Should we neglect the present favorable and inviting period, and an Independance be hereafter effected by any other means, we must charge the consequence to ourselves, or to those rather, whose narrow and prejudiced souls, are habitually opposing the measure, without either inquiring or reflecting. There are reasons to be given in support of Independance, which men should rather privately think of, than be publicly told of. We ought not now to be debating whether we shall be independant or not, but, anxious to accomplish it on a firm, secure, and honorable basis, and uneasy rather that it is not yet began upon. Every day convinces us of its necessity. Even the Tories (if such beings yet remain among us) should, of all men, be the most solicitous to promote it; for, as the appointment of committees at first, protected them from popular rage, so, a wise and well established form of government, will be the only certain means of continuing it securely to them. Wherefore, if they have not virtue enough to be Whigs, they ought to have prudence enough to wish for Independance.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input: Additionally, it is necessary to consider which option is the most feasible and practical: reconciliation or independence, with some occasional observations. Furthermore, in support of the first option, it would be possible to cite the opinions of some of the most capable and experienced individuals on this continent, whose views on this matter have not yet been publicly disclosed. Moreover, it is essentially a self-evident proposition that no nation can achieve significant prominence while in a state of foreign dependence, with limited commercial opportunities and restricted legislative authority. In essence, America has not yet experienced true opulence, and although its progress is unparalleled in the history of other nations, it is still in its formative stages compared to what it could potentially achieve if it had full control over its legislative powers. It is worth noting that England is currently coveting something that would ultimately be of no benefit to it, while the continent is hesitating on a matter that will ultimately lead to its downfall if neglected. Moreover, the benefits to England would accrue from America's commerce, not its conquest, and this commerce would likely continue to a significant extent even if the two countries were as independent of each other as France and Spain, since in many areas, neither country could find a more suitable market. Additionally, the independence of this country from Britain or any other nation is now the primary and sole objective worthy of consideration, and like all other truths that are discovered through necessity, it will become increasingly clear and compelling with each passing day.
output:
Secondly. Which is the easiest and most practicable plan, reconciliation or independance? with some occasional remarks.

In support of the first, I could, if I judged it proper, produce the opinion of some of the ablest and most experienced men on this continent; and whose sentiments, on that head, are not yet publicly known. It is in reality a self-evident position: For no nation in a state of foreign dependance, limited in its commerce, and cramped and fettered in its legislative powers, can ever arrive at any material eminence. America doth not yet know what opulence is; and although the progress which she hath made stands unparalleled in the history of other nations, it is but childhood, compared with what she would be capable of arriving at, had she, as she ought to have, the legislative powers in her own hands. England is, at this time, proudly coveting what would do her no good, were she to accomplish it; and the Continent hesitating on a matter, which will be her final ruin if neglected. It is the commerce and not the conquest of America, by which England is to be benefited, and that would in a great measure continue, were the countries as independant of each other as France and Spain; because in many articles, neither can go to a better market. But it is the independance of this country of Britain or any other, which is now the main and only object worthy of contention, and which, like all other truths discovered by necessity, will appear clearer and stronger every day.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input:
It is unreasonable to believe that France or Spain would provide assistance if our intention is solely to use that help to mend the divide and fortify the relationship between Britain and America. These nations would ultimately face negative repercussions from such an outcome. 

Furthermore, as long as we declare ourselves as subjects of Britain, foreign nations will view us as rebels. This situation poses a potential threat to their stability, as it is unusual for individuals to take up arms while still identifying as subjects. While we may understand this contradiction, the concept of combining resistance with subjection is too complex for most people to grasp.
output:
Secondly. - It is unreasonable to suppose, that France or Spain will give us any kind of assistance, if we mean only, to make use of that assistance for the purpose of repairing the breach, and strengthening the connection between Britain and America; because, those powers would be sufferers by the consequences.

Thirdly. - While we profess ourselves the subjects of Britain, we must, in the eye of foreign nations, be considered as rebels. The precedent is somewhat dangerous to their peace, for men to be in arms under the name of subjects; we, on the spot, can solve the paradox: but to unite resistance and subjection, requires an idea much too refined for common understanding.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input:
It is worth noting that one who adopts nature as a guide is not easily dislodged from his position, and upon that basis, it may be stated generally that independence, being a single and simple principle contained within ourselves, whereas reconciliation is an exceedingly intricate and complicated matter in which a treacherous and capricious court is involved, provides an answer that is beyond doubt.

Furthermore, the present condition of America is truly alarming to every individual capable of reflection. There exists no law, no government, and no other mode of authority than that which is founded upon and granted by courtesy. Moreover, the people are held together by an unprecedented concurrence of sentiment, which is nevertheless subject to change and which every concealed adversary endeavours to dissolve. Additionally, the current situation may be described as legislation without law, wisdom without a plan, and constitution without a name, and, what is remarkably astonishing, as perfect independence contending for dependence. It is worth noting that this instance is without precedent; such a case has never existed before, and who can determine what the outcome may be? In essence, the property of no individual is secure within the present unsteady system of affairs. Furthermore, the mind of the multitude is left without direction, and, seeing no fixed object before them, they pursue whatever fancy or opinion may suggest. Moreover, nothing is regarded as criminal; there is no such thing as treason, and therefore every individual considers himself at liberty to act as he pleases. Additionally, the Tories would not have dared to assemble offensively had they known that their lives, by that act, were forfeited to the laws of the state. It is worth noting that a distinction should be drawn between English soldiers taken in battle and inhabitants of America taken in arms. The former are prisoners, whereas the latter are traitors. The one forfeits his liberty, while the other forfeits his head.
output:
He who takes nature for his guide is not easily beaten out of his argument, and on that ground, I answer generally - That independance being a single simple line, contained within ourselves; and reconciliation, a matter exceedingly perplexed and complicated, and in which, a treacherous capricious court is to interfere, gives the answer without a doubt.

The present state of America is truly alarming to every man who is capable of reflexion. Without law, without government, without any other mode of power than what is founded on, and granted by courtesy. Held together by an unexampled concurrence of sentiment, which is nevertheless subject to change, and which every secret enemy is endeavouring to dissolve. Our present condition, is, Legislation without law; wisdom without a plan; constitution without a name; and, what is strangely astonishing, perfect Independance contending for dependance. The instance is without a precedent; the case never existed before; and who can tell what may be the event? The property of no man is secure in the present unbraced system of things. The mind of the multitude is left at random, and seeing no fixed object before them, they pursue such as fancy or opinion starts. Nothing is criminal; there is no such thing as treason; wherefore, every one thinks himself at liberty to act as he pleases. The Tories dared not have assembled offensively, had they known that their lives, by that act, were forfeited to the laws of the state. A line of distinction should be drawn, between, English soldiers taken in battle, and inhabitants of America taken in arms. The first are prisoners, but the latter traitors. The one forfeits his liberty, the other his head.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input: This highlights the concern that involving religion in political disputes can diminish its overall value and pose significant risks to society. It also suggests that many individuals within religious groups may not support the political statements being made, which raises questions about their involvement and endorsement. Ultimately, this indicates that such political engagement could undermine the continental harmony and friendships that have been fostered through recent generous donations, which is crucial for the well-being of everyone involved.
output:
First, Because it tends to the decrease and reproach of all religion whatever, and is of the utmost danger to society, to make it a party in political disputes.

Secondly, Because it exhibits a body of men, numbers of whom disavow the publishing political testimonies, as being concerned therein and approvers thereof.

Thirdly, Because it hath a tendency to undo that continental harmony and friendship which yourselves by your late liberal and charitable donations hath lent a hand to establish; and the preservation of which is of the utmost consequence to us all.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input:
In the following sections, the author has deliberately refrained from including personal remarks about individuals. The text does not contain compliments or criticisms directed at specific persons. This suggests that those who are wise and worthy do not require validation through written works, while those with misguided or hostile opinions will likely abandon them without excessive effort aimed at changing their views.

The struggle for America can be seen as a struggle for all humanity. Various circumstances have arisen, and will continue to arise, that are not limited to specific locales but are universal in nature, affecting the principles held by all supporters of humanity. The destruction of a nation through violence, the waging of war against the natural rights of all people, and the eradication of those who defend these rights concern everyone who possesses the capacity for empathy. This highlights the importance of collective responsibility beyond political affiliations.
output:
In the following sheets, the author hath studiously avoided every thing which is personal among ourselves. Compliments as well as censure to individuals make no part thereof. The wise, and the worthy, need not the triumph of a pamphlet; and those whose sentiments are injudicious, or unfriendly, will cease of themselves unless too much pains are bestowed upon their conversion.

The cause of America is in a great measure the cause of all mankind. Many circumstances hath, and will arise, which are not local, but universal, and through which the principles of all Lovers of Mankind are affected, and in the Event of which, their Affections are interested. The laying a Country desolate with Fire and Sword, declaring War against the natural rights of all Mankind, and extirpating the Defenders thereof from the Face of the Earth, is the Concern of every Man to whom Nature hath given the Power of feeling; of which Class, regardless of Party Censure, is the
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input: In the context of managing a fleet, many people make significant mistakes regarding crew composition; it is not essential for one-fourth of the crew to be composed of experienced sailors. The privateer known as the Terrible, captained by Captain Death, engaged in the most intense battles during the last war with fewer than twenty sailors aboard, despite having over two hundred men overall. A small number of skilled and sociable sailors can quickly train a sufficient number of capable land-based workers in the fundamental tasks required on a ship. This highlights that there may never be a more opportune time to engage in maritime activities than now, given that timber is readily available, fisheries are currently underutilized, and many sailors and shipbuilders are unemployed. Warships with seventy to eighty guns were constructed in New England forty years ago, suggesting that similar achievements can be replicated today. Shipbuilding is a source of great pride for America, and it is anticipated that the nation will eventually surpass all others in this field. Most eastern empires are landlocked and therefore lack the ability to compete in maritime endeavors. Africa is largely in a state of underdevelopment, and no European power possesses both extensive coastlines and a wealth of internal resources. While nature has granted one region a coastal advantage, it has limited another; America is uniquely positioned with both resources. Additionally, the vast expanse of Russia is largely cut off from the sea, meaning that its abundant forests, tar, iron, and cordage primarily serve as commodities for trade rather than supporting a strong naval presence.
output: In point of manning a fleet, people in general run into great errors; it is not necessary that one fourth part should be sailors. The Terrible privateer, Captain Death, stood the hottest engagement of any ship last war, yet had not twenty sailors on board, though her complement of men was upwards of two hundred. A few able and social sailors will soon instruct a sufficient number of active landmen in the common work of a ship. Wherefore, we never can be more capable to begin on maritime matters than now, while our timber is standing, our fisheries blocked up, and our sailors and shipwrights out of employ. Men of war, of seventy and eighty guns were built forty years ago in New-England, and why not the same now? Ship-building is America's greatest pride, and in which, she will in time excel the whole world. The great empires of the east are mostly inland, and consequently excluded from the possibility of rivalling her. Africa is in a state of barbarism; and no power in Europe, hath either such an extent of coast, or such an internal supply of materials. Where nature hath given the one, she has withheld the other; to America only hath she been liberal of both. The vast empire of Russia is almost shut out from the sea; wherefore, her boundless forests, her tar, iron, and cordage are only articles of commerce.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input: Individuals with passive temperaments tend to downplay the severity of Britain's offenses, holding out hope for a positive outcome and advocating for reconciliation. This highlights the importance of examining human emotions and the natural consequences of Britain's actions. When considering the doctrine of reconciliation, it becomes clear that it is challenging to love, honor, and faithfully serve a power that has brought destruction and violence to one's land. If it is not possible to do so, then delaying reconciliation will ultimately lead to ruin for future generations. This suggests that any connection with Britain, a nation that can no longer be loved or respected, will be forced and unnatural, driven solely by short-term convenience. Such a connection is likely to deteriorate over time, leading to a more dire situation than the initial one. Those who claim they can overlook Britain's violations must be asked: have you personally experienced the loss of your home, property, or loved ones at their hands? Have you been left to suffer alongside your destitute family? If not, then you may not fully understand the perspectives of those who have. Ultimately, if you have endured such hardships and can still reconcile with those responsible, it raises questions about your character and values. This suggests that you may be prioritizing self-interest over personal integrity, and that your actions may be driven by cowardice rather than conviction.
output: Men of passive tempers look somewhat lightly over the offences of Britain, and, still hoping for the best, are apt to call out, "Come, come, we shall be friends again, for all this." But examine the passions and feelings of mankind, Bring the doctrine of reconciliation to the touchstone of nature, and then tell me, whether you can hereafter love, honour, and faithfully serve the power that hath carried fire and sword into your land? If you cannot do all these, then are you only deceiving yourselves, and by your delay bringing ruin upon posterity. Your future connection with Britain, whom you can neither love nor honour, will be forced and unnatural, and being formed only on the plan of present convenience, will in a little time fall into a relapse more wretched than the first. But if you say, you can still pass the violations over, then I ask, Hath your house been burnt? Hath your property been destroyed before your face? Are your wife and children destitute of a bed to lie on, or bread to live on? Have you lost a parent or a child by their hands, and yourself the ruined and wretched survivor? If you have not, then are you not a judge of those who have. But if you have, and still can shake hands with the murderers, then are you unworthy of the name of husband, father, friend, or lover, and whatever may be your rank or title in life, you have the heart of a coward, and the spirit of a sycophant.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input: Although unnecessary offense should be carefully avoided, it is reasonable to believe that all supporters of the doctrine of reconciliation may be grouped into the following categories. The first consists of interested men, who cannot be trusted. The second consists of weak men, who cannot see. The third consists of prejudiced men, who will not see. The fourth consists of a certain set of moderate men, who think better of the European world than it deserves. This last class, by an ill-judged deliberation, will ultimately cause more calamities to this continent than all the other three combined.
output: Though I would carefully avoid giving unnecessary offence, yet I am inclined to believe, that all those who espouse the doctrine of reconciliation, may be included within the following descriptions. Interested men, who are not to be trusted; weak men, who cannot see; prejudiced men, who will not see; and a certain set of moderate men, who think better of the European world than it deserves; and this last class, by an ill-judged deliberation, will be the cause of more calamities to this continent, than all the other three.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input:
It is worth noting that there exists a certain delicacy regarding the origins and manner in which this matter must first be addressed. Furthermore, it appears most agreeable and consistent that this initiative should originate from an intermediary body situated between the governed and the governing authorities, specifically, between Congress and the populace. Consequently, a Continental Conference should be convened in the following manner and for the following purpose.

A committee comprising twenty-six members of Congress, specifically two representatives from each colony, shall be established. Additionally, two members from each House of Assembly or Provincial Convention shall be included, along with five representatives of the general populace. These representatives will be selected in the capital city or town of each province, representing the entire province, and will be chosen by any qualified voters who deem it appropriate to attend from all regions of the province for this purpose. Alternatively, if it is more convenient, the representatives may be selected from two or three of the most populous areas within the province. In this assembled conference, the two essential principles of governance—knowledge and power—will be united. The members of Congress, Assemblies, or Conventions, having gained experience in national matters, will serve as capable and valuable advisors, and the entire body, empowered by the people, will possess a legitimate authority.
output:
But as there is a peculiar delicacy, from whom, or in what manner, this business must first arise, and as it seems most agreeable and consistent that it should come from some intermediate body between the governed and the governors, that is, between the Congress and the people, let a Continental Conference be held, in the following manner, and for the following purpose.

A committee of twenty-six members of Congress, viz. two for each colony. Two members from each House of Assembly, or Provincial Convention; and five representatives of the people at large, to be chosen in the capital city or town of each province, for, and in behalf of the whole province, by as many qualified voters as shall think proper to attend from all parts of the province for that purpose; or, if more convenient, the representatives may be chosen in two or three of the most populous parts thereof. In this conference, thus assembled, will be united, the two grand principles of business, knowledge and power. The members of Congress, Assemblies, or Conventions, by having had experience in national concerns, will be able and useful counsellors, and the whole, being impowered by the people, will have a truly legal authority.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input: It is worth noting that the elevation of one individual above all others cannot be substantiated by the principles of natural equality, nor can it be defended based on scriptural authority. The will of the Almighty, as articulated by Gideon and the prophet Samuel, explicitly rejects the concept of governance by kings. Furthermore, the anti-monarchical passages within scripture have often been conveniently overlooked in monarchical systems, yet they certainly deserve the consideration of nations still in the process of establishing their governments. The directive to "Render unto Cæsar the things which are Cæsar's" serves as a judicial principle; however, it does not provide a foundation for monarchical governance, as the Jews during that period were devoid of a king and were subjugated to Roman authority.
output: As the exalting one man so greatly above the rest cannot be justified on the equal rights of nature, so neither can it be defended on the authority of scripture; for the will of the Almighty, as declared by Gideon and the prophet Samuel, expressly disapproves of government by kings. All anti-monarchical parts of scripture have been very smoothly glossed over in monarchical governments, but they undoubtedly merit the attention of countries which have their governments yet to form. "Render unto Cæsar the things which are Cæsar's" is the scripture doctrine of courts, yet it is no support of monarchical government, for the Jews at that time were without a king, and in a state of vassalage to the Romans.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input:
Additionally, it is evident that when William the Conqueror subdued England, he imposed law through the exercise of military power; and until we consent to the legitimate and authoritative occupation of the seat of government in America, we will be vulnerable to the possibility of it being filled by some opportunistic individual who may subject us to similar treatment, thereby prompting the question of what will become of our freedom and our property.

Furthermore, with regard to religion, it is worth noting that I consider it to be the indispensable duty of all government to safeguard the rights of all individuals who conscientiously profess a particular faith, and I am not aware of any other role that government should play in this regard. Moreover, if an individual were to relinquish the narrow-mindedness and selfishness that characterize the attitudes of many individuals in various professions, they would immediately be freed from their concerns regarding this matter. In essence, suspicion is a characteristic that is often associated with individuals of limited perspective, and it is detrimental to the well-being of society as a whole. It is worth noting that, for my part, I sincerely and conscientiously believe that it is the will of the divine authority that there should be a diversity of religious opinions among us, as this affords a broader scope for the expression of Christian kindness. Additionally, were we all to hold the same beliefs, our religious inclinations would lack the opportunity for testing and verification, and on this liberal principle, I view the various denominations among us as being akin to members of the same family, differing only in their specific affiliations.
output:
When William the Conqueror subdued England, he gave them law at the point of the sword; and until we consent, that the seat of government, in America, be legally and authoritatively occupied, we shall be in danger of having it filled by some fortunate ruffian, who may treat us in the same manner, and then, where will be our freedom? where our property?

As to religion, I hold it to be the indispensable duty of all government, to protect all conscientious professors thereof, and I know of no other business which government hath to do therewith. Let a man throw aside that narrowness of soul, that selfishness of principle, which the niggards of all professions are so unwilling to part with, and he will be at once delivered of his fears on that head. Suspicion is the companion of mean souls, and the bane of all good society. For myself, I fully and conscientiously believe, that it is the will of the Almighty, that there should be diversity of religious opinions among us: It affords a larger field for our Christian kindness. Were we all of one way of thinking, our religious dispositions would want matter for probation; and on this liberal principle, I look on the various denominations among us, to be like children of the same family, differing only, in what is called, their Christian names.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input:
In England, a king has limited responsibilities, which are primarily focused on waging war and distributing positions, resulting in the impoverishment of the nation and the creation of conflict. Furthermore, this role is relatively uncomplicated, yet it comes with a substantial annual budget of eight hundred thousand sterling and a significant amount of admiration. Nevertheless, one honest individual is of greater value to society and in the eyes of a higher power than all the rulers who have ever held power.

In the subsequent sections, the presentation will be based on straightforward facts, clear arguments, and sensible reasoning. Additionally, the only prerequisite for the reader is to approach the subject without preconceived notions and biases, allowing their rational thinking and emotions to guide their judgment. Moreover, it is essential for the reader to maintain an open-minded and impartial perspective, considering the broader implications and long-term effects, rather than solely focusing on the present moment.
output:
In England a king hath little more to do than to make war and give away places; which in plain terms, is to impoverish the nation and set it together by the ears. A pretty business indeed for a man to be allowed eight hundred thousand sterling a year for, and worshipped into the bargain! Of more worth is one honest man to society and in the sight of God, than all the crowned ruffians that ever lived.

In the following pages I offer nothing more than simple facts, plain arguments, and common sense; and have no other preliminaries to settle with the reader, than that he will divest himself of prejudice and prepossession, and suffer his reason and his feelings to determine for themselves; that he will put on, or rather that he will not put off, the true character of a man, and generously enlarge his views beyond the present day.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input: The observation that people often make unfounded statements without proper reflection is evident in discussions about historical events. A common assertion is that if a rupture had occurred forty or fifty years later, the Continent would have been better positioned to rid itself of dependence. However, this argument overlooks the fact that our current military capability stems from the experience gained during the last war, which would have faded over time. By the time of such a hypothetical future, the Continent would likely lack military leadership or knowledgeable officers, and future generations could be as uninformed about military matters as ancient civilizations. This highlights that the present moment is more advantageous than any future point. The reasoning is as follows: after the last war, we had experience but lacked troop numbers; conversely, in forty or fifty years, there may be an abundance of troops without the requisite experience. Therefore, the optimal moment for action is the present, as it balances existing military knowledge with the potential for growth in numbers.
output: I have frequently amused myself both in public and private companies, with silently remarking, the specious errors of those who speak without reflecting. And among the many which I have heard, the following seems the most general, viz. that had this rupture happened forty or fifty years hence, instead of now, the Continent would have been more able to have shaken off the dependance. To which I reply, that our military ability, at this time, arises from the experience gained in the last war, and which in forty or fifty years time, would have been totally extinct. The Continent, would not, by that time, have had a General, or even a military officer left; and we, or those who may succeed us, would have been as ignorant of martial matters as the ancient Indians: And this single position, closely attended to, will unanswerably prove, that the present time is preferable to all others. The argument turns thus - at the conclusion of the last war, we had experience, but wanted numbers; and forty or fifty years hence, we should have numbers, without experience; wherefore, the proper point of time, must be some particular point between the two extremes, in which a sufficiency of the former remains, and a proper increase of the latter is obtained: And that point of time is the present time.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input:
Currently, as British subjects, we are unable to gain recognition or audience abroad. The established protocol of all courts is not in our favor, and this will remain the case until we achieve independence, thereby earning a position comparable to that of other nations. Furthermore, this status will enable us to participate as equals in the international community.

Initially, these developments may seem unusual and challenging. However, as with previous steps we have taken, they will eventually become familiar and acceptable. Meanwhile, until independence is formally declared, the Continent will experience a sense of unease, similar to that of an individual who continually postpones an unpleasant task. Nevertheless, it is acknowledged that this task must be undertaken, and accordingly, it will continue to be a source of concern, with the awareness of its necessity constantly present. Additionally, the Continent will wish for a resolution to this situation, and will be motivated to bring it to a conclusion.
output:
Under our present denomination of British subjects, we can neither be received nor heard abroad: The custom of all courts is against us, and will be so, until, by an independance, we take rank with other nations.

These proceedings may at first appear strange and difficult; but, like all other steps which we have already passed over, will in a little time become familiar and agreeable; and, until an independance is declared, the Continent will feel itself like a man who continues putting off some unpleasant business from day to day, yet knows it must be done, hates to set about it, wishes it over, and is continually haunted with the thoughts of its necessity.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input: The act of taking up arms solely to enforce the repeal of a financial law appears unwarranted by both divine law and human sentiments, similar to the enforcement of obedience to such a law through violence. This suggests that the ends do not justify the means, as the lives of individuals are too precious to be risked over trivial matters. The justification for using arms arises from the violence inflicted upon individuals, the destruction of property by armed forces, and the invasion of the country. Ultimately, once it became necessary to defend against such aggression, all subjection to Britain should have ended, marking the beginning of American independence from the moment the first gun was fired. This perspective underscores a consistent rationale, informed by a series of events beyond the control of the colonies, rather than being driven by whim or ambition.
output: Besides, the taking up arms, merely to enforce the repeal of a pecuniary law, seems as unwarrantable by the divine law, and as repugnant to human feelings, as the taking up arms to enforce obedience thereto. The object, on either side, doth not justify the means; for the lives of men are too valuable to be cast away on such trifles. It is the violence which is done and threatened to our persons; the destruction of our property by an armed force; the invasion of our country by fire and sword, which conscientiously qualifies the use of arms: And the instant, in which such a mode of defence became necessary, all subjection to Britain ought to have ceased; and the independancy of America, should have been considered, as dating its æra from, and published by, the first musket that was fired against her. This line is a line of consistency; neither drawn by caprice, nor extended by ambition; but produced by a chain of events, of which the colonies were not the authors.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input: The debt that a nation incurs should not be a concern if the work is completed. It is essential for a nation to have some level of debt. A national debt serves as a national bond; when it does not accrue interest, it poses no significant issue. Currently, Britain carries a debt exceeding one hundred and forty million sterling, for which it pays more than four million in interest. In exchange for this debt, Britain maintains a substantial navy. In contrast, America has no debt and lacks a navy. However, with just one-twentieth of the British national debt, America could establish a navy that is twice the size of Britain’s. Presently, the value of England's navy is approximately three and a half million sterling.
output: The debt we may contract doth not deserve our regard if the work be but accomplished. No nation ought to be without a debt. A national debt is a national bond; and when it bears no interest, is in no case a grievance. Britain is oppressed with a debt of upwards of one hundred and forty millions sterling, for which she pays upwards of four millions interest. And as a compensation for her debt, she has a large navy; America is without a debt, and without a navy; yet for the twentieth part of the English national debt, could have a navy as large again. The navy of England is not worth, at this time, more than three millions and an half sterling.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input: The relationship between America and British politics suggests that America is not a primary concern for England; rather, England prioritizes its own interests when considering America's welfare. This highlights that England may restrict America's growth when it does not align with its own objectives or poses a threat to them. This situation raises concerns about the implications of such governance. It indicates that changing the name of a relationship does not transform the underlying dynamics between adversaries. To illustrate the dangers of pursuing reconciliation, one could argue that it would be strategically advantageous for the king to repeal certain acts to regain control over the provinces. This would allow him to achieve what he cannot accomplish through direct force, suggesting that reconciliation could lead to detrimental outcomes.
output: America is only a secondary object in the system of British politics, England consults the good of this country, no farther than it answers her own purpose. Wherefore, her own interest leads her to suppress the growth of ours in every case which doth not promote her advantage, or in the least interferes with it. A pretty state we should soon be in under such a second-hand government, considering what has happened! Men do not change from enemies to friends by the alteration of a name: And in order to shew that reconciliation now is a dangerous doctrine, I affirm, that it would be policy in the king at this time, to repeal the acts for the sake of reinstating himself in the government of the provinces; in order, that he may accomplish by craft and subtilty, in the long run, what he cannot do by force and violence in the short one. Reconciliation and ruin are nearly related.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input:
It is challenging to overcome local or long-standing prejudices. However, if we allow ourselves to analyze the components of the English constitution, we will discover that they consist of the remnants of two ancient tyrannies, mixed with some new republican elements. 

The third aspect is the new republican elements represented by the Commons, whose virtue is essential for the freedom of England. 

The first two elements, being hereditary, exist independently of the people. Therefore, in a constitutional context, they do not contribute to the freedom of the state.
output:
I know it is difficult to get over local or long standing prejudices, yet if we will suffer ourselves to examine the component parts of the English constitution, we shall find them to be the base remains of two ancient tyrannies, compounded with some new republican materials.

Thirdly. - The new republican materials, in the persons of the commons, on whose virtue depends the freedom of England.

The two first, by being hereditary, are independent of the people; wherefore in a constitutional sense they contribute nothing towards the freedom of the state.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input:
In instances when individuals have diverged from the correct path, it is not surprising that they encounter difficulties and failures. Furthermore, it is apparent from the manner in which you have conducted your testimony that engaging in politics, as a collective of religious individuals, is not an appropriate course of action for you. Although it may seem well-suited to your perspective, it remains a disordered amalgamation of good and bad elements that have been improperly combined, leading to conclusions that are both unnatural and unjust.

We acknowledge the initial two pages of your testimony, which, in total, do not exceed four pages, and we anticipate a reciprocal degree of respect from you. This expectation arises from the understanding that the desire for peace transcends the boundaries of Quakerism; it is, in fact, a fundamental aspiration shared by all human beings, regardless of their religious affiliations. On this basis, as individuals striving to establish an independent constitution for ourselves, we surpass others in our hope, purpose, and objectives. Our vision is one of everlasting peace. We have grown weary of conflict with Britain and perceive no viable resolution other than a definitive separation. Our actions are consistent; we endure the current adversities and burdens in the pursuit of fostering an unending and uninterrupted peace. We are actively striving, and will persist in our efforts, to sever and dissolve a connection that has already inundated our land with bloodshed; a connection that, as long as it persists, will inevitably lead to further calamities for both nations.
output:
When men have departed from the right way, it is no wonder that they stumble and fall. And it is evident from the manner in which ye have managed your testimony, that politics, (as a religious body of men) is not your proper Walk; for however well adapted it might appear to you, it is, nevertheless, a jumble of good and bad put unwisely together, and the conclusion drawn therefrom, both unnatural and unjust.

The two first pages, (and the whole doth not make four) we give you credit for, and expect the same civility from you, because the love and desire of peace is not confined to Quakerism, it is the natural, as well the religious wish of all denominations of men. And on this ground, as men labouring to establish an Independant Constitution of our own, do we exceed all others in our hope, end, and aim. Our plan is peace for ever. We are tired of contention with Britain, and can see no real end to it but in a final separation. We act consistently, because for the sake of introducing an endless and uninterrupted peace, do we bear the evils and burthens of the present day. We are endeavoring, and will steadily continue to endeavour, to separate and dissolve a connexion which hath already filled our land with blood; and which, while the name of it remains, will be the fatal cause of future mischiefs to both countries.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input: Those who speak of harmony and reconciliation, can you bring back the time that has passed? Can you restore innocence to prostitution? Neither can you reconcile Britain and America. The final bond is now severed, as the people of England are presenting addresses against us. There are wounds that nature cannot forgive; she would cease to be nature if she did. Just as a lover cannot forgive the assailant of his beloved, the continent cannot forgive the atrocities committed by Britain. The Almighty has instilled in us these enduring feelings for good and wise reasons. They serve as the guardians of His image within our hearts. They set us apart from the common herd. The social contract would unravel, and justice would be eliminated from the earth, or exist only sporadically, if we were indifferent to the bonds of affection. The robber and the murderer would often go unpunished if the injuries to our temper did not compel us toward justice.
output: Ye that tell us of harmony and reconciliation, can ye restore to us the time that is past? Can ye give to prostitution its former innocence? Neither can ye reconcile Britain and America. The last cord now is broken, the people of England are presenting addresses against us. There are injuries which nature cannot forgive; she would cease to be nature if she did. As well can the lover forgive the ravisher of his mistress, as the continent forgive the murders of Britain. The Almighty hath implanted in us these unextinguishable feelings for good and wise purposes. They are the guardians of his image in our hearts. They distinguish us from the herd of common animals. The social compact would dissolve, and justice be extirpated the earth, or have only a casual existence were we callous to the touches of affection. The robber, and the murderer, would often escape unpunished, did not the injuries which our tempers sustain, provoke us into justice.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input:
Thomas Anello, also known as Massanello, was a fisherman from Naples who successfully incited his fellow countrymen in the public marketplace against the oppression of the Spaniards, to whom the region was then subjected. This fervor led to a revolt, and in the span of a single day, he ascended to the position of king.

Furthermore, it is worth noting that to engage in discussions of friendship with individuals in whom our rational judgment prohibits us from placing trust, and with whom our emotions have been painfully affected through numerous channels, is an exercise in madness and folly. Each passing day erodes the remnants of kinship that exist between us and them. Is there any rational basis to anticipate that as this relationship deteriorates, our affection will somehow flourish, or that we will find common ground more easily when we face an increasing number of significant issues over which to disagree?
output:
¹ Thomas Anello, otherwise Massanello, a fisherman of Naples, who after spiriting up his countrymen in the public market place, against the oppressions of the Spaniards, to whom the place was then subject, prompted them to revolt, and in the space of a day became king.

To talk of friendship with those in whom our reason forbids us to have faith, and our affections wounded through a thousand pores instruct us to detest, is madness and folly. Every day wears out the little remains of kindred between us and them, and can there be any reason to hope, that as the relationship expires, the affection will increase, or that we shall agree better, when we have ten times more and greater concerns to quarrel over than ever?
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input:
It hardly needs to be said that the crown is the dominant element in the English constitution, and it is self-evident that its entire importance comes simply from its role as the source of offices and pensions. This highlights that while we have been wise enough to shut and lock a door against absolute monarchy, we have at the same time been foolish enough to put the crown in possession of the key.

The prejudice of Englishmen in favor of their own system of government by king, lords, and commons arises as much or more from national pride as from reason. Individuals are undoubtedly safer in England than in some other countries, but the will of the king is as much the law of the land in Britain as in France, with this difference: instead of coming directly from his mouth, it is delivered to the people in the more imposing form of an act of parliament. Ultimately, the fate of Charles the First has only made kings more subtle, not more just.
output:
That the crown is this overbearing part in the English constitution needs not be mentioned, and that it derives its whole consequence merely from being the giver of places and pensions is self-evident, wherefore, though we have been wise enough to shut and lock a door against absolute monarchy, we at the same time have been foolish enough to put the crown in possession of the key.

The prejudice of Englishmen, in favour of their own government by king, lords and commons, arises as much or more from national pride than reason. Individuals are undoubtedly safer in England than in some other countries, but the will of the king is as much the law of the land in Britain as in France, with this difference, that instead of proceeding directly from his mouth, it is handed to the people under the more formidable shape of an act of parliament. For the fate of Charles the first, hath only made kings more subtle - not more just.

input: The king has the authority to veto legislation in England, as any law requires his approval. This raises questions about the appropriateness of a young individual, often just twenty-one years old, having the power to reject laws proposed by millions who are older and more experienced. This situation highlights a certain absurdity in governance. However, it is important to recognize that the context differs significantly between England and America. The king's veto is considerably more perilous in America, where he is less likely to approve legislation aimed at strengthening defense, compared to his approach in England, where he generally supports such measures. Ultimately, the implications of the king's veto in America are much more severe than in England.
output: But the king you will say has a negative in England; the people there can make no laws without his consent. In point of right and good order, there is something very ridiculous, that a youth of twenty-one (which hath often happened) shall say to several millions of people, older and wiser than himself, I forbid this or that act of yours to be law. But in this place I decline this sort of reply, though I will never cease to expose the absurdity of it, and only answer, that England being the King's residence, and America not so, makes quite another case. The king's negative here is ten times more dangerous and fatal than it can be in England, for there he will scarcely refuse his consent to a bill for putting England into as strong a state of defence as possible, and in America he would never suffer such a bill to be passed.
