The king retains significant governing powers, which grants him a negative influence over the legislation of the entire continent. Given his history as a staunch opponent of liberty and his evident desire for arbitrary authority, one must question whether he is a suitable individual to dictate, "You shall make no laws without my approval." It is common knowledge among the inhabitants of America that, under the current constitution, this continent can only enact laws with the king's consent. Furthermore, it is evident that, based on past events, he will permit only those laws that serve his interests. 

The absence of laws in America can enslave us just as effectively as if we were subjected to laws imposed from England. Once matters are settled, it is clear that the full power of the crown will be applied to keep this continent subdued and compliant. Instead of advancing, we risk regressing or becoming embroiled in constant disputes and futile petitions. We are already more empowered than the king desires, and it is likely he will strive to diminish our status in the future. 

To distill the issue to its essence, can a power that is envious of our success be deemed appropriate for governance? Anyone who responds negatively to this question embodies the spirit of independence, which fundamentally revolves around whether we will have the authority to create our own laws or whether the king, our foremost adversary, will dictate, "There will be no laws except those I approve."
output: First. The powers of governing still remaining in the hands of the king, he will have a negative over the whole legislation of this continent. And as he hath shewn himself such an inveterate enemy to liberty, and discovered such a thirst for arbitrary power; is he, or is he not, a proper man to say to these colonies, "You shall make no laws but what I please." And is there any inhabitant in America so ignorant, as not to know, that according to what is called the present constitution, that this continent can make no laws but what the king gives leave to; and is there any man so unwise, as not to see, that (considering what has happened) he will suffer no law to be made here, but such as suit his purpose. We may be as effectually enslaved by the want of laws in America, as by submitting to laws made for us in England. After matters are made up (as it is called) can there be any doubt, but the whole power of the crown will be exerted, to keep this continent as low and humble as possible? Instead of going forward we shall go backward, or be perpetually quarrelling or ridiculously petitioning. - We are already greater than the king wishes us to be, and will he not hereafter endeavour to make us less? To bring the matter to one point. Is the power who is jealous of our prosperity, a proper power to govern us? Whoever says No to this question is an independant, for independancy means no more, than, whether we shall make our own laws, or whether the king, the greatest enemy this continent hath, or can have, shall tell us "there shall be no laws but such as I like."

Generally, even the most primitive creatures do not harm their own offspring, and similarly, savage societies do not wage war on their family members. Therefore, the claim, if accurate, would be a source of shame for Britain. Nevertheless, this statement is not entirely true, and the term "parent country" has been used in a misleading manner by the king and his supporters, who have a hidden agenda to influence the vulnerable minds of the people.

In reality, Europe, rather than England, is the parent country of America. Historically, this new world has served as a refuge for individuals who have been persecuted for their beliefs in civil and religious liberty, originating from various parts of Europe. These people have fled to America, not because they were escaping the nurturing care of a mother country, but rather because they were seeking to escape the oppressive treatment of a tyrannical power. Furthermore, it is worth noting that the same tyrannical forces that drove the initial emigrants away from their homes continue to pursue their descendants to this day, which is particularly relevant in the case of England.
output: But Britain is the parent country, say some. Then the more shame upon her conduct. Even brutes do not devour their young, nor savages make war upon their families; wherefore the assertion, if true, turns to her reproach; but it happens not to be true, or only partly so, and the phrase parent or mother country hath been jesuitically adopted by the king and his parasites, with a low papistical design of gaining an unfair bias on the credulous weakness of our minds. Europe, and not England, is the parent country of America. This new world hath been the asylum for the persecuted lovers of civil and religious liberty from every part of Europe. Hither have they fled, not from the tender embraces of the mother, but from the cruelty of the monster; and it is so far true of England, that the same tyranny which drove the first emigrants from home, pursues their descendants still.

Ultimately, this contrast underscores the potential benefits of republican governments, which are founded on more natural principles and may be better equipped to negotiate disputes and maintain peace.
output:
The colonies have manifested such a spirit of good order and obedience to continental government, as is sufficient to make every reasonable person easy and happy on that head. No man can assign the least pretence for his fears, on any other grounds, than such as are truly childish and ridiculous, viz. that one colony will be striving for superiority over another.

Where there are no distinctions there can be no superiority, perfect equality affords no temptation. The republics of Europe are all (and we may say always) in peace. Holland and Swisserland are without wars, foreign or domestic: Monarchical governments, it is true, are never long at rest; the crown itself is a temptation to enterprizing ruffians at home; and that degree of pride and insolence ever attendant on regal authority, swells into a rupture with foreign powers, in instances, where a republican government, by being formed on more natural principles, would negociate the mistake.

Moreover, our significant strength resides not in mere numbers but in our unity; nevertheless, our current numbers are adequate to withstand the forces of the entire world. At present, the continent boasts the largest assembly of armed and disciplined personnel of any power on Earth. We have reached a level of strength where no single colony can sustain itself independently, and when united, we possess the capacity to achieve our objectives. Any lesser or greater outcome could have dire consequences. Our land forces are already sufficient, and regarding naval matters, we cannot ignore the fact that Britain would never permit an American warship to be constructed as long as the continent remained under her control. Therefore, we would not be further advanced in that domain a century from now than we are today; in truth, we would likely be at a disadvantage, as the timber resources of the country continue to deplete, and what remains will ultimately be distant and challenging to obtain.
output:
As all men allow the measure, and vary only in their opinion of the time, let us, in order to remove mistakes, take a general survey of things, and endeavour, if possible, to find out the very time. But we need not go far, the inquiry ceases at once, for, the time hath found us. The general concurrence, the glorious union of all things prove the fact.

It is not in numbers, but in unity, that our great strength lies; yet our present numbers are sufficient to repel the force of all the world. The Continent hath, at this time, the largest body of armed and disciplined men of any power under Heaven; and is just arrived at that pitch of strength, in which no single colony is able to support itself, and the whole, when united, can accomplish the matter, and either more, or, less than this, might be fatal in its effects. Our land force is already sufficient, and as to naval affairs, we cannot be insensible, that Britain would never suffer an American man of war to be built, while the continent remained in her hands. Wherefore, we should be no forwarder an hundred years hence in that branch, than we are now; but the truth is, we should be less so, because the timber of the country is every day diminishing, and that, which will remain at last, will be far off and difficult to procure.

input:
Seldom, if ever, does complete truth reside within any human disclosure; it is infrequent for there to exist a situation in which something is entirely unadulterated or without error. Nevertheless, in this instance, although the actions may be misguided, the emotions are authentic, which may render the distinction less significant. Mr. Knightley could not attribute to Emma a more forgiving heart than she already possessed, nor a heart more willing to accept his own.

In reality, he had been entirely unaware of his own influence. He had followed her into the shrubbery without any intention of testing it. His purpose in approaching her, driven by concern regarding her reaction to Frank Churchill's engagement, was devoid of any selfish motive; he merely sought, should she provide an opportunity, to comfort or advise her. The remainder of the encounter was a spontaneous response to the sentiments he experienced in that moment. The reassuring revelation of her complete indifference towards Frank Churchill, along with her heart being entirely disengaged from him, had sparked the hope that, in time, he might earn her affection; however, this was not an immediate aspiration—he had simply, in a fleeting triumph of eagerness over judgment, desired confirmation that she did not prohibit his attempts to win her heart. The more elevated hopes that gradually emerged were all the more enchanting. The affection he had wished to cultivate, if possible, was already his! Within a span of half an hour, he transitioned from a state of deep distress to a condition so akin to perfect happiness that it could only be described as such.
output:
Seldom, very seldom, does complete truth belong to any human disclosure; seldom can it happen that something is not a little disguised, or a little mistaken; but where, as in this case, though the conduct is mistaken, the feelings are not, it may not be very material. - Mr. Knightley could not impute to Emma a more relenting heart than she possessed, or a heart more disposed to accept of his.

He had, in fact, been wholly unsuspicious of his own influence. He had followed her into the shrubbery with no idea of trying it. He had come, in his anxiety to see how she bore Frank Churchill’s engagement, with no selfish view, no view at all, but of endeavouring, if she allowed him an opening, to soothe or to counsel her. - The rest had been the work of the moment, the immediate effect of what he heard, on his feelings. The delightful assurance of her total indifference towards Frank Churchill, of her having a heart completely disengaged from him, had given birth to the hope, that, in time, he might gain her affection himself; - but it had been no present hope - he had only, in the momentary conquest of eagerness over judgment, aspired to be told that she did not forbid his attempt to attach her. - The superior hopes which gradually opened were so much the more enchanting. - The affection, which he had been asking to be allowed to create, if he could, was already his! - Within half an hour, he had passed from a thoroughly distressed state of mind, to something so like perfect happiness, that it could bear no other name.

When they all sat down it was better; to her taste a great deal better, for Frank Churchill grew talkative and gay, making her his first object. To amuse her, and be agreeable in her eyes, seemed all that he cared for - and Emma, glad to be enlivened, not sorry to be flattered, was gay and easy too, and gave him all the friendly encouragement, the admission to be gallant, which she had ever given in the first and most animating period of their acquaintance; but which now, in her own estimation, meant nothing, though in the judgment of most people looking on it must have had such an appearance as no English word but flirtation could very well describe. “Mr. Frank Churchill and Miss Woodhouse flirted together excessively.” They were laying themselves open to that very phrase - and to having it sent off in a letter to Maple Grove by one lady, to Ireland by another. Suddenly, Hook came face to face with Peter. The other onlookers stepped back, creating a circle around them. 

For some time, the two adversaries studied each other. Hook displayed a slight shudder, while Peter wore an enigmatic smile. 

Without further conversation, they engaged in combat. Initially, neither fighter gained the upper hand. Peter demonstrated exceptional skill as a swordsman, parrying rapidly and countering with feints that occasionally slipped past Hook's defenses. However, Peter's shorter reach hindered him from delivering a decisive blow. Hook, while not lacking in skill, was somewhat less agile with his wrist movements. He advanced with force, hoping to end the duel with a signature thrust he had learned from Barbecue in Rio. To his surprise, this thrust was repeatedly deflected. Frustrated, Hook attempted to close the distance and strike with his iron hook, which had been swinging through the air. Peter evaded the hook and lunged aggressively, piercing Hook in the ribs. Upon seeing his own blood, which he found distasteful, Hook dropped his sword and realized that he was at Peter's mercy.
output:
Thus suddenly Hook found himself face to face with Peter. The others drew back and formed a ring around them.

For long the two enemies looked at one another, Hook shuddering slightly, and Peter with the strange smile upon his face.

Without more words they fell to, and for a space there was no advantage to either blade. Peter was a superb swordsman, and parried with dazzling rapidity; ever and anon he followed up a feint with a lunge that got past his foe’s defence, but his shorter reach stood him in ill stead, and he could not drive the steel home. Hook, scarcely his inferior in brilliancy, but not quite so nimble in wrist play, forced him back by the weight of his onset, hoping suddenly to end all with a favourite thrust, taught him long ago by Barbecue at Rio; but to his astonishment he found this thrust turned aside again and again. Then he sought to close and give the quietus with his iron hook, which all this time had been pawing the air; but Peter doubled under it and, lunging fiercely, pierced him in the ribs. At the sight of his own blood, whose peculiar colour, you remember, was offensive to him, the sword fell from Hook’s hand, and he was at Peter’s mercy.

Had she haughtily unhanded him (and we should have loved to write it of her), she would have been hurled through the air like the others, and then Hook would probably not have been present at the tying of the children; and had he not been at the tying he would not have discovered Slightly’s secret, and without the secret he could not presently have made his foul attempt on Peter’s life.

input: The concept of dualism is also evident in the human condition. This highlights the idea that every excess is accompanied by a corresponding defect, and every defect by an excess. Every positive aspect has a negative counterpart, and every evil has a redeeming quality. Furthermore, every faculty that is capable of experiencing pleasure is also subject to a penalty for its abuse, emphasizing the importance of moderation. This suggests that for every advantage, there is a corresponding disadvantage, and for every gain, there is a loss. Ultimately, the pursuit of wealth and material possessions can have unintended consequences, as nature tends to balance excess with deficiency. If an individual accumulates too much wealth, their quality of life may suffer as a result. Nature inherently resists monopolies and exceptions, and the natural world tends to seek equilibrium. This is evident in the way that the varieties of human condition tend to equalize themselves over time, as some circumstance or event invariably arises to humble the powerful, the wealthy, and the fortunate, placing them on a more level footing with others. For example, an individual who is overly strong and fierce may be tempered by their love and concern for their family, which can soften their demeanor and make them more courteous. This process illustrates how nature maintains balance and equilibrium, transforming even the most hardened individuals into more gentle and compassionate beings.
output: The same dualism underlies the nature and condition of man. Every excess causes a defect; every defect an excess. Every sweet hath its sour; every evil its good. Every faculty which is a receiver of pleasure has an equal penalty put on its abuse. It is to answer for its moderation with its life. For every grain of wit there is a grain of folly. For everything you have missed, you have gained something else; and for everything you gain, you lose something. If riches increase, they are increased that use them. If the gatherer gathers too much, nature takes out of the man what she puts into his chest, swells the estate, but kills the owner. Nature hates monopolies and exceptions. The waves of the sea do not more speedily seek a level from their loftiest tossing, than the varieties of condition tend to equalize themselves. There is always some leveling circumstance that puts down the overbearing, the strong, the rich, the fortunate, substantially on the same ground with all others. Is a man too strong and fierce for society, and by temper and position a bad citizen, - a morose ruffian, with a dash of the pirate in him; - nature sends him a troop of pretty sons and daughters, who are getting along in the dame's classes at the village school, and love and fear for them smooths his grim scowl to courtesy. Thus she contrives to intenerate the granite and felspar, takes the boar out and puts the lamb in, and keeps her balance true.

output: Ever since I was a boy, I have wished to write a discourse on Compensation: for it seemed to me when very young, that on this subject life was ahead of theology, and the people knew more than the preachers taught. The documents, too, from which the doctrine is to be drawn, charmed my fancy by their endless variety, and lay always before me, even in sleep; for they are the tools in our hands, the bread in our basket, the transactions of the street, the farm, and the dwelling-house, greetings, relations, debts and credits, the influence of character, the nature and endowment of all men. It seemed to me, also, that in it might be shown men a ray of divinity, the present action of the soul of this world, clean from all vestige of tradition, and so the heart of man might be bathed by an inundation of eternal love, conversing with that which he knows was always and always must be, because it really is now. It appeared, moreover, that if this doctrine could be stated in terms with any resemblance to those bright intuitions in which this truth is sometimes revealed to us, it would be a star in many dark hours and crooked passages in our journey that would not suffer us to lose our way.

Matthew Arnold, in a speech about Emerson given in Boston, provided a thoughtful assessment of Emerson's position in the literary hierarchy. While some may perceive Arnold's perspective as lacking appreciation, more objective readers are likely to find merit in his evaluation of the prominent American figure.

After analyzing Emerson's poetry, Arnold concludes that he does not consider Emerson to be among the great poets or the great writers of literature. He identifies great writers as individuals such as Cicero, Plato, Bacon, Pascal, Swift, and Voltaire—those who possess a natural genius for style. Arnold notes that the presence of impressive passages in someone's work does not necessarily indicate that they are a great writer. Although Emerson includes passages of noble and moving eloquence, sharp wit, and keen observations of nature, Arnold maintains that he does not classify Emerson as a great writer. This perspective aligns with Carlyle's critique of Emerson's literary and poetic works, which he describes as too ethereal, speculative, and theoretical, suggesting a preference for more concrete and tangible expressions in writing.
output:
Matthew Arnold, in an address on Emerson delivered in Boston, gave an excellent estimate of the rank we should accord to him in the great hierarchy of letters. Some, perhaps, will think that Arnold was unappreciative and cold, but dispassionate readers will be inclined to agree with his judgment of our great American.

After a review of the poetical works of Emerson the English critic draws his conclusions as follows:

"I do not then place Emerson among the great poets. But I go farther, and say that I do not place him among the great writers, the great men of letters. Who are the great men of letters? They are men like Cicero, Plato, Bacon, Pascal, Swift, Voltaire - writers with, in the first place, a genius and instinct for style.... Brilliant and powerful passages in a man's writings do not prove his possession of it. Emerson has passages of noble and pathetic eloquence; he has passages of shrewd and felicitous wit; he has crisp epigram; he has passages of exquisitely touched observation of nature. Yet he is not a great writer.... Carlyle formulates perfectly the defects of his friend's poetic and literary productions when he says: 'For me it is too ethereal, speculative, theoretic; I will have all things condense themselves, take shape and body, if they are to have my sympathy.'...

input: Games of strength constituted a hallmark of the public games in Greece, which encompassed both athletic and intellectual contests of diverse forms. These grand national festivals exerted a profound influence across Greece, serving as a reliable bond of unity among the numerous independent states and significantly contributing to the collective effort to resist foreign invasions. In the context of Greek society, the accomplished athlete was venerated almost to the status of a deity, with documented instances of altars being constructed and sacrifices offered in their honor. Furthermore, the meticulous care and fostering of the physique, inspired by this national ethos, represent one of the most notable characteristics of Greek culture, a quality that could be judiciously emulated in contemporary society.
output: [Footnote 1: Games of strength. The public games of Greece were athletic and intellectual contests of various kinds. There were four of importance: the Olympic, held every four years; the Pythian, held every third Olympic year; and the Nemean and Isthmian, held alternate years between the Olympic periods. input: I am afraid to speak or act in any way that might be considered treason against the majesty of love, which is the genius and god of gifts and to whom we must not presume to prescribe. Let love give kingdoms or flower leaves indifferently. There are people from whom we always expect fairy tokens; let us not stop expecting them. This is a prerogative, and it is not to be limited by our municipal rules. For the rest, I like to see that we cannot be bought and sold. The best of hospitality and generosity is also not a matter of will, but of fate. I find that I am not much to you; you do not need me; you do not feel me; then I am thrust out of doors, even though you offer me house and lands. No services have any value, but only likeness. When I have tried to join myself to others through services, it proved to be an intellectual trick, and nothing more. They eat your service like apples and leave you out. But love them, and they feel for you and delight in you all the time.

input: These fleeting pleasures and subtle pains exist for curiosity, not for actual living. They should not be indulged. Engaging in such pursuits is akin to weaving cobwebs instead of fabric. Our friendships often reach shallow and unsatisfactory conclusions because we have infused them with ephemeral qualities, rather than the resilience of genuine human connection. The principles of friendship are profound, serious, and timeless, intertwined with the laws of nature and morality. However, we have focused on immediate gratification, seeking quick satisfaction. We grasp at the slowest fruits in the expansive garden of existence, fruits that require many seasons to ripen. We pursue our friends not with reverence but with a possessive desire that seeks to claim them as our own. This effort is in vain. We are equipped with subtle oppositions that emerge upon meeting, transforming all lyrical beauty into mundane reality. Most individuals lower themselves to meet one another. All interactions necessitate compromise, and, alarmingly, the unique essence of each beautiful nature fades as they draw closer. Actual society, even among the virtuous and talented, becomes a constant source of disappointment. After careful planning for encounters, we find ourselves plagued by frustrating misunderstandings, unexpected indifference, and sudden outbursts of wit and vitality during moments that should celebrate friendship and intellectual exchange. Our abilities do not function as they should, leading both individuals to find solace in solitude.
output: 8. Yet these uneasy pleasures and fine pains are for curiosity, and not for life. They are not to be indulged. This is to weave cobweb, and not cloth. Our friendships hurry to short and poor conclusions, because we have made them a texture of wine and dreams, instead of the tough fiber of the human heart. The laws of friendship are great, austere, and eternal, of one web with the laws of nature and of morals. But we have aimed at a swift and petty benefit, to suck a sudden sweetness. We snatch at the slowest fruit in the whole garden of God, which many summers and many winters must ripen. We seek our friend not sacredly but with an adulterate passion which would appropriate him to ourselves. In vain. We are armed all over with subtle antagonisms, which, as soon as we meet, begin to play, and translate all poetry into stale prose. Almost all people descend to meet. All association must be a compromise, and, what is worst, the very flower and aroma of the flower of each of the beautiful natures disappears as they approach each other. What a perpetual disappointment is actual society, even of the virtuous and gifted! After interviews have been compassed with long foresight, we must be tormented presently by baffled blows, by sudden, unseasonable apathies, by epilepsies of wit and of animal spirits, in the heyday of friendship and thought. Our faculties do not play us true, and both parties are relieved by solitude.

input:
Additionally, the discourses entitled Nature and The American Scholar embody the fundamental principles of Emerson's philosophical, poetic, and moral instruction. In essence, it is worth noting that Emerson, like all great educators, possessed a relatively limited number of core principles and theories that formed the basis of his teachings. Furthermore, these essential principles of existence can be succinctly articulated in a brief phrase, encompassing concepts such as self-reliance, cultural refinement, intellectual and moral autonomy, the divine nature of humanity and the natural world, the importance of labor, and the pursuit of lofty ideals.

Moreover, Emerson devoted the latter portion of his life to lecturing and literary pursuits. It is worth noting that his son, Dr. Edward Emerson, provided a fascinating account of the process by which his father's lectures were constructed. Moreover, throughout his life, Emerson maintained a journal, which he referred to as his intellectual repository. The ideas and thoughts recorded in this journal were meticulously indexed, and a significant number of them ultimately appeared in his published works, having been carefully selected, expanded, and refined over time. Additionally, these thoughts were initially recorded in a chronological manner, without regard to order or organization, but were later categorized, elaborated upon, and illustrated, ultimately being incorporated into lectures or discourses, and subjected to repeated scrutiny and revision before being finally refined and published in essay form.
output:
These two discourses, Nature and The American Scholar, strike the keynote of Emerson's philosophical, poetical, and moral teachings. In fact he had, as every great teacher has, only a limited number of principles and theories to teach. These principles of life can all be enumerated in twenty words - self-reliance, culture, intellectual and moral independence, the divinity of nature and man, the necessity of labor, and high ideals.

Emerson spent the latter part of his life in lecturing and in literary work. His son, Dr. Edward Emerson, gave an interesting account of how these lectures were constructed. "All through his life he kept a journal. This book, he said, was his 'Savings Bank.' The thoughts thus received and garnered in his journals were indexed, and a great many of them appeared in his published works. They were religiously set down just as they came, in no order except chronological, but later they were grouped, enlarged or pruned, illustrated, worked into a lecture or discourse, and, after having in this capacity undergone repeated testing and rearranging, were finally carefully sifted and more rigidly pruned, and were printed as essays."

input: This law often shapes the regulations of cities and nations. It may be futile to build or conspire against it, as mismanagement tends not to persist for long. While it may seem that no checks exist against a new wrongdoing, these checks likely exist and will eventually surface. In the case of a harsh government, the safety of the leader may be compromised. Similarly, excessive taxation can lead to minimal revenue. If the criminal justice system is excessively harsh, juries may be less likely to convict. Conversely, if the laws are too lenient, individuals may seek private retribution. In a highly energized democracy, citizens may react with intensified vigor, making life feel more vibrant. Ultimately, the true essence and contentment of human life often appear to transcend the extremes of circumstance, adapting relatively well across various conditions. The impact of individual character tends to remain consistent across different forms of governance, whether in Turkey or New England. Historically, even under the ancient despots of Egypt, it seems that individuals were as free as cultural conditions would permit.
output: This law writes the laws of cities and nations. It is in vain to build or plot or combine against it. Things refuse to be mismanaged long. Res nolunt diu male administrari. Though no checks to a new evil appear, the checks exist, and will appear. If the government is cruel, the governor's life is not safe. If you tax too high, the revenue will yield nothing. If you make the criminal code sanguinary, juries will not convict. If the law is too mild, private vengeance comes in. If the government is a terrific democracy, the pressure is resisted by an overcharge of energy in the citizen, and life glows with a fiercer flame. The true life and satisfactions of man seem to elude the utmost rigors or felicities of condition, and to establish themselves with great indifferency under all varieties of circumstances. Under all governments the influence of character remains the same, - in Turkey and in New England about alike. Under the primeval despots of Egypt, history honestly confesses that man must have been as free as culture could make him.

input: The world can often be seen encapsulated in a drop of dew. While a microscope may struggle to detect the tiny organisms, it is important to recognize that being small does not necessarily diminish their complexity. Features such as vision, hearing, taste, smell, movement, resistance, appetite, and reproductive systems can all exist within these minute beings. Similarly, we may find that our lives are reflected in every action we take. The idea of omnipresence suggests that a divine essence can be found in even the smallest elements, like moss and cobwebs. The essence of the universe seems to manifest within each specific point. Where there is goodness, one may also find evil; where there is attraction, there can also be aversion; and where there is strength, there may exist limitations. Overall, this perspective highlights the interconnected nature of existence.
output: The world globes itself in a drop of dew. The microscope cannot find the animalcule which is less perfect for being little. Eyes, ears, taste, smell, motion, resistance, appetite, and organs of reproduction that take hold on eternity, - all find room to consist in the small creature. So do we put our life into every act. The true doctrine of omnipresence is, that God reappears with all his parts in every moss and cobweb. The value of the universe contrives to throw itself into every point. If the good is there, so is the evil; if the affinity, so the repulsion; if the force, so the limitation.

input: Virtues are generally seen as the exception rather than the rule. There is the man and his virtues. Men perform what is called a good action, such as an act of courage or charity, much as they would pay a fine to make up for their daily absence from parade. Their works are done as an apology or excuse for their living in the world, as invalids and the insane pay a high board. Their virtues are penances. I do not wish to atone, but to live. My life is for itself and not for a spectacle. I much prefer that it should be of a lower strain, so long as it is genuine and consistent, than that it should be glittering and unsteady. I wish it to be sound and sweet, and not to need diet and bleeding. I ask primary evidence that you are a man, and refuse this appeal from the man to his actions. I know that for myself it makes no difference whether I do or refrain from those actions which are considered excellent. I cannot consent to pay for a privilege where I have an intrinsic right. Few and mean as my gifts may be, I actually am, and do not need for my own assurance or the assurance of my fellows any secondary testimony. This highlights a preference for authentic existence over performed virtue. Ultimately, the passage suggests that being genuinely oneself requires no external validation.
output: Virtues are, in the popular estimate, rather the exception than the rule. There is the man and his virtues. Men do what is called a good action, as some piece of courage or charity, much as they would pay a fine in expiation of daily non-appearance on parade. Their works are done as an apology or extenuation of their living in the world, - as invalids and the insane pay a high board. Their virtues are penances. I do not wish to expiate, but to live. This address was given at Cambridge in 1837, before the Harvard Chapter of the Phi Beta Kappa Society, a college fraternity whose members are typically drawn from the top twenty-five students in each graduating class. I greet you at the beginning of our literary year. Our anniversary is one of hope, and perhaps not enough of labor. input: The actions and events of our childhood and youth now exist as subjects of tranquil observation. They remain suspended like vivid images in the atmosphere. Conversely, our recent actions and the matters currently at hand elude our capacity for speculation. Our emotions still flow through these experiences. We are as unaware of them as we are of our feet, hands, or brains. The new deed remains an integral part of life, temporarily immersed within our unconscious existence. During a moment of contemplation, it detaches itself from life much like a ripe fruit, transforming into a thought within the mind. Instantly, it is elevated and transfigured; the perishable has assumed an incorruptible state. Henceforth, it becomes an object of beauty, regardless of its humble origin and surroundings. Furthermore, it is important to note the impossibility of anticipating this act. In its immature form, it is incapable of flight, radiance, or vibrancy; it exists merely as a dull grub. However, without any prior notice, the same entity unfurls magnificent wings and emerges as an angel of wisdom. Thus, there exists no fact or event in our personal history that will not, in due time, shed its adhesive and inert quality, astounding us by ascending from our being into the celestial realm. The cradle and infancy, school and playground, the fears associated with boys, dogs, and reprimands, the affection for young girls and berries, along with many other experiences that once dominated our perception, have already faded. Friends and family, profession and political affiliations, town and countryside, nation and world must also rise and resonate in harmony.
output: The actions and events of our childhood and youth are now matters of calmest observation. They lie like fair pictures in the air. Not so with our recent actions, - with the business which we now have in hand. On this we are quite unable to speculate. Our affections as yet circulate through it. We no more feel or know it than we feel the feet, or the hand, or the brain of our body. The new deed is yet a part of life, - remains for a time immersed in our unconscious life. In some contemplative hour it detaches itself from the life like a ripe fruit, to become a thought of the mind. Instantly it is raised, transfigured; the corruptible has put on incorruption. Henceforth it is an object of beauty, however base its origin and neighborhood. Observe, too, the impossibility of antedating this act. In its grub state it cannot fly, it cannot shine, it is a dull grub. But suddenly, without observation, the selfsame thing unfurls beautiful wings, and is an angel of wisdom. So is there no fact, no event, in our private history, which shall not, sooner or later, lose its adhesive, inert form, and astonish us by soaring from our body into the empyrean. Cradle and infancy, school and playground, the fear of boys, and dogs, and ferules, the love of little maids and berries, and many another fact that once filled the whole sky, are gone already; friend and relative, profession and party, town and country, nation and world, must also soar and sing.

input: It is foolish to fear that our ties may become too spiritual, as though in that way we might lose some genuine affection. Whatever correction of our common views we make from insight, nature will surely confirm us in, and though it may appear to deprive us of some pleasure, it will repay us with a greater one. Let us feel, if we choose, the absolute isolation of the individual. We are certain that we possess everything within ourselves. We travel to Europe, or we pursue particular persons, or we read books, in the instinctive belief that these will draw it forth and reveal us to ourselves. We are all beggars. The persons are such as we are; Europe is an old, faded garment of the dead; the books are their ghosts. Let us abandon this idolatry. Let us renounce this mendicancy. Let us even bid our dearest friends farewell and defy them, saying, "Who are you? Release me. I will be dependent no longer." Ah! Do you not see, my brother, that in this way we part only to meet again on a higher plane, and to belong to one another only the more because we belong more to ourselves? A friend is two-faced: he looks to the past and the future. He is the child of all my preceding hours, the prophet of those to come, and the herald of a greater friend.
output: 22. It is foolish to be afraid of making our ties too spiritual, as if so we could lose any genuine love. Let us feel, if we will, the absolute insulation of man. We are sure that we have all in us. We go to Europe, or we pursue persons, or we read books, in the instinctive faith that these will call it out and reveal us to ourselves. Beggars all. The persons are such as we; the Europe, an old faded garment of dead persons; the books, their ghosts. Let us drop this idolatry. Let us give over this mendicancy. Let us even bid our dearest friends farewell, and defy them, saying, "Who are you? Unhand me. I will be dependent no more." input: It is worth noting that we now find ourselves as a collective, lacking individuality. Humanity does not hold reverence for one another, nor is the brilliance of intellect encouraged to remain introspective in order to connect with the vast internal depths of thought; rather, it seeks external validation, soliciting a mere cup of water from the vessels of others. Additionally, it is essential for each individual to embark on their journey alone. I find greater solace in the quietude of a church before the commencement of the service than in any delivered sermon. The individuals present appear distant, cool, and pure, each encircled by their own sacred space or sanctuary. Therefore, let us always choose to remain seated in contemplation. Why should we bear the shortcomings of our friends, spouses, parents, or children simply because they occupy our shared space or share our lineage? I recognize that every individual shares the essence of my being, and I, in turn, share the essence of all humanity. However, I shall not adopt their irritability or folly, nor shall I feel shame on their behalf. Furthermore, the nature of one's solitude must transcend mere physical separation; it should be spiritual and uplifting. At times, it may seem as if the entire world conspires to inundate you with trivial demands. Friends, clients, children, illness, fear, want, and charity all simultaneously knock at your door and implore, "Join us." However, it is vital to maintain your dignity; do not descend into their chaos. The annoyance that others may inflict upon me is a consequence of my own weak curiosity. No individual can approach me without my consent. In essence, "What we cherish, we possess, yet through desire, we deprive ourselves of that very affection."
output: But now we are a mob. Man does not stand in awe of man, nor is his genius admonished to stay at home to put itself in communication with the internal ocean, but it goes abroad to beg a cup of water of the urns of other men. We must go alone. I like the silent church before the service begins, better than any preaching. How far off, how cool, how chaste the persons look, begirt each one with a precinct or sanctuary! So let us always sit. Why should we assume the faults of our friend, or wife, or father, or child, because they sit around our hearth, or are said to have the same blood? All men have my blood, and I have all men's. Not for that will I adopt their petulance or folly, even to the extent of being ashamed of it. But your isolation must not be mechanical, but spiritual, that is, must be elevation. At times the whole world seems to be in conspiracy to importune you with emphatic trifles. Friend, client, child, sickness, fear, want, charity, all knock at once at thy closet door, and say, "Come out unto us." But keep thy state; come not into their confusion. The power men possess to annoy men, I give them by a weak curiosity. No man can come near me but through my act. "What we love that we have, but by desire we bereave ourselves of the love."

In the works of earlier English dramatists, particularly in the plays of Beaumont and Fletcher, there is a consistent acknowledgment of gentility. Noble behavior appears easily identifiable within the society of their time, much like distinguishing colors in the American populace today. When a character such as Rodrigo, Pedro, or Valerio makes an entrance, even if he is unfamiliar, the duke or governor immediately recognizes him as a gentleman and extends endless civilities. In contrast, all others are regarded as lesser individuals.

This appreciation for personal qualities is mirrored in their works, which often feature heroic characters and dialogues. In plays like Bonduca, Sophocles, the Mad Lover, and the Double Marriage, the speakers exhibit earnestness and sincerity, allowing the dialogue to elevate into poetry with minimal plot developments. For instance, in a notable scene, the Roman Martius has triumphed over Athens, except for the indomitable spirits of Sophocles, the duke of Athens, and his wife, Dorigen. Martius becomes infatuated with Dorigen’s beauty and attempts to spare her husband’s life. However, Sophocles refuses to plead for his own life, despite knowing that a simple request could secure it, leading to the impending execution of both men.
output: 1. In the elder English dramatists, and mainly in the plays of Beaumont and Fletcher, there is a constant recognition of gentility, as if a noble behavior were as easily marked in the society of their age, as color is in our American population. When any Rodrigo, Pedro, or Valerio enters, though he be a stranger, the duke or governor exclaims, This is a gentleman, - and proffers civilities without end; but all the rest are slag and refuse. In harmony with this delight in personal advantages, there is in their plays a certain heroic cast of character and dialogue, - as in Bonduca, Sophocles, the Mad Lover, the Double Marriage, - wherein the speaker is so earnest and cordial, and on such deep grounds of character, that the dialogue, on the slightest additional incident in the plot, rises naturally into poetry. Among many texts, take the following. The Roman Martius has conquered Athens - all but the invincible spirits of Sophocles, the duke of Athens, and Dorigen, his wife. The beauty of the latter inflames Martius, and he seeks to save her husband; but Sophocles will not ask his life, although assured, that a word will save him, and the execution of both proceeds.

It can be argued that virtues such as truth, frankness, courage, love, humility, and prudence may often be interconnected, as they tend to contribute to a person's overall well-being. While it is uncertain whether all matter will ultimately be found to be composed of a single element, such as oxygen or hydrogen, it is possible that the world of human behavior and actions may be viewed as being made up of a unified whole, with many principles and values being intertwined. As we explore the world around us, we may find that many of our actions and decisions can be related to a set of fundamental principles, which can be thought of as a kind of moral framework.

The eye and its field of vision can be seen as a representation of this idea, with the horizon forming a kind of boundary or limit. This pattern of a central point surrounded by a circumference is repeated throughout nature, and may be considered a symbol of great significance. The concept of a circle with its center everywhere and its circumference nowhere, as described by St. Augustine, can be seen as a powerful metaphor for the nature of the world and our place in it. Throughout our lives, we may be constantly learning and interpreting the meaning of this and other forms, and one possible lesson is that every action has consequences and may be part of a larger cycle of cause and effect. Additionally, it may be possible to draw a larger circle around any given action or event, suggesting that there is always more to learn and discover, and that every ending can also be a new beginning. In summary, the world and our experiences in it may be characterized by a series of interconnected patterns and cycles, with every event and action being part of a larger whole.
output:
Thus truth, frankness, courage, love, humility, and all the virtues range themselves on the side of prudence, or the art of securing a present well-being. I do not know if all matter will be found to be made of one element, as oxygen or hydrogen, at last, but the world of manners and actions is wrought of one stuff, and begin where we will we are pretty sure in a short space to be mumbling our ten commandments.

The eye is the first circle; the horizon which it forms is the second; and throughout nature this primary picture is repeated without end. It is the highest emblem in the cipher of the world. St. Augustine described the nature of God as a circle whose centre was everywhere and its circumference nowhere. We are all our lifetime reading the copious sense of this first of forms. One moral we have already deduced in considering the circular or compensatory character of every human action. Another analogy we shall now trace, that every action admits of being outdone. Our life is an apprenticeship to the truth that around every circle another can be drawn; that there is no end in nature, but every end is a beginning; that there is always another dawn risen on mid-noon, and under every deep a lower deep opens.

input: The key to every man is his thought. However sturdy and defiant he may appear, he has a helm that he obeys, an idea according to which all his facts are classified. He can only be reformed by showing him a new idea that commands his own. The life of man is a self-evolving circle, which, from a ring imperceptibly small, rushes outward on all sides to new and larger circles, and this without end. The extent to which this generation of circles, wheel without wheel, will go depends on the force or truth of the individual soul. This highlights that each thought, having formed itself into a circular wave of circumstance—such as an empire, the rules of an art, a local usage, or a religious rite—exerts an inert effort to heap itself on that ridge, to solidify, and to hem in the life. But if the soul is quick and strong, it bursts over that boundary on all sides and expands another orbit on the great deep, which also runs up into a high wave, with an attempt again to stop and to bind. Ultimately, the heart refuses to be imprisoned; in its first and narrowest pulses, it already tends outward with a vast force and toward immense and innumerable expansions.

input: Wisdom will never allow us to be on unfriendly terms with any person or group of people. We hold back sympathy and intimacy from others, as though we were waiting for some better sympathy and intimacy to arrive. But from where, and when? Tomorrow will be much like today. Life is wasted while we are preparing to live. Our friends and fellow workers pass away from us. We can hardly say that we see new men and new women approaching us. We are too old to care about fashion, and too old to expect the support of anyone greater or more powerful. This suggests that we should take pleasure in the affections and habits that grow near us. These old shoes are comfortable on the feet. We can undoubtedly find faults easily in the company we keep, and we can easily mention prouder names that appeal more to our fancy. Every person's imagination has its own friends, and life would be pleasant with such companions. But if you cannot have them on good mutual terms, you cannot have them at all. If our ambition, rather than the divine, shapes and forms these new relationships, their virtue is lost, just as strawberries lose their flavor when grown in garden beds. Ultimately, this highlights the importance of accepting and valuing the connections already within our reach.
output: Wisdom will never let us stand with any man or men on an unfriendly footing. We refuse sympathy and intimacy with people, as if we waited for some better sympathy and intimacy to come. But whence and when? To-morrow will be like to-day. Life wastes itself whilst we are preparing to live. Our friends and fellow-workers die off from us. Scarcely can we say we see new men, new women, approaching us. We are too old to regard fashion, too old to expect patronage of any greater or more powerful. Let us suck the sweetness of those affections and consuetudes that grow near us. These old shoes are easy to the feet. Undoubtedly we can easily pick faults in our company, can easily whisper names prouder and that tickle the fancy more. Every man's imagination hath its friends; and pleasant would life be with such companions. But if you cannot have them on good mutual terms, you cannot have them. If not the Deity but our ambition hews and shapes the new relations, their virtue escapes, as strawberries lose their flavor in garden beds.

input: The novel can be described as lacking a conventional plot and featuring only one character. It serves as a psychological exploration of a young Parisian who seems to spend his life attempting to embody the passions and ideas of various eras, rather than his own in the nineteenth century. In a way, he appears to synthesize the diverse moods that humanity has experienced over time, appreciating both the artificial renunciations that some might call virtue and the more instinctive rebellions that others may refer to as sin. The writing style is notable for its intricate quality, combining vividness and obscurity, and it is rich with slang, older expressions, technical terminology, and elaborate rephrasings. This style is characteristic of some of the most esteemed figures within the French Symbolist movement. The metaphors presented could be seen as both extravagant and delicately nuanced. The sensory experiences depicted often draw from mystical philosophy, making it difficult at times to discern whether the reader is engaging with the spiritual revelations of a medieval saint or the troubling admissions of a contemporary sinner. The book may be perceived as unsettling, with a lingering scent of incense that seems to permeate its pages and affect the mind. The rhythmic flow of the sentences, marked by intricate refrains and carefully repeated phrases, can induce a state of reverie in the reader, leading them to lose track of the waning day and the encroaching shadows. In summary, this novel offers a complex and immersive reading experience that can provoke deep reflection.
output: It was a novel without a plot and with only one character, being, indeed, simply a psychological study of a certain young Parisian who spent his life trying to realize in the nineteenth century all the passions and modes of thought that belonged to every century except his own, and to sum up, as it were, in himself the various moods through which the world-spirit had ever passed, loving for their mere artificiality those renunciations that men have unwisely called virtue, as much as those natural rebellions that wise men still call sin. The style in which it was written was that curious jewelled style, vivid and obscure at once, full of argot and of archaisms, of technical expressions and of elaborate paraphrases, that characterizes the work of some of the finest artists of the French school of Symbolistes. There were in it metaphors as monstrous as orchids and as subtle in colour. The life of the senses was described in the terms of mystical philosophy. One hardly knew at times whether one was reading the spiritual ecstasies of some mediæval saint or the morbid confessions of a modern sinner. It was a poisonous book. The heavy odour of incense seemed to cling about its pages and to trouble the brain. The mere cadence of the sentences, the subtle monotony of their music, so full as it was of complex refrains and movements elaborately repeated, produced in the mind of the lad, as he passed from chapter to chapter, a form of reverie, a malady of dreaming, that made him unconscious of the falling day and creeping shadows.

input: You are unchanged. I wonder what your future will hold. Do not jeopardize it with renunciations. At this moment, you embody perfection. Do not render yourself incomplete. You are entirely flawless now. You need not deny this; you are aware of it. Moreover, Dorian, do not mislead yourself. Life is not controlled by will or intention. Instead, it is a matter of nerves, fibers, and the slowly developed cells where thought resides and passion dreams. You may believe yourself to be safe and strong. However, it only takes a particular hue in a room, a morning sky, a cherished perfume that evokes subtle memories, a line from a long-forgotten poem, or a melody from a piece of music you no longer play—these are the elements that shape our lives. Browning has addressed this in his writing; yet, our senses evoke these experiences for us. There are times when the scent of lilacs suddenly envelops me, compelling me to relive the most peculiar month of my life. I wish I could swap places with you, Dorian. The world has judged us both, but it has always revered you. This admiration will endure. You represent what the age seeks and fears it has discovered. I am grateful that you have never created anything tangible—no sculptures, no paintings, no external expressions. Life itself has been your art. You have composed your existence into music. Your days are your sonnets.
output: “Yes, you are the same. I wonder what the rest of your life will be. Don’t spoil it by renunciations. At present you are a perfect type. Don’t make yourself incomplete. You are quite flawless now. You need not shake your head: you know you are. Besides, Dorian, don’t deceive yourself. Life is not governed by will or intention. Life is a question of nerves, and fibres, and slowly built-up cells in which thought hides itself and passion has its dreams. You may fancy yourself safe and think yourself strong. But a chance tone of colour in a room or a morning sky, a particular perfume that you had once loved and that brings subtle memories with it, a line from a forgotten poem that you had come across again, a cadence from a piece of music that you had ceased to play - I tell you, Dorian, that it is on things like these that our lives depend. Browning writes about that somewhere; but our own senses will imagine them for us. There are moments when the odour of lilas blanc passes suddenly across me, and I have to live the strangest month of my life over again. I wish I could change places with you, Dorian. The world has cried out against us both, but it has always worshipped you. It always will worship you. You are the type of what the age is searching for, and what it is afraid it has found. I am so glad that you have never done anything, never carved a statue, or painted a picture, or produced anything outside of yourself! Life has been your art. You have set yourself to music. Your days are your sonnets.”

output:

“People like you - the wilful sunbeams of life - don’t commit crimes, Dorian. But I am much obliged for the compliment, all the same. And now tell me - reach me the matches, like a good boy - thanks - what are your actual relations with Sibyl Vane?”

output:

input:
There is a rather lovely garden. I’m not sure I’ve ever seen one quite like it—it tends to feel large and shady, with box-bordered paths and long grape-covered arbors that have seats beneath them.

There may have been some legal trouble, I believe, perhaps something involving heirs and co-heirs; in any case, the place tends to have been empty for years.

That can often spoil my sense of ghostliness, I’m afraid, but I don’t really mind—there seems to be something strange about the house, and I can feel it.

I even mentioned it to John one moonlit evening, but he said what I felt was likely a draught, and he shut the window.
output:
There is a delicious garden! I never saw such a garden - large and shady, full of box-bordered paths, and lined with long grape-covered arbors with seats under them.

There was some legal trouble, I believe, something about the heirs and co-heirs; anyhow, the place has been empty for years.

That spoils my ghostliness, I am afraid; but I don’t care - there is something strange about the house - I can feel it.

I even said so to John one moonlight evening, but he said what I felt was a draught, and shut the window.

output:

One notable feature of this paper is that it tends to appear different as the lighting conditions change, although this may not be immediately apparent to everyone. It's worth noting that this characteristic seems to have gone unnoticed by others, but it's something that can be observed.

When sunlight enters through the east window, particularly the first direct beam of light, the paper's appearance can change relatively quickly, to the point where it may be difficult to fully appreciate the extent of the transformation. Overall, the paper's design and appearance can be quite dynamic and sensitive to its surroundings.
output:
The outside pattern is a florid arabesque, reminding one of a fungus. If you can imagine a toadstool in joints, an interminable string of toadstools, budding and sprouting in endless convolutions, - why, that is something like it.

There is one marked peculiarity about this paper, a thing nobody seems to notice but myself, and that is that it changes as the light changes.

When the sun shoots in through the east window - I always watch for that first long, straight ray - it changes so quickly that I never can quite believe it.

input:
This is a large, airy room that takes up nearly the entire floor, with windows facing in all directions and an abundance of air and sunlight. It appears to have served first as a nursery and later as a playroom and gymnasium, since the windows are barred for the safety of small children and there are rings and other fixtures set into the walls.

The wallpaper is dull enough to confuse the eye as it tries to follow the pattern, and pronounced enough to be constantly irritating and to invite close study. When one traces the lame, uncertain curves for even a short distance, they suddenly seem to destroy themselves, plunging off at outrageous angles and dissolving into unheard-of contradictions.
output:
It is a big, airy room, the whole floor nearly, with windows that look all ways, and air and sunshine galore. It was nursery first and then playground and gymnasium, I should judge; for the windows are barred for little children, and there are rings and things in the walls.

It is dull enough to confuse the eye in following, pronounced enough to constantly irritate, and provoke study, and when you follow the lame, uncertain curves for a little distance they suddenly commit suicide - plunge off at outrageous angles, destroy themselves in unheard-of contradictions.

input: I tend to avoid looking out the windows, as there are numerous women outside who move quickly. This highlights my desire for a sense of security. output:
I don’t like to look out of the windows even - there are so many of those creeping women, and they creep so fast.

But I am securely fastened now by my well-hidden rope - you don’t get me out in the road there!

I suppose I shall have to get back behind the pattern when it comes night, and that is hard!

It is so pleasant to be out in this great room and creep around as I please!

output:

We have been here two weeks, and I haven’t felt like writing before, since that first day.

I am sitting by the window now, up in this atrocious nursery, and there is nothing to hinder my writing as much as I please, save lack of strength.

I felt it was an appropriate moment to communicate my concerns, so I expressed to him that I did not feel I was improving and requested that he take me away. 

John responded that the repairs at home were incomplete and that he could not leave town at that time. He added that if my safety were at risk, he would act differently. He reassured me, stating that I was indeed making progress, even if I could not perceive it. As a doctor, he emphasized his expertise, noting that I was gaining weight and color, and that my appetite had improved. He conveyed that he felt much more at ease regarding my condition.
output:
The faint figure behind seemed to shake the pattern, just as if she wanted to get out.

I got up softly and went to feel and see if the paper did move, and when I came back John was awake.

I thought it was a good time to talk, so I told him that I really was not gaining here, and that I wished he would take me away.

“The repairs are not done at home, and I cannot possibly leave town just now. Of course if you were in any danger I could and would, but you really are better, dear, whether you can see it or not. I am a doctor, dear, and I know. You are gaining flesh and color, your appetite is better. I feel really much easier about you.”

input: The appearance of the paper changes significantly depending on the lighting conditions. This highlights the dramatic effect that different types of light can have on its perception. output:

At night in any kind of light, in twilight, candlelight, lamplight, and worst of all by moonlight, it becomes bars! The outside pattern I mean, and the woman behind it is as plain as can be.

By daylight she is subdued, quiet. I fancy it is the pattern that keeps her so still. It is so puzzling. It keeps me quiet by the hour.

output:

But there is something else about that paper - the smell! I noticed it the moment we came into the room, but with so much air and sun it was not bad. Now we have had a week of fog and rain, and whether the windows are open or not, the smell is here.

input: I remember the gentle wink that the knobs of our large, antique bureau used to possess, and there was one chair that consistently appeared to be a steadfast companion. I often felt that if any of the other objects appeared too intimidating, I could always retreat into that chair and find safety. Furthermore, the furniture in this room is not merely uncoordinated; rather, it is a collection we were compelled to bring up from downstairs. I surmise that when this space was utilized as a playroom, the items from the nursery had to be removed, and it is not surprising. I have never witnessed such extensive damage as that which the children have inflicted in this room.
output:
I remember what a kindly wink the knobs of our big old bureau used to have, and there was one chair that always seemed like a strong friend.

I used to feel that if any of the other things looked too fierce I could always hop into that chair and be safe.

The furniture in this room is no worse than inharmonious, however, for we had to bring it all from downstairs. I suppose when this was used as a playroom they had to take the nursery things out, and no wonder! I never saw such ravages as the children have made here.

She chuckled and mentioned that she wouldn’t mind taking care of it herself, but she suggested that I should be careful not to overexert myself. 

She seemed to be trying to encourage me to leave the room, as it was quite obvious what was happening. However, I explained that it felt so peaceful, empty, and tidy now that I thought I might lie down again and rest for a while; I asked her not to disturb me even for dinner, saying that I would call out when I woke up.

Now, she is no longer here, and neither are the servants or any belongings. The only thing remaining is that large bedframe, securely fastened, with the canvas mattress we discovered resting on it.
output:
She laughed and said she wouldn’t mind doing it herself, but I must not get tired.

She tried to get me out of the room - it was too patent! But I said it was so quiet and empty and clean now that I believed I would lie down again and sleep all I could; and not to wake me even for dinner - I would call when I woke.

So now she is gone, and the servants are gone, and the things are gone, and there is nothing left but that great bedstead nailed down, with the canvas mattress we found on it.

input:
Through careful observation at night, a significant realization has emerged. There are moments when it appears that numerous women are present, while at other times, only one is discernible. This individual moves quickly, causing a noticeable disturbance. 

In brightly lit areas, she remains still, while in darker sections, she grips the bars and shakes them vigorously. This behavior suggests a persistent effort to escape. However, the intricate pattern of the bars creates an insurmountable barrier, which may explain its multitude of complex shapes.
output:
Through watching so much at night, when it changes so, I have finally found out.

Sometimes I think there are a great many women behind, and sometimes only one, and she crawls around fast, and her crawling shakes it all over.

Then in the very bright spots she keeps still, and in the very shady spots she just takes hold of the bars and shakes them hard.

And she is all the time trying to climb through. But nobody could climb through that pattern - it strangles so; I think that is why it has so many heads.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman

input:
Then I removed all the paper that I could access while standing on the floor. It adheres stubbornly, and the pattern seems to revel in it. The disfigured faces and bulbous eyes, along with the grotesque fungal formations, exude an air of mocking derision.

Furthermore, I find myself becoming increasingly frustrated, prompting thoughts of desperate actions. The notion of leaping from the window may seem like an admirable exertion, yet the bars are too sturdy to even consider attempting such a feat.

Additionally, I would refrain from taking such an action. I am fully aware that such a step would be regarded as improper and could easily be misinterpreted.
output:
Then I peeled off all the paper I could reach standing on the floor. It sticks horribly and the pattern just enjoys it! All those strangled heads and bulbous eyes and waddling fungus growths just shriek with derision!

I am getting angry enough to do something desperate. To jump out of the window would be admirable exercise, but the bars are too strong even to try.

Besides I wouldn’t do it. Of course not. I know well enough that a step like that is improper and might be misconstrued.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman

input:
It resembles a woman bending down and moving cautiously behind the pattern. I find it unsettling. I start to think that I wish John would take me away from this place. 

It is difficult to discuss my condition with John because he is very knowledgeable and deeply cares for me. 

I dislike seeing it at times; it moves so slowly and always seems to enter through one window or another. 

John was asleep, and I did not want to disturb him, so I remained quiet and observed the moonlight on the undulating wallpaper until I felt uneasy.
output:
And it is like a woman stooping down and creeping about behind that pattern. I don’t like it a bit. I wonder - I begin to think - I wish John would take me away from here!

It is so hard to talk with John about my case, because he is so wise, and because he loves me so.

I hate to see it sometimes, it creeps so slowly, and always comes in by one window or another.

John was asleep and I hated to waken him, so I kept still and watched the moonlight on that undulating wallpaper till I felt creepy.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman

input:
The current weather conditions are unpleasant. During the night, the presence of a particular issue becomes pronounced. This highlights a problem that has been ongoing. 

Initially, this issue was a significant source of disturbance. The situation was so bothersome that drastic measures, such as destroying the house, were considered in an attempt to eliminate the underlying cause of the problem, which is a strong smell. 

A notable feature of the room is a distinctive mark located on the wall, near the baseboard. The mark is a streak that continues around the room, passing behind each piece of furniture with the exception of the bed. It appears as a long, straight, and even smear, suggesting that it may have been created by repeated rubbing.
output:
In this damp weather it is awful. I wake up in the night and find it hanging over me.

It used to disturb me at first. I thought seriously of burning the house - to reach the smell.

There is a very funny mark on this wall, low down, near the mopboard. A streak that runs round the room. It goes behind every piece of furniture, except the bed, a long, straight, even smooch, as if it had been rubbed over and over.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman

input:
Additionally, there exists a recurring location where the pattern appears to be distorted, resembling a broken form, and two rounded shapes, akin to eyes, are oriented in an inverted manner. Furthermore, it is worth noting that the persistence and audacity of this phenomenon evoke a strong sense of irritation in me. Moreover, these shapes seem to be omnipresent, extending in various directions, and their unblinking nature is particularly striking. In essence, the uniformity of the pattern is disrupted at one point, where two sections fail to align, resulting in the shapes being staggered, with one positioned slightly higher than the other.

It is worth noting that the degree of expression exhibited by this inanimate object is remarkable, particularly in light of the fact that such entities are generally not renowned for their expressive qualities. Moreover, as a child, I would often lie awake and derive a considerable amount of fascination and fear from observing plain walls and unadorned furniture, which would provide me with more entertainment than many children could find in a repository of toys.
output:
There is a recurrent spot where the pattern lolls like a broken neck and two bulbous eyes stare at you upside-down.

I get positively angry with the impertinence of it and the everlastingness. Up and down and sideways they crawl, and those absurd, unblinking eyes are everywhere. There is one place where two breadths didn’t match, and the eyes go all up and down the line, one a little higher than the other.

I never saw so much expression in an inanimate thing before, and we all know how much expression they have! I used to lie awake as a child and get more entertainment and terror out of blank walls and plain furniture than most children could find in a toy-store.
title: The Yellow Wallpaper
author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman

input: When outside, it seems that one may need to move along the ground, where the surroundings are often green rather than yellow. However, in this space, I can move easily along the floor, and my shoulder fits nicely into the narrow curve along the wall, which helps me avoid losing my way. I continued to move in that manner, but I glanced back at him occasionally. I found myself wondering why he might have fainted. Nevertheless, he did, and he lay directly in my path by the wall, which meant I had to navigate over him each time I moved. In summary, this situation created a challenge for my movements as I continued to traverse the space.
output:
For outside you have to creep on the ground, and everything is green instead of yellow.

But here I can creep smoothly on the floor, and my shoulder just fits in that long smooch around the wall, so I cannot lose my way.

I kept on creeping just the same, but I looked at him over my shoulder.

Now why should that man have fainted? But he did, and right across my path by the wall, so that I had to creep over him every time!

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman

input:
Today marks the final day, which is sufficient for the situation at hand. John will remain in town overnight and will not leave until this evening. 

Jennie expressed a desire to stay with me, indicating her intention to offer companionship. However, I informed her that I would likely sleep more soundly alone for the night.

This highlights a strategic decision, as I was not truly alone. Once the moonlight appeared and I observed Jennie struggling with the pattern, I felt compelled to get up and assist her.
output:
Hurrah! This is the last day, but it is enough. John is to stay in town over night, and won’t be out until this evening.

Jennie wanted to sleep with me - the sly thing! but I told her I should undoubtedly rest better for a night all alone.

That was clever, for really I wasn’t alone a bit! As soon as it was moonlight, and that poor thing began to crawl and shake the pattern, I got up and ran to help her.

input:
John is unaware of the extent of my suffering. He believes there is no justification for my distress, which is sufficient for him.

The discomfort I experience primarily stems from nervousness. It is challenging for me to feel that I am not fulfilling my responsibilities.

I intended to be a source of support for John, providing him with genuine rest and comfort; instead, I find myself feeling like a burden.

It is difficult for others to understand the effort required for me to accomplish even simple tasks, such as dressing, entertaining, and managing various responsibilities.
output:
John does not know how much I really suffer. He knows there is no reason to suffer, and that satisfies him.

Of course it is only nervousness. It does weigh on me so not to do my duty in any way!

I meant to be such a help to John, such a real rest and comfort, and here I am a comparative burden already!

Nobody would believe what an effort it is to do what little I am able - to dress and entertain, and order things.

I don’t blame her at all. It can often feel very humiliating to be caught creeping around in daylight.

I always lock the door when I creep in the daytime. I can’t do it at night, because I know John would likely suspect something right away.

And John tends to be so strange now that I don’t want to irritate him. I wish he would take another room. Besides, I don’t want anyone else to get that woman out at night but me.

I often wonder whether I might be able to see her out of all the windows at once.
output:

I always lock the door when I creep by daylight. I can’t do it at night, for I know John would suspect something at once.

input:
I am becoming quite attached to the room, despite its wallpaper. In fact, it may be due to the wallpaper that I feel this way. 

I lie here on this large, immovable bed, which I believe is nailed down. I spend hours tracing the pattern with my eyes. It is almost like a form of exercise, I assure you. I begin, let us say, in the bottom corner where the wallpaper remains untouched. I resolve for the thousandth time to follow that seemingly pointless pattern to some sort of conclusion.
output:
I’m getting really fond of the room in spite of the wallpaper. Perhaps because of the wallpaper.

I lie here on this great immovable bed - it is nailed down, I believe - and follow that pattern about by the hour. It is as good as gymnastics, I assure you. I start, we’ll say, at the bottom, down in the corner over there where it has not been touched, and I determine for the thousandth time that I will follow that pointless pattern to some sort of a conclusion.
