author: Frederick Douglass

input: We had been in jail for only about twenty minutes when a group of slave traders and their agents rushed in to look at us and determine whether we were for sale. I had never seen such people before. I felt surrounded by fiends from hell. A band of pirates could not have resembled their father, the devil, more closely. They laughed and grinned at us, saying, "Ah, my boys! We have got you, haven't we?" After taunting us in various ways, they examined us one by one to determine our value. They impudently asked if we would like to have them as masters. We gave them no answer and left them to figure it out as best they could. Then they cursed and swore at us, telling us they could drive the devil out of us very quickly if we were only in their hands.
output: We had been in jail scarcely twenty minutes, when a swarm of slave traders, and agents for slave traders, flocked into jail to look at us, and to ascertain if we were for sale. Such a set of beings I never saw before! I felt myself surrounded by so many fiends from perdition. A band of pirates never looked more like their father, the devil. They laughed and grinned over us, saying, “Ah, my boys! we have got you, haven’t we?” And after taunting us in various ways, they one by one went into an examination of us, with intent to ascertain our value. They would impudently ask us if we would not like to have them for our masters. We would make them no answer, and leave them to find out as best they could. Then they would curse and swear at us, telling us that they could take the devil out of us in a very little while, if we were only in their hands.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input:
The family of my master consisted of two sons, Andrew and Richard, as well as one daughter, Lucretia, and her husband, Captain Thomas Auld. Additionally, they resided in a single house located on the home plantation of Colonel Edward Lloyd. My master held the position of clerk and superintendent for Colonel Lloyd, effectively serving as the overseer of the overseers. Meanwhile, I spent two years of my childhood on this plantation with my old master's family. 

During my time on the plantation, I witnessed a significant event that was previously mentioned, and as this location played a crucial role in shaping my initial impressions of slavery, I will provide a description of the plantation and the institution of slavery as it existed there. The plantation is situated approximately twelve miles north of Easton in Talbot county, bordering Miles River. Furthermore, the primary products cultivated on the plantation included tobacco, corn, and wheat, which were produced in substantial quantities. As a result, Colonel Lloyd was able to maintain a large sloop, named Sally Lloyd in honor of one of his daughters, in nearly constant employment transporting these products to the market in Baltimore.

The sloop was commanded by Captain Auld, my master's son-in-law, and was manned by Colonel Lloyd's own slaves, including Peter, Isaac, Rich, and Jake. Nevertheless, these individuals were highly regarded by the other slaves and were considered privileged, as being allowed to visit Baltimore was a significant privilege in the eyes of the slaves. Overall, the experience of working on the sloop was viewed as a notable opportunity, and those who were selected to do so were esteemed by their peers.
output: My master’s family consisted of two sons, Andrew and Richard; one daughter, Lucretia, and her husband, Captain Thomas Auld. They lived in one house, upon the home plantation of Colonel Edward Lloyd. My master was Colonel Lloyd’s clerk and superintendent. He was what might be called the overseer of the overseers. I spent two years of childhood on this plantation in my old master’s family. It was here that I witnessed the bloody transaction recorded in the first chapter; and as I received my first impressions of slavery on this plantation, I will give some description of it, and of slavery as it there existed. The plantation is about twelve miles north of Easton, in Talbot county, and is situated on the border of Miles River. The principal products raised upon it were tobacco, corn, and wheat. These were raised in great abundance; so that, with the products of this and the other farms belonging to him, he was able to keep in almost constant employment a large sloop, in carrying them to market at Baltimore. This sloop was named Sally Lloyd, in honor of one of the colonel’s daughters. My master’s son-in-law, Captain Auld, was master of the vessel; she was otherwise manned by the colonel’s own slaves. Their names were Peter, Isaac, Rich, and Jake. These were esteemed very highly by the other slaves, and looked upon as the privileged ones of the plantation; for it was no small affair, in the eyes of the slaves, to be allowed to see Baltimore.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input: Shortly afterward, they succeeded in tying John. They then turned to Henry, who had returned by this time, and commanded him to cross his hands. "I will not," said Henry, in a firm tone, indicating his readiness to accept the consequences of his refusal. "Will you not?" said Tom Graham, the constable. "No, I will not," said Henry, in a still stronger tone. With this, two of the constables drew out their shining pistols and swore by their Creator that they would make him cross his hands or kill him. Each cocked his pistol, and with fingers on the trigger, walked up to Henry, saying at the same time that if he did not cross his hands, they would blow his damned heart out. "Shoot me, shoot me," said Henry. "You cannot kill me but once. Shoot, shoot, and be damned. I will not be tied." This he said in a tone of loud defiance. At the same time, with a motion as quick as lightning, he dashed the pistols from the hand of each constable with one single stroke. As he did this, all hands fell upon him, and after beating him for some time, they finally overpowered him and got him tied.
output: In a few moments, they succeeded in tying John. They then turned to Henry, who had by this time returned, and commanded him to cross his hands. “I won’t!” said Henry, in a firm tone, indicating his readiness to meet the consequences of his refusal. “Won’t you?” said Tom Graham, the constable. “No, I won’t!” said Henry, in a still stronger tone. With this, two of the constables pulled out their shining pistols, and swore, by their Creator, that they would make him cross his hands or kill him. Each cocked his pistol, and, with fingers on the trigger, walked up to Henry, saying, at the same time, if he did not cross his hands, they would blow his damned heart out. “Shoot me, shoot me!” said Henry; “you can’t kill me but once. Shoot, shoot, - and be damned! I won’t be tied!” This he said in a tone of loud defiance; and at the same time, with a motion as quick as lightning, he with one single stroke dashed the pistols from the hand of each constable. As he did this, all hands fell upon him, and, after beating him some time, they finally overpowered him, and got him tied.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input: We now began to feel a degree of safety and to prepare ourselves for the duties and responsibilities of a life of freedom. On the morning after our arrival at New Bedford, while at the breakfast table, the question arose as to what name I should be called by. The name given to me by my mother was "Frederick Augustus Washington Bailey." I had, however, dispensed with the two middle names long before I left Maryland, so that I was generally known by the name of "Frederick Bailey." I started from Baltimore bearing the name of "Stanley." When I got to New York, I again changed my name to "Frederick Johnson," and thought that would be the last change. But when I got to New Bedford, I found it necessary to change my name again. This necessity arose because there were so many Johnsons in New Bedford that it was already quite difficult to distinguish between them. I gave Mr. Johnson the privilege of choosing a name for me, but told him he must not take from me the name of "Frederick." I had to hold on to that in order to preserve a sense of my identity. Mr. Johnson had just been reading the "Lady of the Lake" and at once suggested that my name be "Douglass." From that time until now I have been called "Frederick Douglass," and as I am more widely known by that name than by either of the others, I shall continue to use it as my own.
output: We now began to feel a degree of safety, and to prepare ourselves for the duties and responsibilities of a life of freedom. On the morning after our arrival at New Bedford, while at the breakfast-table, the question arose as to what name I should be called by. The name given me by my mother was, “Frederick Augustus Washington Bailey.” I, however, had dispensed with the two middle names long before I left Maryland so that I was generally known by the name of “Frederick Bailey.” I started from Baltimore bearing the name of “Stanley.” When I got to New York, I again changed my name to “Frederick Johnson,” and thought that would be the last change. But when I got to New Bedford, I found it necessary again to change my name. The reason of this necessity was, that there were so many Johnsons in New Bedford, it was already quite difficult to distinguish between them. I gave Mr. Johnson the privilege of choosing me a name, but told him he must not take from me the name of “Frederick.” I must hold on to that, to preserve a sense of my identity. Mr. Johnson had just been reading the “Lady of the Lake,” and at once suggested that my name be “Douglass.” From that time until now I have been called “Frederick Douglass;” and as I am more widely known by that name than by either of the others, I shall continue to use it as my own.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input: During the altercation, I managed, though I cannot explain how, to retrieve my pass and, without being detected, placed it into the fire. At that point, we were all restrained, and just as we were about to depart for the Easton jail, Betsy Freeland, the mother of William Freeland, arrived at the door with her hands filled with biscuits, which she distributed between Henry and John. Furthermore, she proceeded to deliver a speech directed at me, stating, “You devil! You yellow devil! It was you who instigated Henry and John to attempt to escape. Had it not been for your influence, you long-legged mulatto devil, Henry and John would never have considered such an action.” I chose not to respond and was promptly escorted towards St. Michael’s. A moment prior to the altercation with Henry, Mr. Hamilton had suggested the necessity of conducting a search for the protections that he had understood Frederick had written for himself and the others. However, just as he was about to put his proposal into action, his assistance became necessary in restraining Henry. The chaos surrounding the scuffle led them either to forget the suggestion or to consider it too dangerous to pursue under the present circumstances. Consequently, we had not yet been convicted of harboring the intention to escape.
output: During the scuffle, I managed, I know not how, to get my pass out, and, without being discovered, put it into the fire. We were all now tied; and just as we were to leave for Easton jail, Betsy Freeland, mother of William Freeland, came to the door with her hands full of biscuits, and divided them between Henry and John. She then delivered herself of a speech, to the following effect: - addressing herself to me, she said, “You devil! You yellow devil! it was you that put it into the heads of Henry and John to run away. But for you, you long-legged mulatto devil! Henry nor John would never have thought of such a thing.” I made no reply, and was immediately hurried off towards St. Michael’s. Just a moment previous to the scuffle with Henry, Mr. Hamilton suggested the propriety of making a search for the protections which he had understood Frederick had written for himself and the rest. But, just at the moment he was about carrying his proposal into effect, his aid was needed in helping to tie Henry; and the excitement attending the scuffle caused them either to forget, or to deem it unsafe, under the circumstances, to search. So we were not yet convicted of the intention to run away.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input: Following the valuation, the next step involved the division of individuals. It is difficult to convey the mixture of excitement and anxiety that many of us felt during this period. Our future was about to be determined, and we had little say in that decision, similar to the animals among whom we were classified. Just a single word from the white men could, against all our wishes, hopes, and pleas, permanently separate the closest friends, relatives, and the strongest bonds known to people. Alongside the anguish of separation, there was also a profound fear of ending up in the possession of Master Andrew. He was widely regarded as a particularly harsh individual, often seen as a frequent drinker, and his reckless behavior had already squandered much of his father's estate. Many of us felt that being sold to the Georgia traders might be preferable to becoming his property, as we understood that this would likely result in a situation we all found deeply unsettling and frightening. In summary, the uncertainty of the division process left us grappling with intense emotions, fearful of what lay ahead.
output: After the valuation, then came the division. I have no language to express the high excitement and deep anxiety which were felt among us poor slaves during this time. Our fate for life was now to be decided. We had no more voice in that decision than the brutes among whom we were ranked. A single word from the white men was enough - against all our wishes, prayers, and entreaties - to sunder forever the dearest friends, dearest kindred, and strongest ties known to human beings. In addition to the pain of separation, there was the horrid dread of falling into the hands of Master Andrew. He was known to us all as being a most cruel wretch, - a common drunkard, who had, by his reckless mismanagement and profligate dissipation, already wasted a large portion of his father’s property. We all felt that we might as well be sold at once to the Georgia traders, as to pass into his hands; for we knew that that would be our inevitable condition, - a condition held by us all in the utmost horror and dread.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input: Mr. Hopkins occupied the position of overseer for only a brief period. Although the reasons for the brevity of his tenure remain unclear, it can be inferred that he may have lacked the requisite strictness to meet Colonel Lloyd's expectations. Subsequently, Mr. Austin Gore took over the role, a man who exemplified, to a considerable extent, all the essential characteristics required of a first-rate overseer. Mr. Gore had previously demonstrated his capabilities while serving Colonel Lloyd as overseer on one of the out-farms, thus proving himself deserving of the prestigious position of overseer at the home or Great House Farm.
output: Mr. Hopkins remained but a short time in the office of overseer. Why his career was so short, I do not know, but suppose he lacked the necessary severity to suit Colonel Lloyd. Mr. Hopkins was succeeded by Mr. Austin Gore, a man possessing, in an eminent degree, all those traits of character indispensable to what is called a first-rate overseer. Mr. Gore had served Colonel Lloyd, in the capacity of overseer, upon one of the out-farms, and had shown himself worthy of the high station of overseer upon the home or Great House Farm.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input: I was pleased to discover, in your narrative, how early the most overlooked members of society awaken to an understanding of their rights and the injustices they face. Experience serves as a profound teacher. Long before you had learned your alphabet or understood the destination of the "white sails" on the Chesapeake, you began to perceive the suffering of the enslaved. You did not measure their anguish solely by their hunger and deprivation, nor by their physical punishment and labor, but instead by the harsh and debilitating death that looms over their spirits.
output: I was glad to learn, in your story, how early the most neglected of God’s children waken to a sense of their rights, and of the injustice done them. Experience is a keen teacher; and long before you had mastered your A B C, or knew where the “white sails” of the Chesapeake were bound, you began, I see, to gauge the wretchedness of the slave, not by his hunger and want, not by his lashes and toil, but by the cruel and blighting death which gathers over his soul.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input: Shortly after I began living at Baltimore, my old master's youngest son Richard died. About three years and six months later, my old master, Captain Anthony, also died. He left behind only his son Andrew and his daughter Lucretia to share his estate. He died while visiting his daughter at Hillsborough. Because his death was unexpected, he left no will regarding the disposal of his property. A valuation of the property therefore became necessary so that it could be divided equally between Mrs. Lucretia and Master Andrew. I was immediately sent for to be valued along with the other property. Once again, my feelings rose up in detestation of slavery. I now had a new understanding of my degraded condition. Before this, I had become at least partly insensible to my lot, if not entirely so. I left Baltimore with a young heart overwhelmed by sadness and a soul full of apprehension. I took passage with Captain Rowe on the schooner Wild Cat, and after a voyage of about twenty-four hours, I found myself near the place of my birth. I had now been absent from it for almost five years, if not quite that long. Nevertheless, I remembered the place very well. I was only about five years old when I left it to live with my old master on Colonel Lloyd's plantation, so I was now between ten and eleven years old.
output: In a very short time after I went to live at Baltimore, my old master’s youngest son Richard died; and in about three years and six months after his death, my old master, Captain Anthony, died, leaving only his son, Andrew, and daughter, Lucretia, to share his estate. He died while on a visit to see his daughter at Hillsborough. Cut off thus unexpectedly, he left no will as to the disposal of his property. It was therefore necessary to have a valuation of the property, that it might be equally divided between Mrs. Lucretia and Master Andrew. I was immediately sent for, to be valued with the other property. Here again my feelings rose up in detestation of slavery. I had now a new conception of my degraded condition. Prior to this, I had become, if not insensible to my lot, at least partly so. I left Baltimore with a young heart overborne with sadness, and a soul full of apprehension. I took passage with Captain Rowe, in the schooner Wild Cat, and, after a sail of about twenty-four hours, I found myself near the place of my birth. I had now been absent from it almost, if not quite, five years. I, however, remembered the place very well. I was only about five years old when I left it, to go and live with my old master on Colonel Lloyd’s plantation; so that I was now between ten and eleven years old.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input:
In making a firm decision to run away, we went further than Patrick Henry did when he resolved on liberty or death. For us, liberty was doubtful at best, and failure meant almost certain death. As for me, I would rather die than remain in hopeless bondage.

Sandy, one of our group, gave up the idea but still encouraged us. Our group then consisted of Henry Harris, John Harris, Henry Bailey, Charles Roberts, and myself. Henry Bailey was my uncle and belonged to my master. Charles married my aunt; he belonged to my master’s father-in-law, Mr. William Hamilton.
output:
In coming to a fixed determination to run away, we did more than Patrick Henry, when he resolved upon liberty or death. With us it was a doubtful liberty at most, and almost certain death if we failed. For my part, I should prefer death to hopeless bondage.

Sandy, one of our number, gave up the notion, but still encouraged us. Our company then consisted of Henry Harris, John Harris, Henry Bailey, Charles Roberts, and myself. Henry Bailey was my uncle, and belonged to my master. Charles married my aunt: he belonged to my master’s father-in-law, Mr. William Hamilton.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input: In August 1841, I attended an anti-slavery convention in Nantucket, where I had the good fortune to become acquainted with Frederick Douglass, the author of the following Narrative. He was a stranger to nearly everyone in that gathering, but he had recently escaped from the bondage of slavery in the South, and his curiosity had been stirred to learn about the principles and practices of the abolitionists, of whom he had heard only a somewhat vague description while he was enslaved. For that reason, he was prompted to attend the occasion I have mentioned, even though he was then living in New Bedford. Overall, this meeting marked the beginning of my acquaintance with a man whose story would soon reach a wide audience.
output: In the month of August, 1841, I attended an anti-slavery convention in Nantucket, at which it was my happiness to become acquainted with Frederick Douglass, the writer of the following Narrative. He was a stranger to nearly every member of that body; but, having recently made his escape from the southern prison-house of bondage, and feeling his curiosity excited to ascertain the principles and measures of the abolitionists, - of whom he had heard a somewhat vague description while he was a slave, - he was induced to give his attendance, on the occasion alluded to, though at that time a resident in New Bedford.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input:
I have heard that individuals from marginalized backgrounds may now find job opportunities in calking in New Bedford, which could be seen as a positive outcome of anti-slavery efforts. 

About four months after I arrived in New Bedford, a young man approached me and asked if I was interested in subscribing to the “Liberator.” I expressed my interest but mentioned that, having recently escaped from slavery, I was unable to pay for it at that moment. Eventually, I did become a subscriber. Each week, as the paper arrived, I read it with feelings that are difficult to fully capture. It became a crucial part of my life. The messages within ignited a deep passion in me. Its empathy for those still in bondage, its sharp criticisms of slaveholders, its honest revelations about slavery, and its vigorous challenges to those who supported the system brought me a profound sense of joy that I had not experienced before.
output:
I am told that colored persons can now get employment at calking in New Bedford - a result of anti-slavery effort.

In about four months after I went to New Bedford, there came a young man to me, and inquired if I did not wish to take the “Liberator.” I told him I did; but, just having made my escape from slavery, I remarked that I was unable to pay for it then. I, however, finally became a subscriber to it. The paper came, and I read it from week to week with such feelings as it would be quite idle for me to attempt to describe. The paper became my meat and my drink. My soul was set all on fire. Its sympathy for my brethren in bonds - its scathing denunciations of slaveholders - its faithful exposures of slavery - and its powerful attacks upon the upholders of the institution - sent a thrill of joy through my soul, such as I had never felt before!
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input: Colonel Lloyd may have maintained between three to four hundred slaves on his home plantation and owned a significant number on nearby farms that he also managed. The closest farms to the main plantation were known as Wye Town and New Design. Wye Town was overseen by a man named Noah Willis, while New Design was managed by a Mr. Townsend. The overseers of these farms, along with over twenty others, typically received guidance and oversight from the managers of the home plantation, which served as the central hub for all operations. This location may have functioned as a key decision-making center where disputes among overseers were resolved. If a slave were found guilty of a serious offense, became difficult to manage, or showed a desire to escape, they were often brought to this central place, where they might face harsh punishment before being taken to Baltimore and sold to a trader like Austin Woolfolk, as a deterrent to others. Overall, this system illustrates the harsh realities of plantation life under Colonel Lloyd's management.
output: Colonel Lloyd kept from three to four hundred slaves on his home plantation, and owned a large number more on the neighboring farms belonging to him. The names of the farms nearest to the home plantation were Wye Town and New Design. “Wye Town” was under the overseership of a man named Noah Willis. New Design was under the overseership of a Mr. Townsend. The overseers of these, and all the rest of the farms, numbering over twenty, received advice and direction from the managers of the home plantation. This was the great business place. It was the seat of government for the whole twenty farms. All disputes among the overseers were settled here. If a slave was convicted of any high misdemeanor, became unmanageable, or evinced a determination to run away, he was brought immediately here, severely whipped, put on board the sloop, carried to Baltimore, and sold to Austin Woolfolk, or some other slave-trader, as a warning to the slaves remaining.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input:
In the afternoon of that day, we arrived in Annapolis, the state capital. We paused for only a brief moment, so I did not have the opportunity to go ashore. It was the first sizable town I had ever encountered, and while it may appear small when compared to some of the factory villages in New England, I found it impressive for its size—more remarkable than the Great House Farm.

We reached Baltimore early on Sunday morning, landing at Smith's Wharf, close to Bowley's Wharf. On board the sloop, we transported a large flock of sheep. After assisting in driving them to Mr. Curtis's slaughterhouse on Louden Slater's Hill, I was escorted by Rich, one of the crew members from the sloop, to my new home on Alliciana Street, near Mr. Gardner's shipyard at Fells Point.
output:
In the afternoon of that day, we reached Annapolis, the capital of the State. We stopped but a few moments, so that I had no time to go on shore. It was the first large town that I had ever seen, and though it would look small compared with some of our New England factory villages, I thought it a wonderful place for its size - more imposing even than the Great House Farm!

We arrived at Baltimore early on Sunday morning, landing at Smith’s Wharf, not far from Bowley’s Wharf. We had on board the sloop a large flock of sheep; and after aiding in driving them to the slaughterhouse of Mr. Curtis on Louden Slater’s Hill, I was conducted by Rich, one of the hands belonging on board of the sloop, to my new home in Alliciana Street, near Mr. Gardner’s ship-yard, on Fells Point.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input: We did not receive regular allowances of food. Our typical meal consisted of boiled cornmeal, which was referred to as mush. This mush was placed in a large wooden tray or trough and set on the ground. The children would then be called to eat, and they would gather around the trough, eating in a manner that was reminiscent of animals. Some used oyster shells, others used pieces of shingle, and some used their bare hands, as no spoons were provided. This highlights the competitive nature of mealtime, where the fastest eaters received the most food. Additionally, the strongest individuals were able to secure the best positions at the trough. Ultimately, few children left the trough feeling satisfied, suggesting that the food was insufficient to meet their needs.
output: We were not regularly allowanced. Our food was coarse corn meal boiled. This was called mush. It was put into a large wooden tray or trough, and set down upon the ground. The children were then called, like so many pigs, and like so many pigs they would come and devour the mush; some with oyster-shells, others with pieces of shingle, some with naked hands, and none with spoons. He that ate fastest got most; he that was strongest secured the best place; and few left the trough satisfied.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input: Mr. and Mrs. Auld were both present at home and greeted me at the door alongside their young son, Thomas, for whose care I had been entrusted. In that moment, I experienced a sight I had never encountered previously; it was the face of my new mistress, Sophia Auld, radiant with the most benevolent emotions. It is worth noting that a surge of joy coursed through my being upon witnessing her expression. This was a novel and extraordinary sight, illuminating my path with the light of happiness. Little Thomas was informed that his friend Freddy had arrived, and I was instructed to attend to little Thomas; thus, I embarked upon the responsibilities of my new household with an exceedingly optimistic outlook.
output: Mr. and Mrs. Auld were both at home, and met me at the door with their little son Thomas, to take care of whom I had been given. And here I saw what I had never seen before; it was a white face beaming with the most kindly emotions; it was the face of my new mistress, Sophia Auld. I wish I could describe the rapture that flashed through my soul as I beheld it. It was a new and strange sight to me, brightening up my pathway with the light of happiness. Little Thomas was told, there was his Freddy, - and I was told to take care of little Thomas; and thus I entered upon the duties of my new home with the most cheering prospect ahead.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input: Mr. Severe was aptly named, for he was an exceedingly cruel individual. I witnessed him inflict punishment upon a woman, resulting in blood flowing profusely for an extended duration; this occurred in the presence of her distressed children, who were fervently pleading for their mother’s release. He appeared to derive enjoyment from displaying his fiendish brutality. Furthermore, he was known for his profane language. It is worth noting that the very sound of his speech was sufficient to cause any ordinary person to feel a chill run through their veins and their hair to stand on end. Rarely did a sentence escape his lips that was not initiated or concluded with a horrific oath. The field provided a stark backdrop for his cruelty and profanity, transforming it into a site marked by both bloodshed and blasphemy. From dawn until dusk, he was engaged in cursing, raving, and violently assaulting the laborers in the field in the most terrifying manner. His time on this earth was brief, as he passed away shortly after my arrival at Colonel Lloyd’s; he died as he lived, uttering bitter curses and dreadful oaths even in his final moments. The slaves regarded his death as an act of merciful providence.
output: Mr. Severe was rightly named: he was a cruel man. I have seen him whip a woman, causing the blood to run half an hour at the time; and this, too, in the midst of her crying children, pleading for their mother’s release. He seemed to take pleasure in manifesting his fiendish barbarity. Added to his cruelty, he was a profane swearer. It was enough to chill the blood and stiffen the hair of an ordinary man to hear him talk. Scarce a sentence escaped him but that was commenced or concluded by some horrid oath. The field was the place to witness his cruelty and profanity. His presence made it both the field of blood and of blasphemy. From the rising till the going down of the sun, he was cursing, raving, cutting, and slashing among the slaves of the field, in the most frightful manner. His career was short. He died very soon after I went to Colonel Lloyd’s; and he died as he lived, uttering, with his dying groans, bitter curses and horrid oaths. His death was regarded by the slaves as the result of a merciful providence.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input: She left me abruptly, providing no indication of who my father was. The suggestion that my master is my father may or may not be accurate. Regardless of its truth, it is of little significance to my purpose. The stark reality remains that slaveholders have enacted laws establishing that the children of enslaved women will always inherit the status of their mothers. This practice appears to serve their own desires, turning the fulfillment of their immoral impulses into both a profitable and pleasurable endeavor. Through this manipulative arrangement, the slaveholder often occupies both roles of master and father to his enslaved individuals.
output: Called thus suddenly away, she left me without the slightest intimation of who my father was. The whisper that my master was my father, may or may not be true; and, true or false, it is of but little consequence to my purpose whilst the fact remains, in all its glaring odiousness, that slaveholders have ordained, and by law established, that the children of slave women shall in all cases follow the condition of their mothers; and this is done too obviously to administer to their own lusts, and make a gratification of their wicked desires profitable as well as pleasurable; for by this cunning arrangement, the slaveholder, in cases not a few, sustains to his slaves the double relation of master and father.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input: I resided within the household of Master Hugh for a period of approximately seven years. During this interval, I achieved success in acquiring the abilities of reading and writing. In the process of accomplishing this, I was compelled to employ a variety of strategies. I did not have a consistent instructor. My mistress, who had initially begun to educate me with kindness, had, in accordance with the guidance and instruction of her husband, not only discontinued her teaching but had also actively opposed any instruction of me by others. It is worth noting, however, that my mistress did not immediately adopt this manner of treatment. Initially, she lacked the degree of moral corruption necessary to confine me in intellectual obscurity. Furthermore, it was necessary for her to undergo some preparation in the exercise of arbitrary authority in order to become capable of treating me as though I were an animal.
output: I lived in Master Hugh’s family about seven years. During this time, I succeeded in learning to read and write. In accomplishing this, I was compelled to resort to various stratagems. I had no regular teacher. My mistress, who had kindly commenced to instruct me, had, in compliance with the advice and direction of her husband, not only ceased to instruct, but had set her face against my being instructed by any one else. It is due, however, to my mistress to say of her, that she did not adopt this course of treatment immediately. She at first lacked the depravity indispensable to shutting me up in mental darkness. It was at least necessary for her to have some training in the exercise of irresponsible power, to make her equal to the task of treating me as though I were a brute.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input: A sense of horror permeated the plantation, with the exception of Mr. Gore, who remained calm. When questioned by Colonel Lloyd and the narrator's former master about his drastic actions, he explained that Demby had become unmanageable and was setting a harmful example for the other slaves. He contended that allowing such behavior to go unchecked would threaten the existing order on the plantation. Mr. Gore argued that if one slave could evade punishment and survive, it would encourage others to follow suit, ultimately leading to the freedom of the slaves and the subjugation of the whites. His justification was accepted, and he retained his position as overseer on the plantation. His reputation as an overseer spread, and his actions were not subjected to legal scrutiny. The crime occurred in front of slaves, who were unable to file charges or testify against him. Consequently, Mr. Gore, responsible for a grave murder, escaped accountability and criticism from his community. At the time of the narrator's departure from the area, Mr. Gore resided in St. Michael’s, Talbot County, Maryland. If he is still living there, he likely continues to enjoy the same respect and esteem as he did before, despite his violent actions.
output: A thrill of horror flashed through every soul upon the plantation, excepting Mr. Gore. He alone seemed cool and collected. He was asked by Colonel Lloyd and my old master, why he resorted to this extraordinary expedient. His reply was, (as well as I can remember,) that Demby had become unmanageable. He was setting a dangerous example to the other slaves, - one which, if suffered to pass without some such demonstration on his part, would finally lead to the total subversion of all rule and order upon the plantation. He argued that if one slave refused to be corrected, and escaped with his life, the other slaves would soon copy the example; the result of which would be, the freedom of the slaves, and the enslavement of the whites. Mr. Gore’s defence was satisfactory. He was continued in his station as overseer upon the home plantation. His fame as an overseer went abroad. His horrid crime was not even submitted to judicial investigation. It was committed in the presence of slaves, and they of course could neither institute a suit, nor testify against him; and thus the guilty perpetrator of one of the bloodiest and most foul murders goes unwhipped of justice, and uncensured by the community in which he lives. Mr. Gore lived in St. Michael’s, Talbot county, Maryland, when I left there; and if he is still alive, he very probably lives there now; and if so, he is now, as he was then, as highly esteemed and as much respected as though his guilty soul had not been stained with his brother’s blood.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input:
My mother's name was Harriet Bailey, and she was the daughter of Isaac and Betsey Bailey, who were both African American and had a darker skin tone. It's worth noting that my mother's complexion was actually darker than that of either her mother or father. 

My father, on the other hand, was believed to be a white man, a fact that was generally acknowledged by those who discussed my parentage. There was also a rumor that suggested my master might have been my father, but I can neither confirm nor deny this, as I was not given the opportunity to know the truth. Unfortunately, my mother and I were separated at a very young age, before I had a chance to form a bond with her. This was not an unusual practice in the part of Maryland where I grew up, as it was common for children to be taken from their mothers at a relatively early age. In many cases, this would happen before the child was even a year old, and the mother would be sent to work on a farm elsewhere, while the child was left in the care of an older woman who was no longer able to work in the fields. It may be that this separation was intended to suppress the development of a strong emotional bond between the child and the mother, which can often have the effect of weakening the natural affection that exists between them. Overall, it tends to be the case that such separations can have a profound impact on the relationship between a child and their mother.
output:
My mother was named Harriet Bailey. She was the daughter of Isaac and Betsey Bailey, both colored, and quite dark. My mother was of a darker complexion than either my grandmother or grandfather.

My father was a white man. He was admitted to be such by all I ever heard speak of my parentage. The opinion was also whispered that my master was my father; but of the correctness of this opinion, I know nothing; the means of knowing was withheld from me. My mother and I were separated when I was but an infant - before I knew her as my mother. It is a common custom, in the part of Maryland from which I ran away, to part children from their mothers at a very early age. Frequently, before the child has reached its twelfth month, its mother is taken from it, and hired out on some farm a considerable distance off, and the child is placed under the care of an old woman, too old for field labor. For what this separation is done, I do not know, unless it be to hinder the development of the child’s affection toward its mother, and to blunt and destroy the natural affection of the mother for the child. This is the inevitable result.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input:
In reading your life, no one can claim that we have unfairly selected rare instances of cruelty. We know that the bitter drops you have drained from the cup are not incidental aggravations or individual troubles, but are the kind that must always and necessarily be part of the lot of every slave. They are essential ingredients of the system, not occasional results. This highlights how deeply embedded such suffering is in the institution itself.

After all, I shall read your book with trembling for you. Some years ago, when you were beginning to tell me your real name and birthplace, you may remember that I stopped you and preferred to remain ignorant of it all. Apart from a vague description, I continued in this way until the other day, when you read me your memoirs. At the time, I hardly knew whether to thank you for letting me see them, when I reflected that it was still dangerous in Massachusetts for honest men to tell their names. They say the fathers in 1776 signed the Declaration of Independence with the halter about their necks. You, too, publish your declaration of freedom with danger surrounding you. In all the broad lands overshadowed by the Constitution of the United States, there is no single spot, however narrow or desolate, where a fugitive slave can plant himself and say, “I am safe.” The whole armory of Northern law offers no shield for you. I am free to say that, in your place, I would throw the manuscript into the fire. Ultimately, this suggests the extent of the peril you face.
output:
In reading your life, no one can say that we have unfairly picked out some rare specimens of cruelty. We know that the bitter drops, which even you have drained from the cup, are no incidental aggravations, no individual ills, but such as must mingle always and necessarily in the lot of every slave. They are the essential ingredients, not the occasional results, of the system.

After all, I shall read your book with trembling for you. Some years ago, when you were beginning to tell me your real name and birthplace, you may remember I stopped you, and preferred to remain ignorant of all. With the exception of a vague description, so I continued, till the other day, when you read me your memoirs. I hardly knew, at the time, whether to thank you or not for the sight of them, when I reflected that it was still dangerous, in Massachusetts, for honest men to tell their names! They say the fathers, in 1776, signed the Declaration of Independence with the halter about their necks. You, too, publish your declaration of freedom with danger compassing you around. In all the broad lands which the Constitution of the United States overshadows, there is no single spot, - however narrow or desolate, - where a fugitive slave can plant himself and say, “I am safe.” The whole armory of Northern Law has no shield for you. I am free to say that, in your place, I should throw the MS. into the fire.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input: My new mistress proved to be exactly as she appeared when I first encountered her at the door—a woman characterized by a kind heart and refined sensibilities. She had never previously had a slave under her control, and prior to her marriage, she had relied on her own labor for sustenance. By trade, she was a weaver; through her unwavering dedication to her craft, she had largely been shielded from the debilitating and dehumanizing consequences of slavery. I was completely astonished by her kindness. I found myself uncertain about how to conduct myself in her presence. She was entirely distinct from any other white woman I had ever encountered. I could not approach her in the manner to which I was accustomed with other white ladies. My early training was entirely inappropriate in this context. The crouching servility that is often regarded as a desirable trait in a slave did not seem to be effective when directed towards her. Such behavior did not win her favor; in fact, she appeared perturbed by it. She did not consider it disrespectful or rude for a slave to meet her gaze. Even the humblest slave felt completely at ease in her presence, and none departed without feeling uplifted by the encounter. Her countenance radiated warmth and joy, and her voice resonated with soothing harmony.
output: My new mistress proved to be all she appeared when I first met her at the door, - a woman of the kindest heart and finest feelings. She had never had a slave under her control previously to myself, and prior to her marriage she had been dependent upon her own industry for a living. She was by trade a weaver; and by constant application to her business, she had been in a good degree preserved from the blighting and dehumanizing effects of slavery. I was utterly astonished at her goodness. I scarcely knew how to behave towards her. She was entirely unlike any other white woman I had ever seen. I could not approach her as I was accustomed to approach other white ladies. My early instruction was all out of place. The crouching servility, usually so acceptable a quality in a slave, did not answer when manifested toward her. Her favor was not gained by it; she seemed to be disturbed by it. She did not deem it impudent or unmannerly for a slave to look her in the face. The meanest slave was put fully at ease in her presence, and none left without feeling better for having seen her. Her face was made of heavenly smiles, and her voice of tranquil music.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input:
This, in brief, is my view of the religion of this land. To avoid any misunderstanding that might arise from the use of general terms, I mean by the religion of this land that which is revealed in the words, deeds, and actions of those bodies, north and south, that call themselves Christian churches and yet remain in union with slaveholders. It is against religion, as presented by these bodies, that I have felt it my duty to testify.

I conclude these remarks by copying the following portrait of the religion of the South, which is, through communion and fellowship, the religion of the North, and which I soberly affirm is true to the life, without caricature or the slightest exaggeration. It is said to have been drawn several years before the present anti-slavery agitation began by a northern Methodist preacher who, while residing in the South, had an opportunity to see slaveholding morals, manners, and piety with his own eyes. This highlights the gravity of the matter, and ultimately the passage closes with the words, Shall I not visit for these things? saith the Lord. Shall not my soul be avenged on such a nation as this?
output:
Such is, very briefly, my view of the religion of this land; and to avoid any misunderstanding, growing out of the use of general terms, I mean by the religion of this land, that which is revealed in the words, deeds, and actions, of those bodies, north and south, calling themselves Christian churches, and yet in union with slaveholders. It is against religion, as presented by these bodies, that I have felt it my duty to testify.

I conclude these remarks by copying the following portrait of the religion of the south, (which is, by communion and fellowship, the religion of the north,) which I soberly affirm is “true to the life,” and without caricature or the slightest exaggeration. It is said to have been drawn, several years before the present anti-slavery agitation began, by a northern Methodist preacher, who, while residing at the south, had an opportunity to see slaveholding morals, manners, and piety, with his own eyes. “Shall I not visit for these things? saith the Lord. Shall not my soul be avenged on such a nation as this?”
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input: I am aware of such cases, and it may be worth noting that these slaves tend to suffer greater hardships and have more to contend with than others. In the first place, they can often be a constant source of offence to their mistress. She is generally inclined to find fault with them, and they can seldom do anything to please her. She is often never better pleased than when she sees them under the lash, especially when she suspects her husband of showing favors to his mulatto children that he withholds from his black slaves. The master is frequently compelled to sell this class of his slaves, out of deference to the feelings of his white wife. Cruel as the deed may seem to anyone, for a man to sell his own children to human flesh-mongers, it is often the dictate of humanity for him to do so. Unless he does this, he must not only whip them himself, but must also stand by and see one white son tie up his brother, of only a few shades darker complexion than himself, and apply the gory lash to his naked back. If he utters even a word of disapproval, it may be set down to parental partiality and can only make a bad matter worse, both for himself and for the slave he would wish to protect and defend. In short, these individuals often face especially difficult circumstances, and even actions that appear cruel may sometimes be motivated by a desire to lessen greater suffering.
output: I know of such cases; and it is worthy of remark that such slaves invariably suffer greater hardships, and have more to contend with, than others. They are, in the first place, a constant offence to their mistress. She is ever disposed to find fault with them; they can seldom do any thing to please her; she is never better pleased than when she sees them under the lash, especially when she suspects her husband of showing to his mulatto children favors which he withholds from his black slaves. The master is frequently compelled to sell this class of his slaves, out of deference to the feelings of his white wife; and, cruel as the deed may strike any one to be, for a man to sell his own children to human flesh-mongers, it is often the dictate of humanity for him to do so; for, unless he does this, he must not only whip them himself, but must stand by and see one white son tie up his brother, of but few shades darker complexion than himself, and ply the gory lash to his naked back; and if he lisp one word of disapproval, it is set down to his parental partiality, and only makes a bad matter worse, both for himself and the slave whom he would protect and defend.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input: In this connection, one circumstance makes your recollections especially valuable and renders your early insight all the more remarkable. You come from that part of the country where we are told slavery appears with its fairest features. Let us hear, then, what it is at its best estate. Let us gaze on its bright side, if it has one. Afterward, imagination may task its powers to add dark lines to the picture as it travels southward to that Valley of the Shadow of Death, for the colored man, where the Mississippi sweeps along.
output: In connection with this, there is one circumstance which makes your recollections peculiarly valuable, and renders your early insight the more remarkable. You come from that part of the country where we are told slavery appears with its fairest features. Let us hear, then, what it is at its best estate - gaze on its bright side, if it has one; and then imagination may task her powers to add dark lines to the picture, as she travels southward to that (for the colored man) Valley of the Shadow of Death, where the Mississippi sweeps along.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input: I was approximately twelve years of age, and the notion of being enslaved for life began to weigh heavily on my heart. Around this same period, I acquired a book titled “The Columbian Orator.” I seized every opportunity to engage with this text. Among the many captivating topics it presented, I discovered a dialogue between a master and his slave. The slave was depicted as having escaped from his master on three occasions. The dialogue illustrated the conversation that transpired when the slave was recaptured for the third time. Within this exchange, the master presented the complete rationale in support of slavery, all of which was effectively countered by the slave. The slave articulated several astute and impactful responses to his master—responses that had the intended yet unforeseen consequence of leading to the master's voluntary emancipation of the slave.
output: I was now about twelve years old, and the thought of being a slave for life began to bear heavily upon my heart. Just about this time, I got hold of a book entitled “The Columbian Orator.” Every opportunity I got, I used to read this book. Among much of other interesting matter, I found in it a dialogue between a master and his slave. The slave was represented as having run away from his master three times. The dialogue represented the conversation which took place between them, when the slave was retaken the third time. In this dialogue, the whole argument in behalf of slavery was brought forward by the master, all of which was disposed of by the slave. The slave was made to say some very smart as well as impressive things in reply to his master - things which had the desired though unexpected effect; for the conversation resulted in the voluntary emancipation of the slave on the part of the master.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input: Additionally, it is possible that you may be able to recount your experiences without fear of reprisal, given the affection and esteem in which you are held by numerous individuals, owing to your exceptional abilities and your selfless dedication to the welfare of others. Moreover, it is worth noting that the ability of the most vulnerable members of society to testify freely in public against the injustices they have suffered will be attributable solely to your endeavors and the courageous actions of those who, disregarding the laws and constitutional provisions of the nation, are resolute in their determination to provide protection to the marginalized, and to offer sanctuary to the oppressed in their homes, notwithstanding the dictates of the law. Furthermore, in essence, the realization of this goal, whereby the most humble individuals may eventually be able to bear witness in safety to the cruelties they have endured, will be a direct consequence of your tireless efforts and the unwavering commitment of those who are working to create a more just and compassionate society.
output: You, perhaps, may tell your story in safety, endeared as you are to so many warm hearts by rare gifts, and a still rarer devotion of them to the service of others. But it will be owing only to your labors, and the fearless efforts of those who, trampling the laws and Constitution of the country under their feet, are determined that they will “hide the outcast,” and that their hearths shall be, spite of the law, an asylum for the oppressed, if, some time or other, the humblest may stand in our streets, and bear witness in safety against the cruelties of which he has been the victim.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input: When we had gone about halfway to St. Michael's, while the constables who had us in charge were looking ahead, Henry asked me what he should do with his pass. I told him he could eat it along with his biscuit and admit to nothing, and we passed the word around: "Own nothing," and "Own nothing!" we all said. Our confidence in one another tended to remain unshaken. We were resolved to succeed or fail together, after the calamity had happened to us as much as before. We were now prepared for almost anything. We were to be dragged that morning fifteen miles behind horses and then placed in the Easton jail. When we reached St. Michael's, we went through a kind of examination. We all denied that we had ever intended to run away. We did this more to bring out the evidence against us than from any hope of avoiding being sold, for, as I have said, we were ready for that. The fact was, we cared relatively little where we went, as long as we went together. Our greatest concern tended to be about separation. We dreaded that more than almost anything this side of death. We found that the evidence against us was the testimony of one person; our master would not say who it was, but we reached a unanimous decision among ourselves as to who their informant was. We were sent off to the jail at Easton. When we got there, we were handed over to the sheriff, Mr. Joseph Graham, and by him placed in jail. Henry, John, and I were placed in one room together, while Charles and Henry Bailey were placed in another. Their purpose in separating us may have been to prevent us from planning together.
output: When we got about half way to St. Michael’s, while the constables having us in charge were looking ahead, Henry inquired of me what he should do with his pass. I told him to eat it with his biscuit, and own nothing; and we passed the word around, “Own nothing;” and “Own nothing!” said we all. Our confidence in each other was unshaken. We were resolved to succeed or fail together, after the calamity had befallen us as much as before. We were now prepared for any thing. We were to be dragged that morning fifteen miles behind horses, and then to be placed in the Easton jail. When we reached St. Michael’s, we underwent a sort of examination. We all denied that we ever intended to run away. We did this more to bring out the evidence against us, than from any hope of getting clear of being sold; for, as I have said, we were ready for that. The fact was, we cared but little where we went, so we went together. Our greatest concern was about separation. We dreaded that more than any thing this side of death. We found the evidence against us to be the testimony of one person; our master would not tell who it was; but we came to a unanimous decision among ourselves as to who their informant was. We were sent off to the jail at Easton. When we got there, we were delivered up to the sheriff, Mr. Joseph Graham, and by him placed in jail. Henry, John, and myself, were placed in one room together - Charles, and Henry Bailey, in another. Their object in separating us was to hinder concert.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input:
I was rarely subjected to physical punishment by my former master, and my primary sources of discomfort were hunger and cold. Furthermore, I experienced a significant amount of distress due to hunger, but my suffering was even more pronounced due to the cold. Throughout the year, regardless of the season, I was forced to endure the elements with minimal clothing, consisting of a coarse tow linen shirt that barely reached my knees. Additionally, I had no shoes, stockings, jacket, or trousers to provide any protection from the cold. 

Meanwhile, I was also without a bed, which further exacerbated my struggles with the cold. Nevertheless, during the coldest nights, I would often sneak away with a bag that was normally used to transport corn to the mill, and I would use it as a means of survival. I would crawl inside the bag and attempt to sleep on the cold and damp clay floor, with my head inside the bag and my feet exposed. As a result of this prolonged exposure to the cold, my feet would often become severely cracked due to the frost, to the extent that a writing instrument could fit into the deep gashes that formed.
output: I was seldom whipped by my old master, and suffered little from any thing else than hunger and cold. I suffered much from hunger, but much more from cold. In hottest summer and coldest winter, I was kept almost naked - no shoes, no stockings, no jacket, no trousers, nothing on but a coarse tow linen shirt, reaching only to my knees. I had no bed. I must have perished with cold, but that, the coldest nights, I used to steal a bag which was used for carrying corn to the mill. I would crawl into this bag, and there sleep on the cold, damp, clay floor, with my head in and feet out. My feet have been so cracked with the frost, that the pen with which I am writing might be laid in the gashes.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input:
The Christianity practiced in America can be characterized by its tendency to impose strict and burdensome expectations on others, while its adherents often fail to uphold these same standards themselves. This highlights a disconnect between the values they promote and their actual behavior. They often seek to be recognized and respected by others, desiring prominent positions and titles. However, this outward display of piety can be misleading, as it may not reflect their true intentions or actions. Ultimately, this hypocrisy can have severe consequences, as it can prevent individuals from genuinely accessing spiritual guidance and instead lead them further away from it. 

This situation is exacerbated by the fact that these individuals often prioritize superficial aspects of their faith, such as rituals and public displays of devotion, over more fundamental principles like justice, compassion, and sincerity. They may meticulously follow certain rules and traditions, while neglecting the more important aspects of their faith. This suggests a lack of balance and authenticity in their spiritual practice. Furthermore, their emphasis on appearances can lead them to focus on minor details while ignoring more significant issues, creating a sense of moral inconsistency. 

In essence, the criticism is that these individuals present themselves as virtuous and righteous, but beneath this façade, they are often driven by self-interest and a desire for power. This discrepancy between their outward appearance and inner reality is a significant concern, as it can undermine the integrity of their faith and damage their relationships with others.
output: The Christianity of America is a Christianity, of whose votaries it may be as truly said, as it was of the ancient scribes and Pharisees, “They bind heavy burdens, and grievous to be borne, and lay them on men’s shoulders, but they themselves will not move them with one of their fingers. All their works they do for to be seen of men. - They love the uppermost rooms at feasts, and the chief seats in the synagogues,...... and to be called of men, Rabbi, Rabbi. - But woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye shut up the kingdom of heaven against men; for ye neither go in yourselves, neither suffer ye them that are entering to go in. Ye devour widows’ houses, and for a pretence make long prayers; therefore ye shall receive the greater damnation. Ye compass sea and land to make one proselyte, and when he is made, ye make him twofold more the child of hell than yourselves. - Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye pay tithe of mint, and anise, and cumin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith; these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone. Ye blind guides! which strain at a gnat, and swallow a camel. Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye make clean the outside of the cup and of the platter; but within, they are full of extortion and excess. - Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men’s bones, and of all uncleanness. Even so ye also outwardly appear righteous unto men, but within ye are full of hypocrisy and iniquity.”
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input:
The narrative contains numerous impactful events and passages of considerable eloquence and influence. However, one of the most compelling descriptions is that of Douglass's emotional state as he stood on the banks of the Chesapeake Bay, contemplating his fate and the possibility of one day being a free individual. Meanwhile, he watched as vessels sailed away, their white sails billowing in the wind, and he addressed them as if they were imbued with the spirit of freedom. Furthermore, the passage in question is notable for its emotional resonance and grandeur, and it is likely to evoke a strong response from readers.

Additionally, this particular passage is significant because it distills a vast array of thoughts, emotions, and sentiments into a powerful critique of the institution of slavery. Accordingly, it presents a comprehensive argument against the practice of making one human being the property of another, which is a fundamentally reprehensible act. Moreover, the system of slavery is particularly odious because it denies the inherent value and dignity of human beings, reducing them to a state of subjugation and degradation. Nevertheless, it is essential to recognize the inherent evil of this system and to acknowledge the profound implications of its existence.

Ultimately, the presence of slavery in the United States implies a profound disregard for human well-being and a lack of reverence for a higher power. Consequently, it is imperative to bring an end to this unjust system as soon as possible. output: This Narrative contains many affecting incidents, many passages of great eloquence and power; but I think the most thrilling one of them all is the description Douglass gives of his feelings, as he stood soliloquizing respecting his fate, and the chances of his one day being a freeman, on the banks of the Chesapeake Bay - viewing the receding vessels as they flew with their white wings before the breeze, and apostrophizing them as animated by the living spirit of freedom. Compressed into it is a whole Alexandrian library of thought, feeling, and sentiment - all that can, all that need be urged, in the form of expostulation, entreaty, rebuke, against that crime of crimes, - making man the property of his fellow-man! For months my life was despaired of, and when at last I came to myself and became convalescent, I was so weak and emaciated that a medical board determined that not a day should be lost in sending me back to England. I was dispatched, accordingly, in the troopship “Orontes,” and landed a month later on Portsmouth jetty, with my health irretrievably ruined, but with permission from a paternal government to spend the next nine months in attempting to improve it.

output:
“Cocks and hens,” cried the little girl gleefully, pointing at their ill-omened forms, and clapping her hands to make them rise. “Say, did God make this country?”

“He made the country down in Illinois, and He made the Missouri,” the little girl continued. “I guess somebody else made the country in these parts. It’s not nearly so well done. They forgot the water and the trees.”

It was a strange sight had there been anything but the buzzards to see it. Side by side on the narrow shawl knelt the two wanderers, the little prattling child and the reckless, hardened adventurer. Her chubby face, and his haggard, angular visage were both turned up to the cloudless heaven in heartfelt entreaty to that dread being with whom they were face to face, while the two voices - the one thin and clear, the other deep and harsh - united in the entreaty for mercy and forgiveness. The prayer finished, they resumed their seat in the shadow of the boulder until the child fell asleep, nestling upon the broad breast of her protector. He watched over her slumber for some time, but Nature proved to be too strong for him. For three days and three nights he had allowed himself neither rest nor repose. Slowly the eyelids drooped over the tired eyes, and the head sunk lower and lower upon the breast, until the man’s grizzled beard was mixed with the gold tresses of his companion, and both slept the same deep and dreamless slumber.

“The people hold you in high regard,” Hester remarked. “Surely, you are doing good among them. Does this not bring you some comfort?” 

“Further misery, Hester! It only brings me more misery!” the clergyman replied, with a bitter smile. “Regarding the good that I may appear to accomplish, I have no faith in it. It must be nothing but an illusion. What can a ruined soul such as mine possibly achieve in the redemption of other souls, or a tainted soul in their purification? Moreover, concerning the people's reverence, I would prefer it be transformed into scorn and hatred. Can you truly consider it, Hester, a consolation that I must ascend to my pulpit, meeting countless eyes that gaze upward at my face as if the light of heaven illuminated it? Must I witness my congregation yearning for the truth and hanging on my words as if I were speaking with the tongue of Pentecost, only to then look inward and recognize the grim reality of what they idolize? In moments of bitterness and heartache, I have found myself laughing at the stark contrast between my appearance and my true self. And it is in this that Satan also finds amusement!”
output:
“The people reverence thee,” said Hester. “And surely thou workest good among them! Doth this bring thee no comfort?”

“More misery, Hester! - only the more misery!” answered the clergyman, with a bitter smile. “As concerns the good which I may appear to do, I have no faith in it. It must needs be a delusion. What can a ruined soul, like mine, effect towards the redemption of other souls? - or a polluted soul towards their purification? And as for the people’s reverence, would that it were turned to scorn and hatred! Canst thou deem it, Hester, a consolation, that I must stand up in my pulpit, and meet so many eyes turned upward to my face, as if the light of heaven were beaming from it! - must see my flock hungry for the truth, and listening to my words as if a tongue of Pentecost were speaking! - and then look inward, and discern the black reality of what they idolize? I have laughed, in bitterness and agony of heart, at the contrast between what I seem and what I am! And Satan laughs at it!”

In those days, the distance from the prison door to the market-place was not great. Measured by the prisoner’s experience, however, it could perhaps be counted as a journey of some length, for even though her manner was proud, she may well have felt agony with every step taken by those who crowded in to see her, as if her heart had been thrown into the street for everyone to reject and trample on. In our nature, though, there tends to be a provision that is both wonderful and merciful: a sufferer does not usually know the full intensity of what he endures through the torture of the moment, but mainly through the pain that lingers afterward. With an almost calm bearing, then, Hester Prynne passed through this part of her ordeal and came to a kind of platform at the western edge of the market-place. It stood almost beneath the eaves of Boston’s earliest church and seemed to be a permanent fixture there.

She noted that children are particularly sensitive to changes in their environment and suggested that Pearl was missing something familiar that Hester had always worn.

The minister responded by urging Hester to find a way to calm the child immediately. He commented that he would prefer any challenge over dealing with a child's intense emotions, likening Pearl's beauty to that of a witch in its unsettling nature. He implored her to soothe Pearl for his sake.
output:
“I see what ails the child,” whispered Hester to the clergyman, and turning pale in spite of a strong effort to conceal her trouble and annoyance. “Children will not abide any, the slightest, change in the accustomed aspect of things that are daily before their eyes. Pearl misses something which she has always seen me wear!”

“I pray you,” answered the minister, “if thou hast any means of pacifying the child, do it forthwith! Save it were the cankered wrath of an old witch, like Mistress Hibbins,” added he, attempting to smile, “I know nothing that I would not sooner encounter than this passion in a child. In Pearl’s young beauty, as in the wrinkled witch, it has a preternatural effect. Pacify her, if thou lovest me!”

“And why is that?” the physician asked. “Why not, since all the natural forces strongly urge for the confession of sin? These dark weeds have emerged from a buried heart to reveal an unspoken crime.”

“That, good Sir, is merely a figment of your imagination,” the minister replied. “There can be, if I am correct in my intuition, no power, except for Divine mercy, that can disclose the secrets buried within a human heart, whether through spoken words or symbols. The heart, holding guilt for such secrets, must inevitably keep them until the day when all hidden things are revealed. I have not interpreted the Holy Scriptures in such a way as to believe that the revelation of human thoughts and actions is meant to be a part of retribution. That would be a superficial understanding. No; these revelations, unless I am mistaken, are intended to provide intellectual satisfaction to all intelligent beings who will be waiting on that day to see the dark complexities of life clarified. An understanding of human hearts will be essential for the complete resolution of that complexity. Furthermore, I believe that hearts burdened with such painful secrets will share them willingly on that final day, not with reluctance, but with indescribable joy.”
output:
“And wherefore?” rejoined the physician. “Wherefore not; since all the powers of nature call so earnestly for the confession of sin, that these black weeds have sprung up out of a buried heart, to make manifest an unspoken crime?”

“That, good Sir, is but a fantasy of yours,” replied the minister. “There can be, if I forebode aright, no power, short of the Divine mercy, to disclose, whether by uttered words, or by type or emblem, the secrets that may be buried with a human heart. The heart, making itself guilty of such secrets, must perforce hold them, until the day when all hidden things shall be revealed. Nor have I so read or interpreted Holy Writ, as to understand that the disclosure of human thoughts and deeds, then to be made, is intended as a part of the retribution. That, surely, were a shallow view of it. No; these revelations, unless I greatly err, are meant merely to promote the intellectual satisfaction of all intelligent beings, who will stand waiting, on that day, to see the dark problem of this life made plain. A knowledge of men’s hearts will be needful to the completest solution of that problem. And I conceive, moreover, that the hearts holding such miserable secrets as you speak of will yield them up, at that last day, not with reluctance, but with a joy unutterable.”

input: This incident recalled my mind, to some extent, to its former course. There appeared to be here the foundation of a tale. It impressed me as if the ancient Surveyor, in his attire of a century past, and wearing his immortal wig—which was buried with him, yet did not perish in the grave—had met me in the deserted chamber of the Custom-House. In his bearing was the dignity of one who had held his Majesty's commission, and who was therefore illuminated by a ray of the splendor that shone so dazzlingly about the throne. How unlike, alas, is the hang-dog look of a republican official, who, as the servant of the people, feels himself less than the least, and below the lowest, of his masters. With his own ghostly hand, the obscurely seen but majestic figure had imparted to me the scarlet symbol, and the little roll of explanatory manuscript. With his own ghostly voice, he had exhorted me, on the sacred consideration of my filial duty and reverence towards him—who might reasonably regard himself as my official ancestor—to bring his mouldy and moth-eaten lucubrations before the public. "Do this," said the ghost of Mr. Surveyor Pue, emphatically nodding the head that looked so imposing within its memorable wig, "do this, and the profit shall be all your own! You will shortly need it; for it is not in your days as it was in mine, when a man's office was a life-lease, and oftentimes an heirloom. But, I charge you, in this matter of old Mistress Prynne, give to your predecessor's memory the credit which will be rightfully due!" And I said to the ghost of Mr. Surveyor Pue, "I will!"
