input: The case of the Bombay Parsees serves as an intriguing example. When this industrious and enterprising community, descended from Persian fire-worshippers, fled their homeland in the face of the Caliphs, they arrived in Western India and were granted tolerance by the Hindu sovereigns, contingent upon their abstention from beef. Subsequently, when these regions came under the rule of Muslim conquerors, the Parsees secured a continuation of this indulgence, provided they refrained from consuming pork. What initially began as compliance with authority has evolved into a deeply ingrained practice, leading the Parsees to abstain from both beef and pork to this day. Although this dual abstinence is not mandated by their religious beliefs, it has become an established custom within their community; and in the context of Eastern culture, custom often holds a significance akin to religion.
output: The case of the Bombay Parsees is a curious instance in point. When this industrious and enterprising tribe, the descendants of the Persian fire-worshippers, flying from their native country before the Caliphs, arrived in Western India, they were admitted to toleration by the Hindoo sovereigns, on condition of not eating beef. When those regions afterwards fell under the dominion of Mahomedan conquerors, the Parsees obtained from them a continuance of indulgence, on condition of refraining from pork. What was at first obedience to authority became a second nature, and the Parsees to this day abstain both from beef and pork. Though not required by their religion, the double abstinence has had time to grow into a custom of their tribe; and custom, in the East, is a religion.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: To provide a more localized context, the majority of Spaniards perceive it as a significant offense, deeply disrespectful to the Supreme Being, to worship Him in any manner other than that of the Roman Catholic Church; thus, no other form of public worship is considered lawful on Spanish territory. Furthermore, the populations of Southern Europe view a married clergy as not only irreligious but also as unchaste, indecent, and thoroughly distasteful. It is worth noting that one must consider the perspective of Protestants regarding these deeply held convictions and the attempts to enforce them upon non-Catholics. Moreover, if humanity is justified in interfering with one another's liberties in matters that do not pertain to the interests of others, on what grounds can one consistently exclude these situations? Who can rightfully criticize individuals for wishing to eliminate what they perceive as a scandal in the eyes of both God and society? A more compelling argument can hardly be made for prohibiting any actions deemed as personal immorality than for suppressing practices viewed as impious; unless we are willing to adopt the rationale of persecutors and assert that we may oppress others because we are correct, while they must refrain from persecuting us because they are mistaken, we must be cautious about endorsing a principle that we would find profoundly unjust if applied to our own circumstances.
output: To come somewhat nearer home: the majority of Spaniards consider it a gross impiety, offensive in the highest degree to the Supreme Being, to worship him in any other manner than the Roman Catholic; and no other public worship is lawful on Spanish soil. The people of all Southern Europe look upon a married clergy as not only irreligious, but unchaste, indecent, gross, disgusting. What do Protestants think of these perfectly sincere feelings, and of the attempt to enforce them against non-Catholics? Yet, if mankind are justified in interfering with each other's liberty in things which do not concern the interests of others, on what principle is it possible consistently to exclude these cases? or who can blame people for desiring to suppress what they regard as a scandal in the sight of God and man? No stronger case can be shown for prohibiting anything which is regarded as a personal immorality, than is made out for suppressing these practices in the eyes of those who regard them as impieties; and unless we are willing to adopt the logic of persecutors, and to say that we may persecute others because we are right, and that they must not persecute us because they are wrong, we must beware of admitting a principle of which we should resent as a gross injustice the application to ourselves.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: I do not claim that the most unrestricted freedom to express all possible opinions would eliminate the problems of religious or philosophical sectarianism. Whenever people of limited understanding believe strongly in a particular truth, they will assert it, teach it, and often act on it as though no other truth exists, or at least none that could limit or qualify it. I recognize that the tendency of all opinions to become sectarian is not resolved by the freest discussion. Instead, it is often intensified by such discussion, because a truth that should have been acknowledged but was not is rejected all the more forcefully when it is proclaimed by those regarded as opponents. However, the beneficial effect of conflicting opinions is felt not by the passionate partisan but by the calmer and more impartial observer. The serious danger is not the violent conflict between different parts of the truth, but the quiet suppression of half of it. There is always hope when people are compelled to listen to both sides. It is when they attend to only one side that errors harden into prejudices, and truth itself loses its effect by being exaggerated into falsehood. Since the judicial faculty that can intelligently judge between two sides of a question is very rare, especially when only one side is represented by an advocate, truth has no chance unless every side of it, and every opinion that embodies any portion of the truth, not only finds advocates but is advocated in such a way that it is actually heard.
output: I do not pretend that the most unlimited use of the freedom of enunciating all possible opinions would put an end to the evils of religious or philosophical sectarianism. Every truth which men of narrow capacity are in earnest about, is sure to be asserted, inculcated, and in many ways even acted on, as if no other truth existed in the world, or at all events none that could limit or qualify the first. I acknowledge that the tendency of all opinions to become sectarian is not cured by the freest discussion, but is often heightened and exacerbated thereby; the truth which ought to have been, but was not, seen, being rejected all the more violently because proclaimed by persons regarded as opponents. But it is not on the impassioned partisan, it is on the calmer and more disinterested bystander, that this collision of opinions works its salutary effect. Not the violent conflict between parts of the truth, but the quiet suppression of half of it, is the formidable evil: there is always hope when people are forced to listen to both sides; it is when they attend only to one that errors harden into prejudices, and truth itself ceases to have the effect of truth, by being exaggerated into falsehood. And since there are few mental attributes more rare than that judicial faculty which can sit in intelligent judgment between two sides of a question, of which only one is represented by an advocate before it, truth has no chance but in proportion as every side of it, every opinion which embodies any fraction of the truth, not only finds advocates, but is so advocated as to be listened to.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input:
Objections to governmental involvement, as long as it does not infringe on individual liberties, may typically be categorized into three types. 

Firstly, one concern arises when it seems that individuals may be more capable of effectively managing certain tasks than the government. In many cases, those who have a personal stake in a matter may be best suited to handle it or decide how it should be managed. This idea often challenges the previous practices of legislative or governmental interference in everyday business activities. However, this aspect has been explored extensively by political economists and may not be directly relevant to the core principles discussed in this essay. In summary, while objections to government involvement can be understood in various ways, the notion of individual capability often emerges as a central concern.
output:
The objections to government interference, when it is not such as to involve infringement of liberty, may be of three kinds.

The first is, when the thing to be done is likely to be better done by individuals than by the government. Speaking generally, there is no one so fit to conduct any business, or to determine how or by whom it shall be conducted, as those who are personally interested in it. This principle condemns the interferences, once so common, of the legislature, or the officers of government, with the ordinary processes of industry. But this part of the subject has been sufficiently enlarged upon by political economists, and is not particularly related to the principles of this Essay.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: There is something both contemptible and frightful in the nature of the evidence upon which, in recent years, any individual may be judicially declared unfit for the management of his affairs, and after his death his disposal of his property may be set aside, provided there is enough of it to pay the expenses of litigation, which are charged upon the property itself. Furthermore, all the minute details of his daily life are pried into, and whatever is found which, seen through the medium of the perceiving and describing faculties of the lowest of the low, bears an appearance unlike absolute commonplace, is laid before the jury as evidence of insanity, and often with success, the jurors being little, if at all, less vulgar and ignorant than the witnesses. Moreover, the judges, with that extraordinary want of knowledge of human nature and life which continually astonishes us in English lawyers, often help to mislead them. It is worth noting that these trials speak volumes as to the state of feeling and opinion among the vulgar with regard to human liberty. In essence, so far from setting any value on individuality, so far from respecting the rights of each individual to act, in things indifferent, as seems good to his own judgment and inclinations, judges and juries cannot even conceive that a person in a state of sanity can desire such freedom. Additionally, in former days, when it was proposed to burn atheists, charitable people used to suggest putting them in a madhouse instead; it would be nothing surprising nowadays were we to see this done, and the doers applauding themselves, because, instead of persecuting for religion, they had adopted so humane and Christian a mode of treating these unfortunates, not without a silent satisfaction at their having thereby obtained their deserts.
output: There is something both contemptible and frightful in the sort of evidence on which, of late years, any person can be judicially declared unfit for the management of his affairs; and after his death, his disposal of his property can be set aside, if there is enough of it to pay the expenses of litigation - which are charged on the property itself. All the minute details of his daily life are pried into, and whatever is found which, seen through the medium of the perceiving and describing faculties of the lowest of the low, bears an appearance unlike absolute commonplace, is laid before the jury as evidence of insanity, and often with success; the jurors being little, if at all, less vulgar and ignorant than the witnesses; while the judges, with that extraordinary want of knowledge of human nature and life which continually astonishes us in English lawyers, often help to mislead them. These trials speak volumes as to the state of feeling and opinion among the vulgar with regard to human liberty. So far from setting any value on individuality - so far from respecting the rights of each individual to act, in things indifferent, as seems good to his own judgment and inclinations, judges and juries cannot even conceive that a person in a state of sanity can desire such freedom. In former days, when it was proposed to burn atheists, charitable people used to suggest putting them in a madhouse instead: it would be nothing surprising nowadays were we to see this done, and the doers applauding themselves, because, instead of persecuting for religion, they had adopted so humane and Christian a mode of treating these unfortunates, not without a silent satisfaction at their having thereby obtained their deserts.

input: Additionally, it is a common phenomenon that ideals which neglect a significant aspect of what is desirable tend to yield an inferior representation of the remaining aspect. Furthermore, the current standard of approbation results in a suboptimal manifestation of the other half, characterized by a lack of robust energies guided by vigorous rationality, and weak sentiments that are poorly controlled by a conscientious volition. In essence, its outcome is a set of feeble sentiments and energies, which can be readily maintained in outward compliance with established norms without requiring any notable strength of will or rational faculty. Moreover, it is worth noting that energetic personalities on a large scale are becoming increasingly rare and are now largely relegated to the realm of tradition. Currently, there are scarcely any avenues for the expression of energy in this country beyond the realm of commerce. It is worth noting that the energy expended in this domain is still considerable. Moreover, the limited amount of energy that remains after engagement in commercial pursuits is typically directed towards a particular hobby, which may be a useful or even philanthropic endeavor, but is generally a relatively narrow pursuit. Additionally, the greatness of England is now primarily a collective phenomenon, wherein individual contributions are relatively small, and it is only through the habit of collaboration that we appear capable of achieving greatness. Furthermore, this state of affairs is entirely satisfactory to our moral and religious philanthropists. However, it was individuals of a distinctly different character who were responsible for England's past achievements, and it will be necessary to have individuals of a similar caliber to prevent the country's decline.
output: As is usually the case with ideals which exclude one-half of what is desirable, the present standard of approbation produces only an inferior imitation of the other half. Instead of great energies guided by vigorous reason, and strong feelings strongly controlled by a conscientious will, its result is weak feelings and weak energies, which therefore can be kept in outward conformity to rule without any strength either of will or of reason. Already energetic characters on any large scale are becoming merely traditional. There is now scarcely any outlet for energy in this country except business. The energy expended in that may still be regarded as considerable. What little is left from that employment, is expended on some hobby; which may be a useful, even a philanthropic hobby, but is always some one thing, and generally a thing of small dimensions. The greatness of England is now all collective: individually small, we only appear capable of anything great by our habit of combining; and with this our moral and religious philanthropists are perfectly contented. But it was men of another stamp than this that made England what it has been; and men of another stamp will be needed to prevent its decline.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: The amalgamation of these various factors generates a substantial array of influences that are detrimental to Individuality, rendering it challenging to perceive how it may maintain its position. Moreover, it will face increasing obstacles unless the discerning segment of the public recognizes its significance and acknowledges the inherent value of differences, even if those differences do not lead to improvement and may, from their perspective, even be perceived as detrimental. If the principles of Individuality are ever to be championed, the present moment is critical, as there remains much to be accomplished in the process of enforced assimilation. It is primarily in the initial stages that a successful resistance can be mounted against this encroachment. The expectation that others should conform to our own likeness intensifies as it consumes itself. If opposition is postponed until existence is nearly homogenized, all variations from that norm will ultimately be viewed as irreverent, unethical, and even unnatural. Furthermore, humanity rapidly loses the capacity to envision diversity after an extended period of unfamiliarity with it.
output: The combination of all these causes forms so great a mass of influences hostile to Individuality, that it is not easy to see how it can stand its ground. It will do so with increasing difficulty, unless the intelligent part of the public can be made to feel its value - to see that it is good there should be differences, even though not for the better, even though, as it may appear to them, some should be for the worse. If the claims of Individuality are ever to be asserted, the time is now, while much is still wanting to complete the enforced assimilation. It is only in the earlier stages that any stand can be successfully made against the encroachment. The demand that all other people shall resemble ourselves, grows by what it feeds on. If resistance waits till life is reduced nearly to one uniform type, all deviations from that type will come to be considered impious, immoral, even monstrous and contrary to nature. Mankind speedily become unable to conceive diversity, when they have been for some time unaccustomed to see it.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: I answer that this assumes considerably more. A significant difference exists between presuming an opinion to be true because it has not been refuted despite every opportunity for contesting it, and assuming its truth for the purpose of preventing its refutation. Complete liberty to contradict and disprove our opinion is the very condition that justifies us in assuming its truth for purposes of action. On no other terms can a being with human faculties have any rational assurance of being right.
output: I answer that it is assuming very much more. There is the greatest difference between presuming an opinion to be true, because, with every opportunity for contesting it, it has not been refuted, and assuming its truth for the purpose of not permitting its refutation. Complete liberty of contradicting and disproving our opinion, is the very condition which justifies us in assuming its truth for purposes of action; and on no other terms can a being with human faculties have any rational assurance of being right.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: There is a class of people, though fortunately not as numerous as in the past, who consider it sufficient if someone accepts without doubt what they believe to be true, even if that person has no knowledge of the reasons behind the opinion and could not defend it against even the most basic objections. Such people, once they can have their beliefs taught through authority, naturally conclude that no benefit and some harm comes from allowing those beliefs to be questioned. Where their influence is dominant, they make it nearly impossible for the accepted opinion to be rejected wisely and carefully, although it may still be rejected recklessly and ignorantly. This is because completely blocking discussion is rarely possible, and once discussion begins, beliefs not founded on conviction tend to collapse before the slightest appearance of an argument. Setting aside this possibility, however, and assuming that the true opinion remains in the mind but remains as a prejudice, a belief independent of argument and resistant to it, this is not how truth should be held by a rational person. This is not knowing the truth. Truth held in this manner is merely one more superstition, accidentally attached to the words that express a truth.
output: There is a class of persons (happily not quite so numerous as formerly) who think it enough if a person assents undoubtingly to what they think true, though he has no knowledge whatever of the grounds of the opinion, and could not make a tenable defence of it against the most superficial objections. Such persons, if they can once get their creed taught from authority, naturally think that no good, and some harm, comes of its being allowed to be questioned. Where their influence prevails, they make it nearly impossible for the received opinion to be rejected wisely and considerately, though it may still be rejected rashly and ignorantly; for to shut out discussion entirely is seldom possible, and when it once gets in, beliefs not grounded on conviction are apt to give way before the slightest semblance of an argument. Waiving, however, this possibility - assuming that the true opinion abides in the mind, but abides as a prejudice, a belief independent of, and proof against, argument - this is not the way in which truth ought to be held by a rational being. This is not knowing the truth. Truth, thus held, is but one superstition the more, accidentally clinging to the words which enunciate a truth.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: It is not excessive to require that what the wisest of humanity, those most entitled to trust their own judgment, deem necessary to justify their reliance upon it, should be accepted by that diverse assemblage of a few wise and many unwise individuals, commonly referred to as the public. Additionally, the most intolerant of churches, the Roman Catholic Church, even at the canonisation of a saint, permits and patiently attends to a "devil's advocate." Furthermore, it appears that the holiest of individuals cannot be granted posthumous honours until all that could be said against them is known and considered. Moreover, if even the Newtonian philosophy were not allowed to be questioned, humanity could not possess the same complete assurance of its truth as they do at present. In essence, the beliefs for which we have the most justification have no safeguard other than a continual invitation to the entire world to demonstrate them to be unfounded. It is worth noting that if this challenge is not accepted, or is accepted and the attempt proves unsuccessful, we remain far from certainty; however, we have done the utmost that the current state of human reason permits, and we have omitted nothing that could afford the truth an opportunity to reach us. If the lists remain open, we may hope that, should a superior truth exist, it will be discovered when the human mind is capable of receiving it; meanwhile, we may rely upon having attained such an approximation to truth as is possible in our own era. This constitutes the degree of certainty attainable by a fallible being, and this is the sole means of attaining it.
output: It is not too much to require that what the wisest of mankind, those who are best entitled to trust their own judgment, find necessary to warrant their relying on it, should be submitted to by that miscellaneous collection of a few wise and many foolish individuals, called the public. The most intolerant of churches, the Roman Catholic Church, even at the canonisation of a saint, admits, and listens patiently to, a "devil's advocate." The holiest of men, it appears, cannot be admitted to posthumous honours, until all that the devil could say against him is known and weighed. If even the Newtonian philosophy were not permitted to be questioned, mankind could not feel as complete assurance of its truth as they now do. The beliefs which we have most warrant for, have no safeguard to rest on, but a standing invitation to the whole world to prove them unfounded. If the challenge is not accepted, or is accepted and the attempt fails, we are far enough from certainty still; but we have done the best that the existing state of human reason admits of; we have neglected nothing that could give the truth a chance of reaching us: if the lists are kept open, we may hope that if there be a better truth, it will be found when the human mind is capable of receiving it; and in the meantime we may rely on having attained such approach to truth, as is possible in our own day. This is the amount of certainty attainable by a fallible being, and this the sole way of attaining it.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: The distinction presented here between the aspects of an individual's life that pertain solely to themselves and those that concern others is one that many individuals may refuse to acknowledge. Furthermore, one might question how any aspect of the behavior of a member of society could be regarded as insignificant to other members. No individual exists in complete isolation; it is indeed impossible for a person to engage in actions that are seriously or permanently detrimental to themselves without causing repercussions that extend to their immediate connections and often beyond. For instance, if an individual damages their property, they inflict harm upon those who rely on it directly or indirectly, thus generally reducing the resources available to the community. Additionally, if an individual compromises their physical or mental health, they not only bring misfortune upon those who depend on them for a portion of their happiness but also incapacitate themselves from fulfilling the responsibilities they owe to their fellow beings. This may result in them becoming a burden on the kindness or goodwill of others. If such behavior were to occur with great frequency, it is unlikely that any offense would contribute more to the overall reduction of societal well-being. Finally, even if a person's vices or follies appear to cause no direct harm to others, it can be argued that they are nonetheless damaging through their example. Consequently, it is imperative that such individuals are compelled to exercise self-control for the sake of those who might be influenced or misled by the observation or awareness of their conduct.
output: The distinction here pointed out between the part of a person's life which concerns only himself, and that which concerns others, many persons will refuse to admit. How (it may be asked) can any part of the conduct of a member of society be a matter of indifference to the other members? No person is an entirely isolated being; it is impossible for a person to do anything seriously or permanently hurtful to himself, without mischief reaching at least to his near connections, and often far beyond them. If he injures his property, he does harm to those who directly or indirectly derived support from it, and usually diminishes, by a greater or less amount, the general resources of the community. If he deteriorates his bodily or mental faculties, he not only brings evil upon all who depended on him for any portion of their happiness, but disqualifies himself for rendering the services which he owes to his fellow-creatures generally; perhaps becomes a burthen on their affection or benevolence; and if such conduct were very frequent, hardly any offence that is committed would detract more from the general sum of good. Finally, if by his vices or follies a person does no direct harm to others, he is nevertheless (it may be said) injurious by his example; and ought to be compelled to control himself, for the sake of those whom the sight or knowledge of his conduct might corrupt or mislead.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input:
It is important to analyze these two hypotheses individually, as each has a unique aspect of the argument associated with it. We can never be entirely certain that the opinion we seek to suppress is indeed false; even if we were sure, suppressing it would still be problematic.

First, the opinion that is being suppressed by authority may potentially be true. Those who wish to restrict it typically assert that it is false, yet they are not infallible. They do not possess the authority to make definitive judgments for all individuals or to prevent others from forming their own conclusions. To dismiss an opinion simply because one believes it to be false is to equate one's own certainty with absolute certainty. This highlights that all forms of silencing discussion imply a claim to infallibility. This argument against suppression can stand on its own merit, even if it is widely recognized.

It is necessary to consider separately these two hypotheses, each of which has a distinct branch of the argument corresponding to it. We can never be sure that the opinion we are endeavouring to stifle is a false opinion; and if we were sure, stifling it would be an evil still.

First: the opinion which it is attempted to suppress by authority may possibly be true. Those who desire to suppress it, of course deny its truth; but they are not infallible. They have no authority to decide the question for all mankind, and exclude every other person from the means of judging. To refuse a hearing to an opinion, because they are sure that it is false, is to assume that their certainty is the same thing as absolute certainty. All silencing of discussion is an assumption of infallibility. Its condemnation may be allowed to rest on this common argument, not the worse for being common.

input: It is peculiar that individuals recognize the merits of free discussion yet object to it being taken to extremes. They fail to realize that if the arguments are not strong enough to support an extreme case, they are insufficient for any case. It is also strange that they believe they are not claiming infallibility when they assert that free discussion should occur on all potentially questionable subjects. However, they simultaneously think that certain principles or doctrines should not be open to scrutiny because they consider them to be unquestionably true. To label any proposition as certain, while denying others the opportunity to challenge that certainty, assumes that we and those who share our views are the sole arbiters of certainty, and that we do so without considering alternative perspectives.
output: Strange it is, that men should admit the validity of the arguments for free discussion, but object to their being "pushed to an extreme;" not seeing that unless the reasons are good for an extreme case, they are not good for any case. Strange that they should imagine that they are not assuming infallibility, when they acknowledge that there should be free discussion on all subjects which can possibly be doubtful, but think that some particular principle or doctrine should be forbidden to be questioned because it is so certain, that is, because they are certain that it is certain. To call any proposition certain, while there is any one who would deny its certainty if permitted, but who is not permitted, is to assume that we ourselves, and those who agree with us, are the judges of certainty, and judges without hearing the other side.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: The principles are, first, that a person is generally not accountable to society for their actions when those actions mainly concern their own interests and not those of others. Advice, instruction, persuasion, and, if others believe it necessary for their own good, avoidance by other people are often the only measures by which society can justifiably express its dislike or disapproval of such conduct. Second, for actions that may harm the interests of others, the individual can be held accountable and may be subject to social or legal punishments if society considers one or the other necessary for its protection. Overall, these principles suggest that personal conduct tends to be treated as a matter for individual responsibility when it mainly affects the person themselves, while conduct that can affect others may justify some form of social or legal response.
output: The maxims are, first, that the individual is not accountable to society for his actions, in so far as these concern the interests of no person but himself. Advice, instruction, persuasion, and avoidance by other people if thought necessary by them for their own good, are the only measures by which society can justifiably express its dislike or disapprobation of his conduct. Secondly, that for such actions as are prejudicial to the interests of others, the individual is accountable and may be subjected either to social or to legal punishments, if society is of opinion that the one or the other is requisite for its protection.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: It can be argued that society has a right to take preventative measures to protect itself from harm, which may suggest that there are limitations to the idea that individuals should not be interfered with for misconduct that only affects themselves. For instance, in most cases, drunkenness may not be considered a suitable subject for legislative intervention; however, it may be reasonable to impose special restrictions on individuals who have previously been convicted of violent acts while under the influence of alcohol. This could involve penalties for subsequent instances of drunkenness, as well as increased punishment for any additional offences committed while in that state. In such cases, the act of becoming drunk can be seen as a potential harm to others, and therefore may be considered a crime against them. Similarly, idleness is generally not something that can be punished by law, unless it involves a breach of contract or reliance on public support; nevertheless, if an individual's idleness or other avoidable circumstances lead to a failure to fulfill their obligations to others, such as supporting their children, it may not be unreasonable to enforce their compliance through measures like compulsory labour, if necessary. In summary, while individuals generally have the right to make their own choices, society may also have a legitimate interest in intervening in cases where those choices may harm others.
output: The right inherent in society, to ward off crimes against itself by antecedent precautions, suggests the obvious limitations to the maxim, that purely self-regarding misconduct cannot properly be meddled with in the way of prevention or punishment. Drunkenness, for example, in ordinary cases, is not a fit subject for legislative interference; but I should deem it perfectly legitimate that a person, who had once been convicted of any act of violence to others under the influence of drink, should be placed under a special legal restriction, personal to himself; that if he were afterwards found drunk, he should be liable to a penalty, and that if when in that state he committed another offence, the punishment to which he would be liable for that other offence should be increased in severity. The making himself drunk, in a person whom drunkenness excites to do harm to others, is a crime against others. So, again, idleness, except in a person receiving support from the public, or except when it constitutes a breach of contract, cannot without tyranny be made a subject of legal punishment; but if either from idleness or from any other avoidable cause, a man fails to perform his legal duties to others, as for instance to support his children, it is no tyranny to force him to fulfil that obligation, by compulsory labour, if no other means are available.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: John Stuart Mill was born on 20th May 1806. He was a delicate child, and the unusual education his father designed for him may not have been well suited to developing his physical abilities. As he himself said, "I never was a boy; never played cricket." His exercise generally took the form of walks with his father, during which the elder Mill would lecture his son and test him on his studies. It is perhaps not very useful to speculate on what a different approach might have produced. Mill remained delicate throughout his life, but he seems to have been endowed with the kind of intense mental energy that is often found alongside physical weakness. His youth was, in a sense, sacrificed to an idea: his father intended him to carry on his work, and the boy's own individuality tended to be of little importance. A visit to the south of France at the age of fourteen, in the company of the family of General Sir Samuel Bentham, can be said to have had some influence on him. It offered a glimpse of a different atmosphere, though the studious habits of his home life were largely maintained. He also seems to have derived from it his interest in foreign politics, which remained one of his characteristics to the end of his life. In 1823 he was appointed junior clerk in the Examiners' Office at the India House.
output: John Stuart Mill was born on 20th May 1806. He was a delicate child, and the extraordinary education designed by his father was not calculated to develop and improve his physical powers. "I never was a boy," he says; "never played cricket." His exercise was taken in the form of walks with his father, during which the elder Mill lectured his son and examined him on his work. It is idle to speculate on the possible results of a different treatment. Mill remained delicate throughout his life, but was endowed with that intense mental energy which is so often combined with physical weakness. His youth was sacrificed to an idea; he was designed by his father to carry on his work; the individuality of the boy was unimportant. A visit to the south of France at the age of fourteen, in company with the family of General Sir Samuel Bentham, was not without its influence. It was a glimpse of another atmosphere, though the studious habits of his home life were maintained. Moreover, he derived from it his interest in foreign politics, which remained one of his characteristics to the end of his life. In 1823 he was appointed junior clerk in the Examiners' Office at the India House.

input: It's possible that someone who is skeptical of open discussion might argue that it's not necessarily essential for the general public to be aware of all the arguments for and against certain opinions, as presented by philosophers and theologians. They may suggest that it's not crucial for ordinary people to be able to identify and refute every misleading statement or flawed argument made by a skilled opponent. Instead, they might propose that it's sufficient to have experts who can respond to such claims, ensuring that no potentially misleading information goes unchallenged. In this view, individuals who are not experts can trust in the authority of those who have taught them the basic principles of a particular truth, and, acknowledging their own limitations, can be confident that any complex issues that arise have been or can be addressed by those with specialized knowledge and training. Overall, this perspective suggests that the public can rely on experts to handle complex debates and arguments, and that this can be a viable approach to navigating complex issues.
output: To abate the force of these considerations, an enemy of free discussion may be supposed to say, that there is no necessity for mankind in general to know and understand all that can be said against or for their opinions by philosophers and theologians. That it is not needful for common men to be able to expose all the misstatements or fallacies of an ingenious opponent. That it is enough if there is always somebody capable of answering them, so that nothing likely to mislead uninstructed persons remains unrefuted. That simple minds, having been taught the obvious grounds of the truths inculcated on them, may trust to authority for the rest, and being aware that they have neither knowledge nor talent to resolve every difficulty which can be raised, may repose in the assurance that all those which have been raised have been or can be answered, by those who are specially trained to the task.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: The tyranny of the majority, like other forms of tyranny, was initially and is still commonly feared mainly because it operates through the actions of public authorities. However, thoughtful individuals recognized that when society itself acts as the tyrant—society collectively exerting power over the separate individuals who make it up—its methods of oppression are not limited to the actions carried out by its political officials. Society can and does enforce its own demands, and when it issues wrong demands instead of right ones, or any demands at all in matters it should not interfere with, it practices a social tyranny more formidable than many kinds of political oppression. This is because, although it is not usually backed by such extreme penalties, it leaves fewer ways to escape, penetrating much more deeply into the details of life and enslaving the soul itself. This highlights that protection against the tyranny of the magistrate is not enough; there also needs to be protection against the tyranny of prevailing opinion and feeling, against society's tendency to impose its own ideas and practices as rules of conduct on those who dissent, by means other than civil penalties. This includes fettering the development of individuality and, if possible, preventing the formation of any individuality not in harmony with its ways, and compelling all characters to conform to its own model. Ultimately, there is a limit to the legitimate interference of collective opinion with individual independence, and finding and maintaining that limit against encroachment is as indispensable to a good condition of human affairs as protection against political despotism.
output: Like other tyrannies, the tyranny of the majority was at first, and is still vulgarly, held in dread, chiefly as operating through the acts of the public authorities. But reflecting persons perceived that when society is itself the tyrant - society collectively, over the separate individuals who compose it - its means of tyrannising are not restricted to the acts which it may do by the hands of its political functionaries. Society can and does execute its own mandates: and if it issues wrong mandates instead of right, or any mandates at all in things with which it ought not to meddle, it practises a social tyranny more formidable than many kinds of political oppression, since, though not usually upheld by such extreme penalties, it leaves fewer means of escape, penetrating much more deeply into the details of life, and enslaving the soul itself. Protection, therefore, against the tyranny of the magistrate is not enough: there needs protection also against the tyranny of the prevailing opinion and feeling; against the tendency of society to impose, by other means than civil penalties, its own ideas and practices as rules of conduct on those who dissent from them; to fetter the development, and, if possible, prevent the formation, of any individuality not in harmony with its ways, and compel all characters to fashion themselves upon the model of its own. There is a limit to the legitimate interference of collective opinion with individual independence: and to find that limit, and maintain it against encroachment, is as indispensable to a good condition of human affairs, as protection against political despotism.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: In the eighteenth century, many educated individuals, as well as those who followed their lead, tended to admire what was referred to as civilisation, and they may have been impressed by the advancements in modern science, literature, and philosophy. At the same time, they can often be seen to have overestimated the differences between people in modern and ancient times, and may have believed that the differences were largely in their own favour. The ideas of Rousseau, which can be considered paradoxical, may have had a significant impact, potentially disrupting the prevailing one-sided opinions and forcing people to re-evaluate and recombine their ideas in a more nuanced way. It's worth noting that the current opinions of the time may not have been entirely inaccurate, and they may have contained more truth than Rousseau's ideas, with fewer errors. However, Rousseau's doctrine may have introduced some important truths that were lacking in popular opinion, and these ideas have continued to influence thought over time. The value of simplicity, the potential negative effects of artificial society, and the importance of authenticity are concepts that may have been highlighted by Rousseau's work, and they can often be seen to have had a lasting impact on cultivated minds, even if they still need to be reaffirmed and demonstrated through actions, as words alone may not be sufficient to bring about change. In summary, Rousseau's ideas may have played a significant role in shaping opinions and highlighting important truths, and their influence can still be seen today.
output: Thus, in the eighteenth century, when nearly all the instructed, and all those of the uninstructed who were led by them, were lost in admiration of what is called civilisation, and of the marvels of modern science, literature, and philosophy, and while greatly overrating the amount of unlikeness between the men of modern and those of ancient times, indulged the belief that the whole of the difference was in their own favour; with what a salutary shock did the paradoxes of Rousseau explode like bombshells in the midst, dislocating the compact mass of one-sided opinion, and forcing its elements to recombine in a better form and with additional ingredients. Not that the current opinions were on the whole farther from the truth than Rousseau's were; on the contrary, they were nearer to it; they contained more of positive truth, and very much less of error. Nevertheless there lay in Rousseau's doctrine, and has floated down the stream of opinion along with it, a considerable amount of exactly those truths which the popular opinion wanted; and these are the deposit which was left behind when the flood subsided. The superior worth of simplicity of life, the enervating and demoralising effect of the trammels and hypocrisies of artificial society, are ideas which have never been entirely absent from cultivated minds since Rousseau wrote; and they will in time produce their due effect, though at present needing to be asserted as much as ever, and to be asserted by deeds, for words, on this subject, have nearly exhausted their power.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: There is a particular characteristic of the current direction of public opinion that is especially calculated to render it intolerant of any notable manifestation of individuality. The general average of humanity is not only moderate in intellectual capacity, but also moderate in its inclinations; people possess no tastes or desires sufficiently strong to incline them toward unusual conduct, and consequently they do not comprehend those who do possess such tastes or desires, classifying all such persons among the wild and intemperate whom they are accustomed to regard with disdain. Furthermore, in addition to this general circumstance, one need only suppose that a powerful movement has commenced toward the improvement of morals, and it becomes evident what may be expected. In the present age, such a movement has indeed commenced; much has actually been accomplished in the way of increased regularity of conduct and the discouragement of excesses; and a philanthropic spirit prevails, for the exercise of which no more inviting field exists than the moral and prudential improvement of our fellow beings. Moreover, these tendencies of the times dispose the public more than at most former periods to prescribe general rules of conduct and to endeavor to make everyone conform to the approved standard. Additionally, that standard, whether expressed or tacit, is to desire nothing with intensity. Its ideal of character is to be devoid of any marked character; to impair by compression, like the foot of a Chinese lady, every part of human nature that stands out prominently and tends to render the individual markedly dissimilar in outline from commonplace humanity.
output: There is one characteristic of the present direction of public opinion, peculiarly calculated to make it intolerant of any marked demonstration of individuality. The general average of mankind are not only moderate in intellect, but also moderate in inclinations: they have no tastes or wishes strong enough to incline them to do anything unusual, and they consequently do not understand those who have, and class all such with the wild and intemperate whom they are accustomed to look down upon. Now, in addition to this fact which is general, we have only to suppose that a strong movement has set in towards the improvement of morals, and it is evident what we have to expect. In these days such a movement has set in; much has actually been effected in the way of increased regularity of conduct, and discouragement of excesses; and there is a philanthropic spirit abroad, for the exercise of which there is no more inviting field than the moral and prudential improvement of our fellow-creatures. These tendencies of the times cause the public to be more disposed than at most former periods to prescribe general rules of conduct, and endeavour to make every one conform to the approved standard. And that standard, express or tacit, is to desire nothing strongly. Its ideal of character is to be without any marked character; to maim by compression, like a Chinese lady's foot, every part of human nature which stands out prominently, and tends to make the person markedly dissimilar in outline to commonplace humanity.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: It is accurate to assert this perspective within the framework of Calvinistic theory. According to this theory, the predominant transgression of humanity is deemed to be self-will. The entirety of good that humanity can achieve is encapsulated in the concept of obedience. Individuals possess no choice in their actions; thus, they must act in a prescribed manner: any action that is not a duty is considered a sin. Given that human nature is fundamentally corrupt, there is no possibility of redemption for any individual until the corrupt aspects of human nature are eradicated from within. For those who adhere to this worldview, suppressing any of the human faculties, capacities, and sensibilities is not regarded as detrimental. Humanity requires no capacity beyond the ability to submit entirely to the divine will. Should individuals utilize any of their faculties for purposes other than fulfilling what is perceived as the divine will more effectively, it is argued that they would be better off without them. This encapsulates the essence of Calvinism; moreover, a modified interpretation of this theory is embraced by many who do not identify as Calvinists. This modification entails a less austere interpretation of the supposed will of God, positing that it is divine intent for humanity to indulge in certain inclinations. This indulgence is, of course, not to be pursued in the manner individuals may prefer but rather in obedience, adhering to directives established by authoritative sources, thereby imposing uniformity across all individuals in accordance with the requisite conditions of the case.
output: It is so, on the Calvinistic theory. According to that, the one great offence of man is Self-will. All the good of which humanity is capable, is comprised in Obedience. You have no choice; thus you must do, and no otherwise: "whatever is not a duty, is a sin." Human nature being radically corrupt, there is no redemption for any one until human nature is killed within him. To one holding this theory of life, crushing out any of the human faculties, capacities, and susceptibilities, is no evil: man needs no capacity, but that of surrendering himself to the will of God: and if he uses any of his faculties for any other purpose but to do that supposed will more effectually, he is better without them. That is the theory of Calvinism; and it is held, in a mitigated form, by many who do not consider themselves Calvinists; the mitigation consisting in giving a less ascetic interpretation to the alleged will of God; asserting it to be his will that mankind should gratify some of their inclinations; of course not in the manner they themselves prefer, but in the way of obedience, that is, in a way prescribed to them by authority; and, therefore, by the necessary conditions of the case, the same for all.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: If the absence of free discussion were to leave people unaware of the foundations of accepted opinions, it might be viewed as an intellectual issue rather than a moral one. Such a scenario could suggest that the value of these opinions remains intact, especially concerning their impact on character. However, the reality is that without discussion, individuals not only forget the basis of these opinions but often lose the very meaning of the opinions themselves. The words that express these ideas begin to lose their ability to convey thoughts, often communicating only a fraction of their original intent. Instead of fostering a clear understanding and genuine belief, only a few phrases may be memorized without comprehension, or merely the superficial elements of meaning may persist while the deeper significance is lost. This profound issue occupies a significant place in human history and deserves careful examination and reflection.
output: If, however, the mischievous operation of the absence of free discussion, when the received opinions are true, were confined to leaving men ignorant of the grounds of those opinions, it might be thought that this, if an intellectual, is no moral evil, and does not affect the worth of the opinions, regarded in their influence on the character. The fact, however, is, that not only the grounds of the opinion are forgotten in the absence of discussion, but too often the meaning of the opinion itself. The words which convey it, cease to suggest ideas, or suggest only a small portion of those they were originally employed to communicate. Instead of a vivid conception and a living belief, there remain only a few phrases retained by rote; or, if any part, the shell and husk only of the meaning is retained, the finer essence being lost. The great chapter in human history which this fact occupies and fills, cannot be too earnestly studied and meditated on.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: This volume is dedicated to the memory of a significant influence in the author's life, specifically the friend and wife who inspired much of his best work. Her strong sense of truth and justice served as a powerful motivation, and her approval was the author's primary reward. The author acknowledges that this work is as much hers as it is his, though it has not benefited as fully from her input as it could have, given that some critical parts were left for further review that will now not occur. The author expresses a desire to convey the profound thoughts and emotions that remain unspoken due to her passing, suggesting that achieving this would provide greater value to the world than his current writing can offer without her exceptional insight.
output: _To the beloved and deplored memory of her who was the inspirer, and in part the author, of all that is best in my writings - the friend and wife whose exalted sense of truth and right was my strongest incitement, and whose approbation was my chief reward - I dedicate this volume. Like all that I have written for many years, it belongs as much to her as to me; but the work as it stands has had, in a very insufficient degree, the inestimable advantage of her revision; some of the most important portions having been reserved for a more careful re-examination, which they are now never destined to receive. Were I but capable of interpreting to the world one-half the great thoughts and noble feelings which are buried in her grave, I should be the medium of a greater benefit to it than is ever likely to arise from anything that I can write, unprompted and unassisted by her all but unrivalled wisdom._
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: If the arguments presented in this chapter are valid, then the fullest liberty should exist for professing and discussing any doctrine as a matter of ethical conviction, regardless of how immoral that doctrine may be considered. It would therefore be irrelevant and inappropriate to examine here whether the doctrine of tyrannicide deserves that title. I will content myself with stating that this subject has always been one of the open questions of morals. The act of a private citizen in striking down a criminal who has placed himself above the law and beyond the reach of legal punishment or control has been regarded by whole nations, and by some of the best and wisest of men, not as a crime but as an act of exalted virtue. Whether right or wrong, it is not in the nature of assassination but of civil war. As such, I hold that instigation to it in a specific case may be a proper subject of punishment, but only if an overt act has followed and at least a probable connection can be established between the act and the instigation. Even then, it is not a foreign government but the very government assailed that alone, in the exercise of self-defence, can legitimately punish attacks directed against its own existence.
output: If the arguments of the present chapter are of any validity, there ought to exist the fullest liberty of professing and discussing, as a matter of ethical conviction, any doctrine, however immoral it may be considered. It would, therefore, be irrelevant and out of place to examine here, whether the doctrine of Tyrannicide deserves that title. I shall content myself with saying, that the subject has been at all times one of the open questions of morals; that the act of a private citizen in striking down a criminal, who, by raising himself above the law, has placed himself beyond the reach of legal punishment or control, has been accounted by whole nations, and by some of the best and wisest of men, not a crime, but an act of exalted virtue; and that, right or wrong, it is not of the nature of assassination, but of civil war. As such, I hold that the instigation to it, in a specific case, may be a proper subject of punishment, but only if an overt act has followed, and at least a probable connection can be established between the act and the instigation. Even then, it is not a foreign government, but the very government assailed, which alone, in the exercise of self-defence, can legitimately punish attacks directed against its own existence.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: It should not be assumed that because damage or the probability of damage to the interests of others is the only justification for social interference, such interference is therefore always justified. In many cases, an individual who pursues a legitimate goal necessarily and therefore legitimately causes pain or loss to others, or blocks a good that they had a reasonable hope of obtaining. Such conflicts of interest between individuals often arise from bad social institutions, but they are unavoidable as long as those institutions last. Some would be unavoidable under any institutions. Whoever succeeds in an overcrowded profession or in a competitive examination, or whoever is preferred to another in any contest for an object that both desire, gains benefit from the loss of others, from their wasted effort and their disappointment. However, it is generally agreed that the general interest of mankind is better served when people pursue their goals without being deterred by this kind of consequence. In other words, society recognizes no rights, whether legal or moral, for disappointed competitors to be immune from this kind of suffering. Society feels called on to interfere only when the means of success employed are those that it is contrary to the general interest to permit, namely fraud or treachery, and force.
output: In the first place, it must by no means be supposed, because damage, or probability of damage, to the interests of others, can alone justify the interference of society, that therefore it always does justify such interference. In many cases, an individual, in pursuing a legitimate object, necessarily and therefore legitimately causes pain or loss to others, or intercepts a good which they had a reasonable hope of obtaining. Such oppositions of interest between individuals often arise from bad social institutions, but are unavoidable while those institutions last; and some would be unavoidable under any institutions. Whoever succeeds in an overcrowded profession, or in a competitive examination; whoever is preferred to another in any contest for an object which both desire, reaps benefit from the loss of others, from their wasted exertion and their disappointment. But it is, by common admission, better for the general interest of mankind, that persons should pursue their objects undeterred by this sort of consequences. In other words, society admits no rights, either legal or moral, in the disappointed competitors, to immunity from this kind of suffering; and feels called on to interfere, only when means of success have been employed which it is contrary to the general interest to permit - namely, fraud or treachery, and force.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: Let us now move on to the second part of the argument. Setting aside the possibility that any of the accepted beliefs might be incorrect, we will assume their truth and explore how they are likely perceived when their validity is not openly discussed. Even someone who holds a strong opinion might find it challenging to accept that their viewpoint could be mistaken. However, they should consider that, regardless of its truth, if an opinion is not regularly and openly examined, it may come to be seen as a stagnant belief rather than a dynamic truth. In summary, continuous and open dialogue is essential for opinions to remain relevant and meaningful.
output: Let us now pass to the second division of the argument, and dismissing the supposition that any of the received opinions may be false, let us assume them to be true, and examine into the worth of the manner in which they are likely to be held, when their truth is not freely and openly canvassed. However unwillingly a person who has a strong opinion may admit the possibility that his opinion may be false, he ought to be moved by the consideration that however true it may be, if it is not fully, frequently, and fearlessly discussed, it will be held as a dead dogma, not a living truth.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: This passage raises important questions about societal responsibility in guiding individuals who may lack the ability to govern themselves. It suggests that if society recognizes the need to protect children and minors from their own decisions, it should similarly extend that protection to adults who also demonstrate incapacity for self-governance. The text points out that behaviors such as gambling, alcoholism, promiscuity, idleness, and uncleanliness can be as detrimental to personal happiness and societal progress as many actions currently prohibited by law. This highlights the potential argument for law to address these issues within practical limits and social convenience. Furthermore, it proposes that public opinion should actively combat these vices and impose social penalties on those who engage in them. Importantly, the passage clarifies that the aim is not to restrict individual expression or stifle innovative ways of living, but rather to prevent the repetition of historically harmful behaviors that have proven unbeneficial. Ultimately, it asserts that after sufficient time and experience, certain moral or practical truths can be considered established, and society should strive to prevent future generations from repeating the mistakes of the past.
output: And even (it will be added) if the consequences of misconduct could be confined to the vicious or thoughtless individual, ought society to abandon to their own guidance those who are manifestly unfit for it? If protection against themselves is confessedly due to children and persons under age, is not society equally bound to afford it to persons of mature years who are equally incapable of self-government? If gambling, or drunkenness, or incontinence, or idleness, or uncleanliness, are as injurious to happiness, and as great a hindrance to improvement, as many or most of the acts prohibited by law, why (it may be asked) should not law, so far as is consistent with practicability and social convenience, endeavour to repress these also? And as a supplement to the unavoidable imperfections of law, ought not opinion at least to organise a powerful police against these vices, and visit rigidly with social penalties those who are known to practise them? There is no question here (it may be said) about restricting individuality, or impeding the trial of new and original experiments in living. The only things it is sought to prevent are things which have been tried and condemned from the beginning of the world until now; things which experience has shown not to be useful or suitable to any person's individuality. There must be some length of time and amount of experience, after which a moral or prudential truth may be regarded as established: and it is merely desired to prevent generation after generation from falling over the same precipice which has been fatal to their predecessors.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input:
It is worth noting that we have now recognized the necessity of freedom of opinion and freedom of expression for the mental well-being of humanity, which serves as the foundation for all other forms of well-being, on four distinct grounds. We will now briefly summarize these grounds.

Additionally, if any opinion is compelled to remain silent, that opinion may, to our best understanding, be true. To deny this possibility is to presume our own infallibility.

Furthermore, even if the silenced opinion represents an error, it may contain a fragment of truth, and in fact, this is often the case. Since the prevailing opinion on any subject is rarely, if ever, the complete truth, it is only through the confrontation of opposing opinions that the remaining aspects of truth have any opportunity to emerge.
output:
We have now recognised the necessity to the mental well-being of mankind (on which all their other well-being depends) of freedom of opinion, and freedom of the expression of opinion, on four distinct grounds; which we will now briefly recapitulate.

First, if any opinion is compelled to silence, that opinion may, for aught we can certainly know, be true. To deny this is to assume our own infallibility.

Secondly, though the silenced opinion be an error, it may, and very commonly does, contain a portion of truth; and since the general or prevailing opinion on any subject is rarely or never the whole truth, it is only by the collision of adverse opinions, that the remainder of the truth has any chance of being supplied.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: What Mill's wife truly meant to him is something we may never fully know. Yet there is abundant evidence that she was a real and vivid force in his life, one that awakened the latent enthusiasm within his nature. When she died at Avignon, his friends may have regained a companionship that had become somewhat distant, but on a personal level, Mill was the poorer for it. We cannot enter into the sorrow of that loss; we have no right or power to draw back the veil. It is enough to quote his simple words, so eloquent of an unspoken grief: "I can say nothing which could describe, even in the faintest manner, what that loss was and is. But because I know that she would have wished it, I endeavour to make the best of what life I have left, and to work for her purposes with such diminished strength as can be derived from thoughts of her, and communion with her memory." This highlights how deeply her presence shaped his life and purpose, and ultimately, how her memory became a sustaining force in his remaining years.
output: What his wife really was to Mill, we shall, perhaps, never know. But that she was an actual and vivid force, which roused the latent enthusiasm of his nature, we have abundant evidence. And when she died at Avignon, though his friends may have regained an almost estranged companionship, Mill was, personally, the poorer. Into the sorrow of that bereavement we cannot enter: we have no right or power to draw the veil. It is enough to quote the simple words, so eloquent of an unspoken grief - "I can say nothing which could describe, even in the faintest manner, what that loss was and is. But because I know that she would have wished it, I endeavour to make the best of what life I have left, and to work for her purposes with such diminished strength as can be derived from thoughts of her, and communion with her memory."

input: It is now necessary to assert that the situation was fundamentally different for the early Christians. Had the circumstances been otherwise, Christianity would not have evolved from a marginalized group of the disdained Hebrews into the dominant religion of the Roman Empire. When their adversaries remarked, "See how these Christians love one another," they undoubtedly possessed a much deeper understanding of their faith than has been observed in more recent times. This phenomenon likely accounts for the fact that Christianity currently experiences limited growth in its reach, remaining predominantly associated with Europeans and their descendants even after eighteen centuries. Furthermore, even among those who are fervent in their religious beliefs and ascribe significant meaning to their doctrines, it is frequently observed that the aspects of faith that actively engage their thoughts are those influenced by figures such as Calvin or Knox, individuals who are much closer to their own identities. The words of Christ tend to reside passively in their consciousness, exerting little influence beyond the gentle appeal of the language. There are certainly numerous explanations for why sect-specific doctrines maintain greater vitality than those shared across recognized sects and why educators make greater efforts to keep their significance alive; however, one clear reason is that these unique doctrines are more often subjected to scrutiny and must be defended against open challengers. In essence, both instructors and students tend to become complacent in their roles as soon as there is no opposition present.
output: Now we may be well assured that the case was not thus, but far otherwise, with the early Christians. Had it been thus, Christianity never would have expanded from an obscure sect of the despised Hebrews into the religion of the Roman empire. When their enemies said, "See how these Christians love one another" (a remark not likely to be made by anybody now), they assuredly had a much livelier feeling of the meaning of their creed than they have ever had since. And to this cause, probably, it is chiefly owing that Christianity now makes so little progress in extending its domain, and after eighteen centuries, is still nearly confined to Europeans and the descendants of Europeans. Even with the strictly religious, who are much in earnest about their doctrines, and attach a greater amount of meaning to many of them than people in general, it commonly happens that the part which is thus comparatively active in their minds is that which was made by Calvin, or Knox, or some such person much nearer in character to themselves. The sayings of Christ coexist passively in their minds, producing hardly any effect beyond what is caused by mere listening to words so amiable and bland. There are many reasons, doubtless, why doctrines which are the badge of a sect retain more of their vitality than those common to all recognised sects, and why more pains are taken by teachers to keep their meaning alive; but one reason certainly is, that the peculiar doctrines are more questioned, and have to be oftener defended against open gainsayers. Both teachers and learners go to sleep at their post, as soon as there is no enemy in the field.
