author: John Stuart Mill

input: I do not affirm any such proposition. As humanity progresses, the number of doctrines that are no longer contested or doubted will continuously increase; the well-being of humanity can almost be quantified by the quantity and significance of the truths that have reached a state of being uncontested. The cessation of serious controversy concerning one question after another is an essential aspect of the consolidation of opinion, which is beneficial when it pertains to true opinions, while it can be perilous and harmful in the case of erroneous views. Furthermore, although this gradual reduction in the diversity of opinion is necessary in both respects, being simultaneously inevitable and essential, we are not compelled to conclude that all of its outcomes must be advantageous. The loss of such a crucial aid to the intelligent and dynamic comprehension of a truth, which is provided by the need to explain it to or defend it against opponents, although it does not outweigh the benefits of universal recognition, is neither insignificant nor negligible. Where this advantage can no longer be obtained, I must confess that I would appreciate witnessing the educators of humanity striving to offer a substitute; some method of presenting the complexities of the question as vividly to the learner's awareness as if they were being challenged by a dissenting advocate, keen to convert him.
output: I affirm no such thing. As mankind improve, the number of doctrines which are no longer disputed or doubted will be constantly on the increase: and the well-being of mankind may almost be measured by the number and gravity of the truths which have reached the point of being uncontested. The cessation, on one question after another, of serious controversy, is one of the necessary incidents of the consolidation of opinion; a consolidation as salutary in the case of true opinions, as it is dangerous and noxious when the opinions are erroneous. But though this gradual narrowing of the bounds of diversity of opinion is necessary in both senses of the term, being at once inevitable and indispensable, we are not therefore obliged to conclude that all its consequences must be beneficial. The loss of so important an aid to the intelligent and living apprehension of a truth, as is afforded by the necessity of explaining it to, or defending it against, opponents, though not sufficient to outweigh, is no trifling drawback from, the benefit of its universal recognition. Where this advantage can no longer be had, I confess I should like to see the teachers of mankind endeavouring to provide a substitute for it; some contrivance for making the difficulties of the question as present to the learner's consciousness, as if they were pressed upon him by a dissentient champion, eager for his conversion.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: The same principle generally applies to all traditional doctrines, including those pertaining to prudence, knowledge of life, as well as morals and religion. All languages and literatures are replete with overarching observations regarding life, encompassing both its nature and the appropriate manner in which to navigate it. These observations are widely acknowledged, frequently repeated, and often accepted without question; they are regarded as self-evident truths. However, it is worth noting that most individuals do not genuinely comprehend their significance until personal experience, often of a painful nature, has rendered them a reality. Frequently, when one is grappling with an unexpected misfortune or disappointment, they recall a proverb or common saying that has been familiar throughout their life. The significance of this saying, if it had been fully grasped prior to the present circumstance, might have prevented their misfortune. There are indeed various reasons for this phenomenon beyond the mere lack of discourse; many truths cannot be fully appreciated until they have been substantiated by personal experience. Moreover, a greater understanding of even these truths, along with a more profound mental imprint of what was understood, could have been achieved had individuals been accustomed to hearing them debated from multiple perspectives by those with a true understanding. The unfortunate tendency of humanity to cease contemplating a matter once it is no longer in doubt accounts for a significant portion of their errors. A contemporary author has aptly remarked upon "the deep slumber of a decided opinion."
output: The same thing holds true, generally speaking, of all traditional doctrines - those of prudence and knowledge of life, as well as of morals or religion. All languages and literatures are full of general observations on life, both as to what it is, and how to conduct oneself in it; observations which everybody knows, which everybody repeats, or hears with acquiescence, which are received as truisms, yet of which most people first truly learn the meaning, when experience, generally of a painful kind, has made it a reality to them. How often, when smarting under some unforeseen misfortune or disappointment, does a person call to mind some proverb or common saying, familiar to him all his life, the meaning of which, if he had ever before felt it as he does now, would have saved him from the calamity. There are indeed reasons for this, other than the absence of discussion: there are many truths of which the full meaning cannot be realised, until personal experience has brought it home. But much more of the meaning even of these would have been understood, and what was understood would have been far more deeply impressed on the mind, if the man had been accustomed to hear it argued pro and con by people who did understand it. The fatal tendency of mankind to leave off thinking about a thing when it is no longer doubtful, is the cause of half their errors. A contemporary author has well spoken of "the deep slumber of a decided opinion."
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: To frame the argument effectively, it is beneficial to first focus on a specific aspect of the broader thesis, particularly the Liberty of Thought. This aspect is inherently linked to the associated freedoms of speech and writing. While these liberties are recognized to varying degrees in the political morality of nations that uphold religious tolerance and democratic institutions, the underlying philosophical and practical foundations are not as widely understood or appreciated, even among influential figures. This suggests that a deeper understanding of these foundations extends beyond just this topic and is essential for addressing the broader issues at hand. Ultimately, for those familiar with the discourse surrounding this topic over the past three centuries, I ask for patience as I contribute to this ongoing discussion.
output: It will be convenient for the argument, if, instead of at once entering upon the general thesis, we confine ourselves in the first instance to a single branch of it, on which the principle here stated is, if not fully, yet to a certain point, recognised by the current opinions. This one branch is the Liberty of Thought: from which it is impossible to separate the cognate liberty of speaking and of writing. Although these liberties, to some considerable amount, form part of the political morality of all countries which profess religious toleration and free institutions, the grounds, both philosophical and practical, on which they rest, are perhaps not so familiar to the general mind, nor so thoroughly appreciated by many even of the leaders of opinion, as might have been expected. Those grounds, when rightly understood, are of much wider application than to only one division of the subject, and a thorough consideration of this part of the question will be found the best introduction to the remainder. Those to whom nothing which I am about to say will be new, may therefore, I hope, excuse me, if on a subject which for now three centuries has been so often discussed, I venture on one discussion more.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: Thirdly, even if a widely accepted opinion is entirely accurate, it is still important for it to be subjected to vigorous and earnest debate. This highlights the need for critical examination, as without it, most people will accept the opinion without fully understanding its underlying rationale, essentially holding it as a prejudice. Additionally, this suggests that the doctrine itself may be compromised, losing its original meaning and impact on an individual's character and behavior. Ultimately, if this occurs, the doctrine may become a mere formality, lacking the power to inspire positive change, while also occupying space and hindering the development of genuine, heartfelt convictions that arise from reason or personal experience.
output: Thirdly, even if the received opinion be not only true, but the whole truth; unless it is suffered to be, and actually is, vigorously and earnestly contested, it will, by most of those who receive it, be held in the manner of a prejudice, with little comprehension or feeling of its rational grounds. And not only this, but, fourthly, the meaning of the doctrine itself will be in danger of being lost, or enfeebled, and deprived of its vital effect on the character and conduct: the dogma becoming a mere formal profession, inefficacious for good, but cumbering the ground, and preventing the growth of any real and heartfelt conviction, from reason or personal experience.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: It can be challenging to defend the use of punishment to restrain irreligious opinions, as this approach may be difficult to justify without also condoning the actions of historical figures like Marcus Antoninus. When faced with criticism, opponents of religious freedom may acknowledge this potential consequence and argue, similarly to Dr. Johnson, that the persecutors of Christianity may have been justified in their actions. They tend to suggest that persecution can serve as a test of truth, which ultimately prevails, although legal penalties may sometimes be effective in suppressing harmful misconceptions. This line of reasoning in support of religious intolerance is noteworthy and may be worth considering. In summary, the debate surrounding religious freedom and tolerance is complex, and various arguments can be made, with some suggesting that persecution may have a role to play in testing the validity of certain beliefs.
output: Aware of the impossibility of defending the use of punishment for restraining irreligious opinions, by any argument which will not justify Marcus Antoninus, the enemies of religious freedom, when hard pressed, occasionally accept this consequence, and say, with Dr. Johnson, that the persecutors of Christianity were in the right; that persecution is an ordeal through which truth ought to pass, and always passes successfully, legal penalties being, in the end, powerless against truth, though sometimes beneficially effective against mischievous errors. This is a form of the argument for religious intolerance, sufficiently remarkable not to be passed without notice.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: It can be argued that a theory which suggests that truth may be justifiably persecuted because it may not be harmed by it, does not necessarily intend to be hostile to the acceptance of new truths. However, this theory may be seen as lacking in generosity towards the individuals who contribute to the discovery of these new truths. Discovering and sharing new information that is of significant importance to the world, and correcting previous misconceptions, can be a highly valuable service to humanity, as seen in the cases of the early Christians and the Reformers. In some instances, this can be considered one of the most significant contributions a person can make. Nevertheless, it may seem unfortunate that the individuals who make such significant contributions often face severe consequences, such as martyrdom, as a result of their actions. According to this theory, it may be seen as acceptable for the proponents of new ideas to face punishment, similar to the ancient Locrian law, where a person proposing a new law would face immediate punishment if their proposal was not accepted. It tends to be the case that people who support this approach may not place a high value on the benefits of new discoveries, and this view may be more commonly held by those who believe that new truths were once desirable, but are no longer necessary. In summary, this theory may be seen as having a limited perspective on the value of new truths and the treatment of those who discover them.
output: A theory which maintains that truth may justifiably be persecuted because persecution cannot possibly do it any harm, cannot be charged with being intentionally hostile to the reception of new truths; but we cannot commend the generosity of its dealing with the persons to whom mankind are indebted for them. To discover to the world something which deeply concerns it, and of which it was previously ignorant; to prove to it that it had been mistaken on some vital point of temporal or spiritual interest, is as important a service as a human being can render to his fellow-creatures, and in certain cases, as in those of the early Christians and of the Reformers, those who think with Dr. Johnson believe it to have been the most precious gift which could be bestowed on mankind. That the authors of such splendid benefits should be requited by martyrdom; that their reward should be to be dealt with as the vilest of criminals, is not, upon this theory, a deplorable error and misfortune, for which humanity should mourn in sackcloth and ashes, but the normal and justifiable state of things. The propounder of a new truth, according to this doctrine, should stand, as stood, in the legislation of the Locrians, the proposer of a new law, with a halter round his neck, to be instantly tightened if the public assembly did not, on hearing his reasons, then and there adopt his proposition. People who defend this mode of treating benefactors, cannot be supposed to set much value on the benefit; and I believe this view of the subject is mostly confined to the sort of persons who think that new truths may have been desirable once, but that we have had enough of them now.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: The issue highlighted here may not be merely theoretical; it might be reasonable to expect that I would identify specific cases where society today tends to impose its preferences as if they were moral laws. However, my intention is not to write a comprehensive essay on the shortcomings of current moral sentiments, as that topic may be too complex to address briefly and merely as an example. Nevertheless, I believe that providing instances is essential to demonstrate that the principle I am discussing is both significant and applicable in real life, rather than attempting to construct a defense against hypothetical concerns. It can often be observed through numerous examples that the tendency to broaden the scope of what might be viewed as moral authority, to the point where it infringes on the clearly legitimate freedoms of individuals, is a common trait among humans. In sum, this illustrates how societal influences can sometimes challenge personal liberties in the name of moral standards.
output: The evil here pointed out is not one which exists only in theory; and it may perhaps be expected that I should specify the instances in which the public of this age and country improperly invests its own preferences with the character of moral laws. I am not writing an essay on the aberrations of existing moral feeling. That is too weighty a subject to be discussed parenthetically, and by way of illustration. Yet examples are necessary, to show that the principle I maintain is of serious and practical moment, and that I am not endeavouring to erect a barrier against imaginary evils. And it is not difficult to show, by abundant instances, that to extend the bounds of what may be called moral police, until it encroaches on the most unquestionably legitimate liberty of the individual, is one of the most universal of all human propensities.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: This doctrine is intended to apply to human beings who have reached maturity and possess fully developed faculties. It does not pertain to children or young individuals who have not yet reached the age of adulthood as defined by law. Those who require care and protection from others must be safeguarded against their own actions and external harm. This highlights the need for protection and guidance during early stages of development. Similarly, in backward states of society where the population is not yet capable of spontaneous progress, the difficulties are so significant that there may be limited options for overcoming them. In such cases, a ruler who prioritizes improvement may be justified in using various means to achieve their goals, as long as the end result is the betterment of the society. This suggests that despotism can be a legitimate form of government when dealing with societies that are not yet developed, provided that the ultimate goal is improvement and the means used are effective in achieving that end. However, liberty as a principle only becomes applicable when a society has reached a stage where its members can be improved through free and equal discussion. Until that point, implicit obedience to a ruler may be necessary. Ultimately, once a society has reached the capacity for guided improvement through conviction or persuasion, compulsion is no longer justifiable as a means of achieving the greater good, except in cases where it is necessary for the security of others.
output: It is, perhaps, hardly necessary to say that this doctrine is meant to apply only to human beings in the maturity of their faculties. We are not speaking of children, or of young persons below the age which the law may fix as that of manhood or womanhood. Those who are still in a state to require being taken care of by others, must be protected against their own actions as well as against external injury. For the same reason, we may leave out of consideration those backward states of society in which the race itself may be considered as in its nonage. The early difficulties in the way of spontaneous progress are so great, that there is seldom any choice of means for overcoming them; and a ruler full of the spirit of improvement is warranted in the use of any expedients that will attain an end, perhaps otherwise unattainable. Despotism is a legitimate mode of government in dealing with barbarians, provided the end be their improvement, and the means justified by actually effecting that end. Liberty, as a principle, has no application to any state of things anterior to the time when mankind have become capable of being improved by free and equal discussion. Until then, there is nothing for them but implicit obedience to an Akbar or a Charlemagne, if they are so fortunate as to find one. But as soon as mankind have attained the capacity of being guided to their own improvement by conviction or persuasion (a period long since reached in all nations with whom we need here concern ourselves), compulsion, either in the direct form or in that of pains and penalties for non-compliance, is no longer admissible as a means to their own good, and justifiable only for the security of others.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: Additionally, it is necessary for the principles outlined in this text to be more widely accepted as the foundation for examining specific aspects, prior to attempting a consistent application of these principles to the diverse areas of governance and morality, which can only be undertaken with any potential for benefit if this foundation is established. Furthermore, the limited comments that will be presented on specific issues are intended to provide clarification of the principles, rather than to explore their implications in depth. Moreover, the purpose of these comments is not to provide comprehensive applications, but rather to offer examples of how the principles can be applied, which may serve to elucidate the significance and boundaries of the two fundamental maxims that collectively comprise the entirety of the doctrine presented in this essay. In essence, these examples are designed to facilitate the exercise of judgment in striking a balance between the two maxims, particularly in cases where it is uncertain which maxim is most relevant to the situation at hand.
output: The principles asserted in these pages must be more generally admitted as the basis for discussion of details, before a consistent application of them to all the various departments of government and morals can be attempted with any prospect of advantage. The few observations I propose to make on questions of detail, are designed to illustrate the principles, rather than to follow them out to their consequences. I offer, not so much applications, as specimens of application; which may serve to bring into greater clearness the meaning and limits of the two maxims which together form the entire doctrine of this Essay, and to assist the judgment in holding the balance between them, in the cases where it appears doubtful which of them is applicable to the case.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

The Provincial Mayor expressed agreement and, with a furrowed brow, entered a contemplative state, softly articulating thoughts to himself. After a period of reflection, he indicated a newfound clarity. 

He then shared that he had been studying the geometry of four dimensions for some time, noting that some of his findings were intriguing. He provided an example of a series of portraits depicting a man at various ages: eight, fifteen, seventeen, and twenty-three. He explained that these images serve as three-dimensional representations of the man's four-dimensional existence, which is a constant and unchanging entity.
output:
“I think so,” murmured the Provincial Mayor; and, knitting his brows, he lapsed into an introspective state, his lips moving as one who repeats mystic words. “Yes, I think I see it now,” he said after some time, brightening in a quite transitory manner.

“Well, I do not mind telling you I have been at work upon this geometry of Four Dimensions for some time. Some of my results are curious. For instance, here is a portrait of a man at eight years old, another at fifteen, another at seventeen, another at twenty-three, and so on. All these are evidently sections, as it were, Three-Dimensional representations of his Four-Dimensioned being, which is a fixed and unalterable thing.”
title: The Time Machine
author: H. G. Wells

input: She was greatly troubled, yet her unusual affection for me ultimately prevailed. For five nights during our acquaintance, including the final night, she rested her head on my arm while sleeping. However, as I recount my experiences with her, my thoughts begin to blur. It must have been the night before her rescue when I awoke just before dawn. I had been restless, plagued by a disturbing dream in which I was drowning, and sea anemones were brushing against my face with their soft tendrils. I suddenly woke up, harboring a strange notion that a greyish creature had darted out of the room. I attempted to fall asleep again, but I remained uneasy and restless. It was that dim, grey hour when shadows slowly recede from the darkness, creating a colorless and stark environment that felt unreal. I decided to rise and made my way down to the great hall, stepping out onto the flagstones in front of the palace. I thought I would turn my necessity into an opportunity and witness the sunrise.
output: “It troubled her greatly, but in the end her odd affection for me triumphed, and for five of the nights of our acquaintance, including the last night of all, she slept with her head pillowed on my arm. But my story slips away from me as I speak of her. It must have been the night before her rescue that I was awakened about dawn. I had been restless, dreaming most disagreeably that I was drowned, and that sea anemones were feeling over my face with their soft palps. I woke with a start, and with an odd fancy that some greyish animal had just rushed out of the chamber. I tried to get to sleep again, but I felt restless and uncomfortable. It was that dim grey hour when things are just creeping out of darkness, when everything is colourless and clear cut, and yet unreal. I got up, and went down into the great hall, and so out upon the flagstones in front of the palace. I thought I would make a virtue of necessity, and see the sunrise.
title: The Time Machine
author: H. G. Wells

input: He set down his glass and moved toward the staircase door. I noticed once more his lameness and the soft sound of his footsteps. Rising from my seat, I caught a glimpse of his feet as he exited. He wore only a pair of tattered, blood-stained socks. Shortly after, the door closed behind him. I considered following him for a moment, but then I recalled his aversion to any fuss about himself. For a brief time, my thoughts wandered. Then I heard the Editor say, "Remarkable Behaviour of an Eminent Scientist," as he often thought in headlines. This pulled my attention back to the brightly lit dinner table.
output: He put down his glass, and walked towards the staircase door. Again I remarked his lameness and the soft padding sound of his footfall, and standing up in my place, I saw his feet as he went out. He had nothing on them but a pair of tattered, blood-stained socks. Then the door closed upon him. I had half a mind to follow, till I remembered how he detested any fuss about himself. For a minute, perhaps, my mind was wool-gathering. Then, “Remarkable Behaviour of an Eminent Scientist,” I heard the Editor say, thinking (after his wont) in headlines. And this brought my attention back to the bright dinner-table.
title: The Time Machine
author: H. G. Wells

input: Additionally, it was not long before I found myself being grasped by multiple hands, and it was readily apparent that their intention was to pull me back. Furthermore, I ignited another light source and held it up to their faces, which were temporarily blinded by the illumination. It is worth noting that their appearance was utterly unsettling, characterized by pale, chinless faces and large, lidless eyes that seemed to be a pinkish-grey hue, as they stared in a state of confusion and disorientation. Moreover, I did not linger to observe them further, instead opting to retreat once again, and when my second light source had burned out, I ignited my third. In essence, this third light source had nearly exhausted its fuel when I reached the entrance to the shaft. Moreover, I lay down at the edge of the opening, as the pulsating rhythm of the large pump below was causing me to feel lightheaded. Then, as I felt around for the protruding hooks, I experienced a sudden and violent tug on my feet from behind, as if someone was attempting to pull me backward. Nevertheless, I managed to ignite my final light source, although it was promptly extinguished. However, I had already gained a hold on the climbing bars, and by kicking vigorously, I was able to free myself from the grasp of the Morlocks, rapidly ascending the shaft while they remained below, peering and blinking up at me, with the exception of one small creature that pursued me for a short distance and nearly succeeded in seizing my boot as a prize.
output: “In a moment I was clutched by several hands, and there was no mistaking that they were trying to haul me back. I struck another light, and waved it in their dazzled faces. You can scarce imagine how nauseatingly inhuman they looked - those pale, chinless faces and great, lidless, pinkish-grey eyes! - as they stared in their blindness and bewilderment. But I did not stay to look, I promise you: I retreated again, and when my second match had ended, I struck my third. It had almost burnt through when I reached the opening into the shaft. I lay down on the edge, for the throb of the great pump below made me giddy. Then I felt sideways for the projecting hooks, and, as I did so, my feet were grasped from behind, and I was violently tugged backward. I lit my last match … and it incontinently went out. But I had my hand on the climbing bars now, and, kicking violently, I disengaged myself from the clutches of the Morlocks, and was speedily clambering up the shaft, while they stayed peering and blinking up at me: all but one little wretch who followed me for some way, and well-nigh secured my boot as a trophy.
title: The Time Machine
author: H. G. Wells

input: At first, proceeding from the problems of our own age, it seemed clear as daylight to me that the gradual widening of the present merely temporary and social difference between the Capitalist and the Labourer was the key to the whole position. Additionally, it is worth noting that no doubt it will seem grotesque enough to you—and wildly incredible!—and yet even now there are existing circumstances to point that way. Furthermore, there is a tendency to utilise underground space for the less ornamental purposes of civilisation; there is the Metropolitan Railway in London, for instance, there are new electric railways, there are subways, there are underground workrooms and restaurants, and they increase and multiply. Moreover, evidently, I thought, this tendency had increased till Industry had gradually lost its birthright in the sky. In essence, I mean that it had gone deeper and deeper into larger and ever larger underground factories, spending a still-increasing amount of its time therein, till, in the end—! Even now, does not an East-end worker live in such artificial conditions as practically to be cut off from the natural surface of the earth?

input: I then tried to protect myself from the horror that was coming over me by viewing it as a strict punishment for human selfishness. People had been content to live in comfort and pleasure through the labor of others, had taken Necessity as their motto and excuse, and in time Necessity had come back to them. I even tried to feel a Carlyle-like scorn for this miserable aristocracy in decline. But this way of thinking was not possible for me. No matter how great their intellectual decline, the Eloi had retained too much of the human form not to earn my sympathy, and this tended to make me share, whether I wished it or not, in their decline and their fear. In the end, I found that I could not separate myself from the Eloi or regard their suffering as something they simply deserved.
output: “Then I tried to preserve myself from the horror that was coming upon me, by regarding it as a rigorous punishment of human selfishness. Man had been content to live in ease and delight upon the labours of his fellow-man, had taken Necessity as his watchword and excuse, and in the fullness of time Necessity had come home to him. I even tried a Carlyle-like scorn of this wretched aristocracy in decay. But this attitude of mind was impossible. However great their intellectual degradation, the Eloi had kept too much of the human form not to claim my sympathy, and to make me perforce a sharer in their degradation and their Fear.

input: After some time, I got up and started walking through the bushes toward the hill again, perhaps feeling a bit aimless. I reminded myself to be patient. If I wanted to retrieve my machine, it might be wise to leave the sphinx alone. If they intended to take my machine away, then damaging their bronze panels probably wouldn’t help, and if they didn’t, I would likely get it back as soon as I asked. Sitting amongst all those unfamiliar things, facing such a puzzle, may lead to a sense of hopelessness. Then, the humorous aspect of my situation struck me: I had dedicated years to studying and striving to enter this future age, and now I was anxiously eager to escape it. output: “I got up after a time, and began walking aimlessly through the bushes towards the hill again. ‘Patience,’ said I to myself. ‘If you want your machine again you must leave that sphinx alone. If they mean to take your machine away, it’s little good your wrecking their bronze panels, and if they don’t, you will get it back as soon as you can ask for it. To sit among all those unknown things before a puzzle like that is hopeless. That way lies monomania. Face this world. Learn its ways, watch it, be careful of too hasty guesses at its meaning. In the end you will find clues to it all.’ Then suddenly the humour of the situation came into my mind: the thought of the years I had spent in study and toil to get into the future age, and now my passion of anxiety to get out of it. I had made myself the most complicated and the most hopeless trap that ever a man devised. Although it was at my own expense, I could not help myself. I laughed aloud.

input: Additionally, it is still my conviction that the fact that this box of matches had withstood the effects of time for an indefinite number of years was a highly unusual, and indeed fortunate, occurrence. Furthermore, I discovered a substance that was even more unlikely to have survived, namely camphor, which I found in a sealed jar that had, apparently by chance, been effectively hermetically sealed. Initially, I mistook it for paraffin wax and, as a result, broke the glass container, but the distinctive odour of camphor was readily identifiable. In the context of the widespread decay that surrounded me, it was remarkable that this volatile substance had managed to endure, possibly for thousands of centuries. Moreover, it brought to mind a sepia painting I had previously seen, which had been created using the ink of a fossilised Belemnite that must have perished and become fossilised millions of years ago. It is worth noting that I was on the verge of discarding the camphor, but I recalled that it was combustible and burned with a bright, intense flame, thereby rendering it a suitable substitute for a candle, and I consequently placed it in my pocket. Nevertheless, I did not find any explosives or means of breaching the bronze doors, and my iron crowbar remained the most useful item I had discovered up to that point. In essence, I departed from that gallery in a state of considerable elation.
output: “Now, I still think that for this box of matches to have escaped the wear of time for immemorial years was a most strange, as for me it was a most fortunate, thing. Yet, oddly enough, I found a far unlikelier substance, and that was camphor. I found it in a sealed jar, that by chance, I suppose, had been really hermetically sealed. I fancied at first that it was paraffin wax, and smashed the glass accordingly. But the odour of camphor was unmistakable. In the universal decay this volatile substance had chanced to survive, perhaps through many thousands of centuries. It reminded me of a sepia painting I had once seen done from the ink of a fossil Belemnite that must have perished and become fossilised millions of years ago. I was about to throw it away, but I remembered that it was inflammable and burnt with a good bright flame - was, in fact, an excellent candle - and I put it in my pocket. I found no explosives, however, nor any means of breaking down the bronze doors. As yet my iron crowbar was the most helpful thing I had chanced upon. Nevertheless I left that gallery greatly elated.

input: I found myself in a more precarious situation than before. Previously, I had maintained a sense of hope for eventual escape, despite the difficulties I faced, including the distressing loss of the Time Machine. However, this hope was shaken by my new discoveries. Until then, I had attributed my challenges to the simplistic nature of the little people and unknown forces that I believed I could overcome once I understood them. The Morlocks introduced a new and unsettling element, characterized by an inhuman and malevolent quality that instinctively evoked a strong sense of aversion. This highlights a significant shift in my perception, as I transitioned from feeling like a person who had fallen into a pit, focused on finding a way out, to feeling like a trapped animal, aware that a threatening entity would soon be upon me. Ultimately, my situation had become even more dire, with a heightened sense of vulnerability and urgency.
output: “Now, indeed, I seemed in a worse case than before. Hitherto, except during my night’s anguish at the loss of the Time Machine, I had felt a sustaining hope of ultimate escape, but that hope was staggered by these new discoveries. Hitherto I had merely thought myself impeded by the childish simplicity of the little people, and by some unknown forces which I had only to understand to overcome; but there was an altogether new element in the sickening quality of the Morlocks - a something inhuman and malign. Instinctively I loathed them. Before, I had felt as a man might feel who had fallen into a pit: my concern was with the pit and how to get out of it. Now I felt like a beast in a trap, whose enemy would come upon him soon.

input: I took Weena's hand. Subsequently, struck by a sudden idea, I released her grasp and turned towards a machine that featured a lever reminiscent of those found in a signal box. Ascending to the platform and firmly grasping this lever, I applied all of my weight to it sideways. At that moment, Weena, left alone in the central aisle, began to whimper. I had accurately assessed the strength of the lever, as it snapped after a minute of exertion, allowing me to rejoin her armed with a mace that I deemed more than sufficient for any Morlock skull I might encounter. It is worth noting that I felt a strong desire to confront and eliminate a Morlock or two. One might consider it inhumane to wish to harm one’s own descendants; however, it was extraordinarily difficult to sense any humanity within those creatures. Only my reluctance to abandon Weena and the belief that indulging my murderous impulses might jeopardize my Time Machine kept me from advancing down the gallery to confront the brutes I could hear.
output: “I took Weena’s hand. Then, struck with a sudden idea, I left her and turned to a machine from which projected a lever not unlike those in a signal-box. Clambering upon the stand, and grasping this lever in my hands, I put all my weight upon it sideways. Suddenly Weena, deserted in the central aisle, began to whimper. I had judged the strength of the lever pretty correctly, for it snapped after a minute’s strain, and I rejoined her with a mace in my hand more than sufficient, I judged, for any Morlock skull I might encounter. And I longed very much to kill a Morlock or so. Very inhuman, you may think, to want to go killing one’s own descendants! But it was impossible, somehow, to feel any humanity in the things. Only my disinclination to leave Weena, and a persuasion that if I began to slake my thirst for murder my Time Machine might suffer, restrained me from going straight down the gallery and killing the brutes I heard.

input: I had to climb down a shaft that was perhaps two hundred yards deep. The descent was made by means of metal bars projecting from the sides of the well. These bars were suited to a creature much smaller and lighter than myself, so I quickly became cramped and tired during the descent. I was not merely tired. One of the bars suddenly bent under my weight and nearly swung me off into the darkness below. For a moment I hung by one hand, and after that experience I did not dare to rest again. Although my arms and back soon became acutely painful, I continued climbing down the steep descent as quickly as possible. Looking upward, I saw the opening, a small blue disc in which a star was visible, while little Weena’s head appeared as a round black projection. The thudding sound of a machine below grew louder and more oppressive. Everything except that small disc above was profoundly dark, and when I looked up again Weena had disappeared.

output: “We emerged from the Palace while the sun was still in part above the horizon. I was determined to reach the White Sphinx early the next morning, and ere the dusk I purposed pushing through the woods that had stopped me on the previous journey. My plan was to go as far as possible that night, and then, building a fire, to sleep in the protection of its glare. Accordingly, as we went along I gathered any sticks or dried grass I saw, and presently had my arms full of such litter. Thus loaded, our progress was slower than I had anticipated, and besides Weena was tired. And I, also, began to suffer from sleepiness too; so that it was full night before we reached the wood. Upon the shrubby hill of its edge Weena would have stopped, fearing the darkness before us; but a singular sense of impending calamity, that should indeed have served me as a warning, drove me onward. I had been without sleep for a night and two days, and I was feverish and irritable. I felt sleep coming upon me, and the Morlocks with it.

input: Additionally, it is worth noting that, at that particular point in time, none of us fully accepted the validity of the Time Machine. In essence, the Time Traveller was a individual who possessed a level of intellectual sophistication that made him difficult to comprehend; one never felt that they had a complete understanding of his character, as there was always a suspicion of a subtle reserve or a hidden motive behind his apparent frankness. Consequently, those who took him seriously never felt entirely confident in their assessment of his behaviour, as they were aware that placing their trust in him was akin to entrusting delicate items to a vulnerable environment. Moreover, in the interval between that Thursday and the next, none of us engaged in extensive discussions about time travelling, although it is likely that the notion, with its inherent potentialities and paradoxes, remained a topic of consideration for many of us. In essence, the concept of time travelling, with its implausible yet intriguing possibilities, including the potential for anachronisms and confusion, was a subject that continued to occupy our thoughts. Additionally, I was particularly preoccupied with the mechanism of the model, and I recall discussing it with the Medical Man, whom I encountered on Friday at the Linnæan. He mentioned that he had seen a similar device at Tübingen and placed considerable emphasis on the extinguishing of the candle, although he was unable to provide a satisfactory explanation for the underlying principle of the trick.
output: I think that at that time none of us quite believed in the Time Machine. The fact is, the Time Traveller was one of those men who are too clever to be believed: you never felt that you saw all round him; you always suspected some subtle reserve, some ingenuity in ambush, behind his lucid frankness. Had Filby shown the model and explained the matter in the Time Traveller’s words, we should have shown him far less scepticism. For we should have perceived his motives: a pork-butcher could understand Filby. But the Time Traveller had more than a touch of whim among his elements, and we distrusted him. Things that would have made the fame of a less clever man seemed tricks in his hands. It is a mistake to do things too easily. The serious people who took him seriously never felt quite sure of his deportment; they were somehow aware that trusting their reputations for judgment with him was like furnishing a nursery with eggshell china. So I don’t think any of us said very much about time travelling in the interval between that Thursday and the next, though its odd potentialities ran, no doubt, in most of our minds: its plausibility, that is, its practical incredibleness, the curious possibilities of anachronism and of utter confusion it suggested. For my own part, I was particularly preoccupied with the trick of the model. That I remember discussing with the Medical Man, whom I met on Friday at the Linnæan. He said he had seen a similar thing at Tübingen, and laid considerable stress on the blowing-out of the candle. But how the trick was done he could not explain.

input: The narrative describes a journey through time, marked by a fascination with the fate of Earth. Over the course of thirty million years, the sun appears to grow larger and duller in the western sky, while life on Earth diminishes. Eventually, the sun obscures a significant portion of the night sky. The observer notes the absence of crabs and a lifeless scene on the beach, which is now marked by sparse green liverworts and lichens, along with patches of white. A cold atmosphere prevails, accompanied by occasional falling snowflakes. To the northeast, a blanket of snow reflects starlight, revealing pinkish-white hills. The edges of the sea are lined with ice, while the main body of the ocean remains unfrozen, bathed in a reddish hue beneath the perpetual sunset. This suggests a stark transformation in the environment, highlighting a shift toward desolation.
output: “So I travelled, stopping ever and again, in great strides of a thousand years or more, drawn on by the mystery of the earth’s fate, watching with a strange fascination the sun grow larger and duller in the westward sky, and the life of the old earth ebb away. At last, more than thirty million years hence, the huge red-hot dome of the sun had come to obscure nearly a tenth part of the darkling heavens. Then I stopped once more, for the crawling multitude of crabs had disappeared, and the red beach, save for its livid green liverworts and lichens, seemed lifeless. And now it was flecked with white. A bitter cold assailed me. Rare white flakes ever and again came eddying down. To the north-eastward, the glare of snow lay under the starlight of the sable sky, and I could see an undulating crest of hillocks pinkish white. There were fringes of ice along the sea margin, with drifting masses farther out; but the main expanse of that salt ocean, all bloody under the eternal sunset, was still unfrozen.

input: With changes in our circumstances, there tend to be adaptations that follow. It can be worth considering the factors that contribute to human intelligence and vitality, which may include challenges and the presence of freedom. These conditions often favor the survival of the strong, active, and perceptive, while those who are weaker may struggle. Such environments tend to encourage the collaboration of capable individuals, emphasizing qualities such as self-discipline, patience, and decisiveness. The family unit, along with the emotions it evokes—such as intense jealousy, strong affection for children, and parental devotion—may find their basis in the potential threats faced by the young. However, one might observe that these looming dangers are becoming less pronounced, leading to a growing sentiment against traditional notions of marital jealousy, intense maternal instincts, and various forms of passion. These feelings may increasingly be viewed as unnecessary and uncomfortable remnants of a more primitive existence, creating tensions in a more refined and harmonious way of life. In summary, societal shifts may influence how we perceive and respond to familial emotions and relationships.
output: “But with this change in condition comes inevitably adaptations to the change. What, unless biological science is a mass of errors, is the cause of human intelligence and vigour? Hardship and freedom: conditions under which the active, strong, and subtle survive and the weaker go to the wall; conditions that put a premium upon the loyal alliance of capable men, upon self-restraint, patience, and decision. And the institution of the family, and the emotions that arise therein, the fierce jealousy, the tenderness for offspring, parental self-devotion, all found their justification and support in the imminent dangers of the young. Now, where are these imminent dangers? There is a sentiment arising, and it will grow, against connubial jealousy, against fierce maternity, against passion of all sorts; unnecessary things now, and things that make us uncomfortable, savage survivals, discords in a refined and pleasant life.

input: I returned after a period during which I might have been unaware while on the machine. The cycle of days and nights resumed, the sun appeared golden once more, and the sky was blue. I felt I could breathe more easily. The changing shapes of the land seemed to rise and fall. The hands on the dials appeared to move backward. Eventually, I recognized the faint outlines of houses, signs of human life in decline. These, too, transformed and were replaced by others. When the million dial reached zero, I gradually reduced my speed. I started to identify our familiar and charming architecture as the thousands hand reversed to its starting point, and the rhythm of night and day slowed down. Soon, I found myself surrounded by the old walls of the laboratory. With care, I began to slow the mechanism further. This experience suggests a return to familiarity and the gradual re-emergence of the known environment.
output: “So I came back. For a long time I must have been insensible upon the machine. The blinking succession of the days and nights was resumed, the sun got golden again, the sky blue. I breathed with greater freedom. The fluctuating contours of the land ebbed and flowed. The hands spun backward upon the dials. At last I saw again the dim shadows of houses, the evidences of decadent humanity. These, too, changed and passed, and others came. Presently, when the million dial was at zero, I slackened speed. I began to recognise our own pretty and familiar architecture, the thousands hand ran back to the starting-point, the night and day flapped slower and slower. Then the old walls of the laboratory came round me. Very gently, now, I slowed the mechanism down.

I proceeded out of the gallery and into another, which was even larger. At first glance, this new space resembled a military chapel adorned with tattered flags. However, upon closer inspection, I realized that the brown and charred rags hanging from the sides were actually the remnants of books. These books had deteriorated to the point where they had fallen apart, and all traces of print had disappeared. Nevertheless, the presence of warped boards and cracked metallic clasps still told a story. 

Meanwhile, the scene before me was a testament to the enormous amount of wasted labor. The sheer scale of the decay and rot was striking. As I took in the sight, I couldn't help but think of my own work, particularly the Philosophical Transactions and my seventeen papers on physical optics. Additionally, the thought of such a vast amount of knowledge and effort being reduced to nothing more than rotting paper was a sobering one. Furthermore, the experience had a profound impact on my perspective, and it led me to consider the broader implications of such a sombre wilderness of decay.
output: “Well, mace in one hand and Weena in the other, I went out of that gallery and into another and still larger one, which at the first glance reminded me of a military chapel hung with tattered flags. The brown and charred rags that hung from the sides of it, I presently recognised as the decaying vestiges of books. They had long since dropped to pieces, and every semblance of print had left them. But here and there were warped boards and cracked metallic clasps that told the tale well enough. Had I been a literary man I might, perhaps, have moralised upon the futility of all ambition. But as it was, the thing that struck me with keenest force was the enormous waste of labour to which this sombre wilderness of rotting paper testified. At the time I will confess that I thought chiefly of the Philosophical Transactions and my own seventeen papers upon physical optics.

output: “The calm of evening was upon the world as I emerged from the great hall, and the scene was lit by the warm glow of the setting sun. At first things were very confusing. “I must admit,” the Editor remarked with a touch of humor, “these gentlemen here suggest you’ve been traveling into the middle of next week! Could you share your experiences with little Rosebery? I’m curious about what you might offer for it all.” 

The Time Traveller made his way to the designated spot without uttering a word. He smiled in his usual manner. “Where’s my mutton?” he inquired. “It’s quite a pleasure to have meat again!” 

“I would be willing to pay a shilling a line for a detailed account,” the Editor commented. The Time Traveller then nudged his glass toward the Silent Man and tapped it lightly with his fingernail, causing the Silent Man, who had been observing him intently, to jump and pour him some wine. The remainder of the dinner felt somewhat tense. Personally, I found myself grappling with many questions, and I suspect others did as well. The Journalist attempted to ease the atmosphere by sharing stories about Hettie Potter. Meanwhile, the Time Traveller focused on his meal, showing an appetite reminiscent of someone quite famished. The Medical Man leisurely smoked a cigarette, glancing at the Time Traveller from beneath his lashes. The Silent Man appeared somewhat awkward and eagerly drank champagne, perhaps to calm his nerves. Eventually, the Time Traveller set his plate aside and looked around at us. “I suppose I should apologize,” he said. “I was quite hungry. I’ve had an extraordinary experience.” He reached for a cigar and clipped the end. “However, let’s move to the smoking-room. It’s too lengthy a tale for this setting.” With that, he signaled for the bell and walked toward the adjoining room.
output:
“I say,” said the Editor hilariously, “these chaps here say you have been travelling into the middle of next week! Tell us all about little Rosebery, will you? What will you take for the lot?”

The Time Traveller came to the place reserved for him without a word. He smiled quietly, in his old way. “Where’s my mutton?” he said. “What a treat it is to stick a fork into meat again!”

“I’d give a shilling a line for a verbatim note,” said the Editor. The Time Traveller pushed his glass towards the Silent Man and rang it with his fingernail; at which the Silent Man, who had been staring at his face, started convulsively, and poured him wine. The rest of the dinner was uncomfortable. For my own part, sudden questions kept on rising to my lips, and I dare say it was the same with the others. The Journalist tried to relieve the tension by telling anecdotes of Hettie Potter. The Time Traveller devoted his attention to his dinner, and displayed the appetite of a tramp. The Medical Man smoked a cigarette, and watched the Time Traveller through his eyelashes. The Silent Man seemed even more clumsy than usual, and drank champagne with regularity and determination out of sheer nervousness. At last the Time Traveller pushed his plate away, and looked round us. “I suppose I must apologise,” he said. “I was simply starving. I’ve had a most amazing time.” He reached out his hand for a cigar, and cut the end. “But come into the smoking-room. It’s too long a story to tell over greasy plates.” And ringing the bell in passing, he led the way into the adjoining room.

input: Upon closer examination of their features, I observed additional peculiarities in their delicate appearance reminiscent of Dresden china. Their uniformly curly hair ended sharply at the neck and cheeks, with no trace of it on their faces. Their ears were notably small. The mouths were petite, adorned with bright red, thin lips, and their small chins tapered to a point. Their eyes were large and gentle; however, I could not help but feel that there was a certain absence of the interest I might have anticipated from them.
output: “And then, looking more nearly into their features, I saw some further peculiarities in their Dresden china type of prettiness. Their hair, which was uniformly curly, came to a sharp end at the neck and cheek; there was not the faintest suggestion of it on the face, and their ears were singularly minute. The mouths were small, with bright red, rather thin lips, and the little chins ran to a point. The eyes were large and mild; and - this may seem egotism on my part - I fancied even that there was a certain lack of the interest I might have expected in them.
