input: The distinction between act and object in our understanding of things can be considered crucial, as it may have a significant impact on our ability to acquire knowledge. A key characteristic of the mind is its capacity to be aware of things beyond itself. This awareness tends to involve a relationship between the mind and something external to it, which can be seen as the basis of the mind's ability to know things. If we suggest that the things we know must be within the mind, we may be either unnecessarily limiting the mind's capacity for knowledge or simply stating the obvious. We may be stating the obvious if by "within the mind" we mean the same as "being considered by the mind," i.e., simply being perceived by the mind. However, if this is the case, we would need to acknowledge that what is, in this sense, within the mind, may not necessarily be a mental entity. Upon closer examination of the nature of knowledge, it appears that Berkeley's argument may be flawed in both its substance and form, and his reasons for believing that "ideas" - or the objects of perception - must be mental, seem to lack validity. As a result, his arguments in support of idealism can often be dismissed. It remains to be seen whether there are any other valid grounds for this philosophical position, and a thorough review of the topic may help to provide a clearer understanding of the issue.
output: This question of the distinction between act and object in our apprehending of things is vitally important, since our whole power of acquiring knowledge is bound up with it. The faculty of being acquainted with things other than itself is the main characteristic of a mind. Acquaintance with objects essentially consists in a relation between the mind and something other than the mind; it is this that constitutes the mind's power of knowing things. If we say that the things known must be in the mind, we are either unduly limiting the mind's power of knowing, or we are uttering a mere tautology. We are uttering a mere tautology if we mean by 'in the mind' the same as by 'before the mind', i.e. if we mean merely being apprehended by the mind. But if we mean this, we shall have to admit that what, in this sense, is in the mind, may nevertheless be not mental. Thus when we realize the nature of knowledge, Berkeley's argument is seen to be wrong in substance as well as in form, and his grounds for supposing that 'ideas' - i.e. the objects apprehended - must be mental, are found to have no validity whatever. Hence his grounds in favour of idealism may be dismissed. It remains to see whether there are any other grounds.
title: The Problems of Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell

input:
The term 'physical object' may be used to refer to what we consider the real table, if it exists. This leads us to examine the relationship between sense-data and physical objects. The entirety of physical objects can be referred to as 'matter'. Therefore, we might reformulate our two primary questions as follows: (1) Is matter something that exists? (2) If it does exist, what might its characteristics be?

Bishop Berkeley, who lived from 1685 to 1753, was one of the first philosophers to prominently argue that the immediate objects of our senses may not exist independently of us. In his work, Three Dialogues between Hylas and Philonous, he aims to demonstrate that matter does not exist at all, suggesting instead that the world consists solely of minds and their ideas. Hylas, who previously believed in matter, struggles to counter Philonous's arguments, which often reveal contradictions and paradoxes in Hylas's position, ultimately making the denial of matter appear almost reasonable. The arguments presented vary in their strength; some are quite significant and logically sound, while others may seem confused or overly debatable. Nevertheless, Berkeley's contribution is significant in that he illustrates that denying the existence of matter can be done without falling into absurdity, and that if there are entities existing independently of us, they cannot be the immediate objects of our sensory experiences.
output:
The real table, if it exists, we will call a 'physical object'. Thus we have to consider the relation of sense-data to physical objects. The collection of all physical objects is called 'matter'. Thus our two questions may be re-stated as follows: (1) Is there any such thing as matter? (2) If so, what is its nature?

The philosopher who first brought prominently forward the reasons for regarding the immediate objects of our senses as not existing independently of us was Bishop Berkeley (1685-1753). His Three Dialogues between Hylas and Philonous, in Opposition to Sceptics and Atheists, undertake to prove that there is no such thing as matter at all, and that the world consists of nothing but minds and their ideas. Hylas has hitherto believed in matter, but he is no match for Philonous, who mercilessly drives him into contradictions and paradoxes, and makes his own denial of matter seem, in the end, as if it were almost common sense. The arguments employed are of very different value: some are important and sound, others are confused or quibbling. But Berkeley retains the merit of having shown that the existence of matter is capable of being denied without absurdity, and that if there are any things that exist independently of us they cannot be the immediate objects of our sensations.
title: The Problems of Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell

input: One way to rephrase our theory is to consider a belief like "Othello believes that Desdemona loves Cassio." In this context, we can refer to Desdemona and Cassio as the object-terms, while the act of loving serves as the object-relation. If we identify a complex unity, such as "Desdemona's love for Cassio," which consists of the object-terms connected by the object-relation in the same sequence as they appear in the belief, we can refer to this complex unity as the fact that corresponds to the belief. Therefore, a belief may be considered true if there exists a corresponding fact, while it tends to be false in the absence of such a fact. In summary, the truth of a belief is often linked to the existence of a corresponding fact.
output: We may restate our theory as follows: If we take such a belief as 'Othello believes that Desdemona loves Cassio', we will call Desdemona and Cassio the object-terms, and loving the object-relation. If there is a complex unity 'Desdemona's love for Cassio', consisting of the object-terms related by the object-relation in the same order as they have in the belief, then this complex unity is called the fact corresponding to the belief. Thus a belief is true when there is a corresponding fact, and is false when there is no corresponding fact.
title: The Problems of Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell

input: This perspective presents significant challenges, specifically two major difficulties. The first challenge is the assumption that only one coherent set of beliefs can exist. A novelist, with enough creativity, could construct an alternate history that aligns perfectly with our existing knowledge yet diverges entirely from what actually occurred. Similarly, in scientific fields, it is common to encounter multiple hypotheses that explain all known facts about a particular topic. While scientists strive to gather evidence that eliminates all but one hypothesis, there is no guarantee that they will always achieve this goal.
output: There is, however, a great difficulty in this view, or rather two great difficulties. The first is that there is no reason to suppose that only one coherent body of beliefs is possible. It may be that, with sufficient imagination, a novelist might invent a past for the world that would perfectly fit on to what we know, and yet be quite different from the real past. In more scientific matters, it is certain that there are often two or more hypotheses which account for all the known facts on some subject, and although, in such cases, men of science endeavour to find facts which will rule out all the hypotheses except one, there is no reason why they should always succeed.
title: The Problems of Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell

input: It may be observed that there are different levels of familiarity when it comes to understanding individuals. For example, there is the relationship of people who knew Bismarck personally; then there is the perspective of those who are familiar with him solely through historical accounts. Next, there is the enigmatic figure often referred to as the man with the iron mask, followed by the idea of the longest-lived individual. These categories tend to represent progressively greater distances from direct knowledge. The first group may have the closest connection to true acquaintance, while the second group can usually claim to understand 'who Bismarck was.' In the third category, while we may not know the identity of the man in the iron mask, we can still hold various pieces of information about him that are not directly derived from the fact of his wearing an iron mask. Lastly, in the fourth category, our understanding is limited to what can be logically inferred from the definition of the individual. A similar hierarchy may be found in the realm of general concepts. Just as many specific instances are often understood through descriptions, knowledge about these descriptions can ultimately be traced back to a more direct familiarity with the items they describe.
output: It will be seen that there are various stages in the removal from acquaintance with particulars: there is Bismarck to people who knew him; Bismarck to those who only know of him through history; the man with the iron mask; the longest-lived of men. These are progressively further removed from acquaintance with particulars; the first comes as near to acquaintance as is possible in regard to another person; in the second, we shall still be said to know 'who Bismarck was'; in the third, we do not know who was the man with the iron mask, though we can know many propositions about him which are not logically deducible from the fact that he wore an iron mask; in the fourth, finally, we know nothing beyond what is logically deducible from the definition of the man. There is a similar hierarchy in the region of universals. Many universals, like many particulars, are only known to us by description. But here, as in the case of particulars, knowledge concerning what is known by description is ultimately reducible to knowledge concerning what is known by acquaintance.
title: The Problems of Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell

input: In addition to general principles, there is another category of self-evident truths that are directly derived from sensation. These truths can be referred to as truths of perception, and the judgements that express them can be called judgements of perception. However, it is necessary to exercise caution when attempting to determine the exact nature of these self-evident truths. The actual sense-data aren't true or false by nature. For instance, a specific patch of colour that is seen simply exists, and it does not possess the characteristics of being true or false. Nevertheless, it is true that this patch exists, it is true that it has a particular shape and degree of brightness, and it is true that it is surrounded by other colours. Meanwhile, the patch itself, like all other elements in the world of sense, is fundamentally different from the things that can be classified as true or false, and therefore it cannot be accurately described as true. Consequently, any self-evident truths that are obtained from our senses must be distinct from the sense-data from which they are derived.
output: In addition to general principles, the other kind of self-evident truths are those immediately derived from sensation. We will call such truths 'truths of perception', and the judgements expressing them we will call 'judgements of perception'. But here a certain amount of care is required in getting at the precise nature of the truths that are self-evident. The actual sense-data are neither true nor false. A particular patch of colour which I see, for example, simply exists: it is not the sort of thing that is true or false. It is true that there is such a patch, true that it has a certain shape and degree of brightness, true that it is surrounded by certain other colours. But the patch itself, like everything else in the world of sense, is of a radically different kind from the things that are true or false, and therefore cannot properly be said to be true. Thus whatever self-evident truths may be obtained from our senses must be different from the sense-data from which they are obtained.
title: The Problems of Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell

input: It is clear that the philosophers concur on one key point, which is that a real table exists, regardless of its specific characteristics. This shared perspective is highly significant, and it is necessary to examine the underlying reasons for accepting this viewpoint before proceeding to the subsequent question of the table's nature. Additionally, the rationale for assuming the existence of a real table will be explored in the following chapter, providing a foundation for further discussion. Furthermore, this examination will enable a more comprehensive understanding of the topic at hand.
output: Now obviously this point in which the philosophers are agreed - the view that there is a real table, whatever its nature may be - is vitally important, and it will be worth while to consider what reasons there are for accepting this view before we go on to the further question as to the nature of the real table. Our next chapter, therefore, will be concerned with the reasons for supposing that there is a real table at all.
title: The Problems of Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell

input: This view certainly contains something sublime, something we might wish to accept. However, when the arguments supporting it are carefully examined, they seem to involve considerable confusion and many unjustified assumptions. The fundamental principle on which the system rests is that whatever is incomplete cannot be self-subsistent but must depend on other things in order to exist. It is maintained that anything which has relations to things outside itself must include some reference to those external things within its own nature, and therefore could not be what it is if those external things did not exist. A man's nature, for example, is made up of his memories and the rest of his knowledge, his loves and hatreds, and so on; thus, without the objects he knows or loves or hates, he could not be what he is. He is essentially and obviously a fragment: regarded as the sum-total of reality, he would be self-contradictory.
output: In this conception, there is undeniably something sublime, something to which we could wish to yield assent. Nevertheless, when the arguments in support of it are carefully examined, they appear to involve much confusion and many unwarrantable assumptions. The fundamental tenet upon which the system is built up is that what is incomplete must be not self-subsistent, but must need the support of other things before it can exist. It is held that whatever has relations to things outside itself must contain some reference to those outside things in its own nature, and could not, therefore, be what it is if those outside things did not exist. A man's nature, for example, is constituted by his memories and the rest of his knowledge, by his loves and hatreds, and so on; thus, but for the objects which he knows or loves or hates, he could not be what he is. He is essentially and obviously a fragment: taken as the sum-total of reality he would be self-contradictory.
title: The Problems of Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell

input: Is there any knowledge in the world that is so certain that no reasonable person could doubt it? At first glance, this question may not appear difficult, but in reality it is one of the most difficult questions that can be asked. Once we recognize the obstacles that stand in the way of a straightforward and confident answer, we will be well prepared to begin the study of philosophy. Philosophy is simply the attempt to answer such ultimate questions, not carelessly and dogmatically, as we do in ordinary life and even in the sciences, but critically, after exploring everything that makes these questions puzzling and after recognizing all the vagueness and confusion that underlie our ordinary ideas.
output: Is there any knowledge in the world which is so certain that no reasonable man could doubt it? This question, which at first sight might not seem difficult, is really one of the most difficult that can be asked. When we have realized the obstacles in the way of a straightforward and confident answer, we shall be well launched on the study of philosophy - for philosophy is merely the attempt to answer such ultimate questions, not carelessly and dogmatically, as we do in ordinary life and even in the sciences, but critically, after exploring all that makes such questions puzzling, and after realizing all the vagueness and confusion that underlie our ordinary ideas.
title: The Problems of Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell

input: Consider a proposition such as "Edinburgh is north of London." In this instance, we observe a relationship between two locations, and it is evident that this relationship exists independently of our awareness of it. When we recognize that Edinburgh is north of London, we acquire knowledge that pertains solely to Edinburgh and London; we do not generate the truth of the proposition through our understanding. On the contrary, we merely discern a fact that existed prior to our awareness. The geographical location of Edinburgh would remain north of that of London, even in the absence of any human to comprehend the concepts of north and south, and even if no minds existed in the universe at all. This assertion, however, is contested by numerous philosophers, either for reasons similar to those of Berkeley or Kant. Nonetheless, we have previously examined these arguments and concluded that they are insufficient. Thus, we may proceed under the assumption that the fact of Edinburgh being north of London does not presuppose any mental involvement. Nevertheless, this fact encompasses the relation "north of," which is a universal concept. It would be contradictory for the entirety of this fact to lack any mental implications if the relation "north of," which is an integral component of the fact, inherently involved mental aspects. Therefore, we must concede that the relation, akin to the terms it connects, is not contingent upon thought but rather belongs to an objective reality that thought can perceive but does not create.
output: Consider such a proposition as 'Edinburgh is north of London'. Here we have a relation between two places, and it seems plain that the relation subsists independently of our knowledge of it. When we come to know that Edinburgh is north of London, we come to know something which has to do only with Edinburgh and London: we do not cause the truth of the proposition by coming to know it, on the contrary we merely apprehend a fact which was there before we knew it. The part of the earth's surface where Edinburgh stands would be north of the part where London stands, even if there were no human being to know about north and south, and even if there were no minds at all in the universe. This is, of course, denied by many philosophers, either for Berkeley's reasons or for Kant's. But we have already considered these reasons, and decided that they are inadequate. We may therefore now assume it to be true that nothing mental is presupposed in the fact that Edinburgh is north of London. But this fact involves the relation 'north of', which is a universal; and it would be impossible for the whole fact to involve nothing mental if the relation 'north of', which is a constituent part of the fact, did involve anything mental. Hence we must admit that the relation, like the terms it relates, is not dependent upon thought, but belongs to the independent world which thought apprehends but does not create.
title: The Problems of Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell

input:
When considering a complex fact, there are two theoretical methods by which it can be understood. Firstly, a complex fact can be known through a judgement, in which its various components are assessed as being related in a specific manner. Additionally, a complex fact can be known through direct acquaintance with the fact itself, which can be broadly referred to as perception, although it is not limited to sensory objects. 

Meanwhile, it is notable that the second method of knowing a complex fact, namely acquaintance, is only feasible when the fact actually exists. In contrast, the first method, which involves judgement, is susceptible to error, as with all forms of judgement. The second method provides a comprehensive understanding of the complex whole, and therefore, it is only possible when the components actually have the relationship that enables them to form a complex. Furthermore, the first method presents the components and the relationship separately, requiring only the existence of the components and the relationship, without necessitating that the relationship actually connects the components in that specific manner.
output: Thus in regard to any complex fact, there are, theoretically, two ways in which it may be known: (1) by means of a judgement, in which its several parts are judged to be related as they are in fact related; (2) by means of acquaintance with the complex fact itself, which may (in a large sense) be called perception, though it is by no means confined to objects of the senses. Now it will be observed that the second way of knowing a complex fact, the way of acquaintance, is only possible when there really is such a fact, while the first way, like all judgement, is liable to error. The second way gives us the complex whole, and is therefore only possible when its parts do actually have that relation which makes them combine to form such a complex. The first way, on the contrary, gives us the parts and the relation severally, and demands only the reality of the parts and the relation: the relation may not relate those parts in that way, and yet the judgement may occur.
title: The Problems of Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell

input: It's possible that one might initially think that knowledge could be defined as having a belief that happens to be true. When our beliefs align with the facts, it may seem that we have gained knowledge about a particular topic. However, this definition may not entirely align with how the term is typically used. For example, consider a person who believes that a former Prime Minister's last name started with the letter B - in this case, their belief would be true, as Sir Henry Campbell Bannerman was indeed a former Prime Minister. Nevertheless, if this person also believed that Mr. Balfour was the former Prime Minister, their belief about the last name starting with B would still be true, but it's unlikely that we would consider this to constitute knowledge. Similarly, a newspaper may predict the outcome of a battle before official confirmation is received, and by chance, their prediction may turn out to be correct, potentially leading some readers to believe it. Although their belief may be true, it's unlikely that we would say they have knowledge, given that their belief is based on speculation rather than verified information. In general, having a true belief does not necessarily mean someone has knowledge, especially if that belief is based on incorrect assumptions. In summary, it appears that having a true belief is not sufficient to qualify as knowledge, particularly when that belief is derived from false or unverified information.
output: At first sight we might imagine that knowledge could be defined as 'true belief'. When what we believe is true, it might be supposed that we had achieved a knowledge of what we believe. But this would not accord with the way in which the word is commonly used. To take a very trivial instance: If a man believes that the late Prime Minister's last name began with a B, he believes what is true, since the late Prime Minister was Sir Henry Campbell Bannerman. But if he believes that Mr. Balfour was the late Prime Minister, he will still believe that the late Prime Minister's last name began with a B, yet this belief, though true, would not be thought to constitute knowledge. If a newspaper, by an intelligent anticipation, announces the result of a battle before any telegram giving the result has been received, it may by good fortune announce what afterwards turns out to be the right result, and it may produce belief in some of its less experienced readers. But in spite of the truth of their belief, they cannot be said to have knowledge. Thus it is clear that a true belief is not knowledge when it is deduced from a false belief.
title: The Problems of Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell

input: The possibility of knowing general propositions without having specific instances to refer to is often overlooked. This highlights that such knowledge relies on understanding the relationships between universals rather than needing direct experience of instances. Knowledge of these general propositions is crucial for much of what is commonly accepted as known. For instance, earlier discussions indicated that understanding physical objects, as distinct from sensory data, is achieved through inference rather than direct acquaintance. Consequently, it is not possible to state any proposition like "this is a physical object" based solely on immediate knowledge. This leads to the conclusion that our understanding of physical objects is based on general knowledge that does not depend on specific instances. While we can provide examples of related sensory experiences, we cannot offer instances of actual physical objects. Therefore, our comprehension of physical objects fundamentally relies on the potential for general knowledge without concrete examples. This principle similarly applies to our understanding of other people's minds or any other category of entities that we do not know through direct experience.
output: This possibility, of knowledge of general propositions of which no instance can be given, is often denied, because it is not perceived that the knowledge of such propositions only requires a knowledge of the relations of universals, and does not require any knowledge of instances of the universals in question. Yet the knowledge of such general propositions is quite vital to a great deal of what is generally admitted to be known. For example, we saw, in our early chapters, that knowledge of physical objects, as opposed to sense-data, is only obtained by an inference, and that they are not things with which we are acquainted. Hence we can never know any proposition of the form 'this is a physical object', where 'this' is something immediately known. It follows that all our knowledge concerning physical objects is such that no actual instance can be given. We can give instances of the associated sense-data, but we cannot give instances of the actual physical objects. Hence our knowledge as to physical objects depends throughout upon this possibility of general knowledge where no instance can be given. And the same applies to our knowledge of other people's minds, or of any other class of things of which no instance is known to us by acquaintance.
title: The Problems of Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell

input: We may find it convenient to speak of things as existing only when they are in time—that is, when we can point to some time at which they exist, though this does not rule out the possibility that they exist at all times. In this sense, thoughts and feelings, minds, and physical objects can be said to exist. Universals, however, do not exist in this sense; we may say instead that they subsist or have being, where "being" is understood as timeless, in contrast to "existence." The world of universals, then, can also be described as the world of being. The world of being tends to be unchangeable, rigid, and exact, and it is often delightful to the mathematician, the logician, the builder of metaphysical systems, and all who love perfection more than life. The world of existence, by contrast, tends to be fleeting and vague, without sharp boundaries or any clear plan or arrangement, yet it contains all thoughts and feelings, all the data of sense, and all physical objects—everything that can do either good or harm, and everything that makes any difference to the value of life and the world. Depending on our temperaments, we may prefer to contemplate one world or the other. The one we do not prefer will probably seem to us a pale shadow of the one we do prefer, and hardly worthy of being regarded as real in any sense. But in truth, both have an equal claim on our impartial attention; both are real, and both are important to the metaphysician. Indeed, as soon as we have distinguished the two worlds, it becomes necessary to consider how they are related.
output: We shall find it convenient only to speak of things existing when they are in time, that is to say, when we can point to some time at which they exist (not excluding the possibility of their existing at all times). Thus thoughts and feelings, minds and physical objects exist. But universals do not exist in this sense; we shall say that they subsist or have being, where 'being' is opposed to 'existence' as being timeless. The world of universals, therefore, may also be described as the world of being. The world of being is unchangeable, rigid, exact, delightful to the mathematician, the logician, the builder of metaphysical systems, and all who love perfection more than life. The world of existence is fleeting, vague, without sharp boundaries, without any clear plan or arrangement, but it contains all thoughts and feelings, all the data of sense, and all physical objects, everything that can do either good or harm, everything that makes any difference to the value of life and the world. According to our temperaments, we shall prefer the contemplation of the one or of the other. The one we do not prefer will probably seem to us a pale shadow of the one we prefer, and hardly worthy to be regarded as in any sense real. But the truth is that both have the same claim on our impartial attention, both are real, and both are important to the metaphysician. Indeed no sooner have we distinguished the two worlds than it becomes necessary to consider their relations.
title: The Problems of Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell

input: Individuals who are not familiar with philosophical speculation might find this doctrine to be obviously unreasonable. Common sense typically perceives tables, chairs, the sun, the moon, and material objects as fundamentally distinct from minds and their contents, suggesting that these material objects could exist independently of consciousness. It is common to believe that matter existed long before the emergence of any minds, making it challenging to consider matter solely as a consequence of mental processes. However, regardless of its validity, idealism should not simply be dismissed as absurd.
output: Those who are unaccustomed to philosophical speculation may be inclined to dismiss such a doctrine as obviously absurd. There is no doubt that common sense regards tables and chairs and the sun and moon and material objects generally as something radically different from minds and the contents of minds, and as having an existence which might continue if minds ceased. We think of matter as having existed long before there were any minds, and it is hard to think of it as a mere product of mental activity. But whether true or false, idealism is not to be dismissed as obviously absurd.
title: The Problems of Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell

input: Common words, including proper names, are generally descriptive in nature. That is to say, the thought present in the mind of an individual who employs a proper name correctly can typically be expressed explicitly only if the proper name is replaced by a description. Furthermore, the description required to express the thought will differ among various individuals, or for the same individual at different times. The only element that remains constant, provided that the name is used correctly, is the object to which the name refers. Moreover, as long as this element remains constant, the particular description involved generally has no bearing on the truth or falsity of the proposition in which the name occurs.
output: Common words, even proper names, are usually really descriptions. That is to say, the thought in the mind of a person using a proper name correctly can generally only be expressed explicitly if we replace the proper name by a description. Moreover, the description required to express the thought will vary for different people, or for the same person at different times. The only thing constant (so long as the name is rightly used) is the object to which the name applies. But so long as this remains constant, the particular description involved usually makes no difference to the truth or falsehood of the proposition in which the name appears.
title: The Problems of Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell

input:
In the subsequent pages, I have primarily focused on those philosophical problems for which I believed it feasible to provide positive and constructive insights, as merely negative criticism appeared to be inappropriate. For this reason, the theory of knowledge occupies a more significant portion of this volume than metaphysics, and certain topics, frequently discussed by philosophers, are addressed only briefly or not at all.

Additionally, I have gained valuable insights from unpublished writings of G. E. Moore and J. M. Keynes; from Moore, I have explored the relationships between sense-data and physical objects, while from Keynes, I have examined the concepts of probability and induction. Furthermore, I have greatly benefited from the critiques and suggestions offered by Professor Gilbert Murray.
output:
In the following pages I have confined myself in the main to those problems of philosophy in regard to which I thought it possible to say something positive and constructive, since merely negative criticism seemed out of place. For this reason, theory of knowledge occupies a larger space than metaphysics in the present volume, and some topics much discussed by philosophers are treated very briefly, if at all.

I have derived valuable assistance from unpublished writings of G. E. Moore and J. M. Keynes: from the former, as regards the relations of sense-data to physical objects, and from the latter as regards probability and induction. I have also profited greatly by the criticisms and suggestions of Professor Gilbert Murray.
title: The Problems of Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell

input: This phenomenon, recognized by those who are not blind, is not considered by science to exist in the external world. It is a result of the interaction between specific waves and the eyes, nerves, and brain of the observer. When scientists describe light as waves, they refer to these waves as the physical basis for our experiences of light. However, light itself, which is perceived by sighted individuals and not by those who are blind, is believed by science not to constitute a part of the world that exists independently of our sensory perception. Similar observations can be made regarding other types of sensory experiences.
output: Now this something, which all of us who are not blind know, is not, according to science, really to be found in the outer world: it is something caused by the action of certain waves upon the eyes and nerves and brain of the person who sees the light. When it is said that light is waves, what is really meant is that waves are the physical cause of our sensations of light. But light itself, the thing which seeing people experience and blind people do not, is not supposed by science to form any part of the world that is independent of us and our senses. And very similar remarks would apply to other kinds of sensations.
title: The Problems of Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell

input: The mind that has become accustomed to the freedom and impartiality of philosophic contemplation will preserve something of the same freedom and impartiality in the realm of action and emotion. Additionally, it will regard its purposes and desires as parts of a whole, without the insistence that arises from viewing them as insignificant fragments in a world in which all else remains unaffected by any individual's deeds. Furthermore, the impartiality that in contemplation is the pure desire for truth is the very same quality of mind that in action is justice and in emotion is that universal love which can be extended to all, and not merely to those considered useful or admirable. Moreover, contemplation enlarges not only the objects of our thoughts but also the objects of our actions and our affections: it renders us citizens of the universe, and not merely of one walled city at war with all the rest. In essence, man's true freedom, and his liberation from the bondage of narrow hopes and fears, consists in this citizenship of the universe.
output: The mind which has become accustomed to the freedom and impartiality of philosophic contemplation will preserve something of the same freedom and impartiality in the world of action and emotion. It will view its purposes and desires as parts of the whole, with the absence of insistence that results from seeing them as infinitesimal fragments in a world of which all the rest is unaffected by any one man's deeds. The impartiality which, in contemplation, is the unalloyed desire for truth, is the very same quality of mind which, in action, is justice, and in emotion is that universal love which can be given to all, and not only to those who are judged useful or admirable. Thus contemplation enlarges not only the objects of our thoughts, but also the objects of our actions and our affections: it makes us citizens of the universe, not only of one walled city at war with all the rest. In this citizenship of the universe consists man's true freedom, and his liberation from the thraldom of narrow hopes and fears.
title: The Problems of Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell

input: Additionally, the criticism in question is not characterized by an unwarranted rejection, but rather by a consideration of each piece of apparent knowledge on its individual merits, resulting in the retention of that which still appears to be knowledge following a thorough examination. Furthermore, it is worth noting that some degree of risk of error inevitably remains, owing to the inherent fallibility of human beings. Moreover, philosophy can rightfully claim that it serves to diminish the risk of error, and in certain instances, it renders this risk so minimal as to be virtually insignificant. In essence, it is not possible to completely eliminate the risk of error in a world where mistakes are inevitable, and it is unlikely that any prudent advocate of philosophy would make such a claim.
output: The criticism aimed at, in a word, is not that which, without reason, determines to reject, but that which considers each piece of apparent knowledge on its merits, and retains whatever still appears to be knowledge when this consideration is completed. That some risk of error remains must be admitted, since human beings are fallible. Philosophy may claim justly that it diminishes the risk of error, and that in some cases it renders the risk so small as to be practically negligible. To do more than this is not possible in a world where mistakes must occur; and more than this no prudent advocate of philosophy would claim to have performed.
title: The Problems of Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell

input: A review of the sources of knowledge reveals important distinctions. First, it is necessary to differentiate between knowledge of things and knowledge of truths. Each type can be classified into two forms: immediate and derivative. Immediate knowledge of things, referred to as acquaintance, can be divided based on whether the objects known are particulars or universals. With particulars, acquaintance includes sense-data and possibly self-awareness. In the case of universals, there is no clear principle to determine which can be known through acquaintance. However, it is evident that those which can be known in this way include sensible qualities, spatial and temporal relations, similarities, and certain abstract logical concepts. Derivative knowledge of things, termed knowledge by description, entails both acquaintance with an entity and an understanding of truths. Immediate knowledge of truths is characterized as intuitive knowledge, where the truths known are referred to as self-evident truths. This category includes statements that reflect sensory experiences, certain abstract logical and arithmetical principles, and, to a lesser extent, some ethical propositions. Derivative knowledge of truths encompasses all that can be inferred from self-evident truths using self-evident deductive principles.
output: We may now take a survey of the sources of our knowledge, as they have appeared in the course of our analysis. We have first to distinguish knowledge of things and knowledge of truths. In each there are two kinds, one immediate and one derivative. Our immediate knowledge of things, which we called acquaintance, consists of two sorts, according as the things known are particulars or universals. Among particulars, we have acquaintance with sense-data and (probably) with ourselves. Among universals, there seems to be no principle by which we can decide which can be known by acquaintance, but it is clear that among those that can be so known are sensible qualities, relations of space and time, similarity, and certain abstract logical universals. Our derivative knowledge of things, which we call knowledge by description, always involves both acquaintance with something and knowledge of truths. Our immediate knowledge of truths may be called intuitive knowledge, and the truths so known may be called self-evident truths. Among such truths are included those which merely state what is given in sense, and also certain abstract logical and arithmetical principles, and (though with less certainty) some ethical propositions. Our derivative knowledge of truths consists of everything that we can deduce from self-evident truths by the use of self-evident principles of deduction.
title: The Problems of Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell

input: In essence, despite the misleading nature of such expectations, they nonetheless persist. The simple occurrence of an event a certain number of times leads both animals and humans to anticipate its recurrence. Thus, our instincts undoubtedly lead us to believe that the sun will rise tomorrow; however, we may find ourselves no better off than the chicken that unexpectedly has its neck wrung. Therefore, it is essential to differentiate between the observation that past uniformities give rise to future expectations and the inquiry into whether there is any justifiable basis for assigning significance to such expectations once the issue of their validity has been addressed.
output: But in spite of the misleadingness of such expectations, they nevertheless exist. The mere fact that something has happened a certain number of times causes animals and men to expect that it will happen again. Thus our instincts certainly cause us to believe that the sun will rise to-morrow, but we may be in no better a position than the chicken which unexpectedly has its neck wrung. We have therefore to distinguish the fact that past uniformities cause expectations as to the future, from the question whether there is any reasonable ground for giving weight to such expectations after the question of their validity has been raised.
title: The Problems of Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell

input:
Generally, philosophers have primarily recognized universals that are named by adjectives or substantives, while those named by verbs and prepositions have been largely overlooked. Furthermore, this oversight has had a significant impact on philosophy, and it can be argued that most metaphysical theories, since the time of Spinoza, have been heavily influenced by it. 
The reason for this influence is largely due to the fact that adjectives and common nouns typically express qualities or properties of individual things, whereas prepositions and verbs tend to express connections between multiple things. Consequently, the neglect of prepositions and verbs led to the assumption that every statement can be viewed as assigning a property to a single thing, rather than as describing a connection between multiple things. Additionally, this assumption resulted in the belief that relations between things cannot exist as entities in their own right. Therefore, it was concluded that either there is only one entity in the universe, or, if multiple entities exist, they cannot interact with each other, since any interaction would imply a relation, which is deemed impossible.
output: Even among philosophers, we may say, broadly, that only those universals which are named by adjectives or substantives have been much or often recognized, while those named by verbs and prepositions have been usually overlooked. This omission has had a very great effect upon philosophy; it is hardly too much to say that most metaphysics, since Spinoza, has been largely determined by it. The way this has occurred is, in outline, as follows: Speaking generally, adjectives and common nouns express qualities or properties of single things, whereas prepositions and verbs tend to express relations between two or more things. Thus the neglect of prepositions and verbs led to the belief that every proposition can be regarded as attributing a property to a single thing, rather than as expressing a relation between two or more things. Hence it was supposed that, ultimately, there can be no such entities as relations between things. Hence either there can be only one thing in the universe, or, if there are many things, they cannot possibly interact in any way, since any interaction would be a relation, and relations are impossible.
title: The Problems of Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell

input: A similar perspective may be relevant when considering any other a priori judgment. When we conclude that two and two equals four, we are not simply assessing our thoughts; rather, we are making a statement about all actual or possible pairs. While it is accurate that our minds are structured in a way that leads us to believe that two and two equals four, this belief does not represent the essence of our assertion. Furthermore, no aspect of our mental framework can validate the statement that two and two equals four. Therefore, our a priori knowledge, assuming it is not mistaken, tends not to be limited to insights about our minds but may also apply to whatever exists in the world, encompassing both mental and non-mental realms. In summary, a priori knowledge can often extend beyond mere self-reflection to encompass broader truths about reality.
output: A similar argument applies to any other a priori judgement. When we judge that two and two are four, we are not making a judgement about our thoughts, but about all actual or possible couples. The fact that our minds are so constituted as to believe that two and two are four, though it is true, is emphatically not what we assert when we assert that two and two are four. And no fact about the constitution of our minds could make it true that two and two are four. Thus our a priori knowledge, if it is not erroneous, is not merely knowledge about the constitution of our minds, but is applicable to whatever the world may contain, both what is mental and what is non-mental.
title: The Problems of Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell

input: The issue of memory presents a significant challenge, as it is often unreliable, which raises questions about the overall reliability of intuitive judgments. This challenge is not trivial. To better understand it, we can focus on specific aspects of memory. Generally, memory tends to be more trustworthy when the experience is vivid and recent. For example, if lightning strikes the house next door just moments ago, my recollection of what I witnessed will be highly dependable, making it unreasonable to doubt the occurrence of the flash. This principle also applies to less vivid experiences, provided they occurred recently. I am completely confident that I was sitting in my current chair just half a minute ago. As I reflect on my day, I recognize varying degrees of certainty regarding my memories: some I trust completely, others I feel almost certain about, some I can verify through reflection and related details, and others I doubt. I am confident that I had breakfast this morning, but if I were to consider it with indifference, uncertainty might arise. Regarding the conversation during breakfast, I find that some parts come to mind easily, others require effort, some involve considerable doubt, and some I cannot recall at all. This indicates a continuous spectrum of clarity in my memories, which affects their reliability.
output: The case of memory, however, raises a difficulty, for it is notoriously fallacious, and thus throws doubt on the trustworthiness of intuitive judgements in general. This difficulty is no light one. But let us first narrow its scope as far as possible. Broadly speaking, memory is trustworthy in proportion to the vividness of the experience and to its nearness in time. If the house next door was struck by lightning half a minute ago, my memory of what I saw and heard will be so reliable that it would be preposterous to doubt whether there had been a flash at all. And the same applies to less vivid experiences, so long as they are recent. I am absolutely certain that half a minute ago I was sitting in the same chair in which I am sitting now. Going backward over the day, I find things of which I am quite certain, other things of which I am almost certain, other things of which I can become certain by thought and by calling up attendant circumstances, and some things of which I am by no means certain. I am quite certain that I ate my breakfast this morning, but if I were as indifferent to my breakfast as a philosopher should be, I should be doubtful. As to the conversation at breakfast, I can recall some of it easily, some with an effort, some only with a large element of doubt, and some not at all. Thus there is a continual gradation in the degree of self-evidence of what I remember, and a corresponding gradation in the trustworthiness of my memory.
title: The Problems of Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell

input: At the start of his philosophy, Kant posed the question, 'How is pure mathematics possible?' This is an interesting and difficult question, and any philosophy that is not purely sceptical must provide some answer to it. We have already seen that the answer given by pure empiricists—that our mathematical knowledge is derived by induction from particular instances—is inadequate, for two reasons. First, the validity of the inductive principle itself cannot be proved by induction. Second, the general propositions of mathematics, such as 'two and two always make four', can clearly be known with certainty from a single instance, and gain nothing from enumerating other cases in which they have been found true. This suggests that our knowledge of the general propositions of mathematics (and the same applies to logic) must be accounted for differently from our merely probable knowledge of empirical generalizations such as 'all men are mortal'.
output: The question which Kant put at the beginning of his philosophy, namely 'How is pure mathematics possible?' is an interesting and difficult one, to which every philosophy which is not purely sceptical must find some answer. The answer of the pure empiricists, that our mathematical knowledge is derived by induction from particular instances, we have already seen to be inadequate, for two reasons: first, that the validity of the inductive principle itself cannot be proved by induction; secondly, that the general propositions of mathematics, such as 'two and two always make four', can obviously be known with certainty by consideration of a single instance, and gain nothing by enumeration of other cases in which they have been found to be true. Thus our knowledge of the general propositions of mathematics (and the same applies to logic) must be accounted for otherwise than our (merely probable) knowledge of empirical generalizations such as 'all men are mortal'.
title: The Problems of Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell

input:
It is evident that the actual table, if it exists, differs fundamentally from our immediate experiences of sight, touch, or hearing. The true essence of the table, should it exist, is not readily accessible to us; rather, it must be inferred from our immediate perceptions. Consequently, two challenging questions emerge: (1) Is there a real table at all? (2) If such a table exists, what kind of object might it be?

In essence, it will be beneficial to consider a few straightforward terms that possess clear and definite meanings as we explore these questions. We shall refer to 'sense-data' as the elements that are immediately recognized through sensation, including aspects such as colors, sounds, smells, textures, and so forth. The term 'sensation' will denote the experience of being immediately aware of these elements. Therefore, when we perceive a color, we experience a sensation of that color; however, the color itself constitutes a sense-datum rather than a sensation. The color represents what we are immediately aware of, while the awareness itself is the sensation. It is clear that to understand anything about the table, we must rely on the sense-data—such as the brown color, oblong shape, and smoothness—that we associate with the table. Nevertheless, for the reasons previously articulated, we cannot assert that the table is synonymous with the sense-data, nor can we claim that the sense-data are direct properties of the table. Consequently, a problem arises regarding the relationship between the sense-data and the real table, assuming that such an entity exists.
output:
Thus it becomes evident that the real table, if there is one, is not the same as what we immediately experience by sight or touch or hearing. The real table, if there is one, is not immediately known to us at all, but must be an inference from what is immediately known. Hence, two very difficult questions at once arise; namely, (1) Is there a real table at all? (2) If so, what sort of object can it be?

It will help us in considering these questions to have a few simple terms of which the meaning is definite and clear. Let us give the name of 'sense-data' to the things that are immediately known in sensation: such things as colours, sounds, smells, hardnesses, roughnesses, and so on. We shall give the name 'sensation' to the experience of being immediately aware of these things. Thus, whenever we see a colour, we have a sensation of the colour, but the colour itself is a sense-datum, not a sensation. The colour is that of which we are immediately aware, and the awareness itself is the sensation. It is plain that if we are to know anything about the table, it must be by means of the sense-data - brown colour, oblong shape, smoothness, etc. - which we associate with the table; but, for the reasons which have been given, we cannot say that the table is the sense-data, or even that the sense-data are directly properties of the table. Thus a problem arises as to the relation of the sense-data to the real table, supposing there is such a thing.
title: The Problems of Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell

input:
Given the existence of physical space and its correspondence to private spaces, it is necessary to determine what can be known about it. The knowledge that can be obtained is limited to what is required to maintain the correspondence. In other words, it is not possible to know the inherent nature of physical space, but rather the arrangement of physical objects that results from their spatial relations. For instance, it is possible to know that the earth, moon, and sun are aligned in a straight line during an eclipse, although the true nature of a physical straight line remains unknown, unlike the visual representation of a straight line in private space.

Meanwhile, the relations of distances in physical space can be understood to a greater extent than the distances themselves. It is possible to know that one distance is greater than another, or that it is situated along the same straight line as another distance. However, it is not possible to have a direct understanding of physical distances, unlike the immediate acquaintance that exists with distances in private spaces, or with sensory data such as colors or sounds. Similarly, the knowledge that can be obtained about physical space is comparable to what a person born blind might learn about visual space through the descriptions of others. Nevertheless, there are certain aspects of physical space that cannot be known, just as a person born blind cannot comprehend certain aspects of visual space. Ultimately, it is possible to know the properties of the relations that maintain the correspondence with sensory data, but the inherent nature of the terms that are related remains unknown.
output: Assuming that there is physical space, and that it does thus correspond to private spaces, what can we know about it? We can know only what is required in order to secure the correspondence. That is to say, we can know nothing of what it is like in itself, but we can know the sort of arrangement of physical objects which results from their spatial relations. We can know, for example, that the earth and moon and sun are in one straight line during an eclipse, though we cannot know what a physical straight line is in itself, as we know the look of a straight line in our visual space. Thus we come to know much more about the relations of distances in physical space than about the distances themselves; we may know that one distance is greater than another, or that it is along the same straight line as the other, but we cannot have that immediate acquaintance with physical distances that we have with distances in our private spaces, or with colours or sounds or other sense-data. We can know all those things about physical space which a man born blind might know through other people about the space of sight; but the kind of things which a man born blind could never know about the space of sight we also cannot know about physical space. We can know the properties of the relations required to preserve the correspondence with sense-data, but we cannot know the nature of the terms between which the relations hold.
title: The Problems of Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell

input: The case of memory makes one important point about self-evidence clear. Self-evidence has degrees. It is not a quality that is simply present or absent. It is a quality that may be more or less present, in gradations ranging from absolute certainty down to an almost imperceptible faintness. Truths of perception and some of the principles of logic have the very highest degree of self-evidence. Truths of immediate memory have an almost equally high degree. The inductive principle has less self-evidence than some of the other principles of logic, such as "what follows from a true premiss must be true." Memories have a diminishing self-evidence as they become remoter and fainter. The truths of logic and mathematics have, broadly speaking, less self-evidence as they become more complicated. Judgements of intrinsic ethical or aesthetic value are apt to have some self-evidence, but not much.
output: One important point about self-evidence is made clear by the case of memory, and that is, that self-evidence has degrees: it is not a quality which is simply present or absent, but a quality which may be more or less present, in gradations ranging from absolute certainty down to an almost imperceptible faintness. Truths of perception and some of the principles of logic have the very highest degree of self-evidence; truths of immediate memory have an almost equally high degree. The inductive principle has less self-evidence than some of the other principles of logic, such as 'what follows from a true premiss must be true'. Memories have a diminishing self-evidence as they become remoter and fainter; the truths of logic and mathematics have (broadly speaking) less self-evidence as they become more complicated. Judgements of intrinsic ethical or aesthetic value are apt to have some self-evidence, but not much.
title: The Problems of Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell

input:
The general principles of science, such as the belief in the reign of law and the belief that every event must have a cause, can be seen as being just as dependent on the inductive principle as the beliefs of everyday life. All such general principles tend to be accepted because people have found countless instances in which they hold true and none in which they are false. However, this does not really provide evidence for their truth in the future, unless the inductive principle itself is assumed.

In this way, any knowledge that, on the basis of experience, tells us something about what has not been experienced may rest on a belief that experience can neither confirm nor disprove, yet which, at least in its more concrete applications, often seems to be as firmly rooted in us as many facts of experience. The existence and justification of such beliefs—since the inductive principle, as we will see, is not the only example—raises some of the most difficult and most widely debated problems in philosophy. In the next chapter, we will briefly consider what might be said to account for this kind of knowledge, as well as its scope and its degree of certainty.
output:
The general principles of science, such as the belief in the reign of law, and the belief that every event must have a cause, are as completely dependent upon the inductive principle as are the beliefs of daily life All such general principles are believed because mankind have found innumerable instances of their truth and no instances of their falsehood. But this affords no evidence for their truth in the future, unless the inductive principle is assumed.

Thus all knowledge which, on a basis of experience tells us something about what is not experienced, is based upon a belief which experience can neither confirm nor confute, yet which, at least in its more concrete applications, appears to be as firmly rooted in us as many of the facts of experience. The existence and justification of such beliefs - for the inductive principle, as we shall see, is not the only example - raises some of the most difficult and most debated problems of philosophy. We will, in the next chapter, consider briefly what may be said to account for such knowledge, and what is its scope and its degree of certainty.
title: The Problems of Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell

input: The only situation that might initially appear to contradict our proposition is one in which an a priori statement asserts that all members of one class of particulars belong to another class, or, equivalently, that all particulars possessing one property also possess another. In such a case, it might seem that we are concerned with the particulars that have the property rather than with the property itself. The statement "two and two are four" is in fact an example of this, since it can be expressed as "any two and any other two are four," or as "any collection formed of two twos is a collection of four." If we can demonstrate that statements of this kind truly deal only with universals, then our proposition may be considered proven.
output: The only case in which it might seem, at first sight, as if our proposition were untrue, is the case in which an a priori proposition states that all of one class of particulars belong to some other class, or (what comes to the same thing) that all particulars having some one property also have some other. In this case it might seem as though we were dealing with the particulars that have the property rather than with the property. The proposition 'two and two are four' is really a case in point, for this may be stated in the form 'any two and any other two are four', or 'any collection formed of two twos is a collection of four'. If we can show that such statements as this really deal only with universals, our proposition may be regarded as proved.

author: Bertrand Russell

input: Returning now to the problem of a priori knowledge, which we left unsolved when we began our consideration of universals, we find ourselves in a position to address it much more satisfactorily than before. Let us return to the proposition "two and two are four." In light of what has been said, it is fairly clear that this proposition states a relation between the universal "two" and the universal "four." This highlights a proposition that we will now attempt to establish: namely, that all a priori knowledge deals exclusively with the relations of universals. This proposition is of great importance, and it goes a long way toward resolving our earlier difficulties concerning a priori knowledge.
output: Returning now to the problem of a priori knowledge, which we left unsolved when we began the consideration of universals, we find ourselves in a position to deal with it in a much more satisfactory manner than was possible before. Let us revert to the proposition 'two and two are four'. It is fairly obvious, in view of what has been said, that this proposition states a relation between the universal 'two' and the universal 'four'. This proposition is of great importance, and goes a long way towards solving our previous difficulties concerning a priori knowledge.

input: The problem tends to arise from the fact that such knowledge is general, while all experience is particular. It may seem strange that we can apparently know some truths in advance about particular things we have not yet experienced, but it is not easy to doubt that logic and arithmetic will apply to them. We do not know who the inhabitants of London a hundred years from now will be, but we know that any two of them and any other two of them will make four. This apparent ability to anticipate facts about things we have no experience of is certainly surprising. Kant's solution to the problem, though not valid in my opinion, is interesting. However, it is very difficult, and different philosophers understand it in different ways. We can therefore give only a very brief outline of it, and even that may be considered misleading by many exponents of Kant's system.
output: The problem arises through the fact that such knowledge is general, whereas all experience is particular. It seems strange that we should apparently be able to know some truths in advance about particular things of which we have as yet no experience; but it cannot easily be doubted that logic and arithmetic will apply to such things. We can, therefore, only give the merest outline of it, and even that will be thought misleading by many exponents of Kant's system.

input: It follows that we cannot prove that the universe as a whole forms a single harmonious system such as Hegel believes that it forms. If we cannot prove this, then we also cannot prove the unreality of space and time and matter and evil, since Hegel deduces this unreality from the fragmentary and relational character of these things. Consequently, we are left to the piecemeal investigation of the world and are unable to know the characters of those parts of the universe that are remote from our experience. This result may be disappointing to those whose hopes have been raised by the systems of philosophers, but it is in harmony with the inductive and scientific temper of our age. Moreover, it is borne out by the whole examination of human knowledge that has occupied our previous chapters.

input: On the contrary, true philosophic contemplation finds its satisfaction in every enlargement of the not-Self, in everything that magnifies the objects contemplated and thereby the subject contemplating. This highlights that in contemplation, anything personal or private—anything that depends on habit, self-interest, or desire—distorts the object and therefore impairs the union the intellect seeks. By creating a barrier between subject and object, such personal and private elements become a prison for the intellect. The free intellect will see as God might see, without a here and now, without hopes and fears, without the restraints of customary beliefs and traditional prejudices, calmly and dispassionately, with the sole and exclusive desire for knowledge—knowledge as impersonal and as purely contemplative as it is possible for man to attain. This suggests that the free intellect will value more the abstract and universal knowledge into which the accidents of private history do not enter, than the knowledge brought by the senses, which must depend on an exclusive and personal point of view and on a body whose sense-organs distort as much as they reveal. Ultimately, this is the knowledge the free intellect most values.
output: The true philosophic contemplation, on the contrary, finds its satisfaction in every enlargement of the not-Self, in everything that magnifies the objects contemplated, and thereby the subject contemplating. Everything, in contemplation, that is personal or private, everything that depends upon habit, self-interest, or desire, distorts the object, and hence impairs the union which the intellect seeks. By thus making a barrier between subject and object, such personal and private things become a prison to the intellect. The free intellect will see as God might see, without a here and now, without hopes and fears, without the trammels of customary beliefs and traditional prejudices, calmly, dispassionately, in the sole and exclusive desire of knowledge - knowledge as impersonal, as purely contemplative, as it is possible for man to attain. author: Bertrand Russell

input:
Kant's "thing in itself" is identical in definition with the physical object, namely, it is the cause of sensations. In the properties deduced from the definition it is not identical, since Kant held, despite some inconsistency regarding cause, that we can know that none of the categories are applicable to the "thing in itself."

Apart from minor grounds on which Kant's philosophy may be criticized, there is one main objection that seems fatal to any attempt to deal with the problem of a priori knowledge by his method. What needs to be accounted for is our certainty that facts must always conform to logic and arithmetic. To say that logic and arithmetic are contributed by us does not account for this. Our nature is as much a fact of the existing world as anything else, and there can be no certainty that it will remain constant. If Kant is right, it might happen that tomorrow our nature would change in such a way that two and two become five. This possibility seems never to have occurred to him, yet it utterly destroys the certainty and universality that he is anxious to vindicate for arithmetical propositions. It is true that this possibility is formally inconsistent with the Kantian view that time itself is a form imposed by the subject upon phenomena, so that our real Self is not in time and has no tomorrow. But he would still have to suppose that the time-order of phenomena is determined by characteristics of what is behind phenomena, and this suffices for the substance of our argument.
output:

In the properties deduced from the definition it is not identical, since Kant held (in spite of some inconsistency as regards cause) that we can know that none of the categories are applicable to the 'thing in itself'.

But he will still have to suppose that the time-order of phenomena is determined by characteristics of what is behind phenomena, and this suffices for the substance of our argument.

input: The principle under consideration can be referred to as the principle of induction, which consists of two components. The first component states that if a certain type of object A has consistently been found to be linked with another type of object B, and there have been no instances where A has been found without B, then the likelihood of A being associated with B in a new instance increases with the number of previous cases where A and B have been linked. This suggests that the frequency of observed associations enhances the probability of a similar association occurring in the future.
output:
The principle we are examining may be called the principle of induction, and its two parts may be stated as follows:

input: The second kind of self-evidence may be that which belongs to judgements in the first instance and is not derived from direct perception of a fact as a single complex whole. This second kind of self-evidence can often have degrees, ranging from the very highest degree down to a bare inclination in favour of the belief. Consider, for example, the case of a horse trotting away from us along a hard road. At first, our certainty that we hear the hoofs tends to be complete; gradually, if we listen intently, there may come a moment when we think perhaps it was imagination, or the blind upstairs, or our own heartbeats; at last we may become doubtful whether there was any noise at all; then we may think we no longer hear anything, and finally we may know we no longer hear anything. In this process, there is a continual gradation of self-evidence, from the highest degree to the least, not in the sense-data themselves, but in the judgements based on them. Overall, then, this second sort of self-evidence tends to admit of degrees, and these degrees belong to our judgements rather than to the sense-data.

input: In regard to probable opinion, one can derive significant assistance from coherence, which we have dismissed as a definition of truth, yet may often function as a useful criterion. A collection of individually probable opinions, when they exhibit mutual coherence, becomes more probable than any single opinion would be on its own. It is through this mechanism that many scientific hypotheses attain their probability. These hypotheses integrate into a coherent framework of probable opinions, thereby elevating their likelihood compared to when they are considered in isolation. The same principle applies to general philosophical hypotheses. In particular instances, such hypotheses may initially appear highly questionable; however, upon evaluating the order and coherence they introduce into a collection of probable opinions, they may approach a state of near certainty. This is especially relevant to distinctions between dreams and waking life. If our dreams, night after night, demonstrated the same coherence as our daytime experiences, we would find it difficult to determine whether to trust our dreams or our waking life. As it stands, the coherence test discredits the dreams and validates the waking experience. Nevertheless, while this test enhances probability when it is successful, it does not yield absolute certainty unless there is already some certainty present within the coherent system. Consequently, the mere organization of probable opinion cannot, in isolation, transform it into indubitable knowledge.
output: In regard to probable opinion, we can derive great assistance from coherence, which we rejected as the definition of truth, but may often use as a criterion. A body of individually probable opinions, if they are mutually coherent, become more probable than any one of them would be individually. It is in this way that many scientific hypotheses acquire their probability. They fit into a coherent system of probable opinions, and thus become more probable than they would be in isolation. The same thing applies to general philosophical hypotheses. Often in a single case such hypotheses may seem highly doubtful, while yet, when we consider the order and coherence which they introduce into a mass of probable opinion, they become pretty nearly certain. This applies, in particular, to such matters as the distinction between dreams and waking life. If our dreams, night after night, were as coherent one with another as our days, we should hardly know whether to believe the dreams or the waking life. As it is, the test of coherence condemns the dreams and confirms the waking life. But this test, though it increases probability where it is successful, never gives absolute certainty, unless there is certainty already at some point in the coherent system. Thus the mere organization of probable opinion will never, by itself, transform it into indubitable knowledge.
