input: The manner in which simplicity is introduced through the supposition that physical objects truly exist can be readily observed. If the cat appears at one moment in one part of the room and at another moment in a different part, it is natural to suppose that it has moved from the one location to the other, traversing a series of intermediate positions. However, if it is merely a collection of sense-data, it cannot have been in any place where I did not perceive it; consequently, we must suppose that it did not exist at all during the intervals when I was not observing it, but instead suddenly came into being in a new location. Furthermore, if the cat exists regardless of whether I see it, we can understand from our own experience how it becomes hungry between one meal and the next; but if it does not exist when I am not seeing it, it appears peculiar that appetite should increase during non-existence as rapidly as during existence. Moreover, if the cat consists only of sense-data, it cannot be hungry, since no hunger other than my own can constitute a sense-datum for me. In essence, the behaviour of the sense-data that represent the cat to me, though it appears quite natural when regarded as an expression of hunger, becomes entirely inexplicable when regarded as mere movements and changes of coloured patches, which are as incapable of hunger as a triangle is of playing football.
output: The way in which simplicity comes in from supposing that there really are physical objects is easily seen. If the cat appears at one moment in one part of the room, and at another in another part, it is natural to suppose that it has moved from the one to the other, passing over a series of intermediate positions. But if it is merely a set of sense-data, it cannot have ever been in any place where I did not see it; thus we shall have to suppose that it did not exist at all while I was not looking, but suddenly sprang into being in a new place. If the cat exists whether I see it or not, we can understand from our own experience how it gets hungry between one meal and the next; but if it does not exist when I am not seeing it, it seems odd that appetite should grow during non-existence as fast as during existence. And if the cat consists only of sense-data, it cannot be hungry, since no hunger but my own can be a sense-datum to me. Thus the behaviour of the sense-data which represent the cat to me, though it seems quite natural when regarded as an expression of hunger, becomes utterly inexplicable when regarded as mere movements and changes of patches of colour, which are as incapable of hunger as a triangle is of playing football.

input: It appears that we have tentatively agreed that physical objects may not be entirely like our sense-data, but can often be viewed as the cause of our sensations. These physical objects are situated in the space of science, which may be referred to as 'physical' space. It is worth noting that, if our sensations are to be caused by physical objects, it is likely that there must be a physical space that contains both these objects and our sense-organs, nerves, and brain. We tend to experience a sensation of touch from an object when we are in close proximity to it, which means that some part of our body occupies a nearby location in physical space. Generally speaking, we see an object when there is no opaque object between the object and our eyes in physical space. Similarly, we can usually only hear, smell, or taste an object when we are sufficiently close to it, or when it comes into contact with our tongue, or is positioned in a suitable location in physical space relative to our body. Unless we consider the object and our body to be in the same physical space, it may be challenging to predict what sensations we will derive from a given object under different circumstances, as the relative positions of the object and our body tend to play a significant role in determining the sensations we experience. In summary, our understanding of physical objects and sensations suggests that they are interconnected and can be understood in the context of physical space.
output: We agreed provisionally that physical objects cannot be quite like our sense-data, but may be regarded as causing our sensations. These physical objects are in the space of science, which we may call 'physical' space. It is important to notice that, if our sensations are to be caused by physical objects, there must be a physical space containing these objects and our sense-organs and nerves and brain. We get a sensation of touch from an object when we are in contact with it; that is to say, when some part of our body occupies a place in physical space quite close to the space occupied by the object. We see an object (roughly speaking) when no opaque body is between the object and our eyes in physical space. Similarly, we only hear or smell or taste an object when we are sufficiently near to it, or when it touches the tongue, or has some suitable position in physical space relatively to our body. We cannot begin to state what different sensations we shall derive from a given object under different circumstances unless we regard the object and our body as both in one physical space, for it is mainly the relative positions of the object and our body that determine what sensations we shall derive from the object.

input: It appears that there may be two types of self-evident truths of perception, which can often be distinguished, although they may ultimately be interconnected. Initially, there is the type that merely confirms the existence of a sense-datum without examining it in detail. For instance, when we see a patch of red, we can form the judgement 'there is a patch of red' or, more precisely, 'that exists'; this tends to be a basic intuitive judgement of perception. On the other hand, a different type of judgement emerges when the object of our senses is complex and we break it down to some extent. If, for example, we see a round patch of red, we may conclude 'that patch of red is round'; this is also a judgement of perception, but it differs from the first type. In this case, we have a single sense-datum with both colour and shape, where the colour is red and the shape is round, and our judgement separates the datum into colour and shape before combining them again to state that the red colour has a round shape. A similar example of this type of judgement is 'this is to the right of that', where 'this' and 'that' are seen at the same time, and the sense-datum contains elements that have a particular relationship to each other, which the judgement then affirms. In summary, these two types of judgements of perception can be distinguished by the level of analysis involved, with one confirming existence and the other examining and combining the components of a sense-datum.
output: It would seem that there are two kinds of self-evident truths of perception, though perhaps in the last analysis the two kinds may coalesce. First, there is the kind which simply asserts the existence of the sense-datum, without in any way analysing it. We see a patch of red, and we judge 'there is such-and-such a patch of red', or more strictly 'there is that'; this is one kind of intuitive judgement of perception. The other kind arises when the object of sense is complex, and we subject it to some degree of analysis. If, for instance, we see a round patch of red, we may judge 'that patch of red is round'. This is again a judgement of perception, but it differs from our previous kind. In our present kind we have a single sense-datum which has both colour and shape: the colour is red and the shape is round. Our judgement analyses the datum into colour and shape, and then recombines them by stating that the red colour is round in shape. Another example of this kind of judgement is 'this is to the right of that', where 'this' and 'that' are seen simultaneously. In this kind of judgement the sense-datum contains constituents which have some relation to each other, and the judgement asserts that these constituents have this relation.

input: Kant's position is that our experiences consist of two distinct elements: one attributed to the object itself, and the other to our own nature. As previously discussed, the physical object differs from its associated sense-data, which arise from the interaction between the object and ourselves. This highlights the complex relationship between the object and our perception of it. Kant's unique perspective lies in how he allocates the contributions of the object and ourselves. He argues that the raw sensory data, such as color and hardness, originates from the object, while our mind supplies the spatial and temporal framework, as well as the relationships between sense-data that emerge from comparison or causal reasoning. This suggests that our understanding of space, time, causality, and comparison is rooted in our own cognitive nature. Ultimately, Kant's reasoning is based on the idea that we possess a priori knowledge of these concepts, but not of the raw sensory material. He asserts that any experience we have will necessarily conform to the characteristics defined by our a priori knowledge, as these characteristics are inherent to our own nature and therefore inescapable in our experience of the world.
output: What Kant maintained was that in all our experience there are two elements to be distinguished, the one due to the object (i.e. to what we have called the 'physical object'), the other due to our own nature. We saw, in discussing matter and sense-data, that the physical object is different from the associated sense-data, and that the sense-data are to be regarded as resulting from an interaction between the physical object and ourselves. So far, we are in agreement with Kant. But what is distinctive of Kant is the way in which he apportions the shares of ourselves and the physical object respectively. He considers that the crude material given in sensation - the colour, hardness, etc. - is due to the object, and that what we supply is the arrangement in space and time, and all the relations between sense-data which result from comparison or from considering one as the cause of the other or in any other way. His chief reason in favour of this view is that we seem to have a priori knowledge as to space and time and causality and comparison, but not as to the actual crude material of sensation. We can be sure, he says, that anything we shall ever experience must show the characteristics affirmed of it in our a priori knowledge, because these characteristics are due to our own nature, and therefore nothing can ever come into our experience without acquiring these characteristics.

When we state that a particular entity exists, we imply that there is only one object that possesses the specified characteristics. The statement that an individual is a specific entity means that this individual has the corresponding property, and no other entity possesses it. For instance, if we say that Mr. A is the Unionist candidate for a particular constituency, it means that Mr. A is a Unionist candidate for that constituency, and no one else holds this position. Similarly, the existence of the Unionist candidate for a constituency implies that someone is a Unionist candidate for that constituency, and no one else is.

Furthermore, when we are familiar with an object that is a specific entity, we are aware that this entity exists. However, it is also possible to know that a specific entity exists without being acquainted with any object that we know to be that entity. Additionally, we may know that a specific entity exists even when we are not familiar with any object that actually is that entity.
output: When we say 'the so-and-so exists', we mean that there is just one object which is the so-and-so. The proposition 'a is the so-and-so' means that a has the property so-and-so, and nothing else has. 'Mr. A. is the Unionist candidate for this constituency' means 'Mr. A. is a Unionist candidate for this constituency, and no one else is'. 'The Unionist candidate for this constituency exists' means 'some one is a Unionist candidate for this constituency, and no one else is'. Thus, when we are acquainted with an object which is the so-and-so, we know that the so-and-so exists; but we may know that the so-and-so exists when we are not acquainted with any object which we know to be the so-and-so, and even when we are not acquainted with any object which, in fact, is the so-and-so.

input: In a neighborhood beyond Dockhead in the Borough of Southwark, Jacob's Island stands surrounded by a muddy ditch. This ditch is six or eight feet deep and fifteen or twenty wide when the tide is in. It was once called Mill Pond, but in the days of this story it is known as Folly Ditch. It is a creek or inlet from the Thames and can always be filled at high water by opening the sluices at the Lead Mills, from which it took its old name. At such times, a stranger looking from one of the wooden bridges across it at Mill Lane will see the inhabitants of the houses on either side lowering buckets, pails, and domestic utensils of all kinds from their back doors and windows to haul the water up. When his eye turns from these operations to the houses themselves, his utmost astonishment will be excited by the scene before him. Crazy wooden galleries are common to the backs of half a dozen houses, with holes from which to look upon the slime beneath. Windows are broken and patched, with poles thrust out on which to dry linen that is never there. Rooms are so small, so filthy, and so confined that the air would seem too tainted even for the dirt and squalor they shelter. Wooden chambers thrust themselves out above the mud and threaten to fall into it, as some have done. Dirt-besmeared walls and decaying foundations are present. Every repulsive lineament of poverty and every loathsome indication of filth, rot, and garbage ornament the banks of Folly Ditch.

output: My little mistress behaved like an angel in coming to wait on me, and cheer my solitude; the confinement brought me exceedingly low. I never considered what she did with herself after tea. And though frequently, when she looked in to bid me good-night, I remarked a fresh colour in her cheeks and a pinkness over her slender fingers, instead of fancying the hue borrowed from a cold ride across the moors, I laid it to the charge of a hot fire in the library.

output:
“For shame! for shame!” she repeated, angrily. “You are worse than twenty foes, you poisonous friend!”

“And I must suffer for her egotism!” she sobbed, as Mrs. Linton left the room. “All, all is against me: she has blighted my single consolation. But she uttered falsehoods, didn’t she? Mr. Heathcliff is not a fiend: he has an honourable soul, and a true one, or how could he remember her?”

“You are leagued with the rest, Ellen!” she replied. “I’ll not listen to your slanders. What malevolence you must have to wish to convince me that there is no happiness in the world!”

This spectacle drove me back immediately; I took my hat, and, after a four-miles’ walk, arrived at Heathcliff’s garden-gate just in time to escape the first feathery flakes of a snow shower.

I instinctively recalled her words from just a few hours earlier: “Incomparably beyond and above us all! Whether still on earth or now in heaven, her spirit is at home with God!”
output: Next morning - bright and cheerful out of doors - stole softened in through the blinds of the silent room, and suffused the couch and its occupant with a mellow, tender glow. Edgar Linton had his head laid on the pillow, and his eyes shut. His young and fair features were almost as deathlike as those of the form beside him, and almost as fixed: but his was the hush of exhausted anguish, and hers of perfect peace. Her brow smooth, her lids closed, her lips wearing the expression of a smile; no angel in heaven could be more beautiful than she appeared. And I partook of the infinite calm in which she lay: my mind was never in a holier frame than while I gazed on that untroubled image of Divine rest. I instinctively echoed the words she had uttered a few hours before: “Incomparably beyond and above us all! Whether still on earth or now in heaven, her spirit is at home with God!”

Oh, I’ve no doubt she’s in hell among you! I guess by her silence, as much as anything, what she feels. You say she is often restless, and anxious-looking: is that a proof of tranquillity? You talk of her mind being unsettled. How the devil could it be otherwise in her frightful isolation? And that insipid, paltry creature attending her from duty and humanity! From pity and charity! “Papa would tell you, Miss,” I answered, hastily, “that they are not worth the trouble of visiting. The moors, where you ramble with him, are much nicer; and Thrushcross Park is the finest place in the world.”

One of the maids mentioning the Fairy Cave, quite turned her head with a desire to fulfil this project: she teased Mr. Linton about it; and he promised she should have the journey when she got older. input: These fascinating narratives evoked in me a range of complex emotions. Was humanity truly capable of being both powerful and virtuous, yet also vicious and base? output: “These wonderful narrations inspired me with strange feelings. Was man, indeed, at once so powerful, so virtuous and magnificent, yet so vicious and base? For a long time I could not conceive how one man could go forth to murder his fellow, or even why there were laws and governments; but when I heard details of vice and bloodshed, my wonder ceased and I turned away with disgust and loathing.

input: It is worth noting that I can scarcely articulate the profound effect these books had on me. They generated an endless array of new images and emotions, which at times elevated me to a state of ecstasy, yet more often plunged me into profound despair. In "The Sorrows of Werter," in addition to the appeal of its straightforward and poignant narrative, numerous opinions are explored and various insights are cast upon topics that had previously remained obscure to me. Consequently, I discovered in this work an inexhaustible source of contemplation and amazement. Furthermore, the portrayal of gentle and domestic customs, coupled with noble sentiments and feelings that transcend the self, resonated deeply with my experiences among my guardians as well as with the persistent desires that resided within me. Moreover, I regarded Werter himself as a more divine entity than any I had ever encountered or envisioned; his character exuded sincerity, leaving a lasting impact. The discussions surrounding death and suicide inspired a sense of wonder within me. Although I did not claim to engage in the merits of the arguments presented, I found myself leaning toward the hero's perspective, mourning his demise without fully grasping its implications.
output: “I can hardly describe to you the effect of these books. They produced in me an infinity of new images and feelings, that sometimes raised me to ecstasy, but more frequently sunk me into the lowest dejection. In the Sorrows of Werter, besides the interest of its simple and affecting story, so many opinions are canvassed and so many lights thrown upon what had hitherto been to me obscure subjects that I found in it a never-ending source of speculation and astonishment. The gentle and domestic manners it described, combined with lofty sentiments and feelings, which had for their object something out of self, accorded well with my experience among my protectors and with the wants which were for ever alive in my own bosom. But I thought Werter himself a more divine being than I had ever beheld or imagined; his character contained no pretension, but it sank deep. The disquisitions upon death and suicide were calculated to fill me with wonder. I did not pretend to enter into the merits of the case, yet I inclined towards the opinions of the hero, whose extinction I wept, without precisely understanding it.

input: I spent the rest of the day in my small dwelling, overcome with despair. The departure of my protectors had severed my last connection to the world. For the first time, feelings of revenge and hatred took hold of me, and I made no effort to suppress them. Instead, I allowed myself to be consumed by these emotions, focusing my thoughts on causing harm and destruction. This highlights the intensity of my emotional state at the time. When I thought about my friends, including De Lacey, Agatha, and the Arabian, my feelings of anger momentarily subsided, replaced by a sense of sadness that brought tears to my eyes. However, as I reflected on their rejection and abandonment, my anger returned, fueled by a deep-seated rage. Ultimately, unable to direct my fury towards any living being, I turned my attention to inanimate objects. As night fell, I gathered various combustible materials around the cottage and, after destroying all remnants of the garden's cultivation, I waited impatiently for the moon to set before proceeding with my actions. This suggests that my emotional turmoil had reached a point where I was driven to act out in destructive ways.
output: “I continued for the remainder of the day in my hovel in a state of utter and stupid despair. My protectors had departed and had broken the only link that held me to the world. For the first time the feelings of revenge and hatred filled my bosom, and I did not strive to control them, but allowing myself to be borne away by the stream, I bent my mind towards injury and death. When I thought of my friends, of the mild voice of De Lacey, the gentle eyes of Agatha, and the exquisite beauty of the Arabian, these thoughts vanished and a gush of tears somewhat soothed me. But again when I reflected that they had spurned and deserted me, anger returned, a rage of anger, and unable to injure anything human, I turned my fury towards inanimate objects. As night advanced, I placed a variety of combustibles around the cottage, and after having destroyed every vestige of cultivation in the garden, I waited with forced impatience until the moon had sunk to commence my operations.

As a result, I experienced a sudden change in perspective, which is perhaps characteristic of young people. I abandoned my former pursuits and viewed natural history and its related fields as imperfect and unproductive. Furthermore, I developed a strong dislike for a field of study that seemed incapable of advancing real knowledge. In response to this shift in my mindset, I turned my attention to mathematics and its related disciplines, as they were based on solid foundations and therefore worthy of consideration.
output: Before this I was not unacquainted with the more obvious laws of electricity. On this occasion a man of great research in natural philosophy was with us, and excited by this catastrophe, he entered on the explanation of a theory which he had formed on the subject of electricity and galvanism, which was at once new and astonishing to me. All that he said threw greatly into the shade Cornelius Agrippa, Albertus Magnus, and Paracelsus, the lords of my imagination; but by some fatality the overthrow of these men disinclined me to pursue my accustomed studies. It seemed to me as if nothing would or could ever be known. All that had so long engaged my attention suddenly grew despicable. By one of those caprices of the mind which we are perhaps most subject to in early youth, I at once gave up my former occupations, set down natural history and all its progeny as a deformed and abortive creation, and entertained the greatest disdain for a would-be science which could never even step within the threshold of real knowledge. In this mood of mind I betook myself to the mathematics and the branches of study appertaining to that science as being built upon secure foundations, and so worthy of my consideration.

input: I am the cousin of the unfortunate child who was murdered, or rather, I am his sister, as I was raised by his parents and have lived with them for a long time, even before his birth. It may be considered inappropriate for me to come forward at this moment, but when I see another person facing the threat of harm due to the cowardice of her so-called friends, I feel compelled to speak in order to share what I know about her character. I am familiar with the accused. I have lived in the same house with her for extended periods, once for five years and another time for nearly two. Throughout that time, she seemed to me to be one of the most kind-hearted and generous individuals I have known. She cared for my aunt, Madame Frankenstein, during her final illness with deep affection and attentiveness. After that, she supported her own mother through a prolonged illness, earning the admiration of everyone around her. Subsequently, she returned to my uncle's house, where she was cherished by all family members. She was deeply attached to the deceased child and treated him with the love of a devoted mother. Personally, I do not hesitate to state that, despite all the accusations against her, I believe in her complete innocence. She had no motive for such an act; regarding the object that serves as the main evidence against her, if she had truly desired it, I would have willingly given it to her, as I hold her in the highest regard.
output: “I am,” said she, “the cousin of the unhappy child who was murdered, or rather his sister, for I was educated by and have lived with his parents ever since and even long before his birth. It may therefore be judged indecent in me to come forward on this occasion, but when I see a fellow creature about to perish through the cowardice of her pretended friends, I wish to be allowed to speak, that I may say what I know of her character. I am well acquainted with the accused. I have lived in the same house with her, at one time for five and at another for nearly two years. During all that period she appeared to me the most amiable and benevolent of human creatures. She nursed Madame Frankenstein, my aunt, in her last illness, with the greatest affection and care and afterwards attended her own mother during a tedious illness, in a manner that excited the admiration of all who knew her, after which she again lived in my uncle’s house, where she was beloved by all the family. She was warmly attached to the child who is now dead and acted towards him like a most affectionate mother. For my own part, I do not hesitate to say that, notwithstanding all the evidence produced against her, I believe and rely on her perfect innocence. She had no temptation for such an action; as to the bauble on which the chief proof rests, if she had earnestly desired it, I should have willingly given it to her, so much do I esteem and value her.”

input: I usually took time to rest during the day and preferred to travel at night when I felt concealed from the sight of others. However, one morning, as I found my path leading through a dense forest, I decided to continue my journey after sunrise. It was one of the early days of spring, and the beauty of the sunlight and the pleasantness of the air brought me a sense of cheer. Emotions of kindness and joy, which I had thought were long gone, began to awaken within me. Slightly surprised by the unfamiliarity of these feelings, I allowed myself to be carried away by them, momentarily forgetting my loneliness and physical appearance, and I found the courage to feel happiness. Gentle tears started to fall down my cheeks, and I even lifted my moist eyes in gratitude toward the sun, which seemed to offer me such joy. In summary, this experience filled me with a renewed sense of hope and gratitude.
output: “I generally rested during the day and travelled only when I was secured by night from the view of man. One morning, however, finding that my path lay through a deep wood, I ventured to continue my journey after the sun had risen; the day, which was one of the first of spring, cheered even me by the loveliness of its sunshine and the balminess of the air. I felt emotions of gentleness and pleasure, that had long appeared dead, revive within me. Half surprised by the novelty of these sensations, I allowed myself to be borne away by them, and forgetting my solitude and deformity, dared to be happy. Soft tears again bedewed my cheeks, and I even raised my humid eyes with thankfulness towards the blessed sun, which bestowed such joy upon me.

Soon after my arrival, my father expressed his desire for my immediate marriage to Elizabeth. I chose to remain silent.

“None on earth can compare. I love Elizabeth and eagerly anticipate our union. Therefore, let the date be established; on that day, I shall dedicate myself, in life or in death, to my cousin's happiness.”

“My dear Victor, it is essential that you do not express yourself in such a manner. Grave misfortunes have befallen us; however, let us draw closer to what remains and redirect our love for those we have lost toward those who still live. Although our circle may be small, it will be bound tightly by the bonds of affection and shared misfortune. Furthermore, as time alleviates your sorrow, new and cherished objects of care will emerge to fill the void left by those from whom we have been so unjustly separated.”
output:
Soon after my arrival my father spoke of my immediate marriage with Elizabeth. I remained silent.

“None on earth. I love Elizabeth and look forward to our union with delight. Let the day therefore be fixed; and on it I will consecrate myself, in life or death, to the happiness of my cousin.”

Our circle will be small but bound close by the ties of affection and mutual misfortune. And when time shall have softened your despair, new and dear objects of care will be born to replace those of whom we have been so cruelly deprived.”

I was aware that my silence caused them distress, and I distinctly recalled my father's words: "I know that while you are pleased with yourself, you will think of us with affection, and we shall hear from you regularly. output: The summer months passed while I was thus engaged, heart and soul, in one pursuit. input: It was morning when I awoke, and my foremost concern was to attend to the fire. I uncovered it, and a gentle breeze quickly transformed it into a vibrant flame. From his oppressed slumber, Young Jerry in his closet was awakened after daybreak and before sunrise, by the presence of his father in the family room. Something had gone wrong with him; at least, so Young Jerry inferred, from the circumstance of his holding Mrs. Cruncher by the ears, and knocking the back of her head against the head-board of the bed.

“You oppose yourself to the profit of the business,” said Jerry, “and me and my partners suffer. You was to honour and obey; why the devil don’t you?”
